title: Started small, weak and untrained at 14-15
statement: He began training at 14-15 as the smallest kid in his class after losing arm wrestling to a girl; he could not do a single push-up and could only train about 10 minutes (knee push-ups, sit-ups, light curls).
numbers: start age 14 or 15; 100, 110 or 120 lb; under 5 ft / 5'5" / ~5'2" at 14-15; 0 push-ups; ~10 min sessions
status: contradicted — start age (14 vs 15), weight (100 vs 110 vs 120 lb) and teen height vary between videos

title: Built training tolerance gradually
statement: His first sessions were about 20 minutes of push-ups, sit-ups and air squats, and he extended them step by step; doing more at the start would have burnt him out.
numbers: 10 min → 20 → 40 min → 1 h → 2 h
scope: his own start as a complete beginner
check: Does a complete beginner start with short sessions (10-20 min) and build duration up gradually?

title: Phase 1: bedroom calisthenics, ages ~14-17
statement: With no gym open to minors, he trained bodyweight at home, curled chairs and rocks and sprinted in the mountains while growing almost a foot.

title: Phase 2: an adjustable dumbbell set, ages 17-20
statement: He trained daily in his bedroom with one adjustable dumbbell set, starting with 5 lb curls, and did unsupported dumbbell rows every day for 4 years because he had no bench.
numbers: ~50 lb dumbbell set; 5 lb curls at the start; 140 → 170 lb by 20 "with decent definition"; daily DB rows for 4 years

title: Push-ups built his chest, not the bench
statement: Hundreds of daily push-ups with no rest days made the biggest single difference to his physique; dropping them for bench was a mistake, and his chest is now only maintained.
numbers: hundreds of push-ups/day, no rest days
status: changed — 2020: loved bench and credited it for his chest; 2023: quit benching for dips and push-ups and called dropping push-ups a mistake

title: Looked untrained for years
statement: Despite years of training he did not look like a lifter for a long time; with average genetics it took about 6 years to look trained and 10+ to look jacked, and his lesson is patience.
numbers: ~150-160 lb at 19 after ~4 years; looked untrained for 5-6 years; barely passable at 5-6 years; really good at 9-10 years

title: Team sports gave him his conditioning
statement: He played football then basketball as a teen, mostly running and hill sprints, but liked the weight room more than the games, which showed him lifting was his path.
numbers: football 2 years, basketball 3 years, ~ages 17-19; ~80% running/hill sprints/fartlek; 5 am sprints

title: First gym and barbell at 20 in the US
statement: He moved to the US for a scholarship master's and entered his first gym at 20 having never touched a barbell.
numbers: 2015, age ~20; ~180 lb (also stated 170-180); first real deadlift 275×5

title: Glad fitness YouTube did not exist back then
statement: He made his best gains knowing nothing about angles, protein timing or optimal volume, and thinks that knowledge might have made him timid; he is also glad he did not start a channel in 2016, when he would have spread misinformation.

title: No supplements for his first 7 years
statement: He used no supplements for years; milk was his only protein source as a teen because whey was not available.
numbers: 7 years without supplements; 1-1.5 L milk/day

title: Bodyweight path from 110 to 220 lb
statement: He went from about 110 lb at 15 to a fat peak of 235-240 lb around age 23, crash-cut to ~205-210, recomped at 210 for about three years, then slowly bulked to 220 lb, which he now maintains.
status: contradicted — weight at 22 given as 200-205 or 220 lb; the 240-lb peak dated ~2017 in one video and 2018-2019 in others; in 2025 he recalled 110 kg in Dec 2019

title: His gains rate halved about every five years
statement: Each five-year block brought roughly half the bodyweight gain of the one before.

title: Best gains came from a tiny surplus held for years
statement: As a skinny teen eating what his parents served, plus a little extra each day, he gained steadily for years without tracking, supplements or ever getting chubby; he calls the clean bulk that poverty forced on him "a blessing".
numbers: +1 bowl of rice or some roast beef/day; ~10-15 lb quality mass/year; 110 → 170 lb in 5 years

title: The dirty bulk to 240 lb was wasted years
statement: His dirty bulk gave the most fat and least muscle of any period, left lasting love handles and a wrecked appetite, and his small-framed 6 ft body could not carry the weight.
numbers: peak 240 lb; 12 eggs/day, pounds of beef and pasta; two foot-long subs + soup ≈ 3,000 kcal for one meal
check: Does the bulk avoid fast, dirty weight gain of the kind that took him to 240 lb?

title: Dysmorphia hid his obesity at 240 lb
statement: At 240 lb he was borderline obese while body dysmorphia told him the bulk was working; broken ribs while squatting, rib pain and swollen ankles after short walks finally made him cut.
numbers: 240 lb; ankles swelling after 10-15 min walks

title: The panic crash cut and rebound
statement: He cut about 30 lb in a panic, found it traumatic, then panic-bulked to 225 lb from dysmorphia before settling; repeated 30-lb gain/cut cycles piled up injuries and stubborn fat.
numbers: 240 → ~210 lb; rebound to 225 lb; crash-cut duration given as ~1 month and ~5 months
status: changed — 2020: he said he lost mostly water and muscle; 2021-2022: the 30 lb lost was almost all fat (the duration also conflicts between videos)

title: Three-year recomp at 210 lb
statement: Holding ~210 lb for about three years, he leaned out while legs grew and strength rose (variations and accessories kept progressing when main lifts stalled); the main benefits were healing, no pain and better mental health, and he calls it his "proudest progress".
scope: his own recomp, at a heavy bodyweight
status: current — start BF given as 17-18% and 18-19% in different videos

title: Slow bulk to 220 lb after the recomp
statement: After the recomp he bulked very slowly to 220 lb and maintains it; reaching 220 with subpar genetics took close attention, not bro splits.
numbers: 210 lb (Nov 2022) → 215 (2023, +5 lb in 12 months) → 220 (Dec 2023 onward)
status: changed — 2020-2022: maintain ~210 and recomp; 2022-2024: slow bulk to 220 and maintain, and in 2024 he wants to be "too big for doors"

title: Body composition beats scale weight
statement: An old photo 10 lb lighter showed him much fatter; at 6 ft he thinks you need about 200 lb to look big.
numbers: 10 lb lighter but fatter; ~200 lb at 6 ft to look big

title: More diet mistakes than training mistakes
statement: He says he made more mistakes in diet than in training, some causing damage he cannot repair.

title: No program at first meant stalling
statement: For his first one to two years he trained randomly (machines, bench) with no program; he still gained but never adapted neurologically and stalled, and a plan would have been far more productive.
numbers: ~1-2 years without a program
check: Does the lifter follow a written plan rather than picking exercises at random?

title: A simple linear dumbbell plan gave his best gains
statement: About three years on a simple linear dumbbell program in his bedroom took him from skinny to visibly trained; he trained full body for three years as a beginner.
numbers: ~3 years linear DB program; 3 years full body

title: Copying YouTube-fitness plans stalled him
statement: Following others' plans after discovering fitness YouTube stopped his growth and left him in pain, e.g. months of machine-only 20-rep pump work with no results.
numbers: 20-rep machine work for months
status: contradicted — in 2020 he said he had never followed anyone else's program (see JRN-27)

title: The powerbuilding era and his biggest plateau
statement: A compound-only program grew some parts and not others, and his own powerbuilding program (BBBS, written 2017) brought "the biggest plateau of his life": barely any gains, constant injuries and damaged mental health, with recovery taking until 2020.
numbers: era ~2017-2021; compound-only for 1.5 years; plateau 2017-2019; BBBS written 7 years in, 2 in a gym

title: From strength chaser to hypertrophy-only
statement: Told that getting strong would make him big, he obsessed over maxing the big three and got injuries and fat instead; that is why he now optimizes purely for hypertrophy and says he "doesn't care about strength".
scope: his own approach; see ch. 7 for his strength principles
check: Is the program judged by muscle growth rather than by maxing the big three?

title: Two years in "intermediate hell"
statement: Novices can do anything but intermediates must program precisely; his old program left him a "lifetime intermediate" and repeatedly injured.
numbers: ~2 years stuck

title: He writes his own programs
statement: He says he writes his own programs because a self-written plan may be less optimal but more suitable, and you learn from its mistakes; his gains tracked his programming skill.
status: contradicted — 2020: "never followed someone else's program"; 2022: he followed others' plans after finding fitness YouTube (JRN-23)

title: The "final program" idea, later dropped
statement: His "final program" took about four years to build and test; he later rejected the idea of a final program because the body keeps evolving.
numbers: ~4 years (2 years running a program to gather data, 6 months writing, 2 years beta testing with 10-15 small changes, one every 1.5-2 months); 1.5-2 years to convert to evolving rep ranges, ~3 to understand them
status: changed — 2021: a "final program" to run indefinitely; 2022: no final program exists; 2023: he no longer liked much of his original novice program

title: Experience-based, not study-based
statement: He learned from YouTube lifters (Alan Thrall for deadlift and press, Candito for squat, Omar Isuf for bench) and his own experiments; he has never read a programming book or changed his training because of a study.
scope: his method; see ch. 13 for his view of science

title: Load jumps too big, range of motion too short
statement: When he first progressed he added 10 lb per side each time and took "forever" to see the jumps were too big after stalling; his recurring sin is stacking weight and shortening range of motion until he resets lighter.
numbers: +10 lb per side per progression
check: Are load increases small enough that range of motion stays full?

title: Never ran 5×5
statement: He used evolving rep ranges from the start but admits 5×5 would have moved him through the novice phase faster; dumbbells-only is fine for novices, but barbell patterns should be learnt early.

title: Years of daily training with no rest days
statement: In his early years he trained every day with no rest days or deloads, plus morning runs, without problems; he says his injuries from that period came from programming, not frequency.
numbers: 7 days/week for ~3 years (~1,000 sessions)

title: Extreme training days without harm
statement: He has trained for many hours a day plus mountain running without rhabdomyolysis; in his view overtraining is at worst junk volume.
numbers: one summer 5-6 h/day; at times 4-5 h/day plus hours of running

title: 2020-2023 standard: 6 days, 2-3 hours
statement: For years he trained six days a week for two to three hours, close to failure, with no deloads, and still progressed year-round; he says most people do not need that long.
numbers: 6 days/week, Sunday off; 2-3 h/session; ~12-15 h/week (~20 h counting everything)
status: changed — superseded by 5 days/week and less volume in 2024 (JRN-37)

title: Why his sessions were long
statement: Volume mattered for him: high-but-not-maximal strength work with little tonnage, then many supersetted variations and accessories; replacing compounds with isolation would take 4-5 h/day, and in 2021 he said he was not strong enough to trade volume for intensity below 5 days.
numbers: isolation-only would need 4-5 h/day; not below 5 days/week (2021)

title: 2023: many exercises, few low-rep sets
statement: In 2023 he still trained six days with many exercises per session, but with only a few low-rep sets each, far less volume than his GVS program.
numbers: 6 days/week; 7-8 exercises/session; 3-4 sets/exercise, very low reps

title: Shift to less volume, less frequency, more intensity
statement: Over 3-4 years his programming moved to less volume, fewer days and more intensity while he kept progressing; he now thinks his first-year YouTube programs were too high in volume and frequency.
numbers: 7 → 6 → 5 days/week
scope: himself; see ch. 3 for his volume and frequency principles
status: changed — 2020-2022: 6-7 days/week, 2-3 h, volume is king; 2024: 5 days/week, less volume, more intensity

title: 2024 routine: evening sessions after work
statement: In 2024 he trained five days a week in the evening after a full workday.
numbers: 5 days/week; ~2-2.5 h door to door incl. warm-ups; gym ~6 to 8-9 pm after an 8-18 workday

title: Training fitted around long work weeks
statement: He fits training around long work weeks, family and channel work, and would cut training time if he could get the same gains.
numbers: 50-60 h work weeks (55 h in 2022); 10-25 h/week of content

title: Strength kept, size lost, on near-zero volume
statement: In grad school he only worked up to 1RM bench and overhead press, kept a 3-plate bench for months, but lost a lot of size.
numbers: 60 h/week of work; 25-30 min sessions; 315 lb bench kept

title: Every part he grew, he trained hard
statement: His most-grown parts are the ones he trained "like a madman"; none "just grew".

title: Biceps and the cheat-curl years
statement: Biceps were always his best part because he put everything into them, mainly years of heavy cheat curls; he reached a 100 lb cheat curl in 2022 and then quit them.
numbers: daily cheat curls ~ages 17-22; heavy weekly cheat curls for ~7-13 years; 100 lb cheat curl (2022); 120 lb EZ and 80 lb DB preacher curls without tendinitis or tears
status: changed — 2020: cheat curls are what grew his biceps; 2022: quit them and said they "are not a good exercise"

title: Arms grew from 10 to 18.4 inches
statement: He built his arms "through isolation, not compounds" despite small wrists and what he calls poor arm genetics; 19 in may take another 2-3 years.
numbers: 10-11 in (puberty/18) → ~13 in (3 years in) → 17.5 cold / 18 pumped (2020) → 18 cold (2022) → ~18.4 (2024); wrists 6-6.5 in

title: Triceps neglected for six years
statement: He barely trained triceps for his first ~6 years and now does catch-up work; in 2024 biceps and abs were his strongest-looking parts and triceps and shoulders his weakest. He wishes someone had told him one year in.
numbers: ~6 years without direct triceps work

title: Shoulders: de-prioritized, then isolation and pressing
statement: He skipped vertical pressing for two years so his arms would outgrow his delts, then in 2022 added overhead press and lateral and rear-delt work; shoulders and traps improved through isolation and more serious pressing.
numbers: 2 years without vertical pressing; 2022 plan: OHP + DB/cable laterals + bent-over raises, 3×/week, 12-16 sets/week, pre-tested 3 months

title: Legs: skipped for five years, then squats
statement: He skipped legs for about his first five years (which gave him a big upper body), then mostly only squatted; his legs visibly grew after two years of frequent squatting, and after an injury he regained 3 plates with bigger legs.
numbers: ~5 years without legs; 26-27 in quads from squats; squats 2-3×/week for ~2 years

title: Hamstrings fixed, thighs reached 28 inches
statement: Five years of squat-only leg work left him quad-dominant; RDLs and hyperextensions added an inch to his thighs during the recomp, and he reached his thigh goal, with leg extensions and adductors next.
numbers: +1 in thigh (2020-2023); 28 in reached after five years (2024); next goal 30 in

title: Same squat every time made him regress
statement: When he only back squatted, or squatted the same way 3×/week, he regressed and got hurt; his legs grew from back squats plus lots of safety-bar and front squats, with leg press, extensions and hack squats filling volume.
numbers: 3×/week same squat = regression

title: Calves: his biggest regret
statement: He never trained calves directly for about nine years (sports built them to 16 in), and not training them sooner is his "biggest bodybuilding regret".
numbers: ~9 years untrained; 16 in (2020)

title: Back: thick but narrow until pull-ups returned
statement: Deadlift-only years gave him a thick but zero-width "surfboard" back, and he hit his upper back only as a helper for other lifts; dropping pull-ups for two years cost back development he regrets, and his lats grew strictly from pull-ups and pullovers once he trained them properly.
numbers: pull-ups fell from 20 reps at 165-170 lb to 2-5 after ~2 years off; back grew a lot in 8 months of proper training

title: Abs built with thousands of crunches
statement: Thousands of anchored crunches a day as a teen built his abs, but five years of hitting only the upper abs left an imbalance; in 2023 he did a moderate weekly dose of sit-ups and leg raises.
numbers: thousands of crunches/day (sometimes an hour); 9-15 sets/week (2023)

title: Forearms grew from isolation, not grippers
statement: Over a decade of grippers gave him a ball of muscle on skinny forearms; reverse curls, wrist curls and arm-wrestling methods grew them, quickly, and they are now his favourite muscle.
numbers: 11-12 years of grippers (to CoC 2.5); big improvement in 6 months of isolation; 13-13.5 in (2020) → ~15 in (2022)

title: Neck: 16 to 18 inches
statement: His neck was 16 in without direct training in 2020; he set an 18-in goal and reached it by 2024.

title: Recent lift choices: dips instead of bench
statement: In 2023-2024 he quit benching in favour of dips and push-ups, went months without deadlifting, and progressed weighted dips steadily.
numbers: no deadlift for 6-7 months (2023); weighted dips +90 lb×5 (2023) → +4 plates (2024)

title: Strength milestones felt like nothing
statement: He felt "absolutely nothing" on hitting the 3-plate bench he was promised would change everything; he says PR culture sells meaningless milestones, and he will never give strength advice or chase a 225-lb overhead press.
numbers: 3-plate (315 lb) bench; 255 lb bench; 225 lb OHP he will never chase

title: Broken ribs squatting at 240 lb
statement: He broke both sides of his ribcage (twice) and tore intercostals squatting at about 240 lb; he still has chronic intercostal pain, managed with a rib routine between warm-ups and top sets.
numbers: ~240 lb bodyweight; ribs broken twice

title: Bench injuries at heavy touch-and-go
statement: In four years of benching he had one pec strain and repeated right-shoulder injuries (rotator cuff, AC), always at heavy touch-and-go sets; at 23 he saw the problem was chronic and changed approach.
numbers: 4 years; ~285-295 lb touch-and-go for 5-6

title: Years of tendinitis, fully healed
statement: Street basketball gave him about two years of debilitating patellar tendinitis, and he had tendinitis in both knees and elbows for years; he healed fully and returned to heavy squats, and three pain-free years "probably saved" his relationship with lifting.
numbers: ~2 years patellar tendinitis; pain from 135 lb to 285-295 lb squats; 3 years tendon-pain-free

title: "No pain, no gain" gave his worst years
statement: Under a "no pain, no gain" mindset he squatted and deadlifted with broken bones and overate; those were his worst years, and his best were when he loved lifting.
scope: himself; see ch. 9 for injury principles
check: Does the approach avoid training through broken bones and serious injuries?

title: No back injury from deadlifting
statement: He had no back injury in four years of conventional deadlifting, crediting avoiding "fishing rod" form and home bed bridges, and pulled heavy every two weeks for two years pain-free.
numbers: 4 years conventional; heavy pulls every 2 weeks for 2 years

title: Scoliosis and the mixed-grip regret
statement: He has had scoliosis since his teens (one shoulder lower) and pulled mixed grip for about two years without competing, which he regrets; it did not grow his forearms.
numbers: ~2 years of mixed grip

title: Normal testosterone, stable since puberty
statement: He had all the signs of low testosterone at 17 (never tested) but fixed his environment; yearly blood tests show T slightly above normal and stable since puberty, with only a minimal rise that cannot explain his mass.

title: Family history of cancer
statement: His great-grandfather, grandfather and father died of prostate (and colon) cancer; he considers himself next in line, uses diet as his main prevention, and would be happy to reach 60.
numbers: happy to reach 60; an uncle screened in his 30s is now in his 70s

title: Corticosteroids at 10-11
statement: Corticosteroids for facial paralysis (Bell's palsy) made him gain weight fast, and he started middle school short, fat and acned.
numbers: ~25 lb in a month, age 10-11

title: Rarely sick
statement: He was not sick from age 15 until an illness in 2023, when he chose training and recovery over making videos.

title: Cold showers and a freezing garage gym
statement: He takes daily cold showers and trains in an unheated garage through long winters with no pump and still grows; he cannot train in humidity.
numbers: cold showers 5+ years; 0 °C / 20-30 °F; 8-month winters

title: Endurance kept, running ability lost
statement: His sports conditioning persisted and four years of giant sets without dedicated cardio preserved his endurance, yet at his current mass he is poor at running and jumping and gasses out quickly outside lifting.
numbers: 4 years of giant sets, no dedicated cardio

title: Training is his mental-health anchor
statement: He gets antsy or achy after 2-3 days off and says the "dark thoughts return" after 3-4; rest days become weighted-carry days.
numbers: antsy after 2-3 days off; dark thoughts after 3-4 days
status: contradicted — 2024: never more than about a week without training since 14; 2023: he stopped training for a year after university rejections and played video games 10 h/day; 2020 mentions breaks and skipped periods

title: Discipline over motivation
statement: He is truly motivated for only a small share of workouts; training is scheduled like work and he goes regardless, e.g. a freezing garage after a 10-hour shift. Motivation he built at 13-14 grew into discipline.
numbers: motivated for ~5% of workouts; 20 °F garage after a 10-h shift
scope: himself; see ch. 2 for mindset principles

title: The "gymcel" phase
statement: From about 18 to 23 he trained without enjoyment, was anxious after missed days, trained through broken ribs until he dreaded the gym and looked down on "normies"; freeing himself from the obsession brought better gains.
numbers: ~ages 18-23

title: From rigid to balanced
statement: He now says he is happiest, has his best gains in years, and can take a week off or move sessions for family; he credits his wife for making him less rigid.
numbers: best gains in ~7 years (2024)
status: changed — 2021: could not go 2 days without lifting and panicked when his schedule broke; 2024: balanced and flexible, though he still needs daily activity

title: Years of bigorexia
statement: Body dysmorphia hid his obesity at 240 lb; he made big progress against it using the practices from his own videos but still sometimes feels tiny.

title: Lifting replaced video games and lasted
statement: He has an addictive personality and drops passions once fed up, but lifting has lasted and he is certain he will bodybuild for life; it displaced video games after a two-month internet outage at 15, and he later quit games because they made him depressed.
numbers: 12-14 h/day of games as a kid; 2-month internet outage at 15
status: contradicted — the age he quit games is given as ~18, 18-19 and ~21

title: Bullied until getting big ended it
statement: He was bullied and beaten until about 14; fighting back stopped it but made him aggressive, and getting big ended fights entirely and gave him peace.
numbers: no fights in 6-7+ years

title: Anger as fuel backfired
statement: Channelling anger and bad memories into heavy lifts made him aggressive outside the gym, so he stopped; he says using trauma as fuel produces more trauma.

title: The mental gains outweigh the physique
statement: Lifting made him better in every aspect of life; he values what it did for his mind and willpower far above the muscle and would give up all his muscle to keep it.
numbers: mental gains worth "15 times" the physique

title: Patience: the journey over the finish line
statement: His early years were enjoyable because the journey mattered; chasing a finish line turned lifting into self-punishment, and he would rather reach his goal five years later with sound joints.
numbers: ~10 years of slow progress; goal "five years later" with healthy joints

title: Average genetics, started early, never quit
statement: He was told as a kid there was no point trying and later that he had good genetics "all along"; he rates his genetics 5/10 and says he is bigger than viewers only because he started sooner and never quit.
numbers: genetics 5/10; physique 6.5/10 (2024)
scope: himself; see ch. 2 for genetics principles

title: Without training he would be 150-160 lb
statement: He believes that without lifting he would weigh about 150-160 lb at 6 ft; friends who did not change their environment stayed the same.
numbers: 150-160 lb at 6 ft

title: Intermediate with some advanced parts
statement: In 2020 he had lifted about ten years but counted only two to three as serious bodybuilding, and called himself intermediate with some advanced parts; advanced means a decade of hard training.
numbers: ~10 years lifting, 2-3 serious (2020); ~15 years (2022-2024)

title: Still expects his best gains ahead
statement: He expects the best gains of his life in his 30s and the coming five years, and still finds weaknesses after 15 years.
numbers: next five years (said 2022 and 2024)

title: A year-long plateau would be his failure
statement: If he spends a year in a plateau, he says he will call himself a failure rather than blame a natural limit.
numbers: 1 year

title: He nearly took drugs in 2016-17
statement: He thought he had hit his natural limit, blamed his testosterone and seriously considered drugs though he was still progressing; he spent hours on tren and deca content and admits he was "one bad day away".

title: What stopped him
statement: Deportation risk as an immigrant, his own research, and meeting users whose lives looked grim stopped him and made him an active opponent; he would not take even a risk-free cycle, and he says young men write weekly saying they quit or never started because of his videos.

title: Naivety protected him as a beginner
statement: As a beginner he did not know what steroids were; his mother thought whey was a steroid.

title: Straight edge
statement: He takes no drugs, has never smoked or been drunk and barely drinks; his issue is dependence. Lifting from 15 kept him away from bad crowds, and one heavy weed experience scared him off.
numbers: a glass of wine every ~2 months (2022)

title: Whole foods for life
statement: After fast food at 15 he committed to whole foods only; a relative's death made him change his diet, and he eats raw garlic and ginger daily.
scope: himself; see ch. 10 for nutrition principles

title: A cleaner environment, a bigger body
statement: His youthful gaming, junk-food, low-sleep lifestyle was "not conducive to gains"; the purer the environment he gives his body, the bigger he gets.

title: Introvert with monk-like priorities
statement: He is an extreme introvert who needs solitude and repetition; he prioritizes lifting and work, then family, and sacrifices social gatherings.

title: Why the channel exists
statement: He started the channel during the 2020 lockdown, after about ten years of lifting, to promote natural bodybuilding and give the advice he wished he had had; he calls it a community, not a route to fame, money or numbers.
numbers: started 2020, ~10 years into lifting

title: From refusing money to Ko-fi funding
statement: He refused monetization and sponsors for years; once he became sole breadwinner, Ko-fi pledges turned the channel into a paid second job, still without ads or sponsors.
numbers: 20-25 unpaid h/week; physique review $10, program review $5
status: changed — 2020-2021: would never make money from the channel; 2023 onward: funded by Ko-fi pledges, no ads or sponsors

title: From refusing to coach to a coaching school
statement: For years he refused to coach, saying he was too impatient and harsh; in 2025 he coaches in a paid School of Strategy and calls it "the best choice of his life".
numbers: ~30 strategy clients + 15 in philosophy/literature (2025); clients quit after ~2 months when he coached earlier
status: changed — 2020-2024: refuses to coach; 2025: coaches ~30+ people

title: Harsh with beginners
statement: He berates beginners because a kick in the butt worked for him, but admits it pushes people away.

title: Channel milestones
statement: The channel was terminated without warning in 2022 and restored within 24 hours with other creators' help, fought long copyright battles over anime clips, and grew to 100K subscribers by 2023 with an almost entirely male audience.
numbers: 50K subs in 3 years; 100K by 2023; audience ~98% male; restored in 24 h

title: Competing: wanted, never done
statement: He has repeatedly talked about entering a natural show but has not competed.
numbers: "someday" cut to 180-190 lb to compete (2024)
status: contradicted — 2020 wanted a natural show (one was cancelled), 2021 would enter an online show without cutting; in 2024 he both said he won't compete because he won't lose weight and that he will someday cut to 180-190 lb to compete

title: Discipline over motivation
statement: Motivation spikes and fades; discipline gets you to the gym. The top level is training without deliberation because it's simply on the schedule and you love it.
numbers: three levels: motivation → discipline → "just doing it"; after 10-15 years he is rarely motivated
status: contradicted — he also once called motivation "the most important half" alongside method, against his usual view that it is too unreliable to carry you
check: Is training run as a fixed habit rather than left to how motivated the lifter feels?

title: Motivational content replaces action
statement: Hype and motivational videos are a dopamine spike that substitutes for training and makes you passive (the "David Goggins effect"); a video should be the spark that sends you to train, not a replacement.
numbers: he'd rather you train 5 min than watch his 5-min video

title: Motivation must come from inside
statement: If you need a crew, a commercial gym or cheering friends to train, your motivation is fragile; lockdown quitters and newcomers who vanished once he stopped babying them show it.

title: Discipline and toughness are learned, not genetic
statement: Discipline, fighting spirit and pain tolerance are habits you can build at any age; calling them genetic is a cop-out. Parents who teach discipline give a head start, never an excuse.
scope: all lifters; teach kids early, since it is harder later

title: Willpower is trainable and finite
statement: Each push-through strengthens willpower and each give-in teaches you your will is weak; habits save willpower for when they fail.
status: current — in 2024 he adds that willpower fluctuates with mood and hormones

title: Schedule training; never ask whether to go
statement: Put training in the schedule like lunch or work and decide once that you train for life; asking yourself if you want to go invites "no".
numbers: his fixed 5-8 pm slot (2020); he can't remember his last skipped session

title: Training is non-negotiable
statement: Bad sleep, a bad meal, rain, cold, homework or work hours don't cancel a session; if the program says train, you train, and if you can't, fix the program or yourself.
scope: all lifters; see MND-13 for his 2024 flexibility

title: Go on the days you don't want to
statement: The reluctant days are the ones to go; the reluctance fades and he has never regretted going.
numbers: reluctance gone within ~40 min

title: Reschedule missed sessions, don't drop them
statement: Push a missed session back and rearrange the week; planned rest days are fine but impromptu skips breed laziness. Repeatedly missing scheduled days signals bad programming or training that isn't fun.
numbers: 1 skipped session every 2 weeks adds up to a year of lost sets; if you skip part of a program for 6 months, move it earlier (laziness) or remove it (not needed)

title: Habit-building tactics
statement: Chain training to an existing habit, give small immediate rewards (a manga page per rest period), make key exercises convenient (superset them), write schedules on paper, make the first task easy, and build up from tiny steps if you can't hold a routine.
numbers: fallback routine: shower → dress → 2-min walk
scope: anyone struggling with consistency; novices get a small weekly taste

title: Discipline is rented, not owned
statement: Rent is due daily: once a good habit is built, never let it slip, because temptation never disappears and restarting is worse than never stopping.

title: Greatness comes from tiny daily repetitions
statement: A physique is "a temple built one rock a day": diligent repetition becomes habit, then discipline, not hyped bursts.

title: Discipline taken too far is a straitjacket
statement: Training should be neither winging it nor the Ten Commandments; you wrote the program, so keep flexibility and don't be its slave.
scope: all lifters, especially rigid or neurotic ones
status: changed — 2020-2022: training is rigid, done as planned regardless of feeling, and a week off for low motivation is dangerous; 2024: rigid discipline is a straitjacket and he keeps no fixed time schedule, doing tasks in order of excitement

title: Adherence and enjoyment come before optimisation
statement: A lift or program you love beats a "better" one you hate; a disliked lift gets skipped or done without intensity. Adherence sits at the top of the muscle-building pyramid.
check: Is the program built from lifts and a structure the lifter enjoys enough to stick with for years?

title: Training must be fun; "bodybuilding must suck" must die
statement: Treating training as duty or punishment led him to injury and resentment; martyrs and grinders who hate their training don't last. He claims the "must suck" idea is pushed by PED users.

title: The ideal program excites you
statement: Before tuning other variables, check that each training day is realistic, doable and exciting; you should never dread it.
scope: anyone writing or choosing a program

title: Protect your love of lifting
statement: Never turn bodybuilding into a job; his top priority is never falling out of love with it, and a lighter, hobby-like attitude keeps the passion for decades. If you lose the love, try a new sport and do only movements you enjoy.
numbers: 10 years in, he wants 50 more

title: Plan training on paper, not by instinct
statement: "Instinctive training" without a plan is lazy dice-rolling; the "educated barbarian" arrives knowing exactly what to do.
scope: all lifters past the very start
status: contradicted — elsewhere he says to listen to instinct when a style feels right and drop what you instinctively know isn't needed

title: Consistency beats intensity and optimisation
statement: The park trainee doing daily chin-ups and push-ups outgains the perfect-program lifter who trains sporadically; years of steady work beat short bursts of madness.
numbers: consistent 1 year > obsessed 2 weeks (2020); a program for 10 years > burning out in 3 months (2020); 10 years done properly > 6 months of madness (2021); 2 years fairly hard > 6 months like a madman (2021); 2 years like a normal person > 2 weeks like a madman (2022)
check: Is the plan sustainable for years rather than maximal for a few weeks?

title: Whoever sticks with it longest wins
statement: Elite physiques come from a small consistency edge, not losing what others skip; do slightly less and let consistency make up the difference, which avoids burnout.
numbers: the ~10% others skip

title: Starting extreme guarantees burnout
statement: Extreme starts (huge deficits, double sessions, copying Goggins on day one) fail and are often a subconscious setup to say "it was too hard"; start where you can touch the bottom.
numbers: example: cutting 2000 kcal while training 2x/day

title: No deadlines on physique goals
statement: Deadlines create stress, rushing and shortcuts, and imply you plan to stop; aim for a goal "whenever it comes".
numbers: "a god physique in 6 months" is marketing and impossible without drugs; finding what you love can take 1-2 years
check: Is the physique goal free of a fixed deadline?

title: Building muscle isn't hard, it's long
statement: Confusing "long" with "hard" makes people quit; it isn't a race, and each session adds one block to the pyramid.
numbers: little changes in 6 weeks; you look different in 3-5 years

title: Lifting is lifelong; age is no excuse
statement: What you gain with work you keep with work; "age cope" (downhill after 25, only maintain after 30) dodges responsibility and becomes self-fulfilling. See NAT-34.
numbers: LaLanne lifted from 13 to 96; men enter their prime in their 30s

title: Most people quit, so sticking with it sets you apart
statement: Most trainees quit early or at the intermediate stage, so simply staying puts you ahead of almost everyone.
numbers: ~70% quit after 6 months of mediocre results (2022); ~90% quit at the intermediate stage (2024); gym manager: of 100 yearly members ~20 remain at 2 months, ~5 at 4-6 months (2024); one hobby for 10 years beats 99%

title: Start now
statement: Don't wait for January 1, a "winter arc" or the perfect plan; "tomorrow" means never and waiting for perfection is laziness in disguise.
numbers: three months is barely a first step; you need a year-round arc

title: Stop program-hopping
statement: If a program still makes you progress, don't change it; almost every methodology works if done long enough, and jumping between fads (including each new program he publishes) keeps naturals in a hope-despair cycle.
check: Is a program that still produces progress kept rather than swapped out for novelty?

title: But don't be stubborn with a method that fails
statement: Stay confident but open: stubbornness cost him years, while a mind that switches constantly is also a problem. A diet or lift is a tool, not an attachment.

title: Aim for an unattainable ideal
statement: Your ultimate ideal should be unrealistic; "realistic" means low standards, and aiming high leaves you with more even when you fall short. A manga physique is a fine ideal.
scope: all lifters; pair with yearly steps (MND-30)
status: contradicted — he says elites state godlike goals aloud and verbal commitment helps, but also that loud announcers lack internal willpower and you shouldn't announce your discipline

title: A star and a ladder
statement: Keep a lifelong goal body plus smaller, realistic yearly objectives.
numbers: project ~2 years ahead, not 20

title: Have a self-chosen goal and a "why"
statement: A clear goal you chose (aesthetics, strength, calisthenics or sport) dictates your program; without one, influencers hand you theirs or "progress" itself becomes the goal. People who train for someone else's goals quit or stay insecure.
scope: intermediates especially; he defines an intermediate as someone who can answer "why do you lift?"
status: contradicted — in 2020 he also advised starting with no definite physique goal and "just train and see"
check: Does the program follow from a goal the lifter chose himself?

title: Keep an evolving goal
statement: A finite or reachable goal (beating a specific person) makes you stop or disappoints once reached; let the goal move.

title: Keep your goal body in sight
statement: Print or draw your goal body and put it where you see it daily, but only after removing self-limiting beliefs, or the picture reminds you of failure.
numbers: bedroom, bathroom, gym

title: Rehearse lifts mentally
statement: Visualise heavy lifts and the evening's sets during the day, and picture the target muscle working; he calls the last "biologically meaningless" but says it boosts belief and effort.
numbers: e.g. plan the evening's 4 sets of OHP during the day; a day of visualising a heavy deadlift turns "a 50% chance into a sure thing"

title: Visualisation works only with action
statement: Visualisation or "manifestation" isn't prayer; it only helps alongside training.

title: Belief is self-fulfilling
statement: Limiting beliefs mean low goals, low effort and poor results (Pygmalion/Galatea effects); believing your body won't grow kills the drive for years. Surround yourself with bigger natural lifters. See GEN-04.
numbers: records unbroken for 10-30 years fall repeatedly once one person breaks one

title: Hold yourself to higher standards than others
statement: Be harder on yourself than on the people around you.
numbers: his scale: 10 for himself, 6-7 for loved ones, 3 for strangers

title: Use high natural standards
statement: Being stronger than the untrained average is not "strong"; fitness should raise standards. Skepticism about historical naturals lowers them; take PED users out of setting the standard.

title: Don't compare yourself to others
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: Beat yesterday's self; comparison leads to depression, ego or lower standards unless you directly compete. A strong lifter with small shoulders may wrongly think he's at his limit.
status: contradicted — elsewhere he calls comparison and competition ("mogging") healthy motivators and says to surround yourself with better people

title: Role models for inspiration, not imitation
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: Take traits, not identities: copying is necessary as a beginner, but fanboyism surrenders individuality and creates an artificial ceiling. Naturals fanboying PED users is the worst case.

title: That includes him
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: Disagree with him, judge his advice by applying it, and stop watching (his channel too) if it confuses or depresses you; he gives concepts, not protocols.
numbers: agreeing with 100% of what he says means you're too green or parasocially bonded

title: Copy elite naturals' mindset, not their methods
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: Elite naturals got big by different methods; their shared mindset matters more than any method.

title: Choose realistic natural role models
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: The bigger the gap to your role model, the worse the dysmorphia; prefer past naturals (LaLanne, 1940s lifters) and people who struggled to grow, not enhanced influencers or genetic outliers. See GEN-30.

title: A fictional ideal is fine as a power fantasy
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: An anime or manga physique works as a goal if you know you won't fully match it; it becomes dysmorphia fuel once you think it's naturally achievable.

title: Learn to program for yourself
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: Programming is the skill that takes you furthest; a subpar program you wrote teaches more than a professional's, and his programs are puzzle pieces meant to teach it. "Take the reins" eventually.
numbers: as important as a 500 lb deadlift
check: Does the lifter understand why his program is built as it is, well enough to adjust it himself?

title: Infer and adapt; avoid dogma
section: Comparison, role models and thinking for yourself
statement: "From one thing, know ten thousand things": adapt principles rather than follow anything as gospel. He follows strongman, powerlifting, arm wrestling and sumo to avoid an echo chamber.

title: Practice before theory
statement: Theory without application is worthless; the lifter without theory is more useful than the theorist without lifting ("pen and sword"), and the most important study is the one you run on yourself.

title: Don't consume more fitness content than you train
statement: More time on YouTube fitness than in the gym is unacceptable, and most of what you watch should be information, not entertainment.
numbers: most people run 70/30 the wrong way

title: Be a student of the game
statement: The best natural physiques belong to nerds obsessed with refining their training; years trained don't equal experience.

title: Novices: habit before theory
statement: For novices, discipline and love for the iron matter more than theory; detailed theory is for advanced lifters chasing small edges.
numbers: novice priority: the habit of training 3x/week

title: Most workouts won't be optimal
statement: Demanding perfection causes paralysis by analysis; get the stimulus first.

title: Lift calm, not hyped
statement: Start sessions calm, neutral and determined and save intensity for the moment you must push; hype isn't replicable, tires your adrenaline response and creates dependence.
numbers: he rates hype "C tier"

title: Anger as fuel is unsustainable
statement: Anger, trauma or resentment can get you started but runs dry and keeps those emotions alive; breaking that cycle improved his life.

title: Feeling isn't strength
statement: Mood shouldn't dictate performance: feeling bad or awkward warm-ups don't mean your strength is gone; if spirit is high, push through.
numbers: example: 275 lb warm-ups felt awkward with 390 lb top sets

title: The ability to push is the first requirement
statement: Intense people gain even without a program, while people who can't push themselves stay small on any program; the best technique fails without strong intent.
numbers: lifting is 50% physical, 50% mind
scope: all lifters; see ch. 3 for intensity

title: Phone away, no socialising
statement: Chatting and scrolling lengthen sessions, rush sets and break rest times; music on shuffle, phone untouched, and a partner only spots and loads plates.

title: Save music for hard sets
statement: Use podcasts or lessons for warm-ups and volume work so music keeps its adrenaline boost for working sets; build a varied shuffled playlist, since all-hype music causes habituation.
numbers: playlist ~300 songs (2000 is too many), e.g. 40 PR / 30 transition / 10 classical; shuffle, never skip

title: Shout only when necessary
statement: A committed mid-set shout re-invigorates you, a timid half-shout psychs you out, and shouting costs mental stamina.

title: Lifting is meditation
statement: Once technique and program are ingrained, the body is busy and the mind rests; lifting can be strenuous without being stressful.
scope: his experience; people who struggle with seated meditation

title: Finish the session
statement: Don't drop the lifts that stress you or skip the end of the session (isolation, calves); that is where mental fortitude is built. Treat every exercise as equally important.

title: Leave the rep you know you'd get
statement: Repeated gym failures build a "loser's mindset" and mental plateaus, while knowing you had another rep builds confidence; with conservative steps a miss costs a rep, never a deload. See ch. 3 for failure as an intensity tool.
status: contradicted — in 2020 he also said a lifter who failed 5 times on the way to a 300 lb squat handles misses far better than one who never failed

title: Strength fuels motivation but isn't the goal
statement: Bodybuilding is about what the weight does to the muscle; detach from main-lift numbers (a squat stalling 3 months is fine if other knee-flexion lifts progress). See ch. 7.
status: contradicted — in 2024 he says both that dropping PR culture made him stronger and that constant PRs keep him in love with the gym

title: Strength is instant gratification
statement: Weight on the bar every week is gratifying, so size-seekers drift into strength training; he thinks this explains 5x5 and Starting Strength's popularity.

title: Be honest whether you want strength or looks
statement: Self-test: does a PR or a new vein in the mirror excite you more? If it's looks, call yourself a bodybuilder and drop the "functional" backstory; "power copers" hide poor muscle gains behind strength.

title: Round numbers create psychological plateaus
statement: He stalled at a 3-plate bench until 325 lb was loaded by mistake and he pressed it easily.
numbers: stuck at 315 lb; pressed 325 lb

title: He stopped measuring during slow recomp
statement: Slow recomposition numbers demoralised him even while his physique improved, so he stopped measuring.

title: A healthy ego carries you forward
statement: "Ego death" in bodybuilding is the death of progression; the problem is a big but fragile ego that rejects criticism.

title: "Ego lifter" is mostly an insult
statement: The label is usually an ad hominem used to shame heavy lifting or straps; squatting ATG because the internet bullied you is the real ego lifting. Still, don't grind reps you know you shouldn't.

title: Admit when you're wrong
statement: It's only wrong to be wrong when you refuse to accept it; his defensiveness about drifting cheat-row form cost him days before he fixed it and grew again. Justifying your form ahead of time means you know it's wrong.

title: Hard work beats talent that doesn't work
section: Talent, limits and plateaus (the mental side)
statement: Talent is double-edged because gifted people quit at the first roadblock; grinders with "garbage genetics" who stayed went further. A talented person who works as hard stays ahead, so work harder. See GEN-08.
numbers: after 2 years of hard work he passed a prodigy

title: Limits are mostly mental
section: Talent, limits and plateaus (the mental side)
statement: Never call something impossible; ask under what conditions it is possible. When he stopped telling his body what it could do, it proved far more capable, and he hasn't found his limit yet.

title: The brain is the limiting factor
section: Talent, limits and plateaus (the mental side)
statement: For naturals the real limiter is knowledge and programming, not the body; plateaus are usually intellectual. Keep the mind ahead of the body or you quit around the intermediate stage.

title: Forever-intermediates are stuck by mindset
section: Talent, limits and plateaus (the mental side)
statement: Being stuck at intermediate is psychological and self-inflicted, never genetic; the biggest downfall is entitlement to gains. What separates intermediate from advanced is time and the decision to keep going.

title: Take full responsibility
statement: "It is not always your fault, but it is always your responsibility": you control your reaction and preparedness, not events. "Injuries just happen" absolves people.

title: Locus of control can be learned
statement: An external locus of control is antithetical to self-improvement but can be switched to internal; it is why "just eat less" doesn't land with someone who feels powerless.

title: Reject the blackpill
statement: Demoralisation is an excuse for passivity and a self-fulfilling prophecy; a depressed person can still gain, a demoralised one never will. He claims many blackpill creators profit from it while living fulfilled lives.

title: Ignore the crabs in the bucket
statement: Ridicule and "genetics talk" hold people down; take advice only from people making something of their lives, never from those who quit and judge from the roadside.

title: Action cures overthinking
statement: Talking about a problem soothes you into inaction; he can explain bodybuilding endlessly but can't give you the drive to go do it.

title: Seek voluntary hardship
statement: Struggle builds the toughness to keep training for years; cold exposure won't make you jacked, but it keeps you training. "If you can train there you can train anywhere."
numbers: his freezer-like garage after 9-hour shifts

title: Pain for its own sake is stupid
statement: Puke-bucket workouts, bragging about limping, training through tendonitis and "seek pain" culture are pointless; growth needs sensible work for years, and ignoring declining health is cowardice.

title: Accepted hardship stops being hardship
statement: Accept the work willingly and early; that's why training feels doable and even enjoyable.

title: Defeat teaches more than victory
statement: A victory confirms your plan; a loss gives you homework. Failing and getting back up prepares you for crises.
scope: all lifters; see MND-61 for the tension with avoiding gym failure

title: Assess a lapse without self-flagellation
statement: After a lapse, reflect and try again; moral self-punishment and pity parties feed the cycle.

title: Look back and see your past stupidity
statement: If you don't look back after a year or two and think you were an idiot, you're stagnating.
numbers: review every 1-2 years (or 5); in 3 years you shouldn't recognise who you were

title: You go up or you go down
statement: There is no stagnation for humans; "maintaining forever" is a bad mindset.

title: Use criticism as a ladder
statement: Elite naturals improve when criticised instead of getting upset; compliments are "sweet poison", though you should accept them graciously.

title: Every lifter meets muscle dysmorphia
statement: Bigorexia ("I am too small") hits every lifter, him included; he considers it more dangerous than other dysmorphias because fulfilment seems doable.
numbers: his own lasting bigorexia came from a dirty bulk ~5 years earlier

title: Dysmorphia has no cure; collaborate with it
statement: The ideal moves as you improve, so feeding it is like paying a blackmailer; filter the drive, neither obey nor silence it. Professional help or medication is fine if needed.

title: Dysmorphia spirals
statement: It drives overly aggressive methods that stall progress, which deepens it; it can lead to scheming instead of training, overtraining, injury, quitting or PEDs, which worsen it.

title: Dysmorphia is socially contagious
statement: It grows from comparison, media, parents and peers; comparing an unpumped mirror reflection with curated photos is harmful, and feeling comfortable only when very lean is dysmorphia.
numbers: he says it has skyrocketed vs 30 years ago

title: Steady maingaining soothes dysmorphic anxiety
statement: Steady, trackable gains calm dysmorphia; big fat-heavy bulks followed by cuts mess with your head. See ch. 11.

title: Love your body and still want more
statement: Self-hatred as fuel works at first, then destroys you; accepting your present state lets you move forward, and pride comes from building the body.
status: changed — 2020: lifting motivation may be an expression of dysmorphia and you collaborate with that drive; 2024: love and acceptance, not self-hatred, kept him going

title: Never being fully satisfied keeps you growing
statement: Fully content people stop progressing; contentment isn't the end, since later progress can come from well-being instead of fighting demons.

title: The barbell is a therapist
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: Lifting is the single best thing for mental health; it reduced his anxiety and kept him together in a crisis.
numbers: endorphin/dopamine highs after ~3-4 months of training; 45 min 2-3x/week at home in grad school; at least 15 min/day during exams; a 6-month break is a break from mental stability

title: Anxious or depressed lifters need structure beyond the gym
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: Don't rely only on training to soothe anxiety or rest days become high-anxiety days; walk outside on rest days, follow an exact A-B-C-D plan without tweaking, and reach stable mood before chasing bodybuilding.
numbers: a stable ~6/10 daily mood first

title: Lifting is central, not your whole life
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: "Gymcelling" (isolating in the gym, believing a better body fixes everything) is a net negative; if you feel good only while training, the solution lies elsewhere, and the gym should build confidence you then use socially.
numbers: 8-10 h/week = "serious lifter" (2020); ~5 h/week needs no lifestyle change and replaces Netflix and Instagram (2024)
status: changed — 2020-2022: serious lifting is 8-10 h/week that replaces hobbies and social time; 2024: ~5 h/week, don't centre your life on the gym

title: Dedication is healthy, obsession isn't
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: But mocking passionate lifters as "gymcels" or "try-hards" is projection by people who never committed.

title: Not everyone must bodybuild
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: Training is non-negotiable, but if you hate the gym do martial arts, swimming or tennis; being average or a happy dad bod is fine.
status: changed — 2020-2022: praise breeds stagnation and lazy people get the mediocre gains they deserve; 2024: his harsh voice turns most people off, empathy works better, and pure willpower ideology "creates one hero and breaks nine"

title: Lifting suits addictive personalities
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: It is the ideal outlet because the body eventually stops you; move a gaming addiction to lifting.

title: Leave the intensity in the gym
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: The gym should drain negative energy so you are calm at home; don't carry competition intensity into daily life.

title: Pick one "king" pursuit
section: The place of lifting in life
statement: Pursuing several disciplines at once (boxing and bodybuilding; calisthenics, powerlifting and bodybuilding) makes you mediocre at each; let the rest serve the king.
numbers: side projects ~1% of total work (his finger push-ups)

title: Bodybuilding is transformation of the spirit
statement: He sees it as more spiritual than physical, with the body as a by-product; purely materialistic motives burn out, and the spiritual view keeps you going when results slow.
numbers: spirit is ~50% of training

title: A strong body builds a strong mind
statement: Changing your body proves you can change anything; lifting gives direct feedback from your own work, and the body is "ridiculously easy to change".

title: Lifting for women is a start, not a reason
statement: It's a legitimate start, but if it stays your main reason you plateau, quit or stop once you have a girlfriend; lift for yourself.

title: "I want to look good" is enough
statement: All training goals are "vain" self-improvement, so admit aesthetics if that's what satisfies you.

title: Focus on the journey, not the result
statement: Result-obsessed lifters quit; results are a by-product, and sometimes you do everything right and nothing happens for a while.

title: Mockery of your lifting comes from envy
statement: Swole shaming ("vain", "narcissist") comes from envy or insecurity and shows your improvement bothers them; keep going and widen the gap. A partner discouraging your lifting may be jealous.
numbers: he says he has faced swole shaming for 10 years

title: Take pride in being above average
statement: Natural lifters should drop fake humility; real humility is objectively assessing where you stand.

title: Envy is destructive
statement: Learn how someone got what you want instead of assuming they cheated; naturals accusing each other of being enhanced is jealousy. Admiration is the useful version.
status: changed — 2020: envy can be a lifelong driving force, a sin only when it turns to resentment; 2021-2024: envy keeps you from working and is "one of the worst sins"

title: PED gains don't stay
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Stop the drugs and most of the muscle goes, because the hormonal environment it grew in is gone, even with PCT and hard training; remove the drug and the physique collapses, remove the training and it largely stays.
numbers: users shrink to normal or mediocre within ~3-4 months off
status: contradicted — he has also said PEDs "have been shown to increase myonuclei" and regaining is slightly easier after use, while later rejecting lasting myonuclei gains "in practice"

title: Natural muscle is kept for life
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Naturals lose muscle slowly and regain it quickly; keeping it only takes eating what you need and training, with no substance dependency. He calls this "the number one reason" to stay natural.
numbers: legs built to 25 in shrink in a layoff but don't drop back to 20 in; some muscle remains into your 80s
status: contradicted — in 2020 he said both that lost size "comes back very fast" and that after 10 years and a full detrain it takes much longer than a year; 2024: naturals "regain it quickly"

title: There is no safe dose
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: No responsible or recreational use exists; use and abuse are the same. Prescription or replacement-dose testosterone causes the same side effects as underground testosterone at the same dose.
check: Does the plan exclude all PEDs, including "low-dose" cycles, SARMs and TRT?

title: Bloodwork doesn't make PEDs safe
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Blood tests don't catch heart damage or cancer early, and individual response can't be known in advance; he compares it to scanning while still smoking.
numbers: some lose their liver within 6 months

title: The physical harms creep in
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Organ failure, heart disease, high blood pressure and hematocrit, cancers, gyno and tendon ruptures; benefits arrive fast and harm builds unnoticed ("boiling frog"), and some damage is permanent.
numbers: oral benefits within ~2 days

title: PEDs cost quality and length of life
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: In his view pros now die around 40, and ex-users alive at 70 are rare survivors with wealth and top care; "Arnold-era guys are still alive" is survivorship bias.
numbers: his rough guess: ~1 in 50 users reaches 70 healthy

title: Natural bodybuilding is the path to health
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Being fit and healthy into your 50s-70s beats being massive for 2-3 years in your 20s; enhanced bodybuilding keeps only the aesthetic by-product.

title: Tendon ruptures are PED injuries
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Pec, biceps, lat and quad tears come from muscle outgrowing connective tissue on drugs; a natural won't snap a tendon unless he ego-lifts or uses very short ranges. Drugs also mask injury signals. See ch. 9.

title: Other costs of PEDs
section: Why stay natural: gains, health, lifespan
statement: Money, unknown product quality, dependence on an illegal supplier, risk of jail, and lifelong TRT logistics (insurance, travel to countries that ban it).

title: There is no such thing as one cycle
statement: Small doses escalate: cycle, PCT, cycle again, then blast-and-cruise with "TRT" as the cruise. "It is far easier never to start than to quit."

title: PEDs are addictive hard drugs
statement: Coming off drops you below baseline (depression, mood swings, low libido), which pushes users back on; he rates the mental dependency "as severe as heroin".

title: Exogenous hormones shut down your own production
statement: Natural production may not restart, oral-only cycles suppress too, and repeated cycling forces permanent blast-and-cruise.
numbers: recovery 3 weeks to 6-8 months, sometimes never; some men spend 12 months failing to restart

title: PEDs don't cure insecurity or dysmorphia
statement: They amplify it; the next cycle never brings the size that makes you happy, and most users start "to fill a void".
numbers: at 19-inch arms he would still feel small

title: PEDs amplify who you are
statement: Hormones shape personality; drugs amplify existing traits and insecurities, and users show only their good days online.
numbers: without hormones, he says enhanced influencers would be in deep depression within about a month

title: Drugs cover up bad training
statement: Users never learn to train, so their only answer to a plateau is more drugs; programming knowledge can be passed on, drug gains cannot.

title: PEDs are "liquid tonnage"
statement: Each injection is like weeks of training ("injected time"), and PEDs cause hypertrophy with no exercise at all, depending on dose.
numbers: 2020 guess: PEDs equal "100-200 hours of training per week"; training alone would need 5-6 h/day of top sets for the extra ~50 lb; the enhanced can grow lifting at ~40% of max

title: Muscle responds to hormone duration, not spikes
statement: Injected testosterone stays flat and high while natural levels fluctuate, so even at an equal dose the injector stays anabolic all the time; naturals build through long, stable exposure (an "anabolic bank").
numbers: example: equal 150 mg

title: Drugs scale with dose
statement: Gains keep rising with dose while food doesn't scale; differences between naturals are small and the real gap is natural vs enhanced.
numbers: naturals ~80-120 vs enhanced ~500 (illustrative, 2021); 3-4x (2022); 10-15x normal (2025); 500 mg ≈ 3x natural production

title: PEDs work enormously
statement: "Steroids just let you train harder" is a fake-natty lie; nobody would risk felonies for black-market vials if they did little, and a proper cycle makes almost anyone look "insane".
numbers: ~3 months of a proper cycle

title: PED response is unpredictable
statement: PEDs create new potential rather than amplifying natural potential, and response and side effects can't be predicted; analysis based on hypothetical steroid results is invalid.
status: contradicted — elsewhere he calls the hyper/non-responder idea "exaggerated" and says non-growers are lazy

title: Steroid mass is partly wet
statement: Mass-gaining steroids add fat and water; huge short-term muscle gains are impossible even on drugs.
numbers: 20 lb of muscle in 2-3 months impossible even on steroids; enhanced pros don't gain 50 lb of muscle a year

title: Enhanced lifters recover from what crushes naturals
statement: Offseason bloating, keeping muscle while cutting and recovering from huge workloads are drug effects; if a cycle lets you keep a training plan, that plan was too harsh to work naturally.
numbers: a brutal back session might take a natural 7-10 days to recover from

title: Enhanced advice doesn't transfer to naturals
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: You can't tell whether an enhanced lifter grew from the stimulus or the drugs; copying IFBB pros is "the worst mistake a natural can make", and most mainstream advice comes from users, directly or second-hand.
scope: naturals; exceptions he grants: John Meadows (partly) and Haviland
status: contradicted — "drug users give bad advice and cannot help naturals grow" vs Meadows "gave great advice" and honest users can be good role models
check: Is the program free of methods copied from enhanced lifters without a natural rationale?

title: Naturals must train heavy and compound-focused
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Machines, cables, light weights and very high reps work only on drugs; every top natural he knows trains heavy, and naturals "must be told they need to get stronger".
numbers: grow-anyway styles that fail naturals: 25-50-rep sets, ~60% intensity, ~40% 1RM
check: Is the program built around heavy compound lifts and progressive overload rather than light pump work?

title: For naturals, programming is everything
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Volume, intensity and frequency can't be ignored; his "holy trinity of fake-natty nonsense" is volume without an intensity window, avoiding compounds and not understanding frequency. A big guy saying these don't matter is probably enhanced.
numbers: "one hard set, twice a week, 20 minutes, no accessories" can't grow naturals
check: Does the program deliberately control volume, intensity and frequency?

title: Enhanced volume is mostly junk
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: A natural should do as little as possible to get as much as possible and never replace hard sets with pump work; copying enhanced volume exceeds natural work capacity and leads to burnout.
numbers: ~80% of pro-routine volume is junk
status: contradicted — a 2020 remark says enhanced and natural volumes are "not very different", against huge pro volume and, elsewhere, easy enhanced workouts with baby weights

title: A pump without fibre damage won't grow a natural
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Pump-chasing came from enhanced pros; Bronze and Silver era lifters saw the pump as a pleasant by-product.

title: Bro splits came from enhanced athletes
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Lazy programming works on drugs; naturals on bro splits stay small, and big bro-splitters aren't natural. "Instinctive training" is also promoted mostly by users.

title: Naturals need frequency
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Muscle protein synthesis lasts a few days after training while users stay anabolic around the clock, so one brutal session a week wastes most of the week; "frequency doesn't matter" is spread mostly by steroid users.
numbers: MPS ~48-72 h; naturals rarely recover from heavy presses within 24 h
check: Is each muscle trained more than once a week?

title: Naturals must isolate lagging parts
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: PEDs give diffuse growth to untrained parts; naturals must train forearms, traps and abs directly.

title: Bulk/cut culture comes from pros
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: "Bulk in winter, cut in summer" and gaining muscle at maintenance come from enhanced pros; a natural should look big all year and avoid yo-yo diets. "No food makes you shredded; that's steroids." See ch. 11.

title: Naturals and pros have different priorities
section: Training consequences: don't copy enhanced lifters
statement: Pros: drugs > diet > recovery > training. Naturals: training > recovery > nutrition > supplements. A good program is the best testosterone booster.

title: Natural gain rate is slow
statement: A natural gains in a decade what a user gains in under a year.
numbers: ~20-40 lb of muscle in 10 years natural; 50-60 lb of solid muscle takes decades

title: Natural men peak in their 30s-40s
statement: Testosterone doesn't "crash at 29/30/40"; the idea of peaking in your 20s comes from YouTube lifters on PEDs. Most muscle is built between your 20s and 50s, and age as an excuse in your 40s is a cope.
numbers: T climbs until ~35-40, stable 20s-50s, falls notably only in the 60s-70s for some; natural legs peak mid-30s; taller lifters may peak late 30s

title: Train through your 20s for your prime
statement: Muscle built young protects you in old age; low T and bad bodies in older men come from years of inactivity, not age itself.
numbers: stopping loses gains within ~2 years, much faster than age does

title: Naturals can get big
statement: Being small means you haven't trained enough, long enough or correctly, not that you're natural; the goal is to look enhanced while natural.

title: Reachable lean natural sizes
statement: He gives height-bodyweight pairs a lean natural can reach after years of proper training; a young natural who gets there will draw steroid accusations. His own numbers are in ch. 1.
numbers: 6'1 at 180-190 lb; 175 cm at 82-90 kg raises no flags; 5'7 at 180 lb and 10-12%; Sandow ~90 kg at ~5'11; 6'3 to 255 lb after a decade (not at ~5% year-round); 6'5 tops out ~280 lb lean

title: The natural-enhanced gap is about 40-60 lb
statement: Pros carry roughly 40-60 lb more lean mass than a natural of the same height, and users would lose ~50 lb in three months off.
numbers: pros of his height ~260 lb on stage vs his ~210; Joel ~200 lb at 13-14% vs Arnold 240-250 lb and leaner

title: Natural arm ceilings
statement: 19-20-inch cold arms are possible naturally; 21 in is doubtful, since old measurements were inflated and fat makes 20 easy. Big arms are an "old man's game".
numbers: 19 in after 15 years is "just a good job"; 50 cm at 6 ft at reasonable body fat (2024); +0.2 in/yr is a big win when advanced; pumped (BFR) measurements add 1-2 in

title: Very lean and very big is the clearest non-natural marker
statement: Naturals can't hold their hormones when very lean, so natural competitors should look big at moderate leanness rather than skeletal; natural shows demanding extreme dryness copy pro standards.
numbers: compete at ~12-15% body fat, not 8%

title: Historical naturals show what's possible
statement: Steve Reeves, 1950s physiques, 1910s-20s Indian bodybuilders and Silver Era physiques are natural benchmarks, and today's naturals are bigger thanks to better methods. He holds that massive drug use is certain only from the 1960s-70s.

title: Naturals have big upper-back and leg potential
statement: There's no special natural limit on upper-back size; upper back and legs are the most underdeveloped areas in naturals, and natural quads and hamstrings have enormous potential.

title: Low T in young men is mostly lifestyle
statement: Video games, junk food, alcohol, porn, no sun and no exercise give the body no reason to produce testosterone, and men damage their hormones then blame genetics. Fix that first.
numbers: ~99% have no genetic condition
scope: young men worried about low T

title: Training raises testosterone over time
statement: Muscle, strength and hormones grow in a positive loop: physique first, better hormones follow. His own blood tests suggest his T kept rising slowly.

title: Normal-range hormones are almost irrelevant for naturals
statement: Big naturals with 10+ years of training have average to above-average T, nothing supraphysiological; low-normal T doesn't stop progress, and the T obsession was imported from PED users.
status: changed — 2020: the hormonal profile is the biggest genetic factor for naturals, small edges compound, and heavy squats/deadlifts are worth doing partly for acute T/GH boosts; from 2022: normal levels are "almost irrelevant"

title: TRT is not natural
statement: Any exogenous hormone, even 50 mg on top of normal production, revokes natural status for life; TRT is replacement, not optimisation, and shuts down your own production.
numbers: he says TRT users end up above the top 0.01% of naturals

title: Real TRT is rare
statement: Real TRT replaces hormones you can't produce because of a diagnosed condition, at low-to-mid natural levels; mostly for men in their 70s-80s or rare young men whose hormones never kicked in. That disqualifies ~99% of YouTube TRT users.
numbers: true teen hypogonadism ~0.2% or less

title: TRT is a gateway and a loophole
statement: Clinics prescribe to men with normal levels and turn them into lifelong customers, with doses creeping up; he likens it to the painkiller epidemic. TRT at 18-25 "rejects life" and is a band-aid over a toxic lifestyle.

title: Worried young men shouldn't get tested
statement: Results tend to confirm the fear and lead to quitting, boosters or a TRT clinic; an untrained, sedentary teen tests low by default. Fix lifestyle and train first.
numbers: fix lifestyle for 6 months (1-2 years if it was terrible) before considering TRT; 3-4 years of better habits before re-testing; no TRT under 25; ~3 years of slow natural gains at 16-17 to kick-start hormones
status: contradicted — in 2020-2022 he also advised yearly bloodwork between ~20 and 45 for naturals

title: Don't plan on TRT later in life
statement: Your body is anabolic now, so grow now; men in their 50s-60s do fine without TRT, and he doesn't plan it himself.

title: "Natural" means never having taken PEDs
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Take them once and you can never be natural again, so users can't cycle off and sell to naturals.

title: Time frame is the best indicator
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Genetics speed progress, but nobody gets 10 years of results in 2; years of nothing followed by sudden huge gains means poor training or drugs.
numbers: suspect a teen his size after 1 year, a 16-year-old with huge arms after 6 months, a huge 19-year-old after 2 years; every lean, muscular natural he met was late 20s with many years of training

title: Size swings are a tell
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Sudden jumps in size and strength, disappearing and returning smaller, hiding in hoodies or camera angles, and a neck that shrinks dramatically suggest cycles.
numbers: jumps over 1-3 months; ~40 lb lost coming off

title: Androgen-sensitive muscles are weak evidence
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Traps, delts, upper chest, upper back and neck blow up on drugs, but naturals can build them; isolated blown-up muscles and a "developed everywhere" look are stronger signs, and clear lagging areas point to natural. Naturals grow along a kinetic chain.
status: changed — 2020: these are "the most suspicious muscles"; 2021: "not signs of steroids"; 2023-2024: weak evidence weighed against overall development

title: Face and skin signs
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Moon face, a face that squares out during size jumps, adult jaw growth (a GH sign), sudden severe back acne and a constant red flush are signs; hair loss and acne also occur naturally, and natural facial masculinisation is slow.

title: Enhanced muscle looks different
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Enhanced muscle looks "impossibly hard" with no fat layer; wet bulks look inflated; "pregnant bellies" and thick waists come from GH and insulin, not compound leg training.

title: Behavioural tells
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Users can't explain how they built the muscle ("they just grow"), downplay what PEDs do, or pair a big lean physique with unimpressive training; sudden changes in mood and voice are suspicious.

title: FFMI is worthless for judging natural status
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: The 25 cutoff comes from a small 1995 study that didn't control for training, and every underestimated body-fat percent counts as muscle. Size-strength gaps, vascularity and "natural" in a title are also invalid signs.
numbers: ~150 athletes; understating body fat by 4-5% gives FFMI 26-27; he was above 25 when overweight

title: Drug tests can't settle natural status
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Only random testing works, YouTubers test on their own schedule, natural leagues are "mostly natural" at best, and nobody can prove a negative, his own status included.
numbers: urine clears in 1-2 days
scope: judging others; he won't enter tested shows until tests detect past use

title: Natty-or-not content mostly hurts viewers
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
