statement: It tells beginners that modest physiques need drugs, lowers standards, pushes them toward PEDs and gives fakes free publicity; focus on your own training, though you should still know whether your advice-giver is enhanced.
status: changed — 2020: sign-based content ("in most cases there are visible signs"); from 2021: harmful and a waste of life, though he still analysed individuals in 2023-2024

title: Judgements depend on the viewer's standards
section: Spotting PED use, and its limits
statement: Ordinary people, French audiences or intermediates call ordinary good physiques unnatural; "Schrödinger's bodybuilder" is first small because he never tried, then big because of genetics.

title: Most users start as young novices
statement: Most people who start PEDs are teens or early intermediates with poor programming, rarely 10-15-year veterans; teens take SARMs "as casually as candy".
numbers: often 4-5 years in; some follow influencers who trained under 6 months natural

title: Why people start
statement: Faster results, less effort, believing they hit their natural limit, fear of weakness or of wasting youth ("too late after 25"), and a phase of romanticising PEDs every user goes through.

title: The temptation is real
statement: Nearly every lifter feels it, him included; understand it instead of calling users stupid. If you keep researching steroids "out of curiosity", you're preparing to take them, and PED use spreads through envy.

title: SARMs aren't safer
statement: They are only less researched; pills avoid needles, so teens start there and move on to orals and injections. Avoid them like steroids.

title: Steroids harm women even more
statement: Women risk permanent virilisation even on supposed Anavar; women can't look like men naturally, and natural men can't get "too muscular" for women.

title: PEDs to escape bad genetics fix nothing
statement: Using drugs to escape your genetics is "odium fati": it creates lifelong dependence; he calls it the "only semi-valid" PED argument, but whiny.

title: The only safe message is "never take PEDs"
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: "Stay natural 5 or 10 years, then cycle" sets a goalpost teens shrink to 2 years; harm-reduction content to a mostly natural, young audience recruits users, who remember only the benefits.
numbers: most lifters are teens around 17
scope: anyone giving advice to young lifters

title: Stigma protects young lifters, but aim for empathy
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Shaming PED use is a useful cultural safeguard and refusing to stigmatise is "cowardice", yet he aims for empathy over insults and prefers environments where nobody needs drugs over bans.
status: contradicted — shaming saves lives vs dismissing users doesn't help and empathy works better

title: Argue on danger, not cheating
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Argue against PEDs on health and facts, not on cheating, morality or pleasure.
status: changed — 2021: PED use is "cheating, though in pro sports it may not be bad"; 2022-2025: calling it cheating is a strawman, the debate is about danger

title: Natural is a baseline; be a "noble natty"
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Pride comes from building a big, strong body natural, not from being natural; a skinny untrained natural advertises for the PED camp. The movement mustn't gatekeep: a repentant ex-user who trains well can qualify.

title: Separate yourself from enhanced culture
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Unfollow enhanced influencers and follow believable, high-level naturals who love training, studying rather than copying them; natural bodybuilding needs its own standards. He stopped watching the Olympia because it worsened his dysmorphia.
numbers: ~90% of fitness subscriptions should be natural creators

title: Blackpill and delusion both come from enhanced standards
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: "Nobody is natural" and "pro looks on rice and broccoli" are two sides of the same distortion; a natural who uses "I'm natural" as an excuse for being small is as harmful as a fake natty.

title: The problem is lying, not use
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Honest enhanced lifters are acceptable, some even good role models; fake natties' real crime is killing trust that naturals can grow.

title: Users aren't bad people
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Adults may harm their own health and he wouldn't outlaw it, but users aren't free from judgement or entitled to taxpayer-funded care; taking PEDs is bad, the people are misguided.
status: changed — 2021: "no compassion" for users who get sick; 2023-2024: pity, not hatred, and empathy over insults

title: Enhanced culture set natural bodybuilding back
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: In his view the supplement industry and enhanced pros grew together and "killed" natural bodybuilding, costing decades of method progress; the genetics obsession is a modern drug-user effect.
numbers: 50-60 years of lost progress
status: changed — 2021: natural bodybuilding is "dead" and natural shows mostly aren't natural; 2022-2025: a "noble natty" movement to build on human potential

title: His channel's mission
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Discourage young people from PEDs and show how to get big naturally; convincing one person makes it worthwhile. Users he knew are part of why the channel exists.

title: His own reasons to stay natural
section: Messaging, culture and the natural movement
statement: Being a role model, a doctor-flagged genetic predisposition that exogenous hormones could trigger (including prostate cancer risk), and his time already going into programming, diet and recovery. He says he has never used, is straight edge, and knows PEDs from users' testimony.
numbers: risk window by his early 30s

title: People he claims are enhanced
statement: He claims Mike O'Hearn, Nether (prohormones), Blaha, Liver King, Katcherian, Zyzz, The Rock, Mike Israetel, Dorian Yates, Mentzer and 70s-80s icons including Arnold ("the first fake natties") used PEDs, and once suspected Joel of GH from face growth; he also argues HIT "proves nothing" because, in his view, Mentzer and Yates used.
status: contradicted — in 2020 he said he would "never name anyone" or run a call-out channel, yet later named many alleged users

title: People he believes are natural
statement: He believes Eric Bugenhagen, Jeff Nippard, Steve Reeves, GVS, Omar Isuf and (2023-2025) Joel are natural, and that Henry Cavill's physique is naturally achievable; he says PED users with average genetics wrongly assume elite naturals cheat.
status: contradicted — his view of Joel: suspected GH from face growth vs believed natural (elite in ~3 years)

title: Genetics exist but are never an excuse
statement: How you play your cards matters more than the cards; whatever your starting point, doing the work decides the outcome, and blaming genetics avoids responsibility. Genetics only make it easier; mindset decides whether a natural gets big.
status: current — see GEN-28 for how much more openly he credits genetics in 2024-2025
check: Is stalled progress traced to method, effort or time before genetics are blamed?

title: "Bad genetics" usually means bad training
statement: Most people who blame genetics have average genetics and are training badly (wrong intensity, too little volume, no direct work, inconsistency) or not hard; compound-only lifters blame genes for muscles they never isolate.

title: No true non-responders or hardgainers
statement: Stagnation always has a reason other than "you"; skinny to big is always possible naturally if the parameters are met, and genetics decide how long you stay skinny, not whether you escape it. He says he has helped many so-called non-responders grow.
scope: all lifters; truly cursed lifters (nerve damage, true T deficiency) exist but are very rare
status: contradicted — "hard gainers do not exist" (2020) vs a true hardgainer has a hormonal handicap and cursed lifters exist but are rare; mostly a difference of degree

title: Belief in bad genetics is self-fulfilling
statement: You give up early, get poor results and take them as proof; two clones told "good" vs "bad" genetics would differ after 10 years. See MND-36.

title: Blaming genetics is cowardice and ingratitude
statement: It moves responsibility outside yourself and insults people born without working limbs; resenting nature leads to self-hatred and stagnation.

title: "Schrödinger's genetics"
statement: Before working you can't know your potential; those who stick with it get called gifted or high-T, those who quit get called low-T.

title: Between delusion and despair
statement: The realistic middle ground between delusion and despair about your genetics is where most gains are made.
status: contradicted — in 2024 he also says "be delusional" and refuse to set your own limits

title: Poor genetics can be a gift; gifted people often waste it
statement: Poor genetics force you to become a grinder, while easy early success makes the gifted conceited: they don't review methods, get fatter and quit. Put on a real regimen they become monsters. See MND-70.
numbers: hard workers overtake the gifted by 16-17

title: Being average is fine
statement: Average muscles still grow, just more slowly; algorithms showing only genetic freaks make average lifters think their genetics are bad. There is no karma: lazy gifted people may outperform you, and resenting it only hurts you.
scope: average lifters; he calls himself "Mr Average"

title: Can everyone build a good physique?
statement: He says no person on Earth lacks the ability to build a good physique.
status: contradicted — the same year he said telling everyone they can achieve anything insults people who lack what it takes

title: There is no locatable natural limit
statement: Progress continues, slower, as long as you keep raising weight, volume and intensity; about 99% of people who say they hit the limit only reached the point where the work stopped seeming worth it, or never had a progressive overload scheme. He calls it "a cultural limit, not a biological one".
status: changed — 2020-2023: no limit, you "progress until you die"; 2024: limits exist but you can't locate them, and self-assessments almost always underestimate
check: Is a plateau treated as a programming problem to solve rather than a natural limit?

title: The "limit" is about time and effort
statement: The defensible version is chronological, not numerical: a point where progress becomes negligible and more needs more volume, frequency and gym time, which people decide isn't worth it.
status: changed — in 2023 he called natural limits "safeguards" of the body's harmony, and in 2025 said you can never build too much muscle naturally because the body has limits

title: Natural potential is not infinite
statement: Natural potential isn't equal to enhanced potential; this tempers his "no limit" rhetoric.
numbers: "270 lb at 5% body fat is impossible naturally" (2021)
status: contradicted — he has also called natural potential "effectively unlimited" and "almost infinite"

title: Claimed-limit timelines are nonsense
statement: After 5-10 years you're nowhere near potential; anyone saying gains stop after a few years is wrong, in his view usually to justify drug use.
numbers: rejected claims: "limit in 2/3 years", "99% of gains in 3 months", gains stop after 3/5/8/10 years; the claimed limit fell from 5 years to 2 over a decade

title: Plateaus are not limits
statement: A 5x5 stall is the scheme's limit, a stalled arm "means it's time for an arm day", and avoiding heavy weights causes plateaus; many beginners take their first plateau as the limit and jump on drugs.
numbers: first plateau around ~1 year

title: Low "natural standards" kill drive
statement: Size tables and rules of thumb for natural maximums are wrong, and he says he disproves them; 18-inch arms or 3D shoulders are not "impossible naturally".
numbers: nattyornot's 184 lb at 6 ft; the French "PDC + 10" rule (height cm − 100 = max kg); he is 183 cm/95 kg

title: Novice gains are only half the story
statement: Novice gains get you about half your potential; the other half comes slowly and most give up. The last pounds of muscle are what make a physique exceptional.
numbers: ~50-60% of potential from novice gains; the last 10-15 lb of muscle; even "20% of remaining gains" separates average from Greek god

title: Everyone passes through every level
statement: Gifted people move through novice and intermediate faster but can't skip any level.
numbers: gifted example: novice for 4 weeks, intermediate for 6 months

title: Elite naturals mainly have time
statement: A big natural is accumulated tonnage, often millions of pounds over a lifetime; no single week or month matters much. When a natural is big you see tonnage, when an enhanced lifter is big you see drugs.
numbers: 3 vs 15 years "is the difference between heaven and hell"; most big naturals have trained 15+ years; 8 years "is not long"

title: A great natural physique takes about 10 years
statement: It takes ~10 uninterrupted years of well-written, high-frequency training, and almost nobody does that; anyone who truly does ends up jacked, and if not, something was wrong. Habits applied today show in 5-10 years.
numbers: ~10 years for average genetics (his own took ~10); about half for the gifted; he thinks only 2-3% of young men would commit
check: Are expectations set on a multi-year (~10-year) horizon rather than months?

title: Don't judge your genetics early
statement: Judge only after years of serious training; judging from your teen body is "idiotic". He says 99.9% of fitness YouTube hasn't trained long enough to talk about genetics.
numbers: ≥1 year (2021-2022); "train hard for 10 years before talking about your genetics" (2023)
status: changed — minimum time before judging genetics went from 1 year (2021-2022) to 10 years (2023)

title: Ten serious years beat almost everyone
statement: Anyone training seriously for 10 years ends up better than about 99% of people, so "everyone has good genetics"; almost no natural actually does it.

title: Most people can reach his level
statement: With a narrow frame and average genetics he reached ~210 lb at 6 ft with a full six-pack; most people could match or pass that naturally if they never stop.
numbers: 6 ft, ~210 lb

title: Realistic gain numbers
statement: He gives concrete benchmarks for normal and gifted progress by height.
numbers: +15 kg in 2 years from skinny (58→74 kg at 176 cm) is realistic for most (2024); +45 lb in 4 years (140→185) or 130→180 lb in 3 years at 19 points to good genetics (2024); 6'2-6'3 peak ~220-250 lb (2024); a 6'1 lifter can approach Reeves at ~215 lb (2022)

title: Small lean lifters claiming a limit aren't doing enough
statement: Lean lifters claiming a limit at modest bodyweight aren't eating or training enough; a natural man should never be outsized by a woman.
numbers: example: 160 lb at 5'10

title: Gym averages differ by culture, not biology
statement: The difference between French and US gym averages is cultural.

title: Freaks exist but are rare
statement: A freak looks great without training or explodes on random training; they're irrelevant unless you compete with them.

title: His genetics scale
statement: He ranks lifters 1-10: "a 5 can only achieve what a 5 can", so rejoice at a 10's potential, go back to your own grind, and as a 5 work twice as hard.
numbers: freaks 10; Alex Leonidas and GVS ~6-7; himself 5; a 185 lb natural might be a 7
status: changed — 2020: genetics "won't be treated as an important factor" on his channel and are irrelevant to reaching potential; 2024-2025: genetics set ceiling and speed, though still no excuse

title: Test of giftedness: how long simple progression lasts
statement: The best operational test is how long you progress on load-only linear progression with the same sets, reps and exercises; longer novice gains suggest better potential.
numbers: most stall within 6-7 months (squat around 200 lb to near three plates); the gifted go ~3 years

title: Don't copy gifted lifters
statement: Gifted lifters succeed despite subpar methods, can't tell what works because everything works, and credit hard work; take advice from a 5-7 who had to figure it out. The same applies to creators who succeed against the grain.

title: Strength giftedness isn't size giftedness
statement: Great leverages or a strong nervous system let some outlift you on day one without much growth; such lifters must train reps and tonnage and not give up on size.
numbers: examples: 400 lb first deadlift; 225x5 OHP on day one

title: Signs of giftedness in beginners
statement: Rapid noob gains, pronounced peaks and valleys between muscles even when small, looking big at a low bodyweight (good insertions, small joints), and teens with six-packs and veins without training. Skinny "tube-armed" beginners can still turn out gifted.

title: Athletic background is mistaken for genetics
statement: Years of sport (a wrestler training daily since childhood, teammates secretly lifting since 13) look like genetics; former athletes progress fast on returning to lifting. He wonders whether myonuclei explain it.
numbers: examples: 3 h/day since age 6; 5-6 h/week since 13

title: Structural stress resistance matters (2020)
statement: In 2020 he called your structure's ability to resist stress (spine shape, joint robustness) the most important genetic factor, so injury advice from someone with a "metal" back doesn't transfer.

title: The best body-fat range for growing is genetic
statement: Some grow well at 11-12% while he'd suffer at 10%.

title: Frame sets potential width
statement: Skeleton, especially clavicle length, sets potential mass and shoulder width and can't be trained; a wide V-taper is a gift, but any training improves your V-taper and delt mass builds width relative to frame.

title: Muscle outweighs frame
statement: A wide frame with no muscle looks bad and a narrow frame with muscle looks good; with a narrow frame and wide waist like his, cover it with as much muscle as possible. "Otter mode" only suits wide clavicles and a small waist.

title: Clavicle angle is genetic
statement: Up-pointing clavicles give capped shoulders and less trap room; down-pointing give more trap room but sloped shoulders; short clavicles make traps pop. Training changes the look, not the angle.

title: Waist and hip width are bone structure
statement: Cutting can't fix a structurally wide waist or hips.

title: Tall lifters need more time and mass
statement: Tall lifters have more absolute potential but more frame to fill, so visual change is slower and they need far more mass to look muscular; they don't gain strength slower, and patient tall lifters "become monsters".
numbers: visual change ~4-5 years vs ~2, or 9 vs 3; 6'2 needs 200+ lb; Toba at 6'10/330 lb is realistic
status: current — an early "tall lifters may progress faster" vs "need more time" conflict was reconciled in 2024: strength at the same speed, visual change slower

title: Short lifters look jacked faster
statement: Short lifters win on proportions in bodybuilding, though they have lower absolute size and strength potential and reach what they call their limit sooner.
numbers: a 5'6 lifter can look great at 160-170 lb in ~2 years; ideal bodybuilding height ~5'7-5'9

title: Tall lifters mustn't use short men's standards
statement: Most YouTubers are 5'7-5'10; tall lifters using their standards fall far short of their potential. Tall lifters can't skip body parts, need more work, must build strength (not machines only) and must hammer long legs.
numbers: a 6'7 using a 5'6 man's standards won't reach a tenth of his potential

title: Limb proportions shape the look and the lifts
statement: Short arms look bigger (a bodybuilding gift); long arms favour pulls, triceps and forearms but make biceps harder, and long-armed lifters get more bench ROM for shoulders while short-armed lifters like him need vertical pressing. Long legs with a short torso make quads hard to grow (hips shoot up in the squat), which is anatomy, not bad form.

title: Insertions change shape, not whether a muscle grows
statement: Long bellies and low insertions look small untrained but have more size potential, a "blessing in disguise"; short bellies pop more in 3D and peak. Balance is what matters.

title: You can't know your insertions until the muscle is trained
statement: "Bad" lats or calves are often just undeveloped; his "high lat insertions" were a cope and turned out fine after proper training.
numbers: ~1.5-2 years of proper training

title: Some shape traits are fixed
statement: Biceps peak and sweep, pec shape (heavy flyes can't widen the chest), the bare triceps tendon near the elbow, ab segment number and placement, and vein position are fixed; the size of abs, calves and biceps is trainable.

title: Small joints don't limit size
statement: Small joints and thin bones make muscle look bigger; thick bones push muscle out but don't build more, though bigger frames carry mass more easily. Wrists don't thicken from training.
numbers: his wrists <6.5 in (later "6 in") with 18 in arms, 13.5+ in forearms, 20 in thighs

title: Thicker joints give more strength potential
statement: So wraps help lifters with small wrists or knees.

title: Grip depends on hand size
statement: Grip depends more on hand size and finger length than forearm strength; small hands limit grip volume and therefore forearm growth, a vicious circle.

title: Calves are not 100% genetic
statement: Calf failure comes from inconsistency and poor exercise choice; big calves usually come from being heavy young or from genetics. Bad insertions limit absolute size but not looking beefy.
numbers: his 16-17 in calves look like 13 because of long tibias

title: Forearms depend on insertions
statement: Forearms aren't purely genetic, but insertions (a high belly) drive their look and potential; people who grew forearms from pulls alone probably have gifted insertions.

title: Small arms are a training problem
statement: Only rare outliers grow arms on compounds alone, and then only biceps or triceps, never both.

title: Dominance mostly reflects training history
statement: Years of bench and OHP make you torso-dominant, and curls plus diamond push-ups make you limb-dominant; some people are genuinely back-gifted.

title: A lagging part needs a different stimulus
statement: No body part refuses to grow, and you can't have bad genetics for a part you never train; perfectly equal development is unrealistic.

title: A gifted lower body saves time
statement: Legs need the most tonnage, so leg genetics are a big time saver.

title: Genetics matter only when advanced
statement: Genetics start to matter when sculpting weak points as an advanced lifter; novices whine most but should care least.

title: Time in an anabolic environment drives size
statement: Cumulative exposure counts, and gain is bounded by your years with a prime hormonal profile, so don't rush bodyweight.
numbers: two years at 300 ng = double the exposure of one; 4 months beats 30 days

title: Teen genetics haven't expressed yet
statement: He claims total testosterone peaks later than free testosterone, so a teen's genetics haven't fully shown.
numbers: total T peaks ~30-35 (sometimes 40+); free T in the early 20s

title: Training ranks first among growth factors
statement: His order: training, health, sleep, nutrition, stress, age, response to training, fibre distribution, insertions, frame, body chemistry; against genetics-first lists like nattyornot's.

title: Noob gains are latent at any age
statement: Age 35 is no doom; noob gains are available at any age, most potent right after puberty.

title: Somatotypes are not real categories
statement: "Ectomorph" just means skinny; the body responds to environment (he went from "ecto" when skinny to "meso" when fat). The real traits are morphology, metabolism, leverages and limb lengths, and outside shape doesn't tell you volume or intensity response.

title: Women's potential differs by region
statement: Women have fewer upper-body androgen receptors, so heavy shoulder and upper-trap work is mostly wasted and that volume goes better on legs; they have good potential for biceps, mid-back and rear delts and can't train in curves they weren't born with.

title: Ethnic generalisations are overstated
statement: In his view not all Black men are gifted, jacked untrained men are outliers everywhere, and selection rather than labour explains them; Asian men's "bad genetics" is a self-limiting belief. He sees South Asians as often having wide clavicles and big legs.

title: Genetics pessimism is spread by enhanced culture
statement: It is the most common self-limiting belief in fitness YouTube; in his view enhanced influencers spread "genetics is everything" (steroids as "injectable genetics") to protect their credibility, and exposé channels and low-standard coaches black-pill viewers.

title: "100% genetics" is cope
statement: Saying bodybuilding is all genetics is cope from people who ran a strength program for years without growing.
numbers: example: Starting Strength for 6 years

title: He rates himself average or below
statement: He started as a 140 lb stick at 18 and 6 ft, was told at 20 he'd hit his limit, and kept growing for years. See ch. 1.
numbers: 140 lb at 18; 170 lb at 20; 210 lb after 7-8 years; ~215 lb in 2023; self-rating "bottom-of-the-barrel", "8 of 10 people have better potential" (2020) → 5/10 (2024)
status: changed — 2020: "bad" genetics with 8 in 10 people better; 2024: "5/10, roughly average"

title: His frame
statement: Very short clavicles and narrow shoulders, a wide waist and narrow hips, tiny wrists, average knees, above-average ankles; his back is thick but not wide and he is trap-dominant.
numbers: shoulders ~3 heads wide vs a 4-head "heroic" ratio

title: His gifts and weak points
statement: Gifts: neck, traps, inner forearms, high pec insertions, short quad attachments and a "metal" lower back. Weak points: lat width, pec gap, calves (long insertions), outer forearms and grip (big palm, short fingers). One arm is biceps-dominant, the other triceps-dominant.
numbers: 16 in neck with no direct work

title: Volume, intensity and frequency form one system
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: Volume, intensity and frequency are one trinity; none works alone, and pushing one while ignoring the others breaks the system.
scope: All trainees; the basis for every programming decision in this chapter.

title: Growth comes from tonnage in a relevant window
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: Hypertrophy is driven by tonnage (reps x weight) accumulated over time, but volume counts only when the load sits in a relevant intensity window.
numbers: 10 reps at 315 lb beats 2 at 350; 300x5 beats 350x1; 135 lb bench for 1000 reps won't make you big.
scope: All trainees; tonnage means hard-set tonnage, never raw reps.

title: Count working sets only
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: Only relevant tonnage from hard sets counts; warm-ups and very light work add tonnage but of low quality.
numbers: 4000 lb of nucleus-overload work is worth about 400 lb of quality work.
scope: All trainees; he still sees warm-ups as mildly useful.

title: Stop a muscle when loads become irrelevant
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: End a muscle's work when it can no longer return to a load relevant to the opening strength work; judge this against absolute (fresh) intensity, not the rising relative intensity of a tired muscle.
numbers: A 300 lb squatter who ends up doing a variation with 150 lb has "dug too deep"; 225x10 squats is easy as an opener but brutal after three other leg lifts.
scope: All trainees; he prefers this in-session cue to MRV guesses.

title: Muscular endurance caps the number of sets
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: The real limit on sets is muscular endurance: being able to return to baseline and repeat. It sets your maximum recoverable volume and differs by body part.
scope: All trainees; bigger muscles have more endurance, so set counts should differ per body part.

title: Tonnage creeps up slowly, driven by set and rep progress
section: The frame: tonnage and the trinity
statement: Tonnage should stay stable and rise slowly without big dips or spikes; let progress in sets and reps drive tonnage, and use tonnage math mainly to diagnose stalls.
numbers: Adding a 10-rep set at 200 lb adds 2000 lb vs 50 lb from adding 5 lb to the bar.
scope: All trainees; don't add sets just to hit a tonnage number.

title: Intensity is a number, not a sensation
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Intensity is load relative to your max (% of 1RM, RPE), or mechanical tension on the target muscle; screaming, burning, pain, nausea or breathlessness are not intensity.

title: Pain and nausea are not growth indicators
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: There is no logical link between pain felt and hypertrophy; "no pain no gain" is in his words a "male power fantasy".

title: Effort is the main hypertrophy variable for naturals
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Intensity (effort) is the most important hypertrophy variable; extra volume is a later lever for continued growth, and "hard sets are king".
scope: Naturals, all levels; someone doing bench, squats, rows and pull-ups hard out-grows someone with perfect exercise selection and no intensity.
status: changed — 2020-21 he called himself volume-skewed and said he responded poorly to intensity; by 2023-24 intensity drives growth and volume is a last resort ("these days intensity").
check: Does the program improve effort per set before it adds more sets?

title: Intensity alone is not a program
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Intensity is not the only variable: a "high intensity" program is really a low-volume one, and bodybuilding needs both; only-heavy and only-volume are emotional positions, not programming.

title: Naturals must lift heavy relative to their strength
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Pump and volume alone don't work for naturals; heavy work puts you in relevant windows, gives high-quality tonnage in little time and builds the strength that drives volume.
scope: Naturals. He claims anyone saying you can grow on pump and volume alone is on PEDs or doesn't lift (his opinion).

title: Heavy work saves time
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Compounds at relevant loads rack up tonnage fast; very light work would need 4-10 h sessions to match it.
numbers: Sets of 100 would take four hours; even if 30% intensity built equal size it is impractical versus 70%.
scope: Bodybuilders with limited gym time (unlike athletes training ~8 h/day).

title: Most gym-goers never get close to failure
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Quality volume means sets very close to failure; stopping when all reps look identical is just warming up, and he disagrees that ~65% effort is enough.
scope: All trainees, especially commercial-gym and science-content audiences.

title: Effort is a skill learned per exercise
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: You learn to push and to grind separately for each exercise; keeping form clean under near-maximal loads only comes from training close to failure regularly.
scope: All trainees; many aesthetics-focused trainees "never learn to push", unlike strength athletes.

title: Absolute vs relative intensity
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Absolute intensity is what you can move fresh and warmed up; relative intensity climbs rep by rep, set by set and through the session as fatigue builds.
numbers: A 70% set is 70% only on rep 1 and can end near 95%; 8 squats starting at 75% end near 100%; set 2's first rep at "80%" is really 81-82%.
scope: All trainees; absolute intensity only changes slowly with strength.

title: Put the highest intensity at the start of the session
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Because relative intensity keeps climbing, programming only by absolute percentages misprograms; optimal intensity exists only at the session's start, which is where strength work belongs.
numbers: 80% at the end of a workout is not 80% at the start; dropping from 3 plates to 1 on rows late in a session means the later work was irrelevant.

title: A set's intensity is the average of its reps
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: A heavy low-rep set can be more intense overall than a long set that only gets hard at the end, so low-rep sets near 90% keep a place.
numbers: In a 20-rep set the first 10-12 reps are easy; 10 squat reps climb only from ~70% to ~78-79% effective intensity vs 100% for a max single.

title: Intensity is not tied to a rep range
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Low reps can be low intensity and high reps high intensity; "low reps for strength, high reps for size" is false, and any range means nothing without effort.
numbers: 95% for 10 reps is possible; a heavy set of 8 is more intense than a light set of 3.

title: "Heavy" is relative to the lifter and context
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Whether a load is heavy depends on the lifter and where it falls in the session; don't let other people's standards push you into ever-lower reps.
numbers: A 120 lb deadlift can be 30% for one lifter and 90% for another; for him 205x12 and 265x2 bench are both heavy; 185x10 close-grip late in a session would be 205-215 as an opener.

title: Raising intensity without adding load
section: Intensity: what it is and how much it matters
statement: Pre-fatigue, supersets, variations and density raise intensity without more weight, but fatigue-inflated intensity should stay marginal, never the foundation of the program.
numbers: Push-ups before bench make a 50% bench act like 65%; the same tonnage in 2 h instead of 4 h is more intense; with supersets, 4x10-15 instead of 3x12-20.
scope: All trainees; planned pre-fatigue helps, unplanned pre-fatigue hinders progression.

title: Work mostly between ~60% and ~95% of 1RM
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: The productive window is roughly 60-95% of 1RM; below ~60% is junk volume, and true maxes above ~95% aren't worth the injury risk or the lost tonnage.
check: Is the bulk of working-set load between about 60% and 95% of 1RM?

title: Average intensity about 85%
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: ~85% is the average across training, not a per-set target; individual days can swing as long as the bulk averages ~85%, and that average sets fatigue, frequency, sets and reps.
numbers: ~85% average; a day at 95% and the next at 65% is fine.
status: contradicted — 2020 he said steady 85-95% beats swinging between 99% and 60%; 2022 he allows swings around an 85% average.

title: Rep range: mostly 6-12, all work 3-15
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: Bodybuilding work sits mostly at 6-12 reps within an overall 3-15 span; above 15-20 is junk, and singles to triples should not make up the bulk.
scope: Looks-focused trainees; only some forearm and neck work goes higher.
status: changed — upper limit fell from 20-35 reps (early 2020) to ~15 (2020-09) and "never 20+" (2024).
check: Do most working sets fall in 6-12 reps, with almost none above 15-20?

title: High-rep sets rarely reach real failure
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: Above ~15-20 reps each extra rep adds little intensity, and cardio, lactic burn or technique stop you before the muscle does. In 2025 he adds that true failure is reachable at 12-15, and higher ranges are more forgiving for grinding.
numbers: First compound of the day ~10 reps, not 15; 10-15 hammer curls are worse than 8-12; 35 reps is "ridiculous"; 3x6-10 DB press beats 180 reps of raises.
scope: All trainees; boredom in high-rep sets is a load-selection problem (2025).

title: Low reps build size too
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: Low reps (3-5, 4-8) work for size and help naturals by raising the absolute intensity used for higher-rep work; he rejects the claim that anything under 5 (or 7-8) reps is useless.
numbers: EZ curls 3x5-8; weighted fat-grip pull-ups 4-8; naturals need 6-10, 4-8 and the occasional 3x5; "low reps" means under 5-6.

title: Never test true 1RMs for hypertrophy
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: True 1RMs have an atrocious fatigue-to-stimulus ratio, give little tonnage and raise injury risk; working up to a max and stopping gives you only the warm-up.
numbers: Curls never below 3-4 reps; weighted dips never need true 1RMs.
scope: Hypertrophy training; rare testing builds strength better than constant maxing.
check: Does the program avoid true 1RM attempts and keep singles-to-triples out of the bulk of the work?

title: Low-rep work is a tonnage trap if overdone
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: A true 3RM gives little tonnage and can't be repeated for four sets, while many easy triples aren't truly intense; with low reps, fewer sets are better.
numbers: 2x3 or 2x5 may beat 3x3 or 5x5 for hypertrophy (2023); only the last set of a 3x3 is near failure.

title: Fixed rep "zones" are myths
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: "6-8 strength / 8-12 size / 12+ endurance", "10-15 is best, never below 8" and "compounds low, isolations high" are wrong as fixed rules; choose 6-10, 8-12 or 10-15 by preference and by what lets you progress.

title: Still, match the rep range to the lift
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: Each lift and muscle has its own best window found by experiment; compounds usually go lower and isolations higher, and heavy/medium/light ranges should stay close together.
numbers: Heavy 3-6/2-5/3-5, medium 6-10/6-12, light 8-10/8-12/8-15; never a 1-rep heavy day with a 20-rep light day; 1-15 is too wide to be useful; rear delts at 3-5 or weighted dips at 10-15 are mismatches.

title: A rep range is a bracket around near-failure
section: Intensity windows: loads and rep ranges
statement: Pick the weight so the target rep lands near failure; without high intensity you plateau in any range.
numbers: Lowering rep ranges ~12-20% across the board raises intensity; 6-10 is more intense than 10-15, and grinding 2 more reps past "failure" at 15 means the load isn't challenging.

title: The target is muscular failure
statement: Count only failure where the target muscle is the limit. Cardio, lactic burn, pump, occlusion or a structural breakdown (artificial or mechanical failure) feel hard but build little and cap tonnage.
numbers: He curls 135 lb for 8 but can't do 40 empty-bar reps (pump fatigue, not muscular failure); 20% of your squat for max reps gives a pump but little stimulus.
scope: All trainees; novices often mistake cardio fatigue for failure. A few artificial-failure sets are acceptable, not as the focus.
status: contradicted — terminology only: "mechanical failure" means structural breakdown in 2020-21 but in 2023 he "defines failure as mechanical failure" (stop when body English appears).

title: Failure = no further clean rep
statement: Failure is the point where you cannot do another rep with clean form; the set ends as soon as you need body English or a torso shift, and partials after failure only move the standard.

title: Never actually miss a rep
statement: "Going to failure" means hitting the last rep you can complete; a missed rep is a programming error that raises injury risk, hurts morale and ruins the rest of the session.
scope: Bodybuilders; missed reps may belong in powerlifting. Failing weekly means the program is wrong.
check: Are loads chosen so that reps are reached at or near failure but never actually missed?

title: Selective failure: isolations yes, squats and hinges no
statement: Take isolation, upper-body presses, rows, pulldowns and other low-risk lifts to failure on every set; keep 1-2 reps in reserve on squats, deadlifts, good mornings and other risky lower-body compounds.
numbers: 0 RIR on isolation, presses, rows; 1-2 RIR on squats and hinges. He personally takes 1 RIR on presses because of a neck/upper-back nerve issue.
status: changed — 2020 "every working set goes to failure" (with a rep kept on strength compounds); from 2022 failure only where it is safe and recoverable.
check: Do isolation and upper-body sets end at 0-1 RIR while squats, deadlifts and good mornings stop 1-2 reps short?

title: Isolation lifts deserve full intensity
statement: Isolations have the best stimulus-to-fatigue ratio and low injury risk, so push them as hard as a deadlift; small muscles respond to intensity like big ones.
numbers: 10-12 cable curls with 10 RIR stimulate nothing; 5x10-15 easy arm work is junk.

title: Failure is a calibration tool, not the goal
statement: Proximity to failure is what matters; failure is the baseline for judging effort, and failing on everything misallocates recovery ("always training to failure is stupid").
numbers: Sets at 70-90% also grow muscle.
scope: All trainees; the opposite swing, fear of failure, is just as wrong.

title: Decide where to fail by recoverability
statement: Failure is fine where you can train the muscle again soon (curls, laterals), not where it blocks a pattern for a week; recovery cost depends on the load at which you fail.
numbers: 4 curl sets to failure recover in ~3 days; 5 hard deadlift sets to failure can stop heavy hinging for ≥1 week.

title: Hard sets must be repeatable within 2-3 days
statement: Keep enough in the tank to train the muscle again in 2-3 days; a set you can only recover from every 15 days is not a good hard set. Repeatability is "the bread and butter of natural bodybuilding".
numbers: Retrain within 2-3 days; 99% efforts are fine if not too often.
check: Can every muscle be trained hard again within 2-3 days of its last session?

title: Reps in reserve on squats and deadlifts
statement: On heavy squats, deadlifts and their variations leave the "danger rep" in the tank for form and injury prevention.
numbers: 2020: exactly 1 RIR, never 2+ (5 possible → do 4; 450x3 becomes 2). 2022-24: 1-2 RIR, often 2 (6 possible → stop at 4; 10 of 12 on good mornings; SSB squats without safeties 2 short).
scope: Squats, deadlifts, good mornings and heavy variations.
status: changed — 2020-11 exactly 1 RIR and "2+ means bad weight selection"; 2022-24 1-2 RIR, usually 2.

title: RIR picks your battles
statement: RIR is not the enemy of failure: before grinding, ask whether the rep is worth the risk that day; the last two grinding reps aren't magic, and heavy compounds benefit most from RIR.
numbers: Dial back the last reps in 1-2 of every 4-5 sessions; 4 of a planned 6 squats is still quality tonnage.

title: Use RIR on low-rep work, starting small
statement: RIR belongs in shorter rep ranges; 0-1 RIR on 10-20-rep sets is pointless. Lifters new to RIR should apply it to one hinge or knee-flexion lift first, not across the whole program.

title: Learn failure before using RPE or RIR
statement: RPE and RIR only mean something once you've trained to failure many times, so beginners must learn failure first.
scope: Beginners (learning a lift at very low RPE is fine); see ch. 12.

title: Percentages vs RPE vs feel
statement: Percentages, RPE and RIR are interchangeable A-tier tools and he recommends % of an estimated 1RM, yet in his own training he uses none of them: a rep range from experience, push to failure, add weight when the top gets easy.
numbers: Find a working load without a 1RM by building to a 12RM.
status: contradicted — he recommends %/RPE but also says "no percentages, push every set to failure", dislikes percentages and doesn't know his own 1RM.

title: Strength-athlete sandbagging doesn't suit bodybuilders
statement: Planned sub-maximal strategies from strength sports (capping at 70%, RIR sandbagging, speed pulls) don't fit bodybuilding; progressing 4-6 reps with reserve "is just sandbagging".
scope: Bodybuilders; for athletes the opposite applies (INT-64).
status: contradicted — he himself keeps 1-2 RIR on squats and hinges (INT-33) while calling RIR on strength work a strength-athlete tool.

title: Safer lower-body lifts go to failure
statement: On lower-body days, take RDLs, hyperextensions, leg extensions and lunges to failure instead of squats and deadlifts; never good mornings to failure without safeties.
numbers: RDLs often to failure, pausing to breathe before the last rep (2023).
scope: Lower-body training; per-exercise detail in ch. 5.

title: Hard sets are the most important sets
statement: A hard set uses a challenging load, ends at muscular failure and is repeatable enough to accumulate tonnage; make as much of your tonnage as possible come from hard sets, including accessories, not only strength work.
numbers: ~10 hard sets fit in one workout across different planes; S tier (2023), "king" (2024).
check: Are most of the program's sets hard sets ending near muscular failure?

title: A growth set moves the muscle off its baseline
statement: A set that produces growth leaves the muscle unable to repeat the same effort within the session; it needs days, not 3-4 minutes, to recover. Too light and the muscle returns to baseline too easily.
numbers: After one all-out set you still get ~80% of the reps, so keep working until loads become irrelevant (VOL-04).

title: Repeatability tests show whether a set was hard
statement: If you can nearly match a set shortly after, it wasn't hard enough.
numbers: 55 push-ups then 53 two minutes later = not damaging; baseline 30, post-bench 30/29 = no stimulus, 30/20 = stimulus; after 12 to failure you should still get ≥8; a true max double shouldn't repeat after 10-15 min.

title: Load checks for too-light work
statement: If you still hit the same back-off numbers after the main work, or the bar flies on squats and deadlifts, the weight is too light; if you could do 7 sets instead of 5 with the same reps, add load.
numbers: Front squat 200x5 fresh and still 200x5 easily after back squats means raise it.

title: Sandbagging: when it is fine and when it isn't
statement: Sandbagging is giving less than full effort without a reason. Chosen sandbagging (warm-ups, planned RIR, a muscle trained again in 2 days) is fine; sandbagging forced by the scheme wastes quality tonnage.
scope: All trainees; it belongs at the start (strength work) and, involuntarily, at the end of a session, not in the middle.

title: Fixed multi-set schemes force sandbagging
statement: 5x5, 5x10, 10x10, 4x10 and fixed 8s or 12s force you to hold back early sets; with real effort reps decline across sets.
numbers: If set 1 of 5x5 were a true 5RM, set 2 would be 3-4 reps; 10 then 9-8 is real; 3x5 beats 5x5; 3x8 bench invites more sandbagging than 3x4.

title: Use evolving (declining) rep ranges
statement: Write ranges so reps trickle down toward failure each set; small brackets mean more intensity and more sandbagging risk, wide ones the reverse.
numbers: 6-10 should read 10/9/8; 8/7/6/5; at low reps a 2-rep window (6-8, not fixed 8 or a wide 5-8); 6-5-4 matches 5-5-5 tonnage with a more intense first set.

title: Too much work forces survival pacing
statement: Piling exercises or huge volume into a session makes you pace and sandbag the top work, turning lifting into cardio with weights; if you pace sets to survive later exercises, the program is badly built.
numbers: Four heavy chest compounds in one session is an example; beginners on 15-rep machine work stop pushing by rep 8.

title: Opening strength work is an appetizer
statement: High intensity lives in 1-3 sets of opening strength work that should prime you, not wreck you; then come variations and accessories at relevant intensity.
numbers: 1-3 strength sets; more than ~4 stops being max effort.
scope: All trainees; top sets drive progression more than they build muscle directly. See ch. 7.

title: Bodybuilding intensity is sustained, not one explosion
statement: Bodybuilding effort is "a steady fire" of repeated hard sets rather than one all-out effort.
numbers: Four sets at 90% beat one at 100%.

title: Back-off sets stay tied to the top weight
statement: Back-off weight is tied to the strength-work weight and still pushed near failure in a sensible rep range; once you'd have to strip the bar, stop doing hard sets on that lift.
numbers: 205 for 6-7 then 135 for AMRAP is a finisher, not a back-off.
status: contradicted — he prescribes reduced-weight back-offs but also says he never takes weight off the bar (460 never becomes 440) and controls intensity with reps and sets.

title: Don't open a session with junk
statement: Never do light high-rep work before the main sets; lifters who know the lifts shouldn't start a program at low intensity, and pyramiding up to 8 reps is just a warm-up.
numbers: E.g. no 4x25 without rest before main work.

title: Grinding: damaging on compounds, useful on good isolations
statement: Grindy compound reps drain you more than anything and the grind-through mentality causes injuries; reps should be challenging, never damaging. On isolations with a good strength curve, slow grinding reps keep you near failure longer and are desirable.
scope: Compounds vs isolations (he never states the split explicitly).
status: contradicted — "never grind" statements vs "grinding is where the muscle works hardest" on preacher curls and JM press.

title: Injury risk is near the max, not at 90%
statement: With solid technique and recovery-matched volume, injury risk rises less with intensity than people think; the danger zone is near a true 1RM.
numbers: 90% carries little more risk than 60%.

title: The pump is a by-product, not a goal
statement: Chasing the pump means light weights, high reps and no attention to failure or load; tension and fibre damage drive growth, and a program can give no pump and still grow you.
numbers: Pump rated C tier (2023); heavy 3-5-rep squats or bench rarely pump yet build more than band presses.
scope: All trainees; a small place remains for light pump work on the triceps long head (2022). He claims pros value the pump because they grow from drugs (his opinion).

title: Techniques are the cherry on top
statement: Drop sets, clusters, tempo, short rests, rest-pause and myo-reps are added to a quality set, never replacing it or hurting the hard sets.
numbers: Myo-reps programmed as top sets are unacceptable.

title: Rest-pause is his preferred technique
statement: At failure, rest briefly while focusing on the muscle, then add reps; post-pause reps must be the hardest of the set. It works best at higher reps, so it pushes rep ranges up.
numbers: Rest 10-20 s (range 3-30 s) → +2-5 reps, ~+10-50% hyper-intense volume; after 8 reps and 15 s ~4 more, on a 3-5 set barely one; start with 1-2 rest-pause sets, on the last set.
scope: Introduce on isolations first, then upper-body compounds, only later lower-body compounds; advanced lifters especially.
status: changed — 2020-21 skeptical, ranked last ("leaks tonnage", "three sets in disguise"); 2023-25 his favourite technique, preferred over drop sets.

title: Drop sets and forced reps: occasional at most
statement: Drop sets on every set are pump-chasing junk; use them only to reach target reps once rest-pause fails. Forced reps, forced negatives and beyond-failure work are an extra set in disguise with a poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio.
numbers: Drop 5-10 lb on cable triceps extensions after failing at 10 of 15; beyond-failure work max 1 set per muscle per day (C tier); drop sets never on strength or main lifts.
scope: Accessories; forced negatives once called "amazing" for biceps (2020).

title: Lengthened partials: may work, not his tool
statement: Lengthened partials may work and many intermediates report gains, but he finds them clunky and hard to standardise and gets more from rest-pause.

title: AMRAPs out of loaded bodybuilding work
statement: AMRAPs don't belong on top sets, strength work or loaded accessories, where the weight should dictate a rep range; keep them for finishers and unweighted calisthenics.
numbers: An AMRAP top set reaching 14 reps is in an irrelevant window; bodyweight pull-ups AMRAP 3-4 sets 1x/wk (2023).
status: changed — 2020 he liked AMRAP pull-ups; 2021 finishers and calisthenics only; 2024 drop AMRAPs from bodybuilding programs.

title: Burnouts and widowmakers are occasional tools
statement: Burnouts and widowmaker squats are occasional high-effort tools, not regular programming.
numbers: Burnout: 20RM to failure, rest 2 min, failure, 1 min, failure, 30 s, failure. Widowmaker: 10RM squat for 20 reps without racking, about once a month, then time to flush fatigue.

title: Slow-tempo work kills intensity
statement: Long-tempo sets are boring, kill focus and intensity, and make fatigue hard to track.
numbers: E.g. 15 reps with 6-s negatives; 10 lb slow laterals without overload or failure.

title: HIT and Mentzer: right on intensity, too far on volume
statement: He sees himself as doing high intensity across many sets; one set to failure every 6-8 days is too little for naturals. Mentzer was right to focus on intensity but went too far.
status: changed — 2020 he called HIT a cult and its advocates "lazy"; 2022-24 he keeps Mentzer's hard-set idea and only rejects the minimal volume.

title: Train with focus, save the hype
statement: No phone, chatting or dates in the gym; think about the next set between sets. Save loud music for top sets so you don't desensitize.
numbers: ~90-95% of sessions with podcasts, classical music or silence.
scope: All trainees; he PRs whenever he trains with his gym buddy.

title: Athletes and fighters: stimulate, don't annihilate
statement: For athletes and fighters, lifting stays sub-maximal and never grinds; all-out effort belongs in competition.
numbers: ~70-80% of capacity with 1-2 RIR.

title: What junk volume is
statement: Junk volume is work outside a relevant intensity window: unchallenging loads, pump chasing, and sets ended by cardio or pump rather than muscular failure.
numbers: Typical case: a 30-rep weight stopped at ~20 by pump; BFR or pump drop sets; 25-rep machine sets.
check: Is the program free of sets that end from burn, pump or breathlessness rather than muscle failure?

title: Junk is relative and mainly hurts when it replaces hard sets
statement: Junk volume depends on your muscular endurance and is mainly a problem when it replaces hard sets or takes time from other muscles; calling every set after a top set junk is Mentzer logic.
numbers: A second set costs about 3-4 minutes.
status: changed — 2021 he called the junk-volume concept "overblown"; 2022-24 he applies the label widely and asks for the "bare effective minimum".

title: Typical junk schemes, including 10x10
statement: 10x10/GVT, 5x10 and 5x20 schemes, 25 chest sets, 13+ biceps sets in a session, 10x20 cable work and many sets of light laterals are typical junk. 10x10 is a band-aid: if you can repeat 10 reps for 10 sets the load is uninteresting.
numbers: On 25 chest sets 60-70% of reps do nothing; on a ~300-rep push day 65-75% is junk; true GVT forces ~55-60% 1RM instead of 70-75%; 3 sets in a relevant window may beat it.

title: Most programs are too greedy
statement: He trims most reviewed programs and says most bodybuilders could cut a fifth to a third of their training for the same results.
numbers: Typical cut 20-30% (sometimes 40-80%); arm programs of 21-30 sets cut by 80%; a chest+biceps day for naturals could lose 45%.

title: Do the least volume that keeps you progressing
statement: Do as little as needed for as much growth as possible: the minimal sets that keep you progressing and injury-free, leaving room to add later. Volume "only serves the purpose of progression".
numbers: By 2024 he places himself "closer to HIT than to 18-20 sets" per muscle.
status: changed — 2020-22 maximalist ("more work always gives more" if you recover, sit at the brink of overtraining, 2-3 h sessions); from 2021 minimal-effective, and by 2024 low on the volume spectrum.
check: Is each muscle's weekly volume the lowest that still produces progress?

title: Both extremes fail: one set and 10x10
statement: HIT's single set is too little for naturals and GVT/10x10 too much; naturals grow in the middle. Multiple hard sets compound reps and give room to modulate effort.
numbers: One set of 17 can't beat 13+10+10+10; 3-4 sets at 240 lb beat 1 at 250; 2024: HIT still beats GVT because it leaves room to add.

title: Minimalism is a tool, not an ideology
statement: Minimal programs fit strength, athletes, beginners and busy people, but tend to build unbalanced physiques for bodybuilders; at an advanced level the maximalist's last ~20% decides things.
numbers: Cuts hurt maximalists more in absolute tonnage (50,000 → 25,000 vs 10,000 → 5,000).
status: contradicted — in 2024 he calls maximalist whole-body isolation the best, yet places himself closer to HIT and says most could cut 20-30%.

title: Too little vs too much: err slightly high
statement: Constantly doing too little gives plateaus and too much gives injury or regression; when guessing, err slightly high, but add conservatively.
status: changed — 2020 "too much is worse than too little"; 2022 too many sets cost at worst some junk volume, so err high.

title: People respond differently to volume and intensity
statement: Some respond more to volume and others to intensity; a muscle that won't grow may need more volume, and someone who can't recover needs less volume and more intensity.
scope: Individual tuning; he saw himself as a volume responder in 2020-22.

title: Train between medium and maximum recoverable volume
statement: Maximum recoverable volume (MRV) is the most work you can recover and grow from; aim between medium and maximum. MRV is individual, found by experiment and only diagnosable after the fact, and it rises with training age.
numbers: ~25% above minimum without passing the max is fine; most people don't overshoot.

title: Signs of too much volume
statement: Lingering soreness or failing to repeat performance session to session signals too much volume; at high weekly sets with slow strength gains, try less volume and more intensity.
numbers: 15-20 weekly sets with slow strength gains → try less.

title: Manual laborers need less gym volume
statement: Office workers can aim at their MRV; manual laborers should stay lower with high intensity and low frequency, and athletes must count the volume from their sport.
numbers: 2 heavy sets of a compound instead of 4-8.

title: A weekly set count means little on its own
statement: Arbitrary weekly numbers ignore frequency, rep range and distribution; the optimal count is whatever produces growth, and ±1-2 sets don't matter. Different body parts naturally take different counts.
numbers: The 10-20 guideline is "mathematically sound but not a hard rule".

title: If you need a number: 8-14 hard sets a week
statement: As a rough answer, 8-14 weekly sets per muscle; at 3x/week and high intensity, 9-15 hard sets is enough to keep growing.
numbers: 8-14 (rough math ~7-14: about 4 sessions per 8 days x 2-4 sets, 2022); 9-15 at 3x/wk (2023).
scope: Intermediate and advanced naturals; back is an exception (VOL-45).
check: Do most muscles get roughly 8-14 hard sets a week?

title: Weekly sets by training level
statement: Novices need few weekly sets and build up; intermediates build toward a cap of about 12.
numbers: Novice 3-6/wk (3 once or twice a week, never 6 at once); intermediate 6-12, cap 12, +2 at a time; 2020: 3 → 9 → 12 hard sets by level.

title: Almost no one needs 16-20 weekly sets
statement: 16-20 weekly sets per muscle is more than almost anyone needs and is impractical to schedule.
numbers: 20 sets/wk would mean 5 sessions x 4 sets or 2 x 10; most lifters do 12-20, about 10 can work for intermediates; an advanced natural on ~4 hard sets/wk may only maintain.
status: contradicted — 2023 back caps reach 20-28 and his own 2023 week had 20 back and 18 shoulder sets; partly explained by the back's tolerance.

title: Two to four sets per exercise, usually three
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: Most exercises get 2-4 sets ("rule of three"); fewer for advanced lifters on taxing lifts, with a 4th set only as icing.
numbers: 2020: accessories almost always 4 (2 too few, 5 too many). 2023: 2-4, usually 3. 2024: 3 for novice/intermediate, 2 for advanced. 2025: 2 per taxing lift if you progress. A 5th-7th set means the load wasn't challenging (2021).
status: changed — 2020 four sets as default; 2023-25 three, then two for advanced lifters.
check: Do most exercises use 2-4 working sets?

title: Heavy low-rep work: one to three sets
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: Heavy strength work gets 1-3 sets, never 5 or 10; one heavy set leaves room for more accessory volume, three means easier accessories.
numbers: 1-3 sets (2020); low-rep compounds 2-3, never more (2024).
scope: Strength work on compounds; see ch. 7.

title: Two to four sets per muscle per session
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: 2-4 sets per muscle per session is the most productive range and is used in all his programs; 6+ sets in one session forces lower frequency.
numbers: 2022: two sets per body part per day is plenty; 2024: 4-6 hard sets per muscle per session already counts as high volume.
check: Does each muscle get about 2-4 hard sets per session rather than 6+ on one day?

title: At most two exercises per muscle per day
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: Use at most two exercises per body part per day; a third variation is excess fatigue.
numbers: 1 for novices, 2 normally, 3 for some advanced; 3+3 sets of two compounds is plenty; after pull-ups and one pulldown the lats are done.
check: Does every muscle get at most two exercises per session?

title: More sets per session means less intensity per set
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: Packing a muscle's sets into one session costs both frequency and per-set intensity; low per-session sets suit high frequency.
numbers: 8-12 sets for a body part in one session costs frequency and intensity; 2+2 sets of two similar exercises avoid the intensity loss of 4 straight sets.

title: Session set totals by split (2024)
section: Sets per exercise and per session
statement: Total sets per session shrink as training days increase.
numbers: 4 days/wk ≈ 20 sets per session; 5 days ≈ 14-15 (cut 15-20%); upper/lower: upper 18-24, lower 16-20; his commercial-gym days ≈ 24 sets in under 2 h, 30-34 is a heavy day.

title: Add volume only on a stall, two sets at a time
statement: Add volume only when load, reps and tonnage stall, in small steps; past a point progress should come from intensity rather than more sets.
numbers: About +2 sets per body part (2-4 max) per adjustment.
check: Are sets added only after progress stalls, and only about two at a time?

title: Never jump volume
statement: Volume spikes bring no results, sickness or overuse injury, and people then wrongly blame volume.
numbers: You can't jump from 9 to 16 sets; don't double volume on becoming intermediate.

title: Introducing a new exercise
statement: Start a new exercise at low volume and build up, trimming other work to make room; or use several sets with very light weight.
numbers: 1-2 sets (~50% of the main lift's volume), trim others to 2, then +1 set every week or two up to 4; adding 4 sets of a brand-new exercise exhausts you.

title: Bringing in a new small muscle
statement: Start direct work for a newly trained small muscle at 2-3 weekly sets and build.
numbers: Biceps 3 → 4 → 6; neck 3 → 6 → 9 → 10-12; abs 2-3; small muscles 3 → 6; weak arms 3 sets then 7-8.
scope: Muscles not trained directly before; see also FRQ-27.

title: Add conservatively, cut liberally
statement: Programming is subtraction as well as addition: be conservative when adding and liberal when removing. "If you can shrink a day, always shrink it."
numbers: If you still progress at 12 sets, drop from 15.

title: Cut sets, not reps; cut strength sets first
statement: To reduce fatigue, cut sets rather than reps, and cut strength-work sets (to 1-3) before lowering back-off intensity.
numbers: Strength work is a small share of tonnage, so cutting it barely matters.

title: Move volume from dominant muscles to weak points
statement: Budget weekly volume: take some from a dominant muscle and spend it on weak points or recovery; dominant parts won't shrink.
numbers: Take 30-40% from a dominant muscle; cutting 20% of dominant-leg volume "makes no difference" (2024).
scope: Intermediate and advanced; e.g. cut leg volume to let the upper body catch up.

title: Maintenance takes about half the volume
statement: Keep intensity and roughly halve the volume to maintain a muscle that has reached your goal; taper it down gradually.
numbers: Taper 8 → 6 → 4 sets/wk; legs: squat 3x5 @2 RIR + RDL 3x12 every 10 days, or 3x6-8 squats. He maintains biceps with intensity alone.
scope: Muscles at goal size; legs need more maintenance tonnage than biceps.

title: Don't cut volume pre-emptively for age or a cut
statement: Lowering volume and intensity in advance because of age causes the muscle loss people then blame on age. During a cut, stay at the edge of the intensity you can handle rather than dropping to ~60%.
scope: Older lifters, dieting lifters; see ch. 11.

title: Work capacity is built gradually
statement: Work capacity is what lets you do the volume that drives growth; it is built and lost gradually, and more muscle raises it.
numbers: Building capacity for 2 h of heavy work may take 3-4 years.

title: "Intermediate syndrome": use a bridge program
statement: Jumping from a low-volume novice program to a high-volume one fails; use a bridge program, because an advanced program "must be earned".
numbers: Intermediates with poor capacity drop the last line of each day.

title: Advanced lifters pack more tonnage into the same time
statement: Advanced lifters need more tonnage but get no more gym time, so they raise density with supersets; eventually the only way to add volume is longer sessions.

title: Strength work is ~20%, the rest makes you grow
statement: Strength work opens the session and gives the highest-quality tonnage but is a minority; the variations and accessories that follow provide most of the growth stimulus.
numbers: ~20% strength vs ~80% variations and accessories; typical 2020 day: 1-3 strength sets + 6-8 back-off/variation/accessory sets.

title: Most tonnage at moderate reps; offset heavy and volume work
statement: The bulk of tonnage sits at 4-12 reps, and "volume work" means above 6 reps. When the strength set is heaviest, the following volume work should be lightest, offsetting tonnage swings with variations.
numbers: 4x6-10 or 4x8-12 beats 4x5; evolving sets swing tonnage hugely (1x4 vs 8-6-4).

title: Count indirect volume
statement: Compounds spread tonnage across several muscles, so count it: bench is triceps and front-delt volume, and a 300 lb squat isn't 300 lb of quad tonnage. Shared structures such as the lower back cap how much you can send through them.
numbers: Send part of back volume through legless moves (~300/700 of 1000 lb).

title: Isolation vs compound share
statement: He has given both an isolation-heavy and a compound-heavy ratio.
numbers: About 2:1 isolation:compound per muscle (2023); compounds should be the program's bulk (2024).
status: contradicted — 2023 isolation 2:1 vs 2024 compounds as the bulk.

title: Upper back is a volume black hole
statement: The upper back takes huge volume and recovers fast, so it gets the most sets, as long as the lower back isn't taxed; most people undertrain it.
numbers: Weekly caps rise by stage: 12 → 20 → 12-24 → 14-28 (covers 99.9% of lifters); arms would not tolerate 20. Naturals start with 1-2 pulls per session (one vertical, one horizontal) at ~4 sets each.

title: Legs respond to minimal, hard volume
statement: Legs grow from intensity and progression, not "a million sets": one quad movement plus one hinge or knee-flexion movement at about 3 hard sets each.
numbers: 2022: 6-7 heavy knee-flexion sets/wk; 2023: ~9 quad + 8 posterior hard sets/wk is enough, 18-24 total at 3x/wk is plenty; 2024: 6 quad + 6 posterior sets/wk for himself.
status: changed — 2020 at least 11-12 heavy squat sets per squat day plus giant-set finishers; 2022-24 minimal hard sets.

title: Chest grows on modest volume, but presses need enough
statement: Chest grows on modest weekly volume and about three exercises is the session limit; still, very low pressing volume (3x5 bench) is too little.
numbers: ~6-8 sets/wk; he does 8-12/wk (2023) then 6/wk (2024); four horizontal presses in a session exceed most people's weekly need; 3x5 bench (15 reps) too little, ≥60 working bench reps wanted (2020).
scope: All trainees; add push-ups or dips, which are easier to recover from.

title: Vertical presses and shoulders tolerate more
statement: Vertical pressing tolerates up to double the horizontal press sets; shoulders get 1-2 isolations plus 1-2 vertical presses per day, and more after a press plus one isolation is junk.
numbers: Shoulders 12-20 sets/wk total, 6-12 isolation; vertical press 6-8/wk, up to 12-16 if you recover fast; he runs 9-12 shoulder sets vs 6 chest (2024).

title: Arms are main lifts, not accessories
statement: Treat arms as main lifts with 2-4 hard sets per muscle per session; bro-style 20 sets/wk per arm muscle is junk. If ~12 weekly arm sets don't grow arms, check progression first, then change exercises or even lower volume.
numbers: ~9 biceps + 9 triceps sets/wk himself (2024); 2 hard biceps sets/wk won't grow trained arms.

title: Small muscles: less per session, recover fast
statement: Small muscles take fewer sets per session but recover quickly; feed them through varied angles, frequency and supersets.
numbers: See the small-muscle reference table at the end of this part.
scope: Rear delts, traps, forearms, neck, abs, calves.

title: Back-off sets: two or three after the work sets
statement: After 1-3 strength sets, usually 2-3 back-off sets of the same pattern with a modest drop. After a 3x3, a heavy 3x8-12 back-off on the same lift is too much, so use a variation.
numbers: 2-3 (sometimes 3-4) back-offs, never 10; after 275 lb work sets go to ~245, not 185 (2024).
status: changed — 2020 back-offs are "a must… free tonnage"; 2023 B tier, better as a variation; 2024 he skips them on dips and non-priority squats.

title: Evolving sets: keep the span narrow
statement: When the number of sets evolves, keep the span to 2-4 sets; it is an advanced tool because swinging sets changes volume far more than swinging reps.
numbers: 2-4 sets (2-5 or 2-6 max, never 1-8); 3-6 bench sets "is already a big range".

title: Match total reps when changing schemes
statement: When swapping set/rep schemes keep total reps similar, or know why you are changing volume.
numbers: 5x5 = 25 ≈ 3x8; 4x4 = 16 ≈ 3x5; replace 5x5 with 5x3-6 or 4x4-7.

title: Finishers and pyramids drift into junk
statement: Pyramids and drop-set finishers drift toward junk; weight progression builds quality tonnage. A finisher only makes sense after real work has used up the muscle.
numbers: Max 2-3 finishers per session (2021); drop sets C tier, finishers D tier (2023).
status: changed — 2021 finishers are fine and build work capacity; 2023 "textbook junk volume" or active recovery at best.

title: Nucleus overload: a light complement, later rated minor
statement: Nucleus overload (NO) is frequent, high-volume, very light work kept easy enough to repeat, used to complement strength work for the same muscle, never to replace it. It is the one exception to intensity windows.
numbers: ~15-30% intensity, 4-25 reps (he corrected an earlier 40-60), ≥5 reps left; months (4-5) to show; spread through other days as supersets, never on the day the muscle gets hard sets; traps NO 2-4x/wk.
status: changed — 2020-22 an advocated accessory method for most body parts; 2023 D tier, ~1-2% of results. Also contradicted on whether NO reaches failure.

title: Train until the day's stimulus is done, then leave
statement: There is no fixed time cap: train as long as the day's stimulus takes, don't drag sessions into junk, and cram the necessary work into the least time.
numbers: 2021: 1h15 target, 10 saved minutes ≈ 2 extra quality sets; a 25-35 min session is fine if you progress; 2024: 45-60 min of hard sets exhausts most people.
status: changed — 2020 advanced lifters must lengthen sessions and naturals "cannot just train an hour a day"; 2021 as short as possible; 2024 don't train to a clock.

title: Normal sessions run 60-90 minutes
statement: About 60-90 min is a normal session and 90 min is "pushing it"; if you're done after 60 min of a planned 90, cut the day. Saying training past 1.5 h is pointless is a myth.
numbers: A program that takes 2 h on paper takes ~30 min more in the gym; giant sets compress sessions to 60-70 min; novices: 3 x 1 h beats 2 x 2 h; ~80% of results come from the first 60-70% of a program (2022).

title: His own session lengths
statement: His own sessions went from multi-hour days toward fewer sets per session.
numbers: 2020: 2-3 h, 6 days/wk (12-15 h/wk, 3 h arm days); 2023: ~2 h, 6 days (1.5-2 h excluding warm-up); 2024: commercial-gym days ≈ 24 sets in under 2 h.
status: changed — longer sessions in 2020, fewer sets by 2024.

title: Frequency is the pillar naturals ignore most
statement: Frequency is one of the three pillars with volume and intensity and the most ignored, so for naturals it matters most; when sets happen comes before how many.
numbers: Frequency rated S tier (2023).
scope: Naturals; a coach who says "do 12 sets whenever" doesn't understand programming.

title: Spread weekly sets over several sessions
statement: The same weekly sets give better results spread out: lumping them forces lighter loads and adds cardio limits and junk, while spreading allows heavier loads, more tonnage and better recovery. Frequency exists to fit volume in.
numbers: 3x3 sets beat 9 in one session; 5+5+5 beats 15 on Monday; 4 back sets 3x/wk beat 10 once; 12 back sets in one day after deadlifts is wasted; 15 sets in one day might need ~100 h of recovery.
scope: All trainees beyond novice; front-loading early in the week is fine unless it turns into junk.

title: Once a week is suboptimal unless you are coasting
statement: Training a muscle once a week is always suboptimal for a natural unless you are deliberately coasting on it; it leaves the muscle idle most of the week and brings soreness and poor work capacity.
numbers: Once-a-week all-out = 4 sessions a month, and a lifter training 4x/week beats you on tonnage.
scope: Naturals. Exceptions he admits: a friend's legs growing on 1x/week (2023) and legs 1x/week while fixing an upper-body weakness (2024).
check: Is every muscle you want to grow trained at least twice a week?

title: Frequency is a recovery schedule
statement: There is no universally optimal frequency, only one that matches the work done to its recovery time; retrain a muscle once it is ready, because leaving it dormant leads to stagnation.
numbers: No hard 72 h rule; 24 or 48 h works if volume and intensity are managed.
scope: All trainees; paper math fails because recovery fluctuates.

title: Choose frequency first, then template and sets per day
statement: Pick frequency first; templates mostly dictate frequency and grouping, and per-session numbers must scale to the number of days.
numbers: A rep range that works on a 6-day PPL fails on a 3-day one.

title: Higher frequency, less per session
statement: The more often you train a muscle, the less volume (and the shorter the session) each time; low frequency needs high volume and intensity per session.
numbers: 48 h recovery pairs with 2-4 sets per muscle per session, 72 h with 4-8; 2-3 chest sets per session are plenty at 2-3x/week.

title: Take only part of the recovery "pot" each session
statement: Recovery is a fixed-size tub: fill it with quality tonnage as often as possible, taking only part of it per session; training once a week doesn't make the tub bigger.
numbers: Take ~30-40% per session; if legs recover in 2 days, train them again after 2 days.

title: Every pattern weekly, compounds 2-3x a week
statement: Technique and strength depend on frequency: every movement pattern should return at least once a week, and compounds should be practised 2-3x a week. Once a lift is automatic, heavy-work frequency can drop.
numbers: A lift done every 15-30 days is relearned each time; a pattern left for a month is "catastrophic".

title: Soreness means frequency is too low
statement: Soreness signals too little frequency, not growth; with proper frequency it disappears.
numbers: Still sore after 6 months on the same program = frequency too low; he hadn't been sore in 2 years while progressing (2021).
scope: All trainees beyond the first months.

title: Never sacrifice intensity for frequency
statement: Frequency should not cost per-set intensity; trading frequency for intensity is fine, and stronger lifters need longer recovery windows.
numbers: 2021-22 examples: 3x/wk at 100% may do better as 5x at 85%; calves trained lightly 40 times a year beat 15 hard sessions; squatting 2x/wk for 5 years beats 5x/wk for 1 year.
scope: All trainees; especially strong, advanced lifters.
status: changed — 2021-22 frequency and consistency beat intensity bursts; 2023 stronger lifters need longer windows; 2024 "never sacrifice intensity for frequency", and training less often let him train harder with unchanged gains.

title: Frequency has limits as a progression tool
statement: Frequency is capped by the days in a week, so it can't drive progress through the intermediate and advanced stages; raising frequency on a stalled isolation keeps the muscle fatigued. Hitting a muscle more than 2-3x/week is earned.
numbers: Only isolations are "spammable" at 2-4x/week; compounds near failure are not.

title: Small muscles more often, big muscles harder with more rest
statement: Small muscles burn out fast in a session but recover fast, so train them more often with less per session; the opposite belief is "backwards".
numbers: Every 2 days is a good default even for small muscles.

title: Frequency also exists inside the session
statement: Intra-session frequency (how sets follow each other, rest and session length) matters too; alternating posterior-chain and quad work lets muscles recover between sets and allows more tonnage.

title: At least ~48 hours between hard sessions for a muscle
section: Spacing between sessions for the same muscle
statement: ~48 h is the default and minimum between hard sessions for the same muscle; don't hit a muscle hard two days in a row.
numbers: 48 h ("a bare minimum", 2024); benching two days in a row is bad even with different variations.
scope: All trainees; light hits are treated separately (FRQ-15).
