status: contradicted — he also calls two days in a row and 90/80/70% Mon-Wed valid (2020, 2022); likely hard vs light hits, not always stated.
check: Are hard sessions for the same muscle at least 48 h apart?

title: Light back-to-back hits are allowed
section: Spacing between sessions for the same muscle
statement: Full recovery matters for peak performance, not for hypertrophy, so lighter hits on consecutive days are fine.
numbers: A light blood-flow movement 24 h after a heavy day (advanced); 90/80/70% Mon-Wed then rest until Saturday; a few pull-ups daily.

title: Match the recovery interval to the template
section: Spacing between sessions for the same muscle
statement: Each template implies a recovery interval for each muscle.
numbers: 24 h = light daily full body; 48 h = upper/lower; 72 h = PPL; full body 3x/wk gives 48-72 h; arms 48-72 h, waiting longer gains nothing.

title: Late view: longer gaps for strong lifters
section: Spacing between sessions for the same muscle
statement: By late 2024 he spaces sessions further apart.
numbers: Upper days 72-90 h apart (2-3 days); legs 72-96 h.
status: changed — earlier default was every ~48 h for upper and legs (FRQ-14, FRQ-19).

title: The last hard session sets the next one
section: Spacing between sessions for the same muscle
statement: Check whether the muscle is back to baseline before retraining it; if a moderate session leaves days of unused rest, move the next one earlier, and if you can't match volume next time, you needed more rest.
numbers: After a heavy Monday squat, do Wednesday's quad accessories without pushing them.

title: Legs about every 48 hours, later twice a week
statement: Legs grow from volume spread out, not a weekly crushing day: a heavy knee flexion or hip hinge about every 2 days, with two leg days a week as the minimum beyond novices.
numbers: ~3x/wk with 3-4 sets for quads or hamstrings per session (2024-05); 2x/wk with 72-96 h between sessions (2024-12), because 3x becomes unrecoverable at ~400s squat / ~500s RDL.
scope: Naturals beyond novice; the lower back is usually what stops people training legs that often.
status: changed — 2020-2024-05 every 48 h / 3x a week; 2024-12 2x a week for strong advanced lifters.
check: Are legs trained at least twice a week?

title: Upper body about three times a week
statement: Upper-body muscles are numerous, less taxing and recover fast, so train them about every 2 days; chest does better 2-3x a week with fewer, more precise sets than on one chest day.
numbers: Upper ~3x/wk; chest 2-3x/wk with 2-3 sets per session; 2024: forearms 3-4x, biceps and chest 2-3x weekly.

title: Horizontal press at least twice, bench under three times
statement: Bench once a week doesn't progress the bench, but raw bench 3+ times a week brings shoulder overuse; press horizontally at least twice and use push-ups, flies or close-grip for extra frequency.
numbers: ≥2x/wk horizontal pressing; bench <3x/wk; 3x/wk as in novice programs is too much; at 5x/wk use shoulder-sparing variations.

title: Vertical pressing about twice a week
statement: Vertical pressing ~2x a week is needed for big shoulders; 3x OHP is overcorrection and once a week at 5x5 is too little. Do both a vertical and a horizontal press on each press day.
numbers: 2x/wk; 2023: the vertical pattern 2-3x/wk, not the same lift.

title: Squat twice a week long term
statement: Once a week is not enough, 2x a week is the long-term sweet spot and 3x is hard to sustain; daily squatting works but builds strength more than size.
numbers: 2x/wk; novices 1-2x; heavy squats 4x/wk was more than he could handle.

title: Deadlift rarely, the hinge pattern more often
statement: The conventional deadlift needs the least frequency of the big lifts (low frequency, high intensity, moderate volume), while the hinge pattern can return every 2-3 days with variations.
numbers: Deadlift every 7-10 days, 1x4-6 is excellent; 2024: max 1-2x/wk after 2+ years of pushing it. Hinge pattern every 2-3 days; he hinged heavy every 2 days (2022).
scope: All trainees; he claims pulling heavy several times a week "just means you're still weak".
status: contradicted — 2020 "only a few times a month" alongside heavy deadlifts 2x/week, and heavy hinging every 2 days in 2022; partly deadlift vs hinge variations.

title: Upper back: most frequency-tolerant, spread over days
statement: The upper back tolerates training nearly every day with varied angles and intensities; train back at least 3x a week, add back movements to the split "as Lego blocks", and never put all back volume on one day.
numbers: ≥3x/wk; per session ≤3 exercises / ~10 sets; e.g. 6 back exercises as 2/2/2 over Mon/Wed/Sat; ~6 sets per day instead of 30 once; no horizontal pull on consecutive days.
status: contradicted — 2022/2024 back can be trained every day if parts rotate; 2023 "never train back every day".
check: Is back work spread over at least three days with no more than ~3 back exercises in any one session?

title: Pull-ups can be done very often
statement: Pull-ups are low-impact and the upper back recovers fast, so they can be done daily, even to failure; grease-the-groove works for them as an exception.
numbers: His 2020 daily pull-ups: 100-120 reps on high days, 30-40 on low days; 40-60 weighted daily (2021). 2023: 1-2x/wk with grip rotation is enough to progress; 2024: calisthenics lifters ≥2x/wk.
status: changed — 2020-21 daily; 2023-24 1-2x a week is enough.

title: Bring in a neglected muscle by frequency first
statement: For a neglected or small muscle, raise frequency (1x → 2x → 3x a week) before adding sets per session.
numbers: Rear delts: 1x3 sets → 2x3 → 2x4 → 3x4 per week; early on 3 sets can leave them sore for 3 days.

title: Arms: biceps on every upper day
statement: Arm intensity is fixed at failure and per-session volume is limited, so arm growth comes from frequency; put biceps work on every upper day, and isolations need more frequency than the compounds they accompany.
numbers: Advanced: biceps and triceps every 2 days or more, with only 6-15 weekly sets.

title: Bodyweight work often, spread through other days
statement: Bodyweight and calisthenics movements, abs and nucleus-overload work are cheap to recover from, so do them often and spread them through other days instead of giving them a day of their own.
numbers: Bodyweight movements 4-5x/wk; a dedicated ab day is a "monumental waste".

title: Four days a week is the sustainable sweet spot
statement: 4 training days a week is his favourite and sustainable for life; 3 is fine, and intermediates need at least 3.
numbers: 4 ideal (4-5 range, 2020); 3 or 6 days are "sub-extreme" (2021); 3 days "perfectly fine" (2024).

title: Advanced means more sessions
statement: Advancing means more sessions per year, not just more sets.
numbers: Intermediate 3 sessions/wk (12/month, 140-150/yr); advanced every other day (~4/wk, 15/month, ~180/yr), about 30 extra sessions a year.
scope: Intermediate → advanced; a regular extra rest day puts you back on the intermediate program.

title: Add days by spreading existing work
statement: Start with 3-4 days and expand; add a day by spreading existing tonnage, not by piling on more, and never jump from 3 to 6 days at the same per-day volume.

title: Long days → add a day; thin days → compress
statement: If sessions run too long, add a day; if days are thin or redundant, compress them.
numbers: Taking 10-15% from each of 3 overloaded days can create a 4th shorter day; 5 → 4 or 3 when compressing.

title: Who six days a week suits
statement: Six days suits fast-recovering novices, advanced lifters who need frequency to accumulate volume, and rare volume responders with poor leverages.
numbers: White-collar workers do well on 4-6 days; 6 days on top of MMA taxes recovery.

title: Busy lifters: two or three full-body days
statement: Busy or sleep-deprived lifters don't need high frequency: 2-3 full-body days, or upper/lower twice with isolation in short gaps. A physique built on 5 days a week can be maintained on 2.
numbers: 30 min = 4-5 hard sets; 2 h/week is already a lot; 10-15 min gaps for isolation; skip training on 16-hour shift days.

title: Daily training is possible but not advised
statement: Training every day works if volume and intensity are reduced and the split never builds enough fatigue to need a day off, but he doesn't advise it for others; for depressed lifters, daily training for structure can come before gains.

title: The bro split is the worst template for naturals
statement: One muscle per day once a week gives too little frequency and too much per-session volume, which fills sessions with junk; the fix is to hit each muscle twice a week.
numbers: 2024 example: six back exercises for 25 sets, where 20% of the work gives ~95% of the gains.
scope: Naturals. In his opinion enhanced lifters can recover from it, and would still grow more with more frequency.
check: Does the split avoid giving any muscle a single big session per week?

title: The gentleman split is his favourite
statement: His preferred template is an upper/lower skeleton whose days are built around synergistic muscle groups and a main compound, with flexible boundaries.
numbers: 4-5 days: 2 upper, 2 lower, optional arm day.
status: changed — terminology: in 2020 he praised a well-built "body-part split" as the best natural template; from 2021 that label means one-muscle-per-day splits and he condemns it, while the same idea lives on as the gentleman split.

title: Upper/lower is the most convenient skeleton
statement: Upper/lower saves warm-up time, groups synergistic muscles and manages fatigue well, so it is the base for most templates; its weakness is poor upper-back frequency, and minimal upper/lower days waste it.
scope: All trainees; don't get stuck in a plain 2-upper/2-lower.

title: Run PPL as pull-push-legs
statement: Never run push-pull-legs: pull day's hinges and rows fatigue the legs and lower back right before squats. Use pull-push-legs (or legs-push-pull) or put a rest day between pull and legs.
numbers: Pull-push-legs-pull-push-legs keeps pull and leg days as far apart as possible (2023).
check: If the program is a PPL, does the leg day avoid directly following the pull day?

title: PPL is a good split
statement: PPL is a very good split with an unwarranted bad reputation; run it about 6x a week (each muscle 2x) or 3x a week, and for 4-5 days just cut a day.
numbers: PPL-rest-repeat allows more intensity than PPLPPL-rest.
status: changed — 2020 standard PPL was lower-body biased and the worst order (push days should include pulling); 2023-24 a very good split in pull-push-legs order.

title: Full body works best three times a week
statement: Full body is best at 3x a week with ~48 h between sessions; it is the hardest template to program because compounds get crammed and small muscles neglected, so skew it to priorities and rotate variations.
numbers: Mon/Wed/Fri; 2x is fine for busy people but thin for intermediates; 4x is the upper limit; 6x unrecoverable except for novices; never back-to-back days.
status: changed — 2020 "not a big fan"; 2023-24 "full-body splits are good splits" and 3x a week is one of the best templates. Day-count advice also varies (2021: 2x too little, 4 the sweet spot).

title: First self-made program: full body or PPL
statement: For a first self-made program use full body or PPL; body-part-style and gentleman splits need more experience and work capacity.
scope: Beginners writing their own program; see ch. 12.

title: Templates for intermediate and advanced lifters
statement: Intermediates run upper/lower twice plus an arm day; advanced lifters run upper/lower three times over 6 days, rotating variations and taking rest days as needed.
numbers: Intermediate 5 days, 60-80 min sessions via supersets; advanced 6 days; upper back every day except arm day.

title: The template's name matters less than its control
statement: The label of a split matters less than how it controls volume, intensity and frequency; the same principle is good or bad depending on how it is applied.

title: Torso/limbs splits risk imbalance
statement: Torso/limbs splits risk imbalance, because torso work already trains the limbs and people overemphasise the torso.

title: Double sessions are valid but rarely needed
statement: AM/PM double sessions work but are hard to program; make the morning the hard session (legs) and the evening the fun one, and for most people one combined session is fine.
scope: He sees them as justified mainly on leg days.

title: Pair synergistic muscles; no "chest day"
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Group synergistic muscles, such as chest with shoulders and triceps since presses train all three; never give triceps or chest a day of its own.

title: Each day is justified by a compound
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Decide what a day is before designing it: build it around at least one main compound and name it by its main pattern ("bench day", "squat day").

title: Upper back, calves, abs and neck fill any day
section: What goes on the same day
statement: The upper back is synergistic with nothing, so it fills gaps in any day; calves, abs, neck and upper back are the easiest superset fillers.

title: Back belongs with legs more than with biceps
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Back and biceps is a low-synergy pairing; back days should carry posterior-chain and leg work ("a leg day in disguise"), e.g. an RDL or paused squat supersetted with chin-ups.
status: contradicted — 2020 he also said back and biceps "fits naturally", and in 2023 he pairs lats with biceps after weighted chins.

title: Don't mix big upper and big lower compounds
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Squat + bench or bench + deadlift in one session means re-warming up, switching the pump and losing synergy; lower days can take traps, neck, abs and forearms but never big upper muscles.

title: Small upper work fits on lower days
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Forearms, grip, neck, traps, rear delts, biceps and long-head triceps fit on lower days, ideally in squat rest periods; avoid shoulders and lateral/medial triceps there because they need warming up.
scope: All trainees; 2023: rear delts "skyrocket" on lower days; 2024: arms and shoulders on lower days are fine if they don't hurt upper-day pressing.
status: contradicted — 2020 he disliked hammer curls, pushdowns and triceps extensions on lower days because they turn it into a body-part split.

title: Split boundaries are flexible
section: What goes on the same day
statement: You are not a slave to the template: calves on upper days, chin-ups on push day, upper back on lower day are fine; rigid splits are "mostly idiotic", and you don't hit every muscle on a "full body" day just because of the label.

title: Touch every upper group on upper days
section: What goes on the same day
statement: Every upper day should touch each upper muscle group at least lightly; small extra doses on non-dedicated days ("stacking pebbles") add frequency, blood flow and some tonnage.
numbers: At least 3 groups including arm isolation and abs per upper day; e.g. push-ups or close-grip on arm day.

title: Alternate horizontal and vertical emphasis
section: What goes on the same day
statement: On two or more upper days, give each a horizontal or vertical focus and alternate which pattern opens mirror days, so each pattern gets priority every week.
numbers: Weak chest and shoulders on 3 upper days/wk: two push days, one horizontal, one vertical.

title: Separate heavy squats and heavy deadlifts
statement: Never do heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day or on consecutive days; if they share a day, make one heavy and the other a lighter variation in a higher rep range, squat first.
numbers: E.g. squat + stiff-leg deadlift, or deadlift + pause squat; heavy hinge on the back day, heavy knee flexion on leg day (2021).
check: Are heavy squats and heavy deadlifts kept off the same day and off consecutive days?

title: One heavy lower pattern opens each lower day
statement: Each lower day opens with one heavy knee flexion or hip hinge; the next heavy-ish movement is the other pattern, and which one leads alternates between days.
numbers: Opener at RIR 0-1; with two squat days, make one quad-focused and one hamstring-focused.

title: Alternate taxing and easy days
statement: Don't stack demanding days: alternate upper and lower and follow a long or taxing day with a lighter one; too many easy days in a row wastes time.
numbers: Push A and push B should not run back to back.

title: Heaviest lower day right before the rest day
statement: Start the week with an upper day and put the heaviest lower or highest-tonnage day right before the rest day or weekend, so rest follows the sessions that drain the most.
numbers: In a 4-day upper/lower, the second lower day goes before the weekend; a 5-on/2-off split peaks in fatigue on Friday.

title: Spread rest days out
statement: Don't train 4-5 days in a row and then take a block off; spread sessions and rest days.
numbers: 2 on/1 off or 2 on/2 off beats packing; 5 sessions over a 7-8 day window; on 3 days a week alternate training and rest; four rest days a week starts to be too many.

title: Write the split as a rotation, not a week
statement: The week is a human invention: write the split as a rotation of days and let rest days float with recovery.
numbers: 8-day cycles; a 4-day program over an 8-day window (on/off) is fine; 1-2 rest days per week depending on fatigue.

title: Place squat days with care
statement: Squat after a rest day or an arms/accessory day, not the day after heavy bench, trap or upper-back work (pre-fatigued shoulder girdle) or heavy lower-back work; you can deadlift after almost any day except squats or deadlifts.
numbers: He deadlifts two days after squatting.

title: Manage mental fatigue across the week
statement: Heavy lower compounds are the most mentally draining, so separate them and keep the window of mentally taxing work short.

title: Schedule around physical work
statement: Blue-collar workers should keep weekdays minimal and intense, put most volume on days off and leave recovery before heavy work days; white-collar workers can train 4-6x a week.

title: An arm day is the least taxing day
statement: An arm day is a low-CNS day: a few upper compounds (close-grip bench, dips, rows) then isolation, never a pump-only day or lower-body lifts; it can double as active recovery.
status: contradicted — order: 2021 curls and extensions first while fresh vs 2020/2023 open with a heavy compound.

title: An arm day is earned and optional
statement: Add an arm day only if big arms are a goal and only once legs are trained at least twice a week with plenty of upper-back work; it adds to arm work on other days rather than replacing it.
numbers: Start 1x/wk; two arm days a week is hard to justify.

title: Where the arm day goes
statement: Put the arm day on a weekend or low-energy day, or between two CNS-heavy lower days, not next to upper days whose arm work it would duplicate.
numbers: 2023: a rest day between the torso day and the arm day.
status: contradicted — 2020 he said an arm day "won't take away" and can sit between heavy days; 2021/2023 never next to upper days.

title: Pyramid of priority within a session
statement: Open with the most demanding, most important lift (heavy low-rep strength work while fresh), then lighter compounds, then isolation; if time runs short, cut from the bottom, never the top.
numbers: Cutting the bottom loses only ~10-20% of gains.
scope: All trainees; exception: a priority muscle can go first.
check: Does each session open with its heaviest, most important lift?

title: At most two strength lifts per workout
statement: Use at most two strength lifts per session, and don't put two non-supersetted strength lifts for different parts of one body part back to back.
numbers: Max 2; three is too much; bench then OHP back to back is bad, back squat then front squat is acceptable.

title: Every session holds both intensity and volume
statement: Don't split training into heavy/light days or strength/volume weeks, which give volume without intensity and intensity without volume; open every day with strength work and vary the emphasis on a spectrum.
status: contradicted — he describes gentleman days as heavy/moderate/pump, says full body needs heavy/medium/light days per muscle, and once suggested alternating strength and giant-set weeks.

title: Put skipped work early, as supersets
statement: Work people tend to skip (neck, abs, calves) goes early in the session, supersetted into the main lifts' rest periods, not at the end; it doesn't hurt main-lift performance.

title: Upper days long, lower days short
statement: Lower lifts hit more muscle and move more tonnage per set, so lower days carry fewer exercises; upper days have many small muscles that need isolation and should look about twice as long on paper.
numbers: Lower 3-5 movements (≤2 giant-set lines), upper 6-8 up to 10 (lower ≈ 60-70% of upper); 2022: 4-6 exercises per day with ≥4 low-fatigue isolations; in PPL legs are the shortest, most intense day.

title: Intense days shorter, voluminous days longer
statement: The more intense the day, the shorter it should be; don't pile volume after a heavy deadlift.

title: Mirror days give rotation
statement: A/B mirror days (same emphasis, different lifts, rep ranges or order) reduce boredom and overuse injuries; train the muscle, not the movement. Novices don't need them.
numbers: Hitting a muscle 3x/week only causes overuse injuries if you repeat the same exercise.

title: Keep rotations simple, strength work regular
statement: Keep rotations simple (A/B) and within the same movement pattern, and keep strength work regular rather than rotated; if alternatives don't share a pattern, the missing work must appear elsewhere.
numbers: 15 squat variations means each is practised ~3 times a year.

title: A good program is flexible
statement: If moving or dropping one exercise breaks a program, it is a bad program; followers can cut exercises or volume freely, and the more advanced you are, the more flexibility you need.
numbers: Since 2024 he runs "a template, not a program": upper or lower days filled from a memorised exercise list.

title: Stick with a good program for years
statement: Run a good program as an endless repeating cycle rather than jumping every 6 months; frequent changes produce artificial PRs, and for a bodybuilder all training is hypertrophy training, so "blocks" make little sense.

title: Fighters and athletes: lifting is secondary
statement: For fighters, lifting is minimal and scheduled away from the sport; an upper-dominant split suits them because lower lifts tax the CNS and tendons more.
numbers: Purists 2 sessions/wk (~1.5 h each); hybrids 3-4x/wk with rotated variations; time split ~70% sport / 20% drills / 10% hypertrophy (advanced 60/20/20); upper-dominant e.g. 4 upper, 2 lower.

title: Novices: three full-body days
statement: Novices do well on 3 full-body days with weekends off; frequency hardly matters for beginners, and they need only one heavy squat and one heavy hinge a week.
numbers: Mon/Wed/Fri, ABA/BAB; any 1-3x/wk works.

title: Women are not programmed like men
statement: A woman not seeking upper-body size gains nothing from training it 3x a week; his women's novice program is 3 full-body days emphasising legs and glutes, and even women wanting a bigger upper body shouldn't get an upper-dominant split.

title: Rest about 2-3 minutes, never more than 5
statement: Rest as little as possible while staying performant; more than 5 min is overkill. He doesn't time rests and goes roughly by feel.
numbers: 2020: 3-5 min strength, 1-2 min straight-set accessories, 3-4 min between heavy low-rep evolving sets; 2021: 2-3 min for strength, 1.5-3 up to 5; 2023: "2 or 3 is fine as long as you recover"; 2024: ~3 min by feel or a song.
scope: All trainees; heavy Bulgarian split squats: he sits 3 min.
status: changed — mild drift from 3-5 min for strength sets (2020) to 2-3 min by feel (2021-24).
check: Do straight sets get roughly 2-3 minutes of rest (not under ~90 s, not over ~5 min)?

title: Rest so the muscle returns to baseline
statement: The aim of rest is for the muscle to be back to baseline for the next set; too-short rests wreck performance and turn training into cardio.
numbers: 20 s between curl sets gives a third of the reps; 15 s with a challenging weight isn't enough; 60-90 s improves conditioning but hurts performance; 100 reps is like 10x10 with no rest.
scope: All trainees; rest-pause is the deliberate exception (INT-56).

title: Same-muscle exercises still need full rest
statement: Between two exercises for the same muscle, rest 2-3 min; performance matters for biceps as much as for quads.
numbers: 2-3 min.
scope: All trainees; supersets of different muscles are fine.

title: Low reps get straight sets and long rests
statement: Low-rep sets run as straight sets with long rests; higher-rep sets can use rest-pause and shorter rests.

title: Rest-based tests
statement: Redoing a set after 3 min should give fewer reps; but a big crash means poor work capacity, and a 1RM you can repeat after 10 min wasn't a true max.
numbers: 6 reps falling to 3-4 after 3 min signals poor work capacity (unless technique or context changed).

title: Don't superset the opening strength work
statement: Heavy opening lifts (squat, deadlift, bench, hinges, heavy knee flexion, weighted chins) run as straight sets with full rest to keep focus and energy; at most pair them with small non-bracing work (neck, abs, curls, rear delts).
numbers: 2024: bench and pull-ups standalone, the rest supersetted, ~1h10 session. Overhead press paired with a pull is an exception.
status: contradicted — he also says resting 5 min after bench is wasted and supersets bench (and his bench back-offs) with rows or pull-ups.
check: Are the session's heavy opening lifts done as straight sets with full rest?

title: Never superset two movements for the same muscle
statement: Pairing two lifts for the same muscle is pre-fatigue or a finisher, a different tool, and a last resort otherwise.
numbers: No face pulls with reverse flies, dips with shoulder press, OHP with lateral raises, or two biceps movements back to back.

title: Leg exercises don't chain into each other
statement: Lower-body supersets are harder because leg lifts tax the cardiovascular system; pair leg lifts with static or non-leg moves, and moving straight from one leg exercise to another is "a cardinal sin of hypertrophy". Keep ab work away from heavy bracing lifts.
numbers: Front squats + leg raises or pull-ups, not + deficit deadlifts.
status: contradicted — he has also paired leg press with leg curl and leg extension with calf raises; probably circuits vs paired isolation, a distinction he doesn't make.

title: Superset all accessory and isolation work
statement: Sitting idle between sets of curls, shrugs, laterals, pushdowns or leg extensions wastes time and tonnage; the target muscle needs rest, the rest of the body doesn't. He uses supersets in all programs, even for novices.
numbers: "An arm day without supersets is wasted time"; without supersets an advanced program would take 5 h. He giant-sets ~80% of his training (2020), "100% giant sets" (2023).
check: Is accessory and isolation work supersetted rather than run as straight sets with long rests?

title: Pair unrelated or antagonist muscles
statement: Supersets of non-competing muscles cost little or no performance, only cardiovascular capacity; the loss grows in a long full-body day.
numbers: Curls have no effect on calf raises right after; a long-head triceps exercise after a press costs at most one rep (he tested it).
status: changed — 2020 he recommended long-head triceps work between press back-off sets; 2024 he no longer believes in that pairing.

title: Default pairings: press with pull
statement: Pair a horizontal press with a horizontal pull and a vertical press with a vertical pull; such a superset is part of a day, not its emphasis.
numbers: Other pairings he gives: curls + face pulls; skullcrushers + dips; weighted pull-ups/dips + calves, neck, forearms or shoulders; RDL + chin-ups, shrugs, calves or rear delts; leg raises after each bench set.

title: Near-free volume to fill rests
statement: Rear delts, leg curls, wrist curls, calves, traps, biceps and abs add stimulus with almost no systemic fatigue, so they slot into rest periods; use machine and warm-up downtime too.
numbers: 3x10-15 leg curls at session end at zero systemic cost; reverse curls right after the last squat warm-up.

title: No rest inside a superset, rest after the round
statement: A superset is exercises back to back with no planned rest, then rest before repeating the round; walking between stations is fine.
numbers: Within: 0 rest (up to ~1 min to walk). After a round: 3-4 min (2021-24), 2-4 min (2022), 2-3 min (2021, 2024), ~2 min (2023); 90 s between rounds is valid, he gives more.

title: Giant sets: 4-5 exercises, most intense first
statement: A giant set is 4+ exercises; 4-5 is the sweet spot and longer ones eat time instead of saving it. Order them from most to least intense, and the last exercise is the one to cut.
numbers: 4-5 exercises, 6 is overkill; 3-4 rounds (2-4 while learning); at most 2 giant-set lines or 4-5 exercises on leg day; arm giant sets 3 exercises x 3-4 rounds.
scope: All trainees; 2023 he rated giant sets C tier for commercial gyms and low capacity.

title: Nonstop giant sets for conditioned lifters
statement: Advanced, conditioned lifters can cycle giant sets nonstop, since with 5 exercises the first has recovered by the time you loop back; isolation-only giant sets work because isolation isn't systemically fatiguing.
numbers: He cycles 5 exercises 4 times at ~7-8 min per round; the last superset of each day gets zero rest between rounds.

title: Build up to giant sets gradually
statement: Progress from easy supersets to hard giant sets, or you'll be cooked and wrongly blame the system; beginners who can't superset yet use short gaps instead of dropping supersets.
numbers: Easy supersets (biceps + triceps) → easy giant sets (+ rear delts) → hard supersets (press + pull) → hard giant sets (press + pull + abs); 1-2 weeks to adapt with ~4 min rest after the giant set; beginner fallback: set, 1 min, next set, then 2-3 min.

title: Superset only what is logistically close
statement: In commercial gyms superset equipment that sits close together and accept the gamble when it doesn't; never force supersets that don't fit, and if you can't superset, split the exercises.

title: End lower days with an isolation giant set
statement: Finish with a giant set of isolations for different muscles, back to back.
numbers: E.g. 3 rounds of leg extensions 10 / leg curls 10 / calf raises 12 / abs 15.

title: Most gym time is rest; supersets reclaim it
statement: Most gym time is spent resting, so supersets cut session length without removing warm-ups, lifts or hard sets.
numbers: 70-80% of gym time is rest; supersets save ~35% (30-40 min of a 2 h program); RDL + pull-ups as straight sets ≈ 24 min of rest vs ~12 min supersetted.

title: Session length as a diagnostic
statement: If the same work fits in 1 h with supersets as in 2 h, the 2 h was lazy rest; know how long your program takes, because cramming 90 min into 60 raises intensity non-optimally.
numbers: Bodyweight sessions ~50-60 min with 2-3 min between supersets; an upper day with a 5-exercise giant set ≤~1.5 h.

title: Don't idle between sets
statement: Naps, baths or phone time between sets are laziness; fill downtime with another exercise, and keep podcasts for strength-work rests.

title: Progressive overload is non-negotiable
statement: Without progressive overload there is no muscle gain; something has to go up for the muscles to go up, and a coach who never mentions it is a "hack".
check: Does the program have a defined way for load, reps or sets to rise over time?

title: The target is tonnage rising over time
statement: The goal is tonnage (volume × intensity × frequency) rising over time within relevant intensity windows; "tonnage is king". Strength helps by raising tonnage per session, but maxing out won't make you big.

title: A natural must eventually get stronger
statement: To keep growing a natural must eventually get stronger; a main lift stuck for years means the physique is stuck too.
numbers: "You can't stay at 225 for a decade"; 2 years without main-lift progress = no physique progress.

title: Strength alone is not size
statement: Strength counts only inside a program that raises tonnage; low-rep-only strength progress gives little muscle long term, and "more weight = faster growth" is the #1 mistake.
numbers: A 300→400 lb squat at constant tonnage adds little leg.

title: The number doesn't matter, the trend does
statement: The absolute weight means nothing; only that it keeps rising. There is no magic hypertrophy rep range: singles to 20s build muscle if taken to fatigue.
numbers: A 225 bench "means nothing", progression does.

title: Overload comes before growth
statement: Overload and growth feed each other (bigger muscle lifts more, more tonnage, bigger muscle), but overload comes first.

title: Performance is the best gauge of growth
statement: Performance and strength progression are the best gauge of hypertrophy; soreness and pump are poor indicators, and a pump with no progress means drop the method.
numbers: Soreness peaks ~48 h later.
scope: All trainees. See SLP-42 on soreness.

title: Body measurements: slow and disputed
statement: Track progress via strength first; body measurements are slow and misleading for programming, yet he also calls them the only reliable way to know a muscle grew and measures every part he specializes.
scope: All trainees; measurements mainly for specialized body parts.
status: contradicted — "the worst way to judge progress" and too slow to guide programming (2020) vs "the only reliable way" to know a muscle grew (2021).

title: Rising lifts at the same bodyweight = muscle
statement: If lifts, volume or tonnage rise at the same bodyweight or without much fat gain, you are adding muscle.

title: Dirty-bulk strength can mislead
statement: Aggressive or dirty bulks create artificial strength gains that stop tracking muscle.

title: Overload has many modes
statement: Overload can come from load, reps, sets, frequency, rest, technique/variation or range of motion; weight on the bar is just "the tip of the iceberg", and more sets and reps at the same weight are valid overload.

title: Bar weight must stay in the mix
statement: Weight on the bar is the simplest, most reliable and easiest lever to log and must stay in the mix, but load-only progression is "designed to fail" because the ability to add weight outpaces recovery (the "Milo paradox").
scope: All trainees past the novice stage.
status: changed — 2020-21: bar weight is the simplest and best method; 2022: weight is the "tip of the iceberg", most natural gains come from accumulated volume; 2024: his own bar-weight obsession caused progression anxiety, yet you must still get stronger.
check: Does the program raise load as well as reps or sets, without relying on load alone?

title: Reps-only or sets-only progression stalls
statement: Adding only reps or only sets at a fixed weight also stalls: the weight becomes too easy, reps drift into low-quality or cardio-limited volume, and sets become junk volume. You need both load and volume.
numbers: Example drift: 12, 13, 14, 15 reps at 225.

title: Order of the levers
statement: Step loading adds stimulus as reps first (evolving range), then sets, then frequency, and weight last, always in small steps; elsewhere he ranks importance as weight, then reps, then sets, then frequency, with drop sets, TUT and pre-exhaustion only "the cherry on top".
numbers: Superset isolation volume grows 2 → 3-4 sets, spreads to other days, only then add weight.
status: contradicted — both orders stated in Dec 2022; the first probably ranks importance and the second gives the order of steps *[inference]*.

title: Volume and frequency are reserve levers
statement: Volume and frequency are pulled when weight progress stops being realistic; intensity rises automatically as load progresses. When daily volume and intensity both stall, frequency is the lever left.

title: Start with minimal volume
statement: Start with minimal volume and keep volume as a gear in reserve; starting high leaves nothing to progress with. "Progressive overload is a loaded rifle": use only the bullets you need.
numbers: Add 1-2 weekly sets only when needed.
scope: All trainees; see ch. 3 for volume amounts.

title: Tempo can't replace load
statement: Slow tempo/TUT is not a substitute for load; tempo is hard to track and drifts with fatigue, so standardise it rather than progress it.
numbers: Moving 25 lb slowly when you can move 50 uses 50% of the muscle; a 5s/5s curl cuts reps to ~20%.
status: changed — 2020: slower tempo listed as an overload method; 2021-24: tempo is standardised, not progressed.

title: Frequency is overload too
statement: Frequency is overload ("load and time"), but more frequency only helps if it produces progression.
scope: All trainees; see ch. 3 for frequency.

title: Load anything that can be loaded
statement: Fixed-load implements (bodyweight, maxed dumbbells) leave only reps, sets, rest or tempo, none equal to adding weight; use dip belts, vests and dumbbells, and slow the tempo only when you've maxed the rack.
scope: Home and calisthenics trainees, anyone at an implement's limit.

title: Evolving rep ranges are the core method
statement: Give each lift a fixed rep range, start near the bottom, add reps weekly, add weight at the top and stay in the same range. He calls it the best way to progress.
numbers: 6-10 example: 6,5 → … → 10,9,8 → jump; ~90-95% of his lifts (2020); "every one of his programs" (2024).
scope: All lifts past the novice stage (see PRG-36 for novices).
check: Does each lift have a rep range with a rule for when to add weight?

title: Add weight when the first set hits the ceiling
statement: Only the first (top) set needs to reach the top of the range, with the others close; waiting for every set to hit the top turns the range back into a static scheme.
status: changed — Jan 2020: on 4×12, go up only if all four sets of 12 are comfortable; from Aug 2020: waiting for all sets makes ranges static; 2024: one set at the top is enough.
check: Is weight added once the first set reaches the top of the range, not only when every set does?

title: Readiness depends on the range
statement: On a heavy low range less is needed to add weight; you needn't max every set.
numbers: On 3-5, 5,4 is enough; on an 8-12 isolation, 11,10; 5-4 or 5-4-3 can be enough.

title: Reps should fall across sets
statement: At the same weight, reps should drop from set to set; identical reps on three or more sets mean sandbagging or too light a load.
numbers: E.g. 12 → 7; 10, 9-8, 8-7; 4×10 repeated after 3 min rest = add weight; 7,7,7 → 8,7,7 is fine if the top set progresses.

title: Straight sets, no pyramids
statement: Use the same weight on all working sets; pyramids and reverse pyramids ("D tier") pile up junk volume.

title: Every set stays inside the range
statement: If a set falls below the floor after a jump, drop the next set and win it back next session; if the first set misses, return to the previous weight. Falling below means the jump was too big or the range was badly set ("too greedy").
numbers: E.g. 7 then 6 on 6-10 after a jump.

title: Evolving sets: add a set, then weight
statement: When the first set tops the range, add a set; at the top set count, add weight and drop back a set, then rebuild.
numbers: OHP 4×8-12 at 100 lb: at 12/11/10 add 2.5 lb and go to 3 sets; if 3 sets can't stay in range after a jump do 2 (e.g. 7, 6), then add the third back; 12 → 15-16 weekly sets, then add load and return to 12.
status: changed — 2020: he avoided evolving set ranges because removing both limits removes structure; 2021: advanced tools that destabilize programs; 2022-24: standard in his programs.

title: Set ranges one set wide
statement: Keep set ranges one set wide; wide set ranges stall progress, especially on compounds. 3-4 sets beats a fixed 4 because you can try a heavier weight without "failing".
numbers: 2-3 or 3-4 sets, not 1-4.

title: Introduce evolving ranges gradually
statement: Evolve reps before sets; beginners keep sets fixed. Convert a program like "a drop of ink": isolation first, then upper compounds, then lower-body lifts (or, 2022, start on strength work and extend to accessories), never everything at once.

title: Rep PRs build into weight PRs
statement: With evolving ranges you nearly always get a rep PR ("forget 10 lb jumps"), and rep PRs accumulate into weight PRs.
numbers: After 15 years he still gets several rep PRs most sessions.

title: Each lift gets its own range, kept stable
statement: Decide each lift's range before placing it in a day; one global range for everything is simplistic. Never change a lift's range just because you failed to add weight, and if you do modify it, stick with the change.
numbers: 1-2 ranges per press (max 4 across presses), one per isolation.

title: Stay in a range at least a month
statement: Stay in a given rep range at least a month; varying ranges across the program and within each day (light/heavy mix) aids progression and freshness.
numbers: ≥1 month per range.

title: Evolving ranges: slower start, fewer plateaus
statement: Evolving ranges progress more slowly at first than static schemes but avoid plateaus and give a steady flow, trading strength speed for volume at a useful intensity without load pressure.
scope: Post-novice lifters; if you regress on them you'd have done better on 3x5.

title: Evolving ranges need tracking and brackets
statement: Evolving ranges require tracking and judgement; their freedom can let tonnage dip, so ranges stay inside strict brackets ("infinite possibilities but a narrow optimum"). Misused, they still produce terrible programs.

title: Open ranges vs fixed rep targets
statement: Two types: open ranges where you take every rep (8-12), and fixed rep targets for strength work where you stop at the target even with reps left, keeping strength a step ahead.
numbers: Fixed targets e.g. 5-4, 6-5-4.
scope: Open ranges for hypertrophy work; fixed targets for strength work.

title: Range width signals intent
statement: A narrow range means quick jumps are expected, a wide one slower progress; a range is a microcosm of a block, not a block.

title: Evolving ranges for novices: disputed
statement: He has said both that novices should not use evolving ranges (hard to track, need beta-testing, dangerous for lazy novices) and that evolving schemes are "very intelligent" and good for novices.
numbers: E.g. a 3-5×4-6 evolving scheme for novices.
status: contradicted — all 2020-21 statements, no clear direction.

title: Ranges that are too narrow fail
statement: Narrow ranges leave no room for set evolution and drift toward sandbagged 5x5; keep at least 4 reps between floor and ceiling.
numbers: Too narrow: 5-6, 6-8, 8-10 ×4 sets, 10-12 ×2-3 sets, 4×8-10 squat; good: 6-10, 8-12; 4-6 "a recipe for plateaus" (2025).
status: changed — 2020 he often prescribed 4-6 (4×4-6 pull-ups/dips, 3×4-6 squat); 2023-25: ≥4 reps between floor and ceiling, 4-6 plateaus.

title: Ranges that are too wide fail
statement: Very wide ranges (top more than 2× the bottom) take forever to earn a jump and invite laziness; 6-12 is about the widest he allows (2024).
status: contradicted — 8-15: too wide because reaching 15 means you'll get 12-13 (2020) vs hitting 15 lets you add ~10 lb and still get 8 (2023).

title: Wide ranges for lifts where reps fall fast
statement: Use a wide range like 6-12 where reps drop fast across sets or the lift is hard to progress; incline and preacher curls plateau easily and need it.
numbers: 5×6-12 drops 12 → 6-7; 8 reps at 40 lb won't survive a jump to 4 reps.
scope: Spoto press, incline/preacher curls and similar lifts.

title: Higher ranges: easy reps, hard jumps
statement: Wider or higher ranges make each added rep easier, but the higher the range, the harder it is to clear and add weight.
numbers: Bottom is 50% of top in 4-8, 60% in 6-10.

title: Adjust the range to a plateau
statement: When stalled in a range, adjust it to the exercise: widen if low reps stall, shrink if high reps stall; try widening first so tonnage climbs at the same weight.

title: When testing a range, start wide
statement: When beta-testing a new range, start wider and narrow it; shrinking is safer than expanding.
numbers: Close-grip bench 6-12 → 6-10.

title: The "543" elevator scheme
statement: For heavy deadlifts and OHP, keep the weight and build sets and reps up a ladder, then add weight and restart at the bottom.
numbers: 1-3 sets of 2-5: 2; 3,2; 4,3,2; 5,4,3; then +10 lb and restart at 2. Deadlift variant 2-3-2-4-3-2-5-3-2; a tight 1, 2-1, 3-2-1 version moves slower but may allow 10 lb jumps.
status: changed — 2020 schemes of 2-5 reps; by 2022 compounds never go below 4 (see PRG-102).

title: Fixed-weight squat and bench ladder
statement: For squat and bench, keep the weight and climb a rep ladder, then add weight and return to the start; a failed session is repeated.
numbers: 4 → 5,4 → 6,5,4 → 7,5,3 → 8,6,4, then +5 lb/side; 6-5-4 (15 reps) isn't enough to jump, 8-6-4 (18) is. Higher-volume version where form breaks at high intensity: 4; 5,4; 6,5,4; 7,6,5; 8,7,6.

title: Strength work: 1-3 sets
statement: Keep strength work to 1-3 sets (4 max); 5-6 sets means sandbagging. Descending reps (5-4-3) keep the tonnage high-quality.
numbers: 1-3 sets, max 4.

title: Autoregulate strength work by sets, not load
statement: Keep the strength-lift weight and autoregulate through sets and reps; a weak day is made up with same-pattern back-offs.
numbers: E.g. 420 lb for 1-3 sets of 4-8; a day of one set of 2 → back-offs 3-4×8-12.
scope: Intermediates with a heavy opening lift.

title: Top sets plus lighter volume sets
statement: Pair a few top-intensity sets with lighter volume or back-off sets; how heavy the strength sets are decides the back-off reps.
numbers: OHP: 2-3 top sets (or 3×2-5) + 3×5 ~20-25 lb lighter, 6 sets total (e.g. 135×5, 155×3, 145×5, 155×2); bench: top set 2-4 then 3×5; strength sets at 3s → back-offs toward 8, at 4s → heavier back-offs (5-8); deadlift 1-3/2-4 with RDL 5-7, 5-8 or 5-10.

title: The 85% rule (step loading)
statement: Build reps and sets at a load until it feels like ~70% effort, then add weight to get back to ~85%, cut sets or reps, and rebuild; never keep piling volume at 70%. Your 85% grows with you.
numbers: Close-grip bench 200 lb at 7/6/5 → build until the first set hits 10 and the last still gets 6 with a 4th set added → 10/9/8 at 200 → 205 lb gives ~7/6/6.

title: Rep-goal system
statement: Maxing every set at the same weight toward a total rep goal, then adding ~5 lb, is "excellent" and essentially evolving ranges by another name; he later prefers RIR for clearer brackets.
numbers: 5x5 → 25-rep goal; 25 reps over 3 sets forces ~7-8 per set; when tired he'd use a 35-rep goal.
status: changed — 2020: rep goals excellent; 2021: RIR preferred; 2023: day-chosen RIR autoregulation "S tier".

title: Eastern-style big jumps
statement: Keep a weight challenging for 4 reps until easy, then make a big jump; leaving reps in reserve doesn't slow progress.
numbers: RIR may cost ~300 lb tonnage now but avoids plateaus and injuries.

title: Static schemes force sandbagging
statement: With static schemes the first set is too easy or the last is ground out; 5x5 progresses fast early, then plateaus hard, and is not a good hypertrophy reference.
check: Past the novice stage, does the program avoid fixed set×rep targets like 5x5 on its main lifts?

title: Static schemes can only add weight
statement: Static schemes progress only by adding weight, force conservative jumps, make tonnage jump in steps, and after a miss you deload below where you started; they never teach plateau handling ("5x5 syndrome").
numbers: Repeating 5x5 needs a PR on five sets at once, which stops working after noob gains.

title: Where static ranges are fine
statement: Static ranges are fine for novices (weight keeps rising regardless) and as deliberate tools: back-off or accessory volume after strength work, a secondary lift you don't push, chin-ups, or the only horizontal press of a low-volume day.
numbers: 3x5 > 5x5 as back-off after an AMRAP top set; he uses 5×4 as a mental break on feeder lifts.

title: An evolving version always beats static
statement: An evolving version of a scheme always beats its static form, and static targets should not be used past the beginner phase.
numbers: 3×4-6 over 3x5; 3-5 sets of 3-5 over 5x5; 3×3-5 over 3x3; 3×6 → use 6-10.

title: Default jump sizes
statement: The default jump is 5 lb per side on barbell lifts and 2.5 lb per side on OHP and curls, with "5 lb per hand" logic for dumbbells.
numbers: 5 lb/side (10 lb total); 2.5 lb/side OHP and curls; intermediate range 2.5-10 lb/side; 5 lb/side proved too much for his curls and OHP.

title: No universal jump
statement: Jump size depends on the lift, the range and the whole program; decide plate loading before choosing the range, and if they don't match change one.
numbers: +5 lb on a 30-rep set = +150 lb tonnage.

title: Failed transitions mean jumps are too big
statement: If you stall or transitions to a new weight fail, halve the jumps; if many transitions fail, rework the plan.
numbers: 2.5-5 lb/side instead of 10; ~40% failed transitions = rework; he never failed a squat/deadlift transition but did on upper lifts until he cut jumps.

title: Small muscles get small jumps
statement: Small muscles need small jumps and microplates; 5 lb plates hurt the ego but are necessary. Don't ego lift small muscles.
numbers: +5 lb total (2.5/hand); arms 2.5-5 lb; microplates down to ~2 lb; never below 6 reps.
scope: Arms, laterals and other small muscles.
status: changed — 2020: avoid microplates unless really advanced; 2021-22: ~2 lb jumps for arms and microloading for presses.

title: Microloading also stalls eventually
statement: Microloading extends linear progression on presses but will also stall; then combine it with rep and set manipulation.

title: Coarse dumbbell jumps need a longer range
statement: With coarse dumbbell jumps, extend the range so you can land at the bottom after the jump.
numbers: 5 kg jumps → range to ~15, landing at 5-6.

title: Jumps shrink over a career
statement: Jump size and how often you add weight shrink exponentially over a career, so slowing early progression extends it.

title: Slow, steady, uninterrupted progress
statement: Slow, steady, uninterrupted progress beats fast gains followed by stalls, injury or regression ("not a shooting star"; the tortoise beats the hare).
numbers: 3 fast months then 3 stalled months kills motivation.
check: Is the program built for small, regular increases rather than fast jumps that end in resets?

title: Deliberately slow linear progression
statement: Bodybuilders should deliberately slow linear progression to delay the big plateau, even to a crawl; there are no strength deadlines, only physique deadlines.
numbers: Slow progress let his linear progression last ~6 years.

title: How fast you got strong matters
statement: Slower strength gain with more accumulated volume gives more hypertrophy; how fast you got strong matters more than how strong you got.
numbers: Take 70% of the gains for 10 years over 120% for two.

title: Gains slow but never stop
statement: For a sensible lifter gains slow but never stop (a car at 1 mph still gets far); intermediate pace is the baseline, and elites progress at your rate but don't quit.
numbers: Novice is ~6 months of a 15-year career; 100 → 20 mph analogy.

title: Each lift progresses at its own rate
statement: The more muscle a lift involves, the faster it progresses; OHP is the slowest after curls.
numbers: +60 lb on OHP can take 2-3 years; compounds can add weight every 1-2 sessions while a curl may sit 3-4 weeks; a row can't gain 10 lb/week for a year; isolation never +50 lb/yr.

title: Realistic post-novice rates
statement: Small yearly gains on isolation and modest gains on compounds are normal and still build muscle.
numbers: Biceps isolation +5-10 lb/yr normal; +5-15 lb on curls significant; lateral raises +10-15 lb/yr with strict form grows shoulders; his squat +20 lb in a year while legs grew.

title: Visible change takes months
statement: Nothing massive happens in 2-3 months; judge changes over months, not weeks.
numbers: Measurements show growth after ~4 months; people notice after 6-12; 2 weeks is too short to judge a rep-range switch.

title: Growth happens when progress gets hard
statement: For intermediates hypertrophy happens exactly when progression gets hard; fast progress on a new lift is neural adaptation, not muscle.

title: "Natural limit" is a programming limit
statement: Plateaus after 8-9 years are methodology, not genetics; long-term lifters stall because they stop making training hard or think they know everything.

title: What counts as a plateau
statement: Repeating a weight or reps for 2-3 sessions is the "breaking point" where gains happen, not a plateau; months at the same weight is one. Plateaus are normal and PRs every session are unrealistic (2023).
numbers: 2-3 sessions = normal; ~6 months = plateau; no lift should stagnate more than ~1 month vs 4-5 months on a compound means the program is wrong (both June 2020).
status: contradicted — stall tolerance of ~1 month vs 4-5 months, both June 2020.

title: Plateaus are a recovery or programming problem
statement: Plateaus come from poor recovery or diet, low effort, bad programming or a bad lift; in bodybuilding they usually mean too much volume to recover from or too little stimulus.
numbers: Outside old age (65-70), regression means program or diet.

title: First response: manipulate volume and intensity
statement: Answer a plateau first with new rep ranges, more volume, widened ranges or frequency, not with new exercises; volume, intensity or supersets bypass the law of accommodation.

title: Never deload and re-run the progression
statement: Taking weight off and re-running the same progression is "a longer run-up at the same wall" and wastes quality tonnage; only drop weight if you hit failure mid-session. A missed 3x5 should become 5,4,3 instead.
numbers: E.g. -10% or back to 70% resets.
scope: All lifts; reset-and-retry is why many quit.
check: Does the program handle stalls without resetting the load and re-running the same progression?

title: Don't swap a lift because it stalled
statement: Swapping a stalled lift dodges the plateau; the "progress" on the new lift is neural relearning, and stalling is when the body must build muscle. Letting failure trigger rotation hurts mental strength.
status: changed — 2020: never let a stall trigger rotation; 2023: only add a variation if you truly can't break the plateau; 2024: move to or add another variation of the pattern when a lift stalls.

title: When truly stuck, add a same-pattern variation
statement: One stimulus alone stalls; add (not swap) a carryover variation of the same pattern as back-offs or on another day. Two variations can give a year of gains before a third is needed.
numbers: Incline curls stuck ~35-45 lb ×12; pull-up plateau → different grip or pulldowns; bench stalled → diversify pressing.

title: Plateau busters
statement: For stuck lifts he endorses back-off sets, drop sets within the range, rest-pause on isolation, and occasional low-rep phases on bench.
numbers: Back-off: max reps then -5-10 lb; rest-pause: 10 reps, rest 30 s, +5, then add weight; rest-pause let him add 2 lb/session instead of sitting at 50 lb.
status: changed — 2021: rest-pause an afterthought that complicates rep/set manipulation; 2024-25: recommended plateau buster.

title: Plateaus are mostly programming-made
statement: Most plateaus are built into programs (novice programs are designed to end in a missed set of five); smart programming goes around the wall.

title: Plateaus can't be fully avoided
statement: Aim for fewer and later plateaus and see them coming ("push them ahead of you").
status: changed — 2021: plateaus "fully avoidable" with smart programming; 2023: they can't be avoided.

title: A deliberate stall is not a plateau
statement: Holding strength work steady (a controlled plateau) while pushing volume or a secondary lift is a "tonnage sacrifice", not a plateau; don't try to progress a main lift and its variation at once.

title: Fixed-increment programs rush the wall
statement: Programs that add a fixed weight every session or week rush novices into the wall and then cycle deloads; "you don't force progressive overload, it happens".
numbers: 5 lb/session; +15/+10/+5 lb/week.

title: Tonnage rises steadily, no roller-coaster
statement: Bodybuilding tonnage should rise steadily with only small planned dips, neither flat nor a roller-coaster; powerlifters wave and peak, bodybuilders don't.
numbers: Never deadlift 40 lb less than last session; after each jump tonnage stays above the previous cycle's low.

title: Strength work is the lighthouse
statement: Strength work opens every session when you're freshest; its 1-3 heavy sets drive progression though they are a small share of session volume. Never superset it; if short on time do only the strength work.
numbers: ~30-35% of session volume.

title: Back-offs balance the strength set
statement: A light opener calls for more back-off volume, a heavy one for lighter back-offs; same-style back-offs let strength progress trickle down, while speed back-offs nearly stall progress. Dropping strength reps is fine only if tonnage is made up elsewhere.
scope: Sessions with a heavy opening lift.

title: Most tonnage lives in variations and accessories
statement: Most tonnage should trickle into variations and accessories; if most of a session's tonnage comes from the first heavy lift, a plateau there drains everything. Variations should progress more slowly than the main lift.

title: Lifts can feed or block each other
statement: Main and secondary lifts feed each other, and similar lower-body lifts allow more tonnage together, but four similar presses compete and block overload.
scope: Program design; deadlift and rows compete for novices.

title: Specialization costs the rest
statement: Single-lift focus phases (e.g. Smolov) cost the rest of the program and leave a tonnage drop; alternating priorities make a staircase that never drops.
numbers: Smolov at most as an occasional 30-week sacrifice.

title: No blocks or peaking for bodybuilders
statement: Bodybuilders don't need strength/hypertrophy blocks, mesocycles, 4-week waves or peaking; the whole year is a hypertrophy block and variation lives inside the program (rotations, evolving ranges). RPE, deloads and mesocycles are powerlifting terms he excludes.
numbers: 12-week labels are irrelevant.
check: Does the program avoid separate strength/hypertrophy blocks and peaking phases?

title: Load never comes down in his programs
statement: In his programs only tonnage rises week to week; intensity and volume are managed within sessions, with no deloads.

title: Linear periodization lives in evolving references
statement: Linear periodization is progressing less often via volume and intensity changes; his programs contain it through evolving references, while pure linear progression (same reps, more weight) eventually fails.

title: Undulating intensity is for peaking
statement: For bodybuilders, dropping to 80% intensity sacrifices for nothing; alternating intense and volume sessions outside blocks is good.

title: Training stages last long
statement: Each training stage lasts months to years; stay in one as long as you progress.
numbers: Beginner ~6 months, novice ~1 year, bridge ~1 year (2022: maybe 3-6 months), intermediate ~2 years; each step 6 months-2 years; stage 1 → 2 ≥1 year, 2 → 3 ≥2 more years.

title: Novice ends when linear progression stops
statement: The novice stage ends when session-to-session linear progression on a few lifts with little volume stops and you need more exercises, days and volume, not when you reach strength standards.
numbers: Other markers: grip limits heavy deadlifts; intermediate ends when 12 weekly sets stop working.

title: Moving up a stage
statement: Move up when you want and can handle more volume or start plateauing: bodyweight → weighted, harder variations, +1 set per superset, more frequency rather than junk volume per session.
numbers: +1 set per superset.

title: Run a program as long as it progresses
statement: Keep a program as long as it progresses; one that works for 3 months then stalls is bad.
numbers: 7-8 months (2020); 6-18 months (2022); 1-2 years or indefinitely (2023-24); his own ran 2-3 years.
status: changed — recommended durations lengthened from 7-8 months (2020) to 1-2 years or indefinitely (2023-24).

title: Program hopping is a plague
statement: Program hopping chases novice neural gains, resets adaptation and costs years; switch only when progress truly stops. "Shock the muscle" and "resensitise" are nonsense; muscle stays responsive.
numbers: If five programs fail, the problem is you.
check: Is the program kept for many months as long as it progresses, rather than swapped every few weeks?

title: Valid reasons to change a program
statement: Change a program when there is no progress, no set/rep manipulation left to push volume, or the exercise selection no longer works; carry over what worked (lifts, references, supersets).

title: Program changes are rare and small
statement: Changes should be rare and small; many changes at once can't be assessed, and one bad day is no reason to panic-modify.
numbers: 6-10 → 6-12 is fine often; replacing a lift is rare.

title: Same template, rotating lifts
statement: Advanced lifters keep the same template and rotate lifts within fixed patterns; complexity and flexibility rise as you advance, while novices stay simple.
status: changed — 2021: his "final program" no longer changes; 2022: no final program exists because the body keeps evolving, and he admits he pushed the idea earlier.

title: Autoregulated rotations within a line
statement: Rotate lifts within the same line of specificity, not in arbitrary 6-week blocks and not because of a stall; start with scheduled biweekly rotations and later choose by recovery. Rotating exercises weekly to "shock" lowers specificity (2024).
numbers: Programs rotate every few years; lifts can rotate every ~8 days.

title: Isolation ranges
statement: Isolation work progresses best in moderate-to-high ranges; never go below 6 on small muscles.
numbers: 8-12 or 10-15 typical; 6-10 too low for isolation (2024); 6-12 for hard-to-progress curls; newcomers 10-15 for tendons.
status: changed — 2020: 3×6-10 "great" for isolation; 2024: 6-10 too low, use 8-12/10-15, with exceptions for hard curls.

title: Compound ranges
statement: Compounds progress in 4-8, 6-10 or 8-12, never below 4; main lifts low, accessories medium, isolation high, accessories never low.
numbers: Max 12 for compounds (2022); his ranges 3-20, mostly 6-12 (2024) or 3-15 (2025); leg press 10-15 not 6; 2020 tiers: main 4-8 or 2-5, accessory 6-10, isolation 8-12/10-15; sub-5-rep sets ~5% of volume (2023).
status: changed — 2020 elevator schemes of 2-5 reps; 2022 never below 4; 2023 sub-5 sets ~5% of volume.

title: Small muscles still need overload
statement: Small muscles need progressive overload scaled to their size; baby weights on arm isolation are a rookie mistake, and 30-rep pump sets or the same 30 lb curls for a year don't grow arms.

title: Prioritize, place first, overload
statement: The #1 way to grow a muscle is to prioritize it with isolation, place it first and progressively overload it; lagging parts trained last get skipped and don't grow.

title: Add load once bodyweight reps pass a threshold
statement: Bodyweight reps stall and stop driving hypertrophy; once clean reps reach a threshold, add load (even 5 lb) and use a lower range.
status: contradicted — thresholds vary (10, 15-20 or 30 pull-ups; 25 or 30 dips), but every version says to add load.

title: Weighted pull-up and dip prescriptions
statement: Weighted sets need a fixed range for tracking; bodyweight sets can be AMRAP.

title: Calisthenics progresses through variations
statement: Calisthenics raises intensity mainly through harder variations (leverage, range, rings, diamond), with loading after mastery.
numbers: Dips use a lower rep range than ring push-ups (2024).

title: Load bodyweight-capped movements
statement: Any movement capped by bodyweight should be loaded once easy: hyperextensions, crunches, leg raises, abs work.
numbers: Hyperextensions 8-12 or 4×10-15 past a 45 lb plate; crunches with a plate; leg raises with ankle weights or a dumbbell; load abs once you could do "sit-ups indefinitely".

title: Log every set
statement: Log weights and reps for every set of every exercise, even curls and even if you don't track food; not counting reps is the easiest way to make no progress.
check: Are weights and reps logged for every working set?

title: Fixed rep standards
statement: Fix ROM, tempo and technique first and keep them constant, or progress is fake; cutting ROM to add weight changes leverage, not muscle. Ugly reps mean retake the weight; tightening form is itself overload.

title: Machines are hard to track
statement: Too many machine sets make progression untrackable; machine users rarely add small plates, yet they should log too.
numbers: 6 plates on leg press → 7 in a year.

title: Judge recovery by expected progress
statement: Judge recovery by your expected rate of progression, not by "listen to your body"; a well-built program lets you predict lifts ~2 months out and hit the planned reps.
numbers: He missed a planned weight fewer than 5 times in ~1.5 years.

title: Learn to write your own program
statement: Learn to program and write your own; you are the subject and reviewer of your own experiment, advanced lifters especially.
status: changed — 2024 nuance: don't write from scratch early; tweak from late novice; write from scratch at late intermediate/early advanced.

title: Alpha-test on paper, beta-test in the gym
statement: Test a new program on paper first, then in the gym, starting slightly under-ambitious; keep an untouched copy and log what works.
numbers: Beta 2-4 weeks (2-3 cycles); alpha ~2-3 months stripping things out; beta ~1 year tweaking.

title: Build up from minimal
statement: Add one lift or a few sets at a time until stable, and ease into new workloads.

title: Flexibility needs regulation skill
statement: Program flexibility goes with the ability to raise tonnage, but more flexibility demands more tracking and autoregulation skill; you can't autoregulate if you've never regulated, and instinct training is winging it.

title: Consistency over cleverness
statement: The best method or exercise is the one you'll stick to for a year or more; a simple method done long beats a smart one done twice.
numbers: Stick with pullovers a full year before judging; 5-10 shoulder lifts for 10 years.

title: Missed sessions cost more than tonnage
statement: Skipped sessions add up to lost progress; keep practicing lifts rather than stopping.
numbers: Skipping 1 in 10 loses 10% of a year; ~2 months off per year can mean 4-6 months without real progress.
scope: All lifters. See FAT-04 on breaks.

title: Regaining strength is not progress
statement: Regaining strength after time off is not progress; after a long break restart slowly with less volume. He claims "Peter Pan lifters" quit and restart to relive newbie gains.
numbers: After a year off, restart with less volume.

title: Scheduled deloads are unnecessary for bodybuilders
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Scheduled deloads are unnecessary or harmful for bodybuilders; needing one means you are "digging a hole" with too much frequency, volume or strength work. A deload is an emergency response to a programming mistake and useless unless injured.
status: changed — 2020: "I never deload"; 2022: he deloads constantly through set/rep management, just not the powerlifter way (see FAT-13).
check: Does the program run without scheduled deload weeks?

title: Deloads exist for peaking
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Deloads are for strength athletes who peak; bodybuilders never peak, so only the recovery half could matter. The term spread with the internet and powerlifting and is absent from earlier bodybuilding eras.
numbers: Term spread ~20 years ago.

title: Trim the program instead of deloading
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Reduce workload yourself before a deload would be needed; doing slightly less means you never need a week off and lose less tonnage than a deload costs.
numbers: Cutting 40-50 min from your week beats a deload; ~25% more work across two weeks (2024).
scope: Anyone drifting toward needing a deload.

title: A week off is detraining
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: A week off, or 3-4 days fully off, is detraining, not deloading; you can only deload from a load. Time off is for injury or when away from the gym.
numbers: Needing 3-4 days off every 2 months means intensity/volume is wrong; a 13-day break is planned detraining.

title: Time off costs performance, not muscle
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Size regresses slowly but neural adaptations detrain fast, so time off costs performance and work capacity; "you shrink during a deload" is an exaggeration.
numbers: A 315 lb squat drops to ~255 lb after 2 weeks off; a 10% loss across 6+ movement patterns is huge.

title: Deload fatigue clears in days
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Fatigue clears in about 3 days of a deload; for the rest of the week nothing grows, and repeated deload weeks add up to a lot of lost work over years.
numbers: ~3 days; a week off every 6-12 weeks; on a 3-day schedule one missed day = ~30% of the week.

title: Coming back stronger proves nothing
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: PRs after rest are expected and only show full performance, or that you were under-recovered; bodybuilding is about maintaining performance, not PRs. Strength may even rise after a break while volume capacity falls.
numbers: 5 days off then stronger means the program was bad.

title: Deload weeks backfire behaviourally
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Knowing a deload is coming makes people overzealous beforehand; classic mesocycles pile low-intensity volume and then overshoot into junk volume, and deloads stop lifters learning day-to-day fatigue management.

title: Deloads produce confirmation bias
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Lifters credit the deload for preventing CNS fatigue that never came, like sacrificing a chicken nightly to keep away a wolf that never existed.

title: No resensitisation breaks
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: Mesocycles, low-volume phases, resensitisation breaks and "mTOR resets" are unnecessary; muscle is never desensitised, a plateaued muscle needs more work, and a good program runs indefinitely.

title: If deloads help you, keep them
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: He is tolerant: some top naturals grow with deloads, and if they help you keep them; if they feel wasted, skip them but manage fatigue another way.

title: If you must deload, keep the usual lifts
section: Fatigue: against deload weeks and time off
statement: The better deload is your usual lifts at low intensity and low volume, keeping blood flow and movement patterns.
numbers: 2 sets at 2 RIR is reasonable (2024).
status: contradicted — 2020: usual lifts at low intensity/volume is the "objectively better deload"; 2024: even an active deload far from failure is wasted for hypertrophy, yet in another 2024 video 2 sets at 2 RIR is reasonable.

title: The deload is built into every week
statement: Evolving reps and sets plus rotations vary volume, intensity and frequency slightly while tonnage stays stable; small dips from rep ranges are the only variation he allows. He opposes blast/cruise, polarized volume/intensity days and clear hard/easy weeks.

title: Micro-deloads by muscle, on the day
statement: Picture each body part flashing red (needs work) or green (needs recovery); reduce a muscle that needs rest or rotate it out, and train a fresh muscle even if a rotation planned rest, so every muscle stays continuously stimulated.
numbers: A muscle needing rest gets one evolving-rep set or is rotated out.

title: Volume, intensity and frequency manage fatigue
statement: Volume, intensity and frequency are one thing: tools to manage fatigue. Any program is a block of fatigue, so get the most from the least.

title: Autoregulation needs built-in mechanisms
statement: Autoregulation needs a menu of rotation options built into the program and suits advanced lifters; small recovery shortfalls can accumulate, so novices should work toward it rather than start with it.

title: Training dictates recovery
statement: Set the optimal work first, then see what recovery it needs, not a fixed 5+1 week block; bodybuilders let training dictate recovery, strength athletes the opposite.

title: Pre-plan easier swaps for bad days
statement: Have easier options ready for bad days and hard weeks; keeping the secondary movement preserves tonnage better than keeping strength work.
numbers: Back extensions or light RDLs for heavy deadlifts; the shrug version on bad deadlift days and no rack pulls; −1 set on the secondary movement on the week's 2nd upper day.

title: Longer cycles drop the heaviest lifts periodically
statement: Running an 8-day program over 6-day weeks makes heavy back squats or conventional deadlifts drop out every few weeks, resting body and mind; the next exposure gives PRs.
numbers: 8-day cycle.

title: No stimulus without fatigue
statement: Stimulus and fatigue are the same thing seen two ways; if you're not fatigued you didn't push enough. Target the maximum fatigue you can recover from, and don't demonize fatigue.
check: Is the program aiming for the most fatigue the lifter can recover from, rather than minimizing fatigue?

title: Accumulate fatigue, don't flush it
statement: Fatigue decays fast and fitness slowly, so a pure flush risks fitness; performance exists to let you accumulate fatigue.
numbers: His formula: performance − fatigue = fitness.

title: Stimulus-to-fatigue ratio is overrated
statement: SFR is an excuse to avoid heavy free-weight compounds; compounds give more of both stimulus and fatigue and are only worse if excess fatigue outruns excess stimulus.
numbers: B tier (2023); ranked 5th (2024).
status: changed — 2022: a simple valid concept; 2023: B tier; 2024: 5th, "an excuse".

title: The deadlift's "bad SFR" is programming
statement: The deadlift easily overshoots recovery through too much volume or poor form, so undershoot slightly ("fill the glass without overflowing").

title: SFR matters where fatigue is low-value
statement: SFR does matter where fatigue lands on tendons and stabilizers rather than the target: machines rest them, squats/deadlifts for abs are terrible SFR, heavy deadlift singles aren't optimal, and chasing full ROM can add needless fatigue. It matters most once many small muscles are isolated.
numbers: Bench 100 fatigue points, 60 to muscle vs chest machine 50, 45 to muscle; heavy deadlift singles ~1 rep at RPE 9.

title: Fatigue scales with load, reps and muscle size
statement: Fatigue is roughly reps × weight, modulated by the lift; adding or removing work for big muscle groups matters more than for small ones.
numbers: 10-15 reps at 50 lb is a lot for laterals and nothing for good mornings; 3 sets of curls add no real fatigue, 3 sets of deadlifts do.

title: Name the type of fatigue
statement: Distinguish muscular, cardiovascular, mechanical, tendon, CNS and mental fatigue; many "fatigue-seeking" methods really target cardio. Muscular fatigue is lost fiber force, rebuilt bigger with food and rest.

title: CNS fatigue barely matters for bodybuilders
statement: Most people can't reach CNS burnout; supposed burnout is usually injury or mismanaged volume and intensity, and you don't need rest days for the CNS.
numbers: D tier (2023); 1.5 years of heavy squats/deadlifts with no burnout.

title: Strength loss blamed on CNS is usually life
statement: If your muscles can move a load, it can't fry your CNS; strength loss blamed on CNS is usually a calorie deficit, poor sleep, stress or a bad day.

title: The CNS is trainable
statement: Undertraining the CNS out of fear limits gains and future work capacity; bodybuilders should grow it to serve the muscles rather than plan around it, and a slightly under-recovered CNS costs little since you don't test 1RMs.

title: Sessions still tax the whole system
statement: Each session still fatigues the nervous system and squats tax it most; squat and bench share CNS and stamina, so the system rather than the legs can limit when you train again. Upper and lower "trees" interfere little.
numbers: A novice's bench lags after squats; deadlifts didn't hurt his bench.

title: Daily low-volume training still accumulates
statement: Even very low daily set counts don't fully recover in 24 h because tendon and nervous fatigue accumulate; Bulgarian-style daily training fails for bodybuilding.
numbers: Even 1-2 sets a day.

title: Leave the gym with energy left
statement: Being wrecked is not a goal; being wiped every session means working dumb, and an arm day should leave you energized.
numbers: ~20% in the tank with high frequency; ~40% after an arm day.

title: Stop when sets turn into junk volume
statement: End the session when fatigue pushes sets out of the useful window; if late work at under half your fresh capacity feels hard, it is junk, and a drained last part of a long session means shorten it and raise intensity.
numbers: A 400 lb squatter barely doing 180 lb ×3 late has dug too deep; drained last 30-40 min of a 90-min session.

title: A good session is repeatable
statement: A good session can be repeated within days and for years; giving everything one day and being out for seven loses to managed daily training, and holding back to survive tomorrow is a scheduling problem.
numbers: Repeatable within ~5 days.

title: Lost reps are the early warning
statement: Losing reps at the same weight signals under-recovery: do less volume that day. For bodybuilders bar weight should never go backward; only volume dips temporarily.
numbers: 300 lb ×4 then ×3 = cut volume; 7 instead of 8-9 is a milder sign.
scope: All lifters; heavy lifts give the most accurate read.

title: Fatigue carries across exercises
statement: Fatigue carries across exercises, even to unrelated muscles, so put the least important lifts last; on full body vary the order, since always skipping the last quarter undertrains a quarter of the body.
numbers: By exercise 5 you underperform; if chin-ups drop inside a biceps giant set, remove a curl.

title: Order: explosive, heavy, then hypertrophy
