statement: Order a day explosive → heavy → hypertrophy, so earlier lifts prime later ones; giant sets run in descending intensity. Never open with a 1RM, which wrecks the rest of the day.

title: Cardio fitness limits sessions
statement: Cardiovascular fatigue limits sessions; supersets with a lower-body compound or whole-workout giant sets sabotage performance. To stop fading before failure, build work capacity and eat before training.

title: Warm-up sets count
statement: Warm-up sets count toward fatigue, so they belong in planning.

title: Squats tax him more than deadlifts
statement: He finds high-bar squats far more taxing than deadlifts, contrary to "experts"; heavy knee flexion wrecks his recovery while frequent heavy hinges don't. He can deadlift heavy and squat two days later, but not the reverse.
numbers: Heavy squat every 8 days worked (2020); with two close lower days, deadlifts first and squats second; if you can't repeat a knee-flexion effort 3 days later, swap to a lighter variation in another range.
scope: His experience; general advice on lower-day order.

title: Never heavy squat and heavy deadlift together
statement: Never do heavy squats and heavy deadlifts in the same session; a heavy squat with a light hinge variation is fine. Lifts on the same "tree" share fatigue, so after a brutal squat day adapt the deadlift range or variation, and two heavy hinges are counterproductive.
check: Does the program keep heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on separate days?

title: Lower-back fatigue is the limiter
statement: Lower-back fatigue limits both legs and upper back; manage it to train legs hard and often, and load the upper back without the legs (DB rows, pullovers, chest-supported rows), using hinge styles that reduce axial load.
numbers: 10×10 chest-supported rows fine; on barbell rows "idiotic".

title: No rows right after heavy pulls
statement: Don't put heavy rows right after squats or deadlifts, in the session or the next day; put heavy rows on an upper day.
numbers: Coan rows on upper day at 3×10-12, superset DB shrugs; pull-ups then pullovers can work.
status: contradicted — 2022: deadlift Monday then barbell rows Tuesday won't work; 2024: lats to failure then RDLs the next day doesn't hurt him, and he doubts one day's training hurts the next (garbled source).

title: Cap deadlift and squat volume
statement: Heavy pulling volume adds up fast: most people should use a deadlift variation for back-offs, never stack deadlifts, back-offs and rack pulls in one day, and choose back-friendly lifts after the heavy pull.
numbers: Deadlift 3 sets of 4-6 is already a lot; squat and RDL 3 sets each, not 4.

title: Lighter knee flexion after a heavy pull
statement: If a heavy pull was 1-2 days earlier, make the next knee-flexion session lighter.
numbers: Pause squats 3×10 or 6-10 reps instead of heavy 3×4.

title: Don't fight for extra deadlift reps
statement: Grinding 2-3 extra heavy deadlift reps can cost the next hinge session in tonnage and adds injury risk; "stimulate, don't annihilate" joints and tendons.
numbers: 2-3 extra reps.

title: Machine squats allow more sets
statement: Belt, hack and leg-press squats cause less systemic and spinal fatigue than barbell squats, so they allow more sets.
numbers: 4 sets vs 3.

title: Don't trash yourself on lower days
statement: Keep reps conservative on lower days; the last lower day may leave you beat up but without back pain. Babying the lower back is justified only if you need it tomorrow.
numbers: His 3-exercise lower days are harder than his 7-exercise upper days.

title: An arm day is a sneaky recovery day
section: Arm days, isolation and low-cost work
statement: An arm or isolation day barely taxes the CNS, its blood flow aids recovery from compounds, and it can replace a rest day; full rest days should become rare as you advance.
numbers: With twice-daily training, a no-compound day makes sense.

title: Light pump sets aid recovery
section: Arm days, isolation and low-cost work
statement: Light pump work days after a heavy session aids recovery.
numbers: E.g. light Saturday pullovers after heavy Monday.
scope: His 2021 view (see SLP-38 on active recovery).

title: Shoulders serve both pressing planes
section: Arm days, isolation and low-cost work
statement: One set of shoulders serves horizontal and vertical pressing, so manage the overlap: keep bench volume low on a heavy OHP day and skip vertical presses when shoulders are fried.
numbers: DB OHP 4×6-12 after dips and upright rows may be overkill.

title: Nucleus overload must stay cheap
section: Arm days, isolation and low-cost work
statement: Nucleus overload stays cheap because it is not made progressively harder; take a bigger share of recovery and hard sets suffer, and small costs add up over a year at high frequency.
numbers: ~2-3% of the recovery bucket; 10-20% is too much.

title: Volume above what you can recover from is wasted
statement: Volume above maximum recoverable volume is wasted, like a surplus that only adds fat; needing 10 low-intensity days to recover shows an unbalanced program.

title: More days raise fatigue
statement: Adding days raises both volume and frequency; if 6 days feels wrong, fit the same volume into 4.
numbers: 4 → 5 days raises both.

title: Fatigue peaks then flushes over the week
statement: Full body 3×/week builds fatigue to a Friday peak that is flushed over the weekend; his programs include days off for that reason.

title: Injuries come from accumulated fatigue
statement: Track past fatigue to prevent injury; injuries come from accumulated fatigue, not that day's work, and perfect form with poorly managed volume still leads to injury.

title: After a break, restart at a third
statement: After a break restart at about a third of usual tonnage; muscle returns fast, and old loads straight away cause injuries.
numbers: ~1/3 of usual tonnage.

title: Overtraining is real but program-relative
statement: Overtraining is individual and relative to the program; train just below its edge, where you still recover but loads become irrelevant past it. The more advanced you are, the less overtraining is possible.
status: contradicted — 2020: called both real and "a myth".

title: Overtraining is really under-recovering
statement: Within-session overtraining is nearly impossible, but you can come back under-rested; skinny, weak under-eaters overtrain easily and grow best on low volume, high intensity and long recovery.

title: Many who think they overtrain are right
statement: Many who think they overtrain really do, because they answer regression with more volume; burnout usually means too much in the gym and too little outside it, so lanky high-metabolism lifters should cut volume and raise calories.
status: contradicted — he also said most people needn't worry about muscular fatigue (2020).

title: No progress = too little or too much stimulus
statement: Lack of progression means too little stimulus or too much; Mentzer's fix of more rest days until training every 5 days makes under-stimulated lifters regress.

title: Mental fatigue is part of recovery
statement: Mental fatigue is an ignored part of recovery and mental stamina is usually lower than physical; feared or repeatedly failed lifts spike stress, confident lifts barely do. Stop when your mind checks out and train again tomorrow; for advanced lifters the brain can become the limiter.

title: Strength work that burns you out: adjust it
statement: If strength work burns you out mentally or in the tendons, lower its intensity or modify the sets.
scope: Lifters with a heavy opening lift.

title: Manual workers train hard but rarely
statement: Manual workers should train intensely but rarely and with low volume, never impairing the ability to work; construction work acts like low-intensity, high-volume, high-frequency training.

title: Sport and lifting share one recovery pot
statement: Sport practice and lifting draw on the same recovery; add a sport gradually, avoid heavy lifting the day before practice or competition, and cut lifting if sparring degrades. Doing three lifting and three martial-arts sessions is chasing two rabbits.
numbers: Start MMA at 1×/week and assess; 40 min of team practice ≈ 15 min of top-set lifting in recovery cost; skill calisthenics (muscle-up, planche) costs real recovery.
scope: Lifters who also play sport or fight.

title: Weighted abs not before heavy lower days
statement: Weighted ab work impairs core rigidity, so don't do it the day before heavy lower work; do it at the end of leg days.

title: Sleep is the most underrated part of recovery
statement: Sleep is as important as diet or more; perfect diet, training and low stress mean nothing without it, and your ability to work harder is limited by your ability to recover. He avoids caffeine to protect it.

title: Most adults need 7-8 hours
statement: Most adults need 7-8 h; the need is largely genetic and falls with age, and the 10-12 h of elite athletes is unrealistic for working people.
status: changed — his own target rose from 7 h (2021) and 7-8 h (2022) to 8-9 h (2024).
check: Does the lifter get at least 7-8 hours of sleep a night?

title: Skipping sleep is quitting the workout halfway
statement: Sleep what you need; cutting an hour to be productive backfires. Between sleep and entertainment, always sleep.
scope: All trainees; he admits regretting nights editing videos.

title: Hypertrophy training raises sleep need
statement: Hypertrophy training raises sleep need because the nervous system needs more rest.

title: You can still grow on poor sleep
statement: You can still gain on sub-par sleep, but sleep matters for mood, hormones and disease risk.
numbers: He slept at 3-4 am during his master's and still made "tremendous" gains.

title: Quality matters as much as quantity
statement: A short optimized night can beat a long poor one; oversleeping can leave you sluggish with no added recovery.

title: Naps are highly anabolic
statement: "Nothing is more anabolic than a nap."
status: changed — 2020: admitted a childhood prejudice against naps; 2024: naps highly anabolic.

title: Early wake-up culture is pointless
statement: Total sleep, volume and tonnage matter, not the clock; wake when your job and biology need you, not to copy celebrities (a "dick-measuring contest").
numbers: 3-5 am wake-ups.

title: Bed before midnight, not for growth hormone
statement: Go to bed before midnight because late-night internet steals sleep; he doubts that sleeping after midnight costs growth hormone and thinks any early-bedtime benefit is minimal.
numbers: Before midnight.

title: Train at your best time
statement: Train when you're strongest, though people adapt to any time.
numbers: He is strongest 5-8 pm and a "zombie" in the morning.

title: Not right before bed; night shifts train before work
statement: Training right before bed revs you up too much; night-shift workers should train before their shift, which also wakes them up.

title: Cool the body before bed
statement: Take a cold shower until cold to the bone or slightly shivering, then sleep in a cool room with the window open, especially in summer.
numbers: Let water hit legs, upper chest and upper back; wipe off without fully drying.

title: No screens before bed
statement: Ban doomscrolling before bed and read instead.
numbers: ≥1.5 h screen-free before bed.
status: changed — 2020: blue light didn't bother him, only susceptible people need to avoid screens; 2024: ban screens ≥1.5 h before bed.

title: The bedroom is for sleep
statement: Keep the bedroom sacred: no phone, TV, laptop or pets if possible, and reserve lying down for sleep so it becomes a sleep trigger.

title: Find your need without an alarm
statement: Find your sleep need by sleeping without alarm, light or noise, and wake without an alarm when possible; don't obsess over cycle lengths, go to bed as early as you can and focus on quality.

title: Insomnia is often psychological
statement: Fear of not sleeping feeds insomnia like a panic attack; don't fight it with pills, let the mind drift, and with poor sleep accept it and organise training around reduced recovery. Tired mornings lead to caffeine abuse and worse sleep.

title: Cut caffeine and toxins
statement: Control caffeine, alcohol and drugs; the health basics are sleep, no toxins, resistance training and moderately low body fat, while thyroid hacks, infrared lights and enemas are bogus.

title: If a deficit hurts sleep, eat late
statement: If dieting hurts your sleep, fast in the day and eat a big meal before bed; sleep matters more than hunger.

title: Avoid crushing an arm in your sleep
statement: Avoid side-sleeping that crushes an arm or shoulder, since pinched nerves can eventually hinder growth; numb arms on waking are harmless if sensation returns. Change position or pillow and use band nerve-decompression drills.

title: Short on sleep: sleep instead of training
statement: If kept up very late, sleep instead of training; forced low-energy sessions gave him bad workouts or injuries. Say no to social pressure that wrecks sleep.
numbers: If forced to choose, a minimal 20-min session (2024).

title: Slightly unwell: train, but not heavy
statement: When slightly unwell, hungry or underslept, still train but avoid heavy work; real flu may be the exception. He claims no cold or flu in ~10 years of training and that training makes the sick feeling go away.

title: A muscle needs ~48-72 hours
statement: A muscle needs about 48 h, up to 72 h, and even a fully trashed muscle is fresh in 4-5 days; no muscle needs a full week off. Avoid the same isolation lift on consecutive days.
numbers: ~48 h, up to 72 h; trashed max 4-5 days; ≥48 h between an arm day and the next upper day; same isolation ≥48 h apart.

title: You don't need 100% recovery
statement: You can retrain before full recovery; a muscle can only be restored to 100%, never beyond, so waiting for or emptying it fully gains nothing, and waiting for 100% pushes people to bro splits. Training early adds fatigue and lengthens the next recovery, a problem only if constant.
numbers: 90-95% (or 90-100%) recovered is enough; even 20% can still grow.
status: contradicted — 2020: training again before full recovery "steals gains" (SLP-24); 2021-22: 20% or 90-95% recovery still grows; reconcilable only as "not constantly".

title: Constantly training under-recovered steals gains
statement: Training the same thing before recovery again and again means training sore, underperforming and growing slower; showing up under-recovered wastes training and risks injury.

title: Bigger muscles cost more recovery
statement: Bigger muscle groups and the lower body cost more recovery and volume sets recovery time; small muscles recover faster, so the 85% rule (PRG-48) must be applied more strictly to big ones.

title: Hard lower-body work now needs 72 h+
statement: Lower-body recovery slows as you get stronger; he now needs ~72 h or more after hard lower work and finds lower body 3×/week too much, so lower reps may suit very taxing lifts. Needing ~10 days before deadlifting again means poor recovery and work capacity.
numbers: 72 h+ (2024-25); after a widowmaker ~72 h to squat light, ~20 h more for optimal (2020); RDL soreness peaks ~48 h; 2 sets of 8-12 Bulgarian split squats left him sore Monday to Friday.
status: changed — 2022: legs every two days without soreness; 2024-25: 72 h+ and lower body 3×/week too much.

title: Upper back recovers very fast
statement: The upper back is small muscles with a big work capacity and recovers fast; pull-ups done with the back allow daily frequency.
numbers: Full upper-back recovery assumed in 48 h (weighted reverse rows 3×6-10); swap DB rows for ring rows on Friday if needed.

title: Recovery figures for other muscles
statement: Muscles differ: chest needs a few days, biceps recover in about 3 days, neck is fast, triceps are slow especially if untrained, lats are sore but always ready, and shoulder sessions should be spread.
numbers: Chest 2-3 days between sessions; biceps 3 days, so 4 sets is fine; 3rd triceps long-head session only if fresh (2023); forearm grip drill every 4-6 days (2020) vs consecutive days with different curls (2024).
status: contradicted — triceps recover very fast (his own, 2020) vs slow especially if untrained (general, 2023), possibly not a real conflict; forearm frequency rose from every 4-6 days (2020) to consecutive days (2024).

title: Recovery speed is individual
statement: Recovery speed varies per muscle and per person; recovery "pots" drain at different rates.
numbers: His triceps recover very fast, his quads take forever (2020).

title: The recovery pot model
statement: Training damage drains a recovery pot whose size is your maximum recoverable volume; keep it relatively full and never empty outside a powerlifting peak. Each muscle and tendon has a pot, pots feed each other (legs also drain the lower-back pot), and time spent with the pot low wastes gains.

title: Spread volume rather than empty the tank
statement: Several partial drains a week give more quality work than one crash to zero; junk volume is lots of fatigue for little stimulus.
numbers: Drain to 40 and refill to 100 twice (120 points) beats one 100-to-0 crash; 9 sets once a week drain to zero, 3 sets ×3/week each drain ~30% for roughly double the quality work.

title: The CNS bucket holds the muscle buckets
statement: The big CNS bucket spends more than any muscle but refills no faster, so leave water in the tank; it keeps refilling while you train other muscles, and its capacity is large and trainable.
numbers: People historically did 8-12 h/day of labour without deloads.

title: Most lifters over-allocate rest
statement: Most lifters overestimate their damage and over-allocate rest, so they over-recover and miss stimulus windows; "gains happen when you rest" is a platitude, since gains are triggered in training and materialize in recovery.

title: Recovery is where growth happens
statement: Growth is actualized in recovery (supercompensation), so training and recovery are equally important; if training is too dense, recovery can matter more than training.
numbers: Curls nonstop for 5 years without rest would never grow biceps.

title: A rest day is programmed
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: A rest day is planned and as important as a training day; an impromptu skip is not a rest day. Let progression, recovery, tendons and psychology set how many you need.
numbers: It can be half a day or 1.5 days with twice-daily sessions.

title: Taxing days go before rest days
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: Put the most taxing (lower-body) days right before rest days or the weekend, giving time to eat and sleep.
numbers: A four-heavy-compound day before a 2-day weekend; 2 full rest days after the lower day before Thursday's full body.

title: Add a rest day if 7 days is too much
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: If training 7 days is too much, add a rest day after day 5; it won't kill gains. Mind what the last day does to the first day of the repeating week.
numbers: No push-ups/dips on day 7 before heavy chest on day 1.

title: Active recovery: early yes, later mostly no
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: He now holds that recovery is just rest: constant active recovery keeps you fatigued, passive couch rest is important, and light walking or mowing is fine.
status: changed — 2020-21: light blood-flow work, light pump, calisthenics and a busy rest day ("not a couch day") aid recovery; 2024: "you do not need active recovery".

title: Optional Sunday session (2023)
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: His 2023 program had an optional Sunday of low-fatigue work plus outdoor activity.
numbers: Calf raises 6-10×10-20; neck flexion/extension 6-10×10-25; shrugs 3-4×15-20; band triceps extensions 3-4×30-50 not to failure; planks 3×1 min; plus hiking, swimming or biking.

title: Off days leave the upper body alone
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: On off days leave chest, shoulders and upper back alone, for mental and physical recovery.

title: His recovery recipe
section: Rest days and active vs passive recovery
statement: Optimal recovery is less frequency, less junk volume, better nutrition and lots of passive rest: eating, sleeping and napping, not cold plunges or runs in the rain.

title: Soreness is not a sign of growth
statement: Soreness isn't a growth signal; strength and tonnage over time are. Constant heavy soreness signals poor adaptation, new programs make you sore from adapting, and trembling or flu-like symptoms aren't growth signs.
check: Is the program judged without using soreness as a measure of success?

title: Soreness should fade with training
statement: Soreness should fade with training age and frequency; still being routinely sore after 5 years means program hopping, and once-weekly muscles stay unconditioned. Once you reach no-soreness, soreness becomes meaningful.
numbers: He trains legs every 2 days and is never sore; new high-volume trainees will be sore 4-7 days; 7 days of leg soreness is a bad sign unless a total beginner, so fix frequency.

title: Feel is an unreliable recovery gauge
statement: Touch-soreness and feel are unreliable recovery gauges; soreness can last a week, and the 48-hour rule is an alternative.
status: contradicted — 2020: feel during and after a workout means nothing for judging volume, yet the same year he said to judge extra tonnage by soreness 4 days later and to "let your body be the judge" for CNS.

title: Exception: a lift that keeps you sore
statement: A lift that keeps you sore for years, like his RDLs, is a good workout.

title: Chronic stress impairs recovery
statement: Chronic stress and mental illness impair recovery and raise injury rates; work stress ruins focus, weight selection and sleep, and lifters who often need deloads may be overtaxed by life.

title: Office jobs recover well, physical jobs add volume
statement: Office jobs give excellent recovery windows as long as you eat enough; blue-collar jobs add volume that must be managed.
numbers: Office workers sit 7-8 h/day.

title: Plateau checklist includes recovery
statement: When stuck, check recovery (eat and sleep more), then the rep range or jumps, then psychology.

title: Age lowers recovery but doesn't force less volume
statement: Age lowers recovery but doesn't force dropping volume; older lifters manage frequency and volume carefully, and you lose muscle by stopping training and diet, not by turning 40.
numbers: At 64, manage frequency/volume carefully.

title: Raising testosterone naturally
statement: Testosterone rises naturally with a clean diet, lots of sleep, low stress and years of rigorous training; any physical activity helps hormones.

title: Cold showers: harmless, not a revolution
statement: Cold showers don't hurt gains and are probably healthy, but won't revolutionise recovery; they chill only the surface, so he doubts protein-synthesis blunting. He suspects (unverified) a testosterone or capillary benefit and hasn't tried ice baths.
numbers: Gained ~40 lb from 20 to 25 taking daily cold showers; cold-only for 5 years (2024), 7 years (2025).
status: changed — 2020: discussed at length as useful for sleep and circulation; 2024: won't revolutionise recovery.

title: Post-training contrast showers
statement: After training a short cold blast while warm, and hot/cold on the forearms, boosts blood flow; only once used to very cold showers, and people with weak hearts should be cautious.
numbers: ~1 min cold blast.

title: Cold exposure and immunity
statement: He credits nutrition, water, sleep and not hiding from the cold for his immunity; adapt with cold showers and going out lightly dressed.
numbers: Lightly dressed around 50 F.

title: Daily sun on the skin
statement: Get sun on your skin daily; he walks shirtless on breaks.
numbers: 20-30 min/day; he walks 30 min.

title: Sauna: probably healthy, growth effect unknown
statement: Sauna is likely good for health, its effect on growth is unknown, and you should watch your heart.

title: Light hand work for blood flow
statement: Blood flow around joints speeds recovery, so light hand work helps: rice bucket B tier, daily foam rolling OK if not too hard. Band finger extensions gave him knuckle tendinitis.

title: Compounds plus isolation, neither alone
statement: A hypertrophy program is compounds for most of the tonnage plus isolation for whatever the compounds miss. Compounds are the "shotgun", isolation the "sniper", and neither works alone.
check: Does the program combine compound lifts for most of the tonnage with isolation for the muscles they miss?

title: Isolation is as serious as compounds
statement: Isolation gets the same priority and effort as compounds, not a token "3 sets of curls" tacked on at the end where it gets skipped. It taxes the nervous system less, so be generous with it.
scope: All; aimed at strength-template followers with small arms.
check: Is isolation work programmed with real sets and effort rather than as optional leftovers?

title: Naturals skew toward compounds
statement: A program that is mostly isolation is how enhanced pros train; for naturals he calls it "garbage". Naturals should lean on compounds.
numbers: 70-75% isolation = the pro/enhanced pattern to avoid
check: Is the program built mainly on compounds rather than ~70%+ isolation?

title: Compound-only training leaves known gaps
statement: Big-three or compound-only programs (he names BBB, Starting Strength, GreySkull) leave the long-head triceps, biceps, forearms, rear/side delts, calves, neck, abs and upper back behind. Adding rows and weighted pull-ups still misses them.
scope: Anyone training for a complete physique.

title: The dominant muscle takes the work
statement: In a compound the strongest muscle does most of the work and leverages decide activation, so some "targeted" muscles barely grow. More total load is not more load on one muscle, and the bigger a prime mover gets the more it steals from small muscles, so skipping isolation early creates deficits that are hard to fix.

title: Which muscles need isolation
statement: Quads, glutes and chest are prime movers in heavy compounds and need little isolation; most other muscles need it, arms more than legs. Hamstrings often stay small in strong naturals despite hinging.
scope: All; compound-only makes more sense for legs than arms.

title: True isolation is a myth, prioritisation is real
statement: No movement isolates one muscle, but each prioritises some muscles, and that is what makes programming possible.

title: A compound is any big multi-joint lift
statement: Any multi-joint lift that recruits a lot of muscle (dips, push-ups) is a compound. The big three are a powerlifting construct and not mandatory for bodybuilders.
scope: Bodybuilders (powerlifters must do the competition lifts).

title: Cover every movement pattern
statement: The bare minimum is a "big ten" that covers every body part. The size patterns are vertical press, horizontal press, knee flexion, hip hinge, horizontal pull and vertical pull. Check each body part when choosing.
numbers: 6 patterns; "big ten" lifts
check: Does the program include a knee flexion, a hip hinge, a horizontal and vertical press, and a horizontal and vertical pull?

title: Minimalism hurts the physique, except legs
statement: Minimalist programs cut exercises "like cost-cutting consultants" and are the enemy of a complete physique. Leg minimalism (one knee flexion plus one hinge) is fine.

title: Isolation is not for "definition"
statement: "Isolation for definition, compounds for size" is bro science; striations come from being lean.

title: Athletes train only purposeful muscle
statement: Athletes and fighters should train only muscle their sport uses, cut most isolation, pick lifts that reproduce the sport's joint angles, and never load the sport movement itself (dumbbell uppercuts, banded punches).

title: Keep the exercise list short
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: Variety comes from what you do with a few lifts, not from many lifts. Too many exercises means each is trained too rarely, technique and tonnage become unstable, and you become "a technician of new tricks rather than a master".
numbers: 20, 45 or 55 lifts named as too many
check: Is each muscle trained with a small set of lifts done often enough to progress?

title: Exercise and variation counts by level
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: The number of exercises per muscle and variations per lift grows with training age but stays small.
numbers: 2020: one method keeps a list of 15-20 lifts per body part to choose from. 2022: he rotates 6-7 favourites per muscle; biceps: beginner 1 exercise, NH 4-6. 2023: variations per lift novice 0-1, intermediate 1-2, advanced 3-5, max 5 "hard" variations per pattern. 2024: novices 1-2 exercises per muscle, never more than 4-5; small variations unlimited.
check: Does a novice program use 1-2 exercises per muscle (never more than 4-5)?

title: Hard vs soft variations
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: A soft variation keeps the pattern and changes the implement, grip, pause or rep range (near-full carryover, unlimited). A hard variation is a different pattern (pull-up vs pulldown, squat vs leg press), is a new skill, and should be capped. Rotate soft variations to prevent overuse without changing the pattern.
numbers: max ~5 hard variations

title: Change a lift only for a reason
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: Add or swap a variation only for a reason: a stall despite changing rep ranges, technique, overuse or injury. Never for boredom-driven novelty or to "shock the muscle" (he rates that D tier); constant switching keeps you relearning.
check: Does every exercise change have a stated reason (stall, overuse, injury, technique) rather than "muscle confusion"?

title: Rotation options must hit the muscle the same way
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: Rotations alternate close variations in one slot (week A / week B). Good pairs: Kroc/Meadows rows, RDL/stiff-leg, V-bar/rope pushdowns, bench/close-grip, dips/pause dips. Bad pairs: bench vs OHP, floor press vs paused bench, deadlift vs RDL, close-grip vs skull crusher, sumo vs conventional deficit. An "or" in his programs means pick one or rotate weekly, never both in one session.

title: Train a lift at least every 10-12 days
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: A lift practised less often than every 10-12 days doesn't belong in the program; heavy rotation that drops a lift to once a month is too rare. Big compounds should stay one variation; isolation can rotate more freely.
numbers: every 10-12 days minimum; weekly rotation only after 6-12 months of training
scope: All; weekly rotation for lifters with 6-12+ months.

title: When to rotate: scheduled or by need
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: He has said both that rotations must be scheduled and that they should only happen "when the muscle needs it". The 2023 version (scheduled for most, autoregulated for advanced) may reconcile them.
status: contradicted — 2020: always schedule rotations, never by feel; 2022: never schedule them (e.g. every two weeks) or trigger them by a plateau; 2023: scheduled for most people, autoregulated for advanced lifters.

title: Don't drop a lift because it plateaus
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: Rotating a lift out at every plateau teaches you to quit and resets you to beginner neural gains; grind through instead. Rotating back exercises every two months means never breaking through.

title: Rotations fight overuse and accommodation
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: Variations and rotations are a tool against overuse injury and accommodation, and give mental freshness. They are his main day-to-day volume-control tool (rated B tier); changing volume and intensity can also get around accommodation.

title: His own roster barely changes
section: How many exercises, variations and rotations
statement: He keeps the same lifts for years.
numbers: ~85% of his lifts unchanged since he started (2020); same program for 4 years (2022)

title: No lift is mandatory
statement: For a bodybuilder every lift, including squat, bench and deadlift, can be replaced by another in the same pattern. If a lift hurts after a fair try, plenty of others do the job.
scope: Bodybuilders; powerlifters must do competition lifts.

title: Fit the lifts to your build
statement: Leverages, height and mobility decide which lifts suit you; the program adapts to the lifter. Drop lifts that don't suit you instead of clinging to them (sunk cost).
scope: All; tall lifters often do better with sumo, low-bar to parallel, RDL/stiff-leg, block pulls, OHP.
check: Were the main lifts chosen to suit the lifter's build and pain-free history?

title: Enjoyment beats theoretical optimality
statement: A lift that is 75% optimal and that you actually do beats a 100% optimal lift you skip. Remove exercises you dislike; advanced lifters especially should refuse them.
numbers: 75% vs 100% optimal

title: Judge a new lift after about three months
statement: Start a new lift light and judge it only after training it seriously for about three months, by progress rather than feel; allow a tuning phase. Only program lifts you have done regularly for 3+ months. Keep a ranked list of lifts done, a "to try" list and an "exercise graveyard".
numbers: ≥3 months trial; tuning phase up to 6 months

title: What makes a good hypertrophy lift
statement: His criteria: stretch under load, high stability, good stimulus-to-fatigue (judged per target muscle), low cardio cost, quick setup, and progressable. A lift without a stretch can't rank above "decent"; if form breaks as soon as you load it, it's useless for hypertrophy.
numbers: setup under ~3 min or it gets skipped
check: Do the main lifts load the target in a stretch, stay stable under load and set up in a few minutes?

title: Prefer lifts with a negative
statement: Most lifts should have a controlled eccentric. Positive-only or explosive lifts (Olympic lifts, Pendlay rows, dumped deadlifts) are weaker for hypertrophy; safely loading a lengthened muscle gives the best gains.

title: Feel and soreness are quick checks only
statement: Mind-muscle connection and soreness are quick ways to see what a lift hits, but long-term progress decides.

title: Staples over gimmicks
statement: Prefer time-tested lifts over influencer variants and combo lifts (hip-thrust-to-floor-press, Cuban press, king squat, Bradford press). One load can't suit two patterns; boring stable lifts beat flashy ones. Intermediates are prime targets for gimmicks.

title: Technicality-to-hypertrophy ratio
statement: Avoid highly technical lifts (full Olympic lifts, advanced ring skills, power cleans for novices) or include them only sparingly. Use block/hang/partial versions, or split the lift into its parts, which he estimates is about 5x better for hypertrophy.
numbers: split version ~5x better for hypertrophy

title: Olympic lifts rank low for size
statement: Olympic lifts are near the bottom for hypertrophy (technical, no eccentric); use hang, block or power versions, or split them into pull, front squat and press. Power cleans have no place in novice programs.
confidence: high — ~10 videos, 2020→2024, one 2024 line says they "can be steered toward hypertrophy"

title: Branch across patterns
statement: Spread work across movement patterns instead of piling variations of one lift; pair antagonists or unrelated muscles. Bench-only pressing invites plateaus and shoulder trouble.

title: Don't be dogmatic about tools
statement: Don't play favourites (barbell-only, big-three-only, machine-only). Bodybuilders compete on a stage, not with implements, so use every tool.

title: Copying feats won't copy a physique
statement: Doing an athlete's signature feats won't give you his physique; borrow only what builds muscle. Gymnasts' arms come from 10+ years at 5-6 hours a day, and 15 pull-ups don't make that back.
numbers: 10+ years, 5-6 h/day (gymnasts)

title: "Functional training" is mostly noise
statement: Every resistance exercise is functional for something; curls are functional for hypertrophy. Most "functional training" talk is nonsense.

title: How much exercise selection matters
statement: He has called exercise selection both paramount and a by-product of programming.
status: contradicted — 2021: "selection dictates how your physique turns out", so it is paramount; also 2021: for naturals selection is a by-product of programming; 2023: only B tier.

title: His roster drifted to stretch-heavy, stable lifts
statement: His own favourites moved from the barbell big lifts to lifts with a better stretch and stimulus-to-fatigue: RDL over deadlift, weighted dips and ring push-ups over bench, heel-elevated/SSB/belt/split squats over back squats, a Smith incline press over the military press. Per-muscle picks are in ch. 6, the big lifts' role in ch. 7.
numbers: 2023-24: deadlift ~once a month; ~80% of squat volume heel-elevated
scope: NH's own training; his recommendations followed.
status: changed — 2020: back squat, bench, deadlift and barbell OHP as the core; 2023-24: RDL, dips/ring push-ups, heel-elevated and split squats, Smith/machine presses.

title: The specificity tree, later downgraded
statement: Early on he organised lifts as a tree: branches are movement patterns, each topped by a king lift that lower lifts must feed, and no lift without close neighbours. Later he rated specificity C tier and "not important for bodybuilding"; closeness is judged by the muscle trained, not carryover.
status: changed — 2020-21: specificity must be respected and the tree governs selection; 2023-24: C tier, not important.

title: Choose exercises before anything else
statement: Build the exercise list before choosing the template, volume, intensity and frequency. "If the exercise selection is rotten, the whole program stinks."

title: Open with the heaviest compound
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Always open with the heaviest, most demanding compound or strength lift, never with isolation (laterals, calf raises, leg extensions, leg curls, pulldowns, shrugs). You are freshest at the start, and the last exercises get skipped, so order by importance.
check: Does each session open with its heaviest compound rather than an isolation lift?

title: Prioritise a weak point with a compound
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Opening with isolation for a weak point is pointless; open with a compound variation that targets it instead (e.g. incline press for upper chest).

title: Upper days long, lower days short
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Upper days are a "laundry list" and lower days a "Post-it", because lower-body lifts bring more volume and systemic fatigue per exercise.

title: Upper days: horizontal and vertical press plus a row
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: An upper day needs a horizontal press and a vertical press, plus a horizontal row; he calls it the "winning combo".

title: Don't stack similar heavy compounds
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Don't put similar heavy compounds back to back or superset two energy-expensive compounds (e.g. squat + snatch-grip deadlift, deadlift + hack squat, RDL + chin-ups). Bi-sets at most; a deadlift goes first, never fourth.
check: Are heavy compounds of the same pattern kept apart rather than stacked or supersetted?

title: No two versions of the same lift in a day
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Two near-identical lifts in one session are redundant (bench + dips, ring dips + ring push-ups, leg press + hack squat, RDL + good morning, two pushdowns); pick one and rotate.

title: Know the purpose of each exercise
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Plan the day by listing body parts, then the lifts; every exercise should have a known purpose, like a recipe.

title: Supersets: different muscles, not the same one
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Superset different or antagonist muscles (safe for beginners). Three or four exercises in a row for the same muscle is the "cardinal sin" unless done on purpose; side raises plus rear flies fatigue each other. In giant sets go from heaviest to higher reps.

title: Don't pre-exhaust the target
section: Order and structure of the session
statement: Pre-exhaustion lowers the target's force output: pec deck before pressing is a mistake, and hamstrings before deadlifts shifts load to the lower back. Light band flies for a pump are fine; lats before barbell rows is more defensible. Pre-fatigue is for advanced lifters only, since earlier it masks poor technique.

title: Free weights stay the base for naturals
statement: Free weights should be most of a natural's training; machines and cables complement them. Machine-only lifters stay small, never learn fatigue management, and their tendons don't adapt.

title: Machines, cables and Smith became legitimate
statement: Machines, cables and the Smith machine are good for stable, hard, joint-friendly sets and extra volume, because they offload stability. Most people misuse them with too much weight and too little range; don't go low-rep on machines.
scope: All, more so in later videos.
status: changed — 2020: machines for advanced lifters only, he was biased against them and used none; 2023-24: free weights and machines equally effective, he moved much of his triceps and pressing work to cables/Smith.

title: Stability is a means, not the goal
statement: Unstable lifts are fine if done consistently, but most top hypertrophy lifts happen to be stable.

title: Calisthenics for the upper body, weights for the legs
statement: Calisthenics are great for the upper body and poor for legs; skills (planche, levers, muscle-ups, one-arm moves) build skill, not muscle. Best bodyweight moves: pull-up, inverted row, push-up, leg raise, rings.
status: changed — 2020: rings have a poor technicality-to-hypertrophy ratio; 2024: calisthenics for the upper body plus free weights for the lower body is his ideal and how he trains.

title: Unilateral work went from disliked to A tier
statement: Unilateral lifts are worthwhile; by 2023-24 he rates them A tier and split squats are his favourite leg lift.
status: changed — 2020: personal bias against unilateral work; 2023-24: A tier, favourite leg lift.

title: Bands are support tools
statement: Bands are good for joints, pump, recovery and finishers but unnecessary as main hypertrophy work.

title: Carries and strongman implements are a small part
statement: Carries, sleds, yokes, Atlas stones and sandbags are a small part of his training and not very effective for hypertrophy, except farmer's carries for traps and forearms.
numbers: about 5% of his training

title: Bodybuilding form: target, pain-free, reproducible
statement: Good bodybuilding form targets the intended muscle, is pain-free and is reproducible every rep; how much you lift is not a criterion. It may mean lifting less at first, but it recovers better and correlates with long-term progress.
check: Is every rep aimed at the target muscle, pain-free and repeatable?

title: Execution is half the result
statement: Execution is about half of results and programming the other half; a great program executed badly won't deliver. Form is "mandatory" to lift for years without setbacks.
numbers: ~50% execution / 50% programming

title: Technique sits between load and range
statement: Technique is S tier because it directs stress to the muscle, but it is individual. His 2024 order: load as the precondition, then technique, range of motion and tempo; time under tension is just a by-product of tempo.

title: Pick the version that works the muscle hardest
statement: Choose the variation or leverage that makes the target work hardest, not the one that makes you strongest; "challenge the muscle with as little weight as possible". For hypertrophy pick the technique that piles up the most tonnage safely over time, even if its 1RM is lower.
check: Is technique chosen to load the target muscle rather than to maximise the weight lifted?

title: Strength form vs bodybuilding form
statement: Powerlifting technique minimises range and maximises explosiveness (arch, low bar, sumo), which puts optimal strength form and optimal bodybuilding form at opposite ends. Earlier he said there is "only form".
status: contradicted — 2021: there is only form, any lift can serve size or strength; later: the two optima sit at opposite ends.

title: No universal form, but universal faults
statement: There is no single perfect form, but some faults are always wrong: lumbar rounding on deadlifts, flaring elbows on bench, knee valgus on squats. Deadlift hip height, upper-back rounding, knee travel, bench touch point and elbow tuck depend on the lifter. Leverages are no excuse for bad form.

title: Neither form police nor "form doesn't matter"
statement: Both extremes are wrong: the "form police" who demand one way, and those who say technique doesn't matter. Rules exist but are flexible guidelines; form policing comes from powerlifting judging and is valid only in competition.

title: Beginners get rigid rules; exotic form is earned
statement: Beginners need strict good-vs-bad rules first. Exotic form (rounding the upper back, Arnold-style body English) is earned, and a strong lifter's sloppy form never justifies it for novices.

title: Beginners chase technique, not weight
statement: Beginners focus on technique; if technique regresses as the weight rises, you are on a dangerous path. Until a lift is mastered, progressive overload trains learning rather than muscle.

title: Warm-up reps and top-set reps look the same
statement: Poor form is a choice: if your warm-ups are clean, your top sets can be too. Warm-up reps and top-set reps must look identical.

title: Good form isn't pretty form
statement: Proper bodybuilding form is not the same as pretty form, and visual cues can't judge danger. Lumbar rounding on deadlifts is a symptom (hips shooting up, lost thoracic extension), not the root cause.

title: Check your own form
statement: Film your lifts about once a month and be honest; his own deadlift drift only showed on video. A technique you feel rock-solid in is likely your strongest, and technique should be verifiable by eye and by how the body feels afterwards.
numbers: film ~1×/month

title: Every technique must be justifiable
statement: Every lift, rep range and frequency should be justifiable; bodybuilding is experimentation, but any technique has to be both effective and safe.

title: The last rep looks like the first
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Bodybuilders own technique from the first rep to the last: the 10th rep looks as crisp as the first, only slower. Near failure only speed changes, never form. Form breakdown is acceptable in strength sport, not for size.
check: Does the last rep of a set look like the first, only slower?

title: Avoid mechanical failure
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Mechanical failure (your structure gives out before the muscle) is bad mainly because tonnage stops going to the target. You want to be limited by the muscle, never by structure. It comes from fixable weak links: thoracic extension, setup, technique (e.g. good-morning squats, hips shooting up on deadlifts).

title: Artificial vs organic mechanical failure
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: "Artificial" mechanical failure (bad technique or bar placement) is correctable. "Organic" mechanical failure is a deliberately weak position (e.g. a crane-style stiff-leg with the bar near the toes) used to fail the target sooner.

title: Weight selection makes or breaks form
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Structural integrity comes mostly from weight selection: perfect form at 400 lb can fall apart at 450. Good technique won't save a bad loading decision, and "there is no bad form" ignores this.
numbers: 400 vs 450 lb example

title: Stop when form starts to break
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: If you sense form breaking, stop and put the bar down. If a squat rep would turn into a good morning or the hips shoot up, rack it and keep that rep in reserve for a later exercise.

title: Ego lifting defined
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Ego lifting is using more weight than the exercise can turn into a justified stimulus; cutting range to lift more counts. "If 10 lb dumbbells challenge you, use them." Accusing others of ego lifting often reveals insecurity.
check: Is the load light enough that range isn't cut and the target does the work?

title: A horsed rep is worth less weight
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: A heaved rep gives roughly the stimulus of a deliberate rep with about 30 lb less; you could cut load ~30% and lift slower for similar hypertrophy (not strength).
numbers: ~30 lb; ~30% load

title: Rep ranges follow how form holds up
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Lifts whose form breaks under heavy loads get higher reps from the start; low reps only where you can grind safely. Isolation needs perfect form and mind-muscle connection, so keep it in higher reps.
numbers: low reps (6-10, 8-12) only where grinding is safe

title: Respect the "red zone"
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Every movement has a red zone, the disadvantaged range that stimulates the muscle most and carries the most risk. Enter it with caution; don't avoid it. Breakdown usually happens at the turn from negative to positive.

title: Don't rush through the bottom
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: Bouncing the bench, dive-bombing squats, slamming deadlifts and touch-and-go reps skip the hardest range and give up tension, technique and joint health.

title: Pristine form vs slightly heavier reps
section: Form breakdown, load and ego lifting
statement: He once said pristine form can leave you on "baby weight" and that slightly ego-lifting with more weight and a better stretch can be better; elsewhere he calls cutting range and body English ego lifting.
status: contradicted — 2023: a bit of ego lifting with more weight and stretch "can be better"; 2023-24: cutting range to lift more and body English are ego lifting.

title: No lumbar flexion under load
statement: Any lumbar flexion under load is form breakdown and wrong for bodybuilders. It is a correctable flaw, not inevitable, and it also kills leg drive. Anyone without a severe spinal condition can find a variation with a fully neutral back.
scope: All loaded squats, hinges and rows.
check: Does the lower back stay neutral on every loaded squat, hinge and row rep?

title: The lower back is a bridge, not a crane
statement: The lower back is a rigid, neutral bridge between legs and upper body; only its angle changes during a rep, never its flexion. The legs produce the power. Lower-back pain the day after deadlifts means you aren't pulling with the legs.

title: Upper-back rounding is tolerable, but drags the lower back
statement: Thoracic rounding is less dangerous than lumbar rounding and acceptable in some contexts, but it tends to pull the lower back into rounding. The spine follows the neck: head down starts the chain.

title: Rounding is usually not a choice
statement: On squats and deadlifts the back usually rounds because the body can't stay upright and reshapes around the bar on the positive. It is a technique and intention issue more than weak muscles; causes include weak core, glutes or thoracic extension, setup and poor cues.

title: Neutral spine is not a vertical torso
statement: The torso can be angled, even horizontal as in Pendlay rows, as long as the spine stays straight. The more the torso leans forward, the more potential for rounding.

title: Simple bracing
statement: Before a pull or squat: shoulders back, breathe and brace, flex the upper back, and keep that spine position through the rep. Bracing is a normal nose breath and tightening the abs as if about to be punched, without a big belly breath, sucking in or a ritual. He rates bracing C tier, mattering on heavy squats and deadlifts.

title: Closed jaw, nose breathing
statement: Keep the jaw clenched and breathe through the nose; an open mouth is a "strength vacuum". On squats hold the breath down and exhale on the way up.

title: Lifting posture is everyday posture
statement: Head pulled up as if by a string, chin up, chest out, shoulders back and down, glutes slightly tense, core braced. Lifting with good form is the best long-term posture fix; hunched computer posture limits depth and feeds rounded deadlifts. He ties this to Musashi's posture advice.

title: Hips shooting up overloads the lower back
statement: When the hips shoot back or up on squats or deadlifts, glute and posterior-chain drive is lost and the lower back takes the load. Reversing the squat too fast causes it.

title: Control the negative
statement: A negative that gravity does for you doesn't count; resist it. "The weight should not lead you." Cables and machines invite dropping it; free weights force control.
check: Is the eccentric of every rep (deadlifts excepted) controlled rather than dropped?

title: The negative sets up the positive
statement: Negative technique dictates positive technique, and slow negatives preserve form. The muscle you feel stretching on the way down is the one you'll feel on the way up.

title: At least about one second down
statement: Control the eccentric for at least ~1 s; beyond that tempo is preference. Pick one sensible tempo and keep it regardless of load.
numbers: ≥ ~1 s eccentric; a 2 s vs 6 s negative ≈ 20 lb of load

title: Slow down most near the stretch
statement: Slow the rep most in the range closest to the stretch; letting the bar drop there is cheating and where injuries happen.

title: The positive is the fatigue gauge
statement: Only control the negative; the positive is where you slow down and fail. Negatives should stay the same speed or get slower through a set, since speeding up means momentum. On the last rep he lengthens the negative.

title: Don't count or exaggerate tempo
statement: Prescribed 3-4 s (or 4-0-1-0) negatives on everything are counterproductive: they cut load and progression and confuse novices. Dropped negatives are just as bad: "too slow and too fast both belong in the garbage". Fixed tempos suit only very advanced lifters.
numbers: 3-4 s on everything = too much
scope: All; fixed tempos for very advanced only.

title: Time under tension is a by-product
statement: Time under tension is overrated (C tier), a by-product of tempo like the pump is of high reps; chasing it means baby weights.

title: Tempo's weight in his hierarchy grew
statement: Tempo is S tier in his 2023 list (control and stretch), yet it ranks last among load, range and tempo: set range and load first, then add tempo. Slow tempo's real job is keeping ego in check.
status: changed — 2020: "slow negative, fast positive"; 2021: don't slow negatives on purpose, TUT overrated; 2023-24: tempo S tier, slow near the stretch, ≥1 s eccentric, still no counting.

title: Explosive but controlled positive
statement: Drive the positive with intent, but not so hard that form breaks (e.g. the bar leaving the shoulders); intent matters more than speed. The first reps at 70-80% should move fast.
numbers: first two reps at 70-80% fast

title: Bar speed doesn't show effort
statement: Lifting speed says nothing about effort: his slow reps may look like a max with 5 reps left, and explosive reps can still build muscle.

title: Fast unloaded negatives and negatives-only are not useful
statement: Fast negatives to "lengthen the muscle faster" are hogwash; the stretch reflex at the bottom stresses the muscle more than extra slow eccentric time. Negatives-only training is impractical and of little relevance.

title: ROM is distance under load, relative to leverages
statement: For hypertrophy, range of motion is how far the load travels under tension, and it depends on leverages; there is no objective "full ROM" (standards come from competition). A tall lifter's parallel squat can travel more than a short lifter's ass-to-grass.

title: Full range by default, within comfort
statement: Longer range generally means more hypertrophy (more stretch, more travel), so full range is the default, but use the range you can do comfortably and sustainably. Trimming a little barely matters; keep at least one full-range leg lift.
check: Is full range (or lengthened-biased range) the default for the main lifts?

title: Effective range is what counts
statement: What matters is the part of the range where the target is under the most stress; extra range only helps if the load challenges the muscle through it.
numbers: pullover example: ~30% effective, trimmed to 70-80% effective

title: Range dictates load, never the reverse
statement: "Let ROM dictate the load, never the load dictate the ROM." There are two valid reasons to limit range: more target recruitment, or better performance (tempo, load, reps). Cutting range to add weight usually removes the most stimulating part.
numbers: if a shallower squat allows more than ~20% extra load vs below parallel, you cut too much

title: Range cuts usually chop the bottom
statement: Most range cutting removes the bottom of the negative (the weakest point), which is exactly the part that matters.
numbers: deadlifts above the knee are ~twice as easy

title: Partials are earned and planned
statement: Partials have a place (A tier in 2023) but are scheduled with intent, never improvised after a failed rep; novices start with full range. The 2021 "odd-lift partial craze" produced small lifters who never built a base.
status: changed — 2020: full range best, novices never use partials; 2021: full range all the time is a mistake; 2023: partials A tier.

title: What a good partial is for
statement: A good partial lets you do more reps with more weight for the target, and can be added deliberately to help full-range progress. Earlier he said partials are for high reps, not for moving very heavy weight.
status: contradicted — 2020: partials for high reps, not heavy weight; 2023: a good partial allows more reps with more weight.

title: Lengthened partials
statement: In 2024 he says lengthened partials likely beat full range, which beats shortened partials, probably because they allow more load and reps in the stretch.
status: contradicted — 2023: lengthened partials C tier, used only for calves; 2024: may beat full range (three months apart).

title: More range isn't always better
statement: Extreme deficits and cambered bars mostly add stress on joints and tendons (pecs, shoulders) rather than muscle.

title: No ROM dogma
statement: "Full range or don't lift" is elitist; combine full range with partials. Finding your best range isn't preaching short range.

title: Build depth gradually
statement: Don't force ranges you lack the mobility or leverage for; build depth gradually like load.

title: The lockout adds almost nothing
statement: At lockout the joints are stacked and the skeleton holds the load, so it contributes almost nothing to hypertrophy (C tier). Lockout and depth standards exist for judging; "joints are meant to lock" is an appeal to nature.
numbers: ~1% of hypertrophy; ~2% extra triceps work on OHP

title: Lock out only when it helps
statement: Lock out if it keeps you in the groove, is pain-free and earns more reps or load; skip it if it throws off technique or hurts. Never locking out "to keep tension" can reduce total tension if it costs reps. Lock out dips for stability.

title: The top squeeze is low value
statement: Squeezing at the top is C/D tier: the muscle is least active there, and removing it doesn't reduce growth. A squeeze only helps you feel the muscle; holding lockout for 2 s is just resting, and thrusting the hips at the top of a squat or deadlift does nothing.
status: changed — 2020: squeeze at the top (slow curl positives for the squeeze; on calf raises the squeeze matters more than the stretch); 2021-24: the squeeze gives no tension, C/D tier.

title: Stretch over squeeze
statement: If you must choose between the top squeeze and the bottom stretch, prioritise the stretch.

title: A bodybuilding pause is short
statement: Pause until momentum is gone, keeping the stretch, with no rocking or heaving; no 20 s pauses. Pauses add a small stretched-tension bonus, not a major driver.

title: Pause reps: useful, used sparingly
statement: Pause reps (B tier) clean up form, protect the red zone and cure fear of the hole, but the stretch reflex adds hypertrophy, so use them sparingly. Regular back-offs may beat paused ones; don't open the day with paused work. Pause squat is the best paused lift, paused bench second (a lifesaver for shoulder pain); pause without pins to keep control.

title: Isometric holds are poor for size
statement: Isometric holds are D tier for hypertrophy (arm wrestlers use them for strength without size); constant tension through the range beats holds.

title: Cheating defined
statement: Cheating is using momentum or leverage to bypass part of the range; a partial is also a cheat. It is not a moral question, only one of effectiveness.

title: Cheat reps: from tool to mostly waste
statement: He now prefers strict reps: cheat reps are mostly wasteful and body English is ego lifting. Cheat only in full control, on safe isolation lifts, and never on the negative.
numbers: old method: 6 strict + 3-4 cheated beats 6 strict
status: changed — 2020-22: cheat reps a legitimate tool (strict reps first, then controlled cheats; he did almost only cheat curls for ~10 years); 2022: strict curls would likely have given the same; 2023: C tier; 2024: ego lifting.
check: Are cheat reps absent, or limited to a few controlled extra reps on safe isolation lifts?

title: Rules if you cheat
statement: Decide before the set; apply the same cheat force every rep (escalating cheat is the problem); the cheat only brings the weight to where the muscle can finish it.
numbers: cheating 10% vs 50% gives very different results

title: Cheating sends tonnage elsewhere
statement: The real problem with cheating is that it's harder to direct tonnage to the target; more weight moved by other muscles doesn't make the target bigger.

title: Body English: rows yes, isolation no
statement: Some body English is fine on heavy back rows (Yates rows, a slight torso shift to finish a hard dumbbell row), not on rear-delt or arm isolation. Stop when reps get dirty.

title: What mind-muscle connection is
statement: Mind-muscle connection is the ability to prioritise a target within a compound so stronger muscles don't take the work: feeling fibres stretch and contract, not the pump. Pump doesn't prove a muscle worked, nor does its absence prove it didn't.

title: Feeling is not recruitment
statement: He doesn't feel his quads when squatting, yet they grow "like weeds". Mind-muscle connection (B tier) matters mainly for muscles that struggle to grow, which is really a form issue; it is no excuse for baby weights.
status: changed — 2020: central to prioritising muscles in compounds; 2021-23: useful mainly for lagging muscles, B tier.

title: Progress without feeling is fine
statement: If you progress without feeling the muscle, don't worry; build the connection when progress stalls. Its value is finding the technique that recruits the muscle.

title: How to build the connection
statement: Build it with isolation work before or after compounds, slower tempo with lighter weights, and stretching the target on the negative; then return to heavier loads. Pump helps too; the "spiritual" route is picturing the ideal muscle.

title: Obsessing over feel keeps you small
statement: Piles of useless reps, lower intensity and zoning out in search of feel keep muscles small. The goal is neither feel nor maximal speed but a challenging weight under control.

title: Stay mentally in the set
statement: Phone use during a set kills focus; checking out may leave a piece missing; pain from an unpadded bar distracts from the muscle.

title: Every lift has a technical rating
statement: Each lift has a technical rating: how much practice it takes to master and keep. Front squat, rings and Olympic lifts rate high.
numbers: curls ~2 weeks to master; snatch ~1 year

title: Technical lifts are "jealous"
statement: High-rated lifts decay fast and must be practised constantly; multi-joint lifts done once a month are relearned every time. Bodybuilders shouldn't invest in technical lifts that don't pay back in growth; easier variations (SSB or cross-arm front squats) lower the rating, and close variations maintain the main lift.

title: Enough skill, then stop
statement: Once neural adaptation to a lift is reached, more skill is useless; there is no point breaking the technical ceiling. "Technique is the enemy of the bodybuilder" [*inference*: this reconciles with TEC-03 as "master enough, no more"].

title: Skill comes fast and largely stays
statement: You lift with your nervous system: technique comes and goes fast, muscle slowly. Skill largely stays once built and relearning is faster; a week off squats or deadlifts often costs nothing, a year off feels wobbly. Once-a-week squatting isn't enough practice for a novice.

title: Learn and tweak lifts light
statement: Introduce movements with a learning curve extremely light; change stance or torso angle only with light weight, never at high intensity.

title: Variations change main-lift form
statement: Variations can bleed into the main lift for better or worse: box squats and good mornings can bake in a good-morning squat, stiff-legs bleed into the deadlift. Keep training the main lift itself. Exaggerating a fault (SSB, good mornings) can also teach the right pattern.

title: Bodyweight swings change technique
statement: Bodyweight changes alter squat, deadlift and bench technique, so aggressive bulk/cut cycles force relearning.

title: Leverages change setup, not the pattern
statement: Leverages change stance, grip, depth and lift choice, not the basic movement. Don't copy anyone's form; apply the pointers, since some techniques only work with the right structure.

title: Tall lifters need adapted technique
statement: Tall lifters need wider stances and grips, low bar, sumo or block pulls, and a longer technical adaptation; shoulder-width dogma fits lifters of about 5'7"-5'9". High-bar and conventional deadlifts force tall lifters into more lean and rounding, and short lifters' ass-to-grass can injure them.
numbers: tall = ≥6'0"-6'2"; standard advice fits ~5'7"-5'9"

title: Some bodies reject a pattern
statement: He cannot squat or pull with a wide stance (narrow hips, large waist). Upper-back rounding on heavy squats or RDLs may simply mean you aren't built for that lift.

title: Warm up with the lift itself
statement: Warm up with lighter sets of the lift itself to rehearse the pattern and get blood moving. No treadmill, no static stretching, no elaborate activation; he dropped band and plate activation. Warm-up reps use the same tempo and technique as top sets and are the place to fix technique (e.g. spotting too much lower back at 135).
check: Is the warm-up done with ramping sets of the first lift, using top-set technique, rather than cardio or activation drills?

title: As many warm-up sets as needed
statement: Do as many warm-up sets as you need; one set before a heavy deadlift is unrealistic. Only the first exercise of a movement pattern needs a full ramp. Warm-ups add volume, and the time needed is individual (longer for squats, older or bigger lifters).
numbers: ≈5-15 sets (he does ~18 on squats); jumps +20-50 lb (2022) or +50 lb over 4-5 sets (2023); 0-1 set for follow-up lifts

title: Warm-ups prime, they don't grow you
statement: Warm-ups aren't hard enough to build muscle but prime you for heavy weight; feel the muscles work and don't rush. High-rep warm-ups pre-fatigue a little, which doesn't matter for bodybuilders, but don't burn energy on high-rep warm-up systems.

title: Mobility comes from lifting through range
statement: Lifting through full range with manageable weight and clean form builds mobility; every loaded exercise is a weighted stretch. Static stretching and foam rolling are at most a supplement, and he doesn't stretch. Extreme fascia stretching is a gimmick.

title: Mobility is a muscular skill
statement: Mobility is a muscular skill on a spectrum ("robust rigidity") with no universal standard. You don't have to squat ass-to-grass, but every inch gained is tonnage. Program heavy lifts suited to your body plus light lifts that push mobility limits.

title: Weighted stretching is underused
statement: Loaded stretching is an underexplored, effective method (B tier); traps grow just from holding weight. The fully lengthened position is the weakest and riskiest.

title: Tight hips and squat stance test
statement: Tight hips limit squat depth and make the hips shoot up on deadlifts. Test with your natural squat stance or a seated figure-four, not toe touching.

title: Straps, not mixed grip
statement: Bodybuilders pull double overhand until grip fails, then strap up. Mixed grip creates imbalance and biceps-tear risk, and hook and mixed grips exist for competition (one deadlift video calls hook grip acceptable). Never mixed grip with straps or on shrugs/rows.
check: Are heavy pulls done double overhand or with straps rather than a mixed grip?

title: Strap anything grip would limit
statement: Use straps wherever grip would limit a non-grip exercise (rows, back work, snatch-grip shrugs, Bulgarian split squats), but not on locked pulldowns; train forearms directly. He straps rows only when needed, usually not on the first set.

title: Stack the wrists on every press
statement: Keep the wrist stacked over the forearm on any press; a bent-back wrist leads to tendinitis. Stacked wrists also make you stronger, and you shouldn't feel your wrists on OHP. Break the stack only for a clear benefit.
check: Are the wrists stacked over the forearms on every press?

title: Thumbless grip where the bar can't roll
statement: A thumbless/false grip deloads the wrist where the grip doesn't need securing (curls, raises, vertical presses, reverse curls, pull-ups). Never on heavy horizontal pressing, where the bar can roll.

title: Grip mechanics
statement: A closed, thumb-wrapped grip is strongest. Set the fingers so the bar can't shift (play halves grip strength); the last three fingers do the gripping. "Squeeze the bar as hard as possible" is mostly myth.

title: The legs move the deadlift
statement: The deadlift is "a leg press against the floor" with the back as a rigid bridge: neutral spine, very deep hips, knee flexion, strong hip drive. "Lift with your legs" is a poor cue because you always do; the problem is overusing the lower back.

title: Deadlift setup
statement: Bar over the whole foot, close to but not touching the shins. Bend the knees slightly, push the butt back and reach, then pull yourself into position so the hamstrings are tense, take the slack out, shoulders over the bar. Torso between vertical and horizontal, never parallel. Dragging the bar up the shins means you sat back too much; shoulders behind the bar means you're squatting it.

title: Patient off the floor
statement: Break the bar from the floor with steadily increasing leg pressure and a neutral spine, not "grip and rip". The bar leaves slowly but never slows down, and everything locks out together. People bend over to fake explosiveness off the floor.

title: The "fishing rod" deadlift
statement: When the knees lock early with a rounded back, the legs leave the lift and the back finishes it, causing the struggle past the knees. Most people who fail at the knee have a setup problem, not a strength problem.

title: No rounded-back deadlifting
statement: No one benefits from a rounded lower back on deadlifts; it is defensible only for elite lifters or a competition PR. Olympic lifters who round do so deliberately with light, controllable weight. Abort the pull if the back rounds.
check: Is any deadlift rep with a rounding lower back aborted rather than ground out?

title: Full deadlift lockout
statement: Unlike other lifts, the deadlift locks out fully: hips, knees and shoulders together with a neutral spine. No leaning back, hip thrusting or hyperextension. A soft lockout usually means thoracic rounding.

title: Deadlifts are positive-only
statement: Don't fight the deadlift negative: put the bar down and reset. Slow negatives tire you and sandbag the positive; a controlled negative gives slightly more hypertrophy, but the concentric-only puller gets more reps and fewer injuries. Use RDLs for eccentric work; no touch-and-go.
numbers: 4 s negatives wreck a novice's core within 3 reps
check: Are deadlifts done positive-only, with reset reps, and eccentric work given to RDLs?

title: Low deadlift reps because structure fails first
statement: Keep deadlift sets low-rep: at high reps thoracic extension gives out before the legs, so 15-rep deadlifts are junk volume. With shaky form, do a few sets of 4-5 and add weight only when confident. Place deadlifts early, not at the end of back day.
numbers: 4-6 reps max, stop around 5-6; shaky form 2-3×4-5

title: Pick a variation that keeps the back neutral
statement: If the floor is a problem, choose a stance or variation that allows a neutral back: sumo, trap bar, blocks/rack (max work off blocks, submax from the floor). No cat-back floor pulls; behind-the-back deadlifts not recommended. Deadlift range is arbitrary anyway (set by plate diameter).
scope: Lifters who can't pull neutral from the floor.

title: How deadlift variations differ
statement: Variations differ in torso angle and knee and hip flexion, and torso angle plus knee flexion decide what's trained. Sumo's sticking point is off the floor, conventional's near lockout; the trap bar has more quad drive.

title: Deadlift odds and ends
statement: Learn leg drive with submaximal conventional deficit deadlifts for about 10 reps, and finish deadlift day with light hyperextensions. No heeled shoes for floor pulls (they add a deficit). If the hips shift, move one foot slightly out; a staggered stance only matters if it hurts.
numbers: deficit deadlifts ~10 reps, submax

title: "Deadlift CNS fatigue" is lower-back strain
statement: What people call deadlift CNS fatigue is usually lower-back strain from pulling with the back; squats are actually more taxing.

title: Squat with the knees first
statement: The squat is knee flexion first: break at the knees and let the hips hinge naturally at depth (limit it, don't resist it). Hinging first turns it into a good morning. Torso angle changes come from the hip, never spinal flexion, and should match on the way down and up.

title: The good-morning squat is the cardinal fault
statement: When the hips rise first and the squat becomes a good morning, the tonnage number stays the same but the lower back takes the load instead of the quads, and it leads to injury. Fix it with technique, thoracic extension, core and glute work and 1 s paused squats, not a box.
numbers: 1 s pause squats
check: Do squat reps rise with chest and hips together rather than turning into a good morning?

title: Knee-dominant stance for size
statement: For size keep the squat knee-dominant: medium-to-narrow stance, toes forward, knees allowed forward (knees past toes is fine); heel elevation or a slant board helps. Very wide stances raise the number but cut quad work, and a copied wide, toes-out stance repeatedly injured him.
status: changed — 2020: slightly wider stance with knees out spares the knee; 2021-24: narrow/medium stance, toes forward, knees forward.

title: Squat depth
statement: Squat as deep as you can without back or knee pain or butt wink (a "power leak"); stop before it. Parallel or a hair below is a fine heavy standard, the last few inches add little, and quarter squats stress the knees and grow nothing. Safety and repeatability beat depth.
numbers: parallel or slightly below

title: Quads are stretched below parallel
statement: Quads keep stretching below parallel; the idea that quads only need a short range is a myth. Graduate to free squats once you can go below parallel, since half squats shear the knee.

title: Controlled descent, no dive-bombing
statement: Control the descent; never dive-bomb (patellar tendinitis, knees shooting forward). The bottom should feel rock solid, like sitting; reverse with a controlled bounce, practised light.

title: Bar and upper back on the back squat
statement: No pad: the bar sits tight on the skin. Use as narrow a grip as you can to pack the upper back (narrow it set by set in warm-ups), never relax thoracic extension, and drive the bar into the traps out of the hole. Grip width still depends on proportions; pad pain fades within 2 weeks to 2 months.

title: Unrack and walk out
statement: Unrack from directly under the bar with minimal knee bend and walk out in about four steps, widening into your stance.
numbers: ~4 steps

title: High bar vs low bar
statement: Try both. Low bar suits tall, lanky lifters (bar over midfoot, back a rigid bridge); high bar suits heeled shoes and knee flexion. On low bar use a thumbless grip and press up from under the bar to spare the wrists.

title: Box squats don't fix squats
statement: On a box most people sit back, rock and good-morning up; the box catches you where the squat gets hard and reinforces forward lean. If used, go straight down and up. Touch-and-go SSB box squats are fine for glutes.

title: No knee valgus
statement: Push the knees out and press through the whole foot. Valgus may be acceptable for a one-rep max athlete but harms tendons over a bodybuilder's many reps; light paused or higher-rep squats help control it.

title: Front squat is a rack-and-thoracic lift
statement: Most front squatters (he says 80%) are limited by thoracic extension and the rack, not the legs; the lift fails when the bar dumps. Elbows high, wrists not cocked back, fingers only stop the roll (a three-finger grip is fine), torso upright. It took him about two years to learn, and he'd tell his past self not to bother.
numbers: ~80% limited by rack/thoracic; ~2 years to learn

title: Safety squat bar folds you forward
statement: The SSB pushes you forward (the opposite of a front squat), taxing the posterior chain. Never use your normal working weight the first time, and don't flip the bar.

title: Machine squats need machine form
statement: Smith machine squats are S tier with feet and hips forward, since the machine replaces the hip hinge; don't copy free-weight form on it, and novices should learn free squats. Belt squats: close stance, vertical torso, knees forward, heels elevated, not too low; wide toes-out stance is misuse.

title: Split squats for quads vs glutes
statement: For quads: front foot close, knee travelling past the toes and tracking the foot, foot straight, slow reps unless you're an athlete. For glutes: front foot further out and the torso leaning onto the thigh as you descend. Prefer split squats to lunges.
