numbers: 8-12 reps (quad bias)

title: Bench: shoulder safety first
statement: On bench, protect the shoulders first: arch, shoulders back and tight, leg drive, elbows tucked not flared. The arch shortens the range and keeps the shoulders "in the pocket"; leg drive adds stability, not magic force. He avoids feet-up bench.
check: Is the bench done with shoulders set back and down and elbows tucked?

title: Elbow flare on bench
statement: He has called flared elbows always wrong and, later, the way to recruit more chest.
status: contradicted — 2020: flaring is objectively bad 100% of the time; 2022: flaring is how you recruit more chest.

title: Grip width on bench
statement: Narrower grips deload the shoulder and allow more pressing volume; wide grips internally rotate it. Tall or broad lifters may need a wider grip.

title: Touch point and the Spoto pause
statement: Touching the chest is a powerlifting requirement; long-armed lifters can cut range. A pause just shy of the chest (Spoto) keeps the pecs loaded and saves the shoulders.
numbers: 1-2 s pause

title: No touch-and-go bench
statement: Touch-and-go bench is mostly ego and momentum and stresses the shoulder; pause instead, which also fixes uneven pressing. The ideal is a controlled negative with a micro-pause.
check: Are bench reps paused or controlled at the chest rather than bounced?

title: Bench negative speed
statement: He preaches slow negatives in general, but on bench he lowers "fairly fast but controlled", using the lats, because slow negatives never helped his positive.
status: contradicted — slow negatives as general philosophy vs fairly fast controlled bench negatives (both 2020).

title: Lower the incline
statement: Most people set the incline too steep, which trains shoulders rather than upper chest; lower it.

title: Dips technique
statement: Lean forward for chest or stay vertical for triceps, and don't switch mid-rep (losing the groove costs ~30% performance). Control the eccentric and pause at the bottom; upper arm parallel to the floor is a legitimate full range, deeper optional. Grip slightly wider than the shoulders; parallel bars are most shoulder-friendly. Lock out at the top for stability.
numbers: ~30% performance lost when switching groove

title: Ring push-ups and spotting
statement: Ring push-ups give a deeper, safer chest stretch than cambered bars; deficit ring push-ups are unnecessary. When spotted, tell the spotter exactly what help and how many reps you want; lift-off should be minimal and even, and you de-rack by extending the elbows.

title: OHP: the bottom is where delts work
statement: On the overhead press the bottom range (shoulders flexed under load) is where the delts work, so start low; pin presses and nose-level starts skip it (worse than skipping lockout). Elbow lockout is optional, but lock the shoulders and push the head "through the window". He never locks his elbows (tendinitis).
numbers: he starts at mid-chest
check: Does each overhead press rep start low (around the chin/upper chest) rather than from nose level?

title: OHP range in his own pressing
statement: In 2020 he said both that he prefers full range down to the collarbone and that he doesn't use full range on the overhead press.
status: contradicted — full range to the collarbone vs not full range (both 2020).

title: OHP details
statement: The real overhead press danger is leaning back until it becomes an incline press; some momentum is fine for novices, but no OHP after squats or deadlifts for them. Stand, brace and hold thoracic extension. Press in the scapular plane with the elbows slightly forward; behind-the-neck only with mobility and a light ramp (he avoids it).

title: OHP rep floor rose
statement: Low reps degraded his overhead press form, so he raised the minimum.
numbers: 2020: ≥5 reps; 2022: never below 6
status: changed — 2020: at least 5 reps; 2022: never below 6.

title: Order presses by shoulder demand
statement: Order presses from most to least shoulder-taxing. Seated vs standing doesn't matter if the legs aren't involved.

title: Pull with the back, arms are hooks
statement: Rows and pulls are done with the back; the arms are hooks, and the back moves and stretches with the weight. Arm-only rowing is a hammer curl.

title: Let the shoulder blades travel on rows
statement: On rows let the scapulae protract so the back gets stretched; the bottom stretch matters most and pulling all the way back can be counterproductive. Constant "shoulders back" is the wrong cue for rows (pull-ups keep scapular engagement).
status: changed — 2020-21: retract the scapulae, novices fail by not retracting; 2024: protraction for the stretch matters more.
check: Do rows let the shoulder blades move forward into a stretch at the bottom?

title: A row is a held deadlift position
statement: On bent-over rows the hamstrings, glutes and lower back hold rigid while the back pulls; floor or touch-and-go rows drift into hip hinges (his own cheat rows turned into RDLs). Novices who can't deadlift can't row safely.

title: Barbell rows: moderate reps, pronated grip
statement: Below 6 reps you jerk the bar with the legs. Barbell rows are somewhat full-body: not too strict, not too cheated. Pronated grip, no supinated or mixed grip.
numbers: 3×6-10, never below 6; 5×5 "terrible"

title: Dumbbell and Kroc rows
statement: Dumbbell rows: both feet on the floor (staggered/tripod), no knee on the bench; pull in an arc so the lat stretches and the weight travels forward; no hip shifts to heave. Kroc rows: weight in front, pronated wrists, upright torso, not too few reps (5-8 invites cheating).
numbers: Kroc rows ≥6-10, prefer 10-15

title: Steer the row with elbows and torso
statement: Flared elbows and a higher touch point bias upper back, traps and rear delts; tucked elbows and a lower touch bias lats (lower also rhomboids). A more horizontal torso means more lats. Never row high to the chest.

title: Rounded-back rows, earned
statement: Rounded-back T-bar rows and deep rounded rack hinges aren't really dangerous with moderate load, an engaged posterior chain and slow tempo, but they fatigue the erectors. The lumbar rule for squats and deadlifts is unchanged.
status: changed — 2020: rounding on rows is bad form and he "never rounds"; 2024: rounded T-bar rows and rack hinges at slow tempo are acceptable earned form.

title: Standardise row reps
statement: The weight must touch the chest or the set is over; cable rows that swing from the hips are cheats.

title: Strict bodybuilding pull-ups
statement: Start from the top with the negative, lower more slowly than you pull, keep the scapulae engaged, stay under the bar in line with the body, and pull with the back. No dangling or kipping, and don't force the head over the bar. Strict reps cost load but give better hypertrophy; keep the same grip and tempo when loaded.
check: Are pull-ups strict (controlled negative, no kipping or dangling)?

title: No dead hang at the bottom of a pull-up
statement: A dead hang at the bottom disengages the lats and scapulae. The lat's maximum stretch is just before you lose retraction, so train that "striking range". Dead hangs are a separate tendon drill; weighted hangs don't grow lats.
numbers: 8 reps in the striking range beat 4 full reps

title: Pull-up grip cues and learning drills
statement: Pressure on the pinkies, rotate the arms outward, elbows close, take the slack out first; use a narrower grip if wide feels all arms. Learn back-pulling with scapular engage/disengage drills on the bar.

title: Pulldowns: vertical, slow, full stretch
statement: Pull in line with the cable, slowly, with the handles overhead rather than in front. Let the stack stretch the lats at the top until just before the shoulders internally rotate. Straps aren't needed on locked pulldowns.
status: changed — 2020: lean back and pull a V-bar to the stomach; 2023-24: don't lean way back, pull in line with the cable (leaning back is valid but he prefers vertical).

title: Pullovers: stretch the rib cage, not the shoulder
statement: Lie across the bench with the hips dropped below the shoulders, slight elbow bend, elbows turned in overhead, inhale on the negative. Stretch the rib cage, not the shoulder: stop when the lat stops stretching, no full shoulder extension, and skip the dead top. If the triceps take over, bend the elbows more or use an EZ bar. Not on the floor or a bed.

title: RDL: bent-knee, negative-first hinge
statement: The RDL is a negative-first hinge with bent knees: start from a rack, push the hips back, keep the bar close (or slightly floating with the weight still under you), go until the plates nearly kiss the floor, no bounce. A stiff-leg lets the bar float away. Most people's RDLs are partials or stiff-legs.
numbers: floating the bar so far that it costs >30% load is too far

title: Good mornings
statement: Knees slightly bent, not locked; no need to reach parallel (he stops around 45°, matching his squat and deadlift). The lower back is a bridge, not a crane; the SSB is the best bar; use safeties, never go to failure, and treat it as the day's main hinge. 2024 hamstring version: narrow stance, feet forward, shoulders past the hips, sets of 12.
numbers: ~45° depth; 6-12 reps, never below 8 in one video; heavy sets of 12 (2024)

title: Hip thrusts
statement: Close stance, full range down to the floor; think about the knees (down-in on the way down, up-out on the way up). The top squeeze does little. Pad the bar.
numbers: always 10+ reps

title: A curl moves only the forearm
statement: Keep the elbows at the sides and move only the forearm. Raising the elbows makes it a front raise, and hip drive turns it into a "supinated clean"; this explains poor biceps more than genetics does.

title: Don't fully straighten on curls
statement: Stop just short of full extension; the last inch stresses the tendon, not the muscle, and disengages the biceps. On preachers stop with the forearm about parallel.
numbers: stop ~45° / slight flexion

title: Curl details
statement: Curl one arm at a time or alternating, start neutral and supinate on the way up, take sets to failure without ego. On incline curls the weak bottom dictates the load; with a controlled negative, momentum extends the stretch; use a thumbless grip.
numbers: curls 6-10 to failure

title: Wall curls and cheating
statement: He first said wall and seated curls don't truly stop cheating, then that wall curls reduce cheating and allow slower negatives.
status: changed — 2021-22: wall curls don't stop cheating; 2024: they reduce cheating and allow slower negatives.

title: Triceps extensions: only the elbow moves, no lockout
statement: On skull crushers lock the shoulder in maximum flexion and move only the elbow (swinging turns it into a pullover); do them on a bench, not the floor; elbows may flare; pause at the bottom. Don't lock the elbows on triceps work: the lengthened part matters. Prefer dumbbells and slow negatives.

title: Lateral and rear-delt raises
statement: Laterals: slow and controlled, no swinging, stop at parallel (higher adds nothing), thumbless grip; seated or leaning versions reduce cheating. Rear delts: don't grip, hook the hand or wrist behind the handle, forearm in line with the upper arm, emphasise the bottom stretch.

title: Calf raises: the bottom is the growth
statement: Never let the heels touch, pause at the bottom, use a slow tempo and don't rebound off the Achilles; the bottom is where growth comes from.
numbers: 15+ reps

title: Abs: stretch and control
statement: Slow negatives, a stretch at the bottom, no swinging or rebounding. Effective range beats maximal range (hanging knee raises beat toes-to-bar).
numbers: 10-12 clean knee raises = well-developed abs

title: Forearms, traps and neck
statement: Forearms: train the muscle, not the tendon; keep the wrist stacked; on finger curls let the bar roll to the fingertips. Traps: let the shoulders protract so the traps catch the bar in a stretch, squeeze back rather than up, torso vertical. Neck: chin tucked, spine stacked, clean slow reps per direction, with a harness rather than plates on the head.
numbers: neck 10-20 reps

title: No separate upper chest; build the whole chest
statement: There is no separate "upper chest" to chase; bench and dips develop it, and people who obsess over it usually have no chest. Splitting the chest into regions is an "isolationist mindset".
scope: All lifters; novices especially shouldn't worry about it. Multi-height cable flies are gimmicky.

title: A stubborn chest needs a press you feel
statement: Grip, arch and dominant delts or triceps can steal bench work ("225 on the bar isn't 225 on the chest"). If you don't feel a press in your chest, switch to push-ups, dumbbells or dips for a while, or superset flies or band work between bench sets.
scope: Lifters whose chest lags despite a decent bench.
check: If the chest lags, is the main press one the lifter actually feels in the chest (or has it been swapped)?

title: Bench press is not mandatory
statement: Dips, push-ups and ring push-ups can replace the bench with no other change to the program. Choose by what agrees with you, and swap the bench if it doesn't hit your chest or keeps injuring you. His chest first grew from home push-ups, and by 2024 he had dropped the bench himself.
scope: All lifters with a muscle goal; not powerlifters.

title: Weighted dips are top tier
statement: Weighted dips ("squat of the upper body") are top tier for chest, triceps and shoulders. They give more pec and shoulder stretch than bench and may stress the pecs more. The shoulder risk is slightly higher, with no safety net.
numbers: He does 3 plates + 2×10 lb for 5.
scope: Those whose shoulders and ribcage tolerate them; growing young men should watch for sternum or rib pain.
status: changed — in 2020 he would not recommend dips over bench; later he ranks them equal or better for hypertrophy.

title: Ring push-ups are among the best chest builders
statement: Ring push-ups, especially weighted (backpack) and decline with the rings to the armpits, free the wrists and elbows, have no floor limit, let the scapulae retract, and bias the upper chest when declined. He ranks them first in his hypertrophy tier list.
numbers: About 5 sets of deep ring push-ups.
scope: All levels; load them once bodyweight is easy.

title: Push-ups aren't only for novices
statement: Loaded, or placed at the end of a press day, push-ups stay effective for advanced lifters.
status: changed — 2020: high-rep push-ups too easy for the advanced and weighted push-ups more risk than reward; 2024: he regrets dropping push-ups because "YouTube said they were for noobs".

title: Flies and ring work add chest volume while sparing the shoulders
statement: The less the shoulder is taxed, the more chest you can stimulate. Use flies, band flies and ring push-ups to grow the chest past dominant shoulders.
numbers: Band flies 8-12 between bench warm-ups; cable flies 3-4x12; ~5 sets deep ring push-ups.

title: Flies are finishers with a bent-arm stretch
statement: Use flies for high reps and supersets, not heavy single sets. Top picks: low-to-high cable fly, bent-arm pec deck, fly press, barrel press, and ring flies (build up from neutral ring push-ups first). Straight-arm DB flies and the straight-arm pec deck are mediocre and risky.
numbers: Low-to-high cable fly 4x15.
status: changed — 2020: "scrap the pec deck"; later the bent-arm pec deck is a top choice.

title: One king press, maybe a second, maybe one isolation
statement: The chest needs one big press, perhaps a second press or accessory and perhaps one isolation; more is pointless unless you specialize in chest.
numbers: 1 main press + 0-1 secondary press + 0-1 isolation.

title: Rotate horizontal presses, including shoulder-friendly variations
statement: Use more than one horizontal press over time, including variations that unload the shoulder: paused, close-grip, slingshot, dumbbell, football/cambered bar, pin or Spoto press. Replace one bench day per week with a paused variation.
numbers: One paused-variation day per week.

title: The dumbbell press is underrated
statement: Start with dumbbells if you don't feel the bench in your chest; dumbbells beat a barbell for incline.
scope: Especially lifters who don't feel the barbell bench.
status: contradicted — in 2020 he also said shifting flat-bench volume to dumbbells likely costs gains.

title: The incline press is a chest/shoulder hybrid
statement: The steeper the incline, the more shoulder. Treat the incline as a priority lift and don't stack it right after a heavy flat press. Dumbbell or Smith incline and weighted incline ring push-ups are his favourites.
status: changed — early on he disliked the barbell incline (front-delt heavy, injury-prone, "incline for upper chest" is bad advice); by 2023-2024 DB/Smith incline are favourites.

title: Low-value chest movements
statement: Floor press (no stretch; 3 years of DB floor press gave him a poor chest), plate/Svend press, standing cable press, pullovers for chest, chain dips, Hindu and one-arm push-ups, finger push-ups.

title: Pair the press with a complement
statement: Horizontal press then vertical press (his favourite bench day), bench supersetted with pullovers, or a heavy horizontal press then ring push-ups.

title: A big chest doesn't need a 3-plate bench
statement: Long-armed lifters bench less but may build bigger chests.
numbers: 3-plate (315 lb) bench is not a requirement.

title: Uneven chest: fix the bar path, add one-arm DB work
statement: An uneven chest comes from uneven shoulder height. Fix the bar path and add one-arm dumbbell bench sets.
numbers: 2-3 one-arm DB bench sets per chest day.

title: Strong chest, weak shoulders: bench once a week
statement: A chest-dominant lifter with lagging shoulders should cut bench to one low-rep session a week (see SHO-06).
numbers: 1x/week, 3x4-6.

title: Pullovers made his chest look thicker
statement: He says pullovers made his chest look thicker from the front, though elsewhere he lists pullovers for chest among low-value moves (CHE-13).
status: contradicted — anecdote vs his rating of pullovers as a chest move.

title: The upper back has the most growth potential in naturals
statement: The upper back is the most underdeveloped area in naturals and the slowest to mature; the best natural backs belong to lifters in their 30s-40s. After 10 years of training, adding upper-back volume made his grow "like weeds".

title: The upper back tolerates the most volume and frequency
statement: The upper back is a "glutton for volume"; train it almost every session. Its limits are the shoulder, biceps and elbow tendons and lower-back fatigue, so favour rows and pulls that spare the lower back. 4 sets of pulldowns won't build big lats.

title: Push/pull balance: from "pull more" to "many need more front"
statement: He now sees many lifters as back-dominant from the "pull twice as much as you push" advice; they need less back and more front volume. Everyone should still do plenty of back work.
status: changed — 2020: do more pulling than pushing; 2024: many reviewees need more pushing.

title: A complete back needs a hinge, a vertical pull and a horizontal pull
statement: The back is several areas, each needing its own pattern; vertical and horizontal pulls are not interchangeable. Deadlifts alone give a thick "fridge" back with no width; pull-ups were the only difference between his flat and his detailed back at the same 210 lb. 6-7 back exercises is "bro-split garbage".
numbers: Masterplan: 1 hinge + 1 vertical + 1 horizontal pull on different days, then +1 pull or shrug; a new hinge alternates weekly (A: deadlift 3x3, B: RDL 3x8-12); 1-2 exercises per area.
scope: All lifters wanting a full back.
check: Does each week include a hip hinge, a vertical pull and a horizontal pull?

title: Open the back day with a heavy pull
statement: Open with a floor pull/hinge, a heavy row or a weighted pull-up, never a light pulldown or machine. Don't burn out on the opener; it doubles as a warm-up.
numbers: 2021: ~90% of people should open pull day with a pull from the floor.
status: changed — 2020-2021: a floor pull; later a heavy row or weighted pull-up is also allowed.

title: Back thickness comes from hinges as well as rows
statement: The upper back works isometrically to stabilize hinge loads, so heavy hinges can replace one or two back exercises; the deadlift's weighted stretch at a 45° torso grows the mid back. Pull-ups alone leave you "flat as paper" from the side.

title: The deadlift's role for the back shrank
statement: The deadlift is now only mediocre for lats, builds a thick back with no V-taper, and ignores the small upper-back muscles.
numbers: 2020: it gave ~85% of his back thickness.
status: changed — 2020: "mandatory" for the back; 2022-2024: mediocre for lats, "fridge back".

title: "Legless" pulls as the bread and butter of upper-back growth
statement: Cable, seal, DB and chest-supported rows and hanging pulls should carry upper-back growth; he expects bigger backs from this approach.
status: changed — in 2021 he still called deadlifts and pull-ups the bread and butter.

title: Pull-ups are the king of lat and upper-back builders
statement: Weighted pull-ups when possible; nearly every natural with big lats built them with pull-ups. They decompress the spine, barely tax the CNS, and pair well with presses and small-muscle work. Weighted beat bodyweight, which beat machines.
numbers: Add weight after 6-8 clean reps (2021) or once you reach 20+ bodyweight reps (2024).
scope: All naturals who can do them.

title: Deadlifts and rows don't build lats; vertical pulls and pullovers do
statement: At a 500-520 lb deadlift he had "essentially no lats" and wrongly blamed his insertions; the tonnage went to the rhomboids and mid traps. Slow pull-ups and pullovers then grew them. Only a few people with particular leverages grow lats from deadlifts.
numbers: 500-520 lb deadlift, no lats.

title: Do pullovers every week, short of failure
statement: Pullovers transformed his lats and ribcage and are his favourite lift; put them in every program, on push or upper days. Dumbbell or machine is best; the cable version is a nightmare to set up. They supplement pull-ups and pulldowns but can't replace them.
numbers: Start 1x/week, then medium-heavy 2-3x/week at 1-2 RIR; 2024: about 95 lb, slow negative, dumbbell nearly to the floor.
scope: All lifters; not for most women (barrel-chest look).
check: Are pullovers done at least weekly, stopping 1-2 reps short of failure?

title: Pullover rep ranges
statement: Keep pullovers in moderate reps; very high reps shift the work to the triceps long head.
numbers: 2020: 4-12, preferably 5-7, 3-8 sets; 2022 NO: a 25RM weight, 3-4x7-10, 2-3x/week for a year; 2023: 3x8-12; 2024: 6-10 experienced, 8-12 novices, 12-20 too high.
status: changed — preferred range moved from 5-7 (2020) to 6-10/8-12 (2024).

title: Pull-up prescriptions for lats
statement: Big lats come from heavy weighted pull-ups plus volume, not light pulldowns. Bodyweight pull-ups can be done daily with varied grips.
numbers: Weighted pull-ups 3-5, 4-8 or 5-8; weighted chin-ups ~6-10, 1x/week, not fully extended (biceps protection); 2020 NO: 40-100 pull-ups a day, 6 days a week.

title: Lat pulldowns: from "replace them" to a top pull-up substitute
statement: Some pulldowns are top tier and the pulldown is the best pull-up substitute, worth rotating in even if you can do pull-ups. Best: close-grip neutral, wide supinated, and the diagonal/iliac pulldown heavy for 8-10 to failure. Wide pronated and behind-the-neck are only decent; the standing cable pulldown is bad.
numbers: Diagonal pulldown 8-10 to failure; women's program 4x10-15.
status: changed — 2020-2021: replace pulldowns with pull-ups, never as the main lift or opener; 2022-2024: some pulldowns are top tier.

title: Pull-up grips have different flavours; vary them
statement: Chin-up = lower/front lat plus biceps and core; pronated = more upper/mid back; neutral = best stretch, most shoulder-friendly; wide = lower lat/V-taper, more traps. The sternum (Gironda) pull-up is the "best of the best" but needs about 10 chest-to-bar reps first.
numbers: ~10 chest-to-bar reps before sternum pull-ups.

title: Lat mind-muscle connection comes from stretch and slow tempo
statement: Very slow, fully stretched pull-ups, one-arm cable rows and wide snatch-grip rows to the sternum build the lat connection. Wide overhand grip is best for him; Pendlay rows lack the bottom stretch.
scope: Lifters who don't feel their lats.

title: Don't stack lat work
statement: One heavy lat movement to exhaustion beats several for a pump; never put two lat movements back to back.

title: Lat menu (2023)
statement: His 2023 lat options with rep ranges.
numbers: Weighted pull-ups 3-5, ring rows 6-10, DB pullovers 6-10, machine pullovers, belt-squat or DB rows, cable pulldowns 8-12, machine 10-15.

title: Ribcage expansion from pullovers is real
statement: Pullovers enlarge the ribcage look; his roughly doubled, which makes his 36 in waist look small. It shrinks if you stop.
numbers: 36 in waist; possible bone change before about age 20-22.
status: changed — 2021-2022: costal cartilage spreads; 2023-2024: intercostal muscle and lat fill.

title: Developed lats show from the side and make the rear delts pop
statement: Well-developed lats protrude from the side and make the rear delts stand out.

title: The serratus is the most underrated aesthetic muscle
statement: The V-taper is shoulders, lats and serratus. Pullovers, vertical pressing and pulling, twisting sit-ups and serratus punches train it; it's never limiting and training it helps the shoulders.

title: Dumbbell rows are top tier and underrated
statement: No lower-back tax, an arc path with full lat stretch, and they fit anywhere in a session. Kroc rows are "incredibly underrated" for traps and upper back and very safe.
numbers: 4x6-12 twice a week (2021), 4x8-12, 3x8-12; Kroc and Meadows rows can alternate weekly.

title: Rows: 8-12 reps, controlled negative and stretch
statement: Low reps break row form. Pendlay rows bias the upper back; Yates rows bias the mid back and lats. Rows grow the upper back, not big biceps.
numbers: 8-12, minimum 8.

title: The barbell row is a hinge/row hybrid
statement: It loads the lower back, so program it as the day's hinge or opener in higher reps, or replace it with supported rows. Never 3x5 or 5x5, never grind; don't put it after squats and deadlifts. It is only "decent" for lats.
scope: All levels; with a fried lower back use seal, DB or ring rows.
status: contradicted — in 2021 he said none of his programs include barbell rows.

title: Seal and chest-supported rows for heavy rowing and tired lower backs
statement: Taking the legs and lower back out suits heavier, lower-rep rowing. The EZ-bar incline chest-supported row is top tier; plate-loaded chest-supported machines and the T-bar are mediocre.
scope: Especially when the lower back is fatigued.
status: current — in 2022 he personally preferred Pendlay rows because he hates a chest pad.

title: Pendlay rows: poor stretch, mediocre for lats
statement: The toughest, most technical row, with no controlled negative. Good for pulling strength and traps, mediocre for lats, not for novices.
numbers: Early: 6-8 reps or 5x5-8.
status: changed — 2022: still did them snatch-grip to the sternum; 2024: "not a good hypertrophy movement; DB rows are better for lats".

title: Inverted and ring rows are underrated
statement: Good bodyweight back builders; supinated versions are safe and good for lats, though hard to load. The body row between dip bars is top tier.
numbers: A 10 kg vest isn't enough load.

title: Grip and torso angle steer the row
statement: Neutral or close grip favours the lats; pronated, wide or high-pull favours traps and upper back. You can superset a row with itself if another exercise sits between; do the weak muscle's grip first.

title: Mid back: Kroc rows or flared-elbow rows
statement: The mid/low traps and rhomboids are best hit by Kroc rows or rows with flared elbows, torso fairly vertical, elbow high. Sternum pull-ups with fat grips also bias them.

title: Low-value rows
statement: Cheat barbell row, renegade row, TRX inverted row, standing cable "shotgun" row, T-bar row ("noob trap"), narrow-handle seated cable row. Cable rows are fine as finishers; one-arm seated cable rows beat two-arm.

title: Low-value lat movements
statement: Front lever, one-arm pull-up, muscle-up, dead hangs (for lats), straight-arm pulldown (pump finisher only), kettlebell swings, Jefferson deadlift.

title: Lower back: stabilization work is mostly enough
statement: Squats, floor pulls and rows cover the lower back through isometric stretch; it rarely needs dedicated work unless injured. Hyperextensions are the best isolation if you want one.
status: contradicted — 2020 he also said deadlifts alone aren't enough and the lower back needs isolating like the core; the "enough" view was restated in 2022.

title: One erector bigger than the other: unilateral hinges
statement: Use single-leg hyperextensions or single-leg RDLs.

title: Mirror-muscle training causes shoulder and back pain
statement: Prioritize the posterior chain in compounds and on dedicated days.

title: Traps grow from weighted stretch: heavy load in the hands
statement: More weight beats more range of motion; perfect-form 50 lb DB shrugs never build big traps. The trap's job is to hold weight in the hands, and he predicts zero-ROM heavy holds may prove optimal.

title: Traps need less direct work than he used to give them
statement: RDLs and floor pulls cover the traps; trap isolation is optional. Shrugs are redundant but nearly free volume for giant sets; naturally big-trapped lifters can skip them. His only trap lift is belt-squat shrugs.
numbers: 2020: about 150 shrugs after every pull.
status: changed — 2020-2021: massive trap NO and shrug finishers (BAK-38); 2023-2024: little direct work.

title: Past the novice stage, deadlifts aren't enough for traps (2020-2022)
statement: Add heavy snatch-grip shrugs, above-knee rack pulls (upper traps work near lockout), high pulls and shrug finishers.
numbers: Snatch-grip shrugs up to 400 lb; a 5-plate deadlift plus shrugs ≈ a 7-plate deadlift for traps.

title: Shrug-finisher rule (2020-2021)
statement: End every floor-pull set with shrugs, then hold for a stretch until you must let go; or shrug at the top of the last RDL set, strip 20 lb and repeat. Trap NO was his best NO result.
numbers: Floor pulls at 135-405 lb; strip 20 lb.

title: Shrug reps: mostly 10-15
statement: Traps take lots of volume; 3x8 or 2 sets is too little.
numbers: Mostly 10-15, range 6-20; 4 sets minimum or 5x10-15; 2022 NO 3-4x10-15 3x/week; shrugs every 3 days is plenty; upright rows 10-15.

title: Trap-biased exercise choices
statement: Good: snatch-grip shrugs (mid-trap stretch, no lower-back fatigue, widen the grip gradually), power/cheat and Kelso shrugs, chest-supported incline shrugs, Kroc rows, above-knee rack pulls, upright rows, strapped carries, heavy belt rows. Poor: slow-tempo shrugs, cable shrugs, overhead shrugs, laterals, band pull-aparts, overhead carries.
numbers: Snatch-grip shrugs 10-15; 2025 belt rows: heavy sets of 10 with a stretch.

title: Shrugs superset with almost anything; change torso angle by region
statement: After OHP, with hammer curls, or with the same bar after stiff-legs, but not heavy shrugs with RDLs. Shrugging in a hip-hinge position targets the mid and lower traps. Use straps.
numbers: After OHP 3-5x10-15.

title: Hang cleans can replace shrugs
statement: Hang cleans or hang clean pulls give trap stretch plus explosiveness.

title: Farmer's walks build traps
statement: Carries done after pre-fatiguing traps, neck and shoulders are "a killer" (programming of carries: FOR-18).
numbers: Finisher 3 × 30 m.

title: Mid and low traps grow from any pulling
statement: Train them through pulling before considering NO for them.

title: Vertical pressing is the bread and butter of delt size
statement: Most shoulder gains come from presses; the incline press is a hybrid and a delt movement first. All his recent shoulder gains came from "spamming" overhead presses. Judge by delt size, not pressing load.
numbers: 70-80% of shoulder gains can come from presses.
check: Does the program include at least one vertical press a week (unless the lifter is shoulder-dominant)?

title: Lateral raises support pressing; they don't replace it
statement: Big round natural shoulders come from pressing plus isolation; spamming raises at the cost of presses is a trendy mistake. Press before laterals, and never put raises right before or after a press.
check: Are lateral raises added after pressing rather than replacing it?

title: Pressing frequency
statement: Vertical presses at least twice a week, building toward three; by 2024, 1-2 vertical presses plus 1-2 isolations.
numbers: 2 vertical presses/week → 3 (two loaded, one bodyweight); 2021: 3-4 heavy presses/week; standing press 4x8-12 or 4x10-15; 6-10 paused; boxers 6-12.
status: changed — from 2-4 presses/week (2020-2021) to 1-2 presses plus 1-2 isolations (2024).

title: Shoulder selection: 1-2 presses + 2-3 isolations
statement: Pick any comfortable press; the only requirement is that the arm moves overhead.
numbers: 1-2 vertical presses + 2-3 isolations, 3-5 shoulder movements total.

title: Shoulder-dominant lifters can cut vertical pressing
statement: If your shoulders dominate the chest and arms, cut vertical pressing. No rule says horizontal pressing must outnumber vertical.
numbers: 2020: at least one vertical press per week.
status: changed — 2020: at least one vertical press weekly for all; later shoulder-dominant lifters may skip it.

title: Chest-dominant with lagging shoulders: skew toward vertical pressing
statement: Make the vertical press the first upper day's main lift and isolate the side and rear delts. Being much stronger vertically than horizontally signals that the shoulders steal chest work (see CHE-17).

title: His overhead press choice evolved
statement: Seated DB and machine presses are top tier. The push press is poor for delt size (legs do the work), the Z press mediocre, the behind-the-neck press fine in a pain-free range.
numbers: 2020: barbell OHP 3x6-8 after bench; 2024: 80° Smith incline press.
status: changed — barbell OHP (2020) → strict from the rack (2023) → in 2024 the military press is a "plateau machine", replaced by an 80° Smith incline.

title: Bodyweight shoulders: deficit handstand push-ups
statement: The more vertical the torso, the more shoulder.
numbers: Tiers: pike C, deficit B, decline A, HSPU S.

title: Side and rear delts are what most naturals lack
statement: The front delt is overdeveloped from pressing; hitting side and rear delts regularly gives capped, 3D delts.

title: Lateral raise reps 8-15, never low
statement: Lateral raises belong in moderate-to-high reps; very low reps (e.g. 4) are a mistake.
numbers: 3x10-12, 4x12-15, cable 10-15, 8-12 (better than 8-10); 2020: 4x20 for control; 3 sets is enough on one day.

title: Lateral raise frequency: down to once a week
statement: By 2024 once a week is enough, and 2-3x often hinders progress.
numbers: 2021: light raises up to 4-5 days/week; 2024: 1x/week.

title: Cable laterals with a cuff are the best lateral raise
statement: Constant tension, no grip limit, and no trap takeover, AC stress or cheating when the pin is at hip level. Lean-away ("Egyptian") raises are excellent. Rotate variations (cable, DB, upright rows, Y-raises) rather than repeating one raise twice a week.
numbers: Cable 10-15.

title: Upright rows are valid
statement: A wrongly demonized side-delt/trap isolation when done with a manageable weight; a wrist-roller handle helped his shoulder pain.
numbers: 10-15 reps; wrist-roller version 30 lb for 10-20.

title: Power raises are for advanced lifters only
statement: Power raises and lying lateral power raises give a great stretch and near-pure side-delt work; build up gradually.

title: Lu raises are overhyped for size
statement: Too light for hypertrophy, but fine for mobility or rehab.

title: Rear delts: frequency is the main pillar, with higher reps
statement: Once a week won't grow rear delts. Use higher reps, often short of failure on bands.
numbers: Face pulls 15-20 (up to 20-25); band face pulls 4x25; bent-over raises 4x10-15; rear-delt flies 8-12; rows 8-15; 10-15 to failure; 2020: 40-200 band face pulls daily.
status: contradicted — in 2020 he said both "you can never do enough rear delt work" and that rear delts have a "striking diminishing return".
check: Are rear delts trained more than once a week?

title: Rear-delt exercise choices
statement: Arnold raises are his favourite rear-delt isolation (2020-2021); ring face pulls are top tier, reverse flies A tier. Face pulls are healthy and good for NO, done seated at the end of push days, but aren't the best builders; rear-delt rows are B tier. Laterals and face pulls aren't interchangeable; bent-over raises can overuse the traps.

title: Don't stack front, side and rear raises with little rest
statement: The rear delts get nothing at the end; two rear-delt isolations in one superset is too much.

title: Front delts need little or no isolation
statement: Presses cover the front delts for most people; prioritize laterals. Front raises are optional extra volume.
numbers: 2020: heavy front raises 4x10 weekly; 2025: front raises 10-15.
status: changed — 2020: did heavy front raises himself; 2021-2022: no front work after pressing; 2025: worthwhile "free volume".

title: Shoulder NO: isolation only, never presses
statement: For nucleus overload use laterals, rear flies and face pulls only.

title: Weak points stay weak
statement: His quads grow on little volume while his shoulders lag on much more; in 2022 he barely pressed because his shoulders "grew too easily".
numbers: Quads 3-6 sets/week vs shoulders 14-15 sets/week (2024); 2022: pressing once per 15 days.

title: Arms need isolation; compounds alone leave them small
statement: He has never seen a natural with big biceps from chin-ups alone; at the bottom of a chin-up the back takes the stretch. If rowing 3 plates didn't grow your biceps, 4 plates won't. "70% of arm gains come from compounds" is made up.
numbers: He reached 16 in arms without a chin-up.
check: Does the program include direct biceps and triceps isolation?

title: Treat arm training as seriously as squat and bench
statement: Progressive overload, intensity and strict form. "Train your arms as an afterthought and they will look like an afterthought." Torso-dominant powerlifter physiques come from programming, not genetics.

title: Pump-only, high-volume arm work is a myth
statement: Light, high-rep, pump-chasing arm work done by feel doesn't build arms.
numbers: Bad example: 3x25 curls, 3x20-30 extensions with 3 min rest; 12-20 by feel is too much; fixed 15-rep biceps work chases the pump.

title: Chin-ups are a back exercise
statement: Chin-ups won't build big biceps alone, but they suit back-and-biceps days and programs without curls.

title: Biceps reps: heavy but not below about 4-6
statement: Biceps respond to heavy, strict curls, but since 2023 he never goes below 4-6 reps and uses stretch curls in higher reps for tendon health.
numbers: 2020: 3-7 strict for 4 sets; 6-10 for most (3-7 advanced); 4-12. 2021: 3-4x3-6 barbell; 3x8-10; 4x6-12. 2023: lowest is close-grip EZ curls 4-8; stretch exercises 10-15. 2024: partial curls to an 8RM. 4x8 beats 5x5 and 4x10.
status: changed — strict 3-7 / 3-6 (2020-2021) → floor of 4-6 plus 10-15 stretch curls (2023).

title: Biceps volume: 3x10 once a week is too little
statement: With one curl in a session do 4x8-12. Once a week can work with a top set plus back-offs.
numbers: 4x8-12; top set 8-10 + 4x8-12 back-offs; up to 5 sets mixing heavy barbell and lighter preacher work.

title: Keep curl selection small
statement: 2-3 curls trained hard, not five curls dissecting the heads; many variations reduce neural adaptation.
numbers: Novice 1 biceps exercise; intermediate 2 biceps + 2-3 triceps; advanced adds one very strict movement per muscle and rotates weekly among three favourites; he used 4-6 as an advanced lifter (2022).

title: A good biceps exercise maximizes biceps use
statement: Stable elbow and shoulder, controllable stretch, no swinging. Top tier (2022): close-grip EZ preacher, close-grip EZ curl, spider curl, behind-the-back cable curl. Excellent: cable, braced concentration, pinwheel, machine curls, arm blaster. Bad: cheat barbell curls ("a supinated clean"), waiter curls, one-arm chin-ups.

title: Preacher curls are a staple
statement: Especially close-grip EZ; the pad lets you go to failure safely. He keeps partial preacher curls because they suit his tendons.
numbers: Minimum 6 reps; 6-12 (8-12 to avoid ego lifting).

title: Incline and stretch curls: from poor to top tier
statement: Biceps work best around 90° elbow flexion; the incline curl trains the lengthened position. Fixes: slight incline only, no bouncing, or cable/Bayesian versions. He now does incline cable and spider curls for elbow pain.
numbers: Incline cable and spider curls 10-15.
status: changed — poor (2020) → C tier (2022) → A/S tier (2023-2024); he admits he "relied on theory over practice".

title: Cheat curls built his biceps, but aren't needed
statement: Cheat curls were his only curl for about 6 years (from 15 to ~22) with no tendinitis, but he calls that survivorship bias. Barbell cheat curls become whole-body moves; dumbbell versions stay more honest. Not for beginners.
numbers: About 4x6 daily.
status: contradicted — a staple that built his arms vs "not the way to big arms"; "curls in general suffice".

title: Find a curl you love; swap any curl that hurts
statement: Nobody hates every curl. Regular curls hurt his shoulders, so he uses cross-body pinwheel curls; hammer curls in front of the body over-recruit the front delt.

title: Head emphasis
statement: The long head grows from almost any curl; the short head and the upper biceps need targeting. Curls bias the distal biceps; short-range rows with fixed shoulders bias the proximal biceps, so doing only curls can mimic poor peak genetics.

title: Brachialis and brachioradialis make the arm look wider
statement: Hammer curls "cost nothing"; he prefers full range for the brachialis (brachioradialis work: FOR-13).
numbers: About 6 sets/week of hammer curls.

title: If forearms or triceps dominate the biceps, favour supinated curls
statement: Cut pronated work and twist the pinky outward, especially with a short biceps insertion.

title: Band curls for tendon health
statement: Band curls don't hurt recovery and suit NO, while high-frequency DB or barbell curls tend to cause tendonitis.
status: contradicted — "mediocre" for building muscle in 2022 (recovery/finisher only) vs "excellent", the only curl he really feels, in 2024.

title: The EZ bar changes wrist comfort, not biceps activation
statement: It mainly changes wrist comfort and forearm involvement; dumbbells make cheating harder.

title: Small isolation needs humility
statement: Strict light curls hit the biceps; most heavy curls are cheated.
numbers: Strict incline curls with about 25 lb; most 135 lb curls are cheated.

title: Maintaining big biceps: high intensity, low volume
statement: Already-big biceps can be kept with little, heavy work.
numbers: EZ curls 2-3x6-8.

title: Presses don't build the triceps for most naturals
statement: He benched 335 with almost no triceps; you can add 200 lb to a bench with little going to the triceps if you're chest- or shoulder-dominant. Those who grow triceps from bench alone are outliers. Beginners should isolate from day one.
numbers: 335 lb bench; 7 years without triceps isolation.
status: changed — 2020 he grew his arms mostly with biceps work; 2024 he regrets 7 years without triceps isolation.

title: The long head needs extensions with shoulder flexion
statement: The long head is the biggest, most neglected part of the triceps. Pressing and pushdowns build the lateral head; overhead extensions, French presses and skull crushers with shoulder flexion hit the long head, which pushes the biceps up. Pullovers give it only a passive stretch.
check: Is there at least one triceps extension done with the shoulder flexed (overhead, French press, skull crusher past vertical)?

title: Long-head reps: mostly 8-12
statement: Small muscles shouldn't always be trained at very high reps; 5x5 is acceptable once a week.
numbers: Lying extensions 4x8-12 or 4x10-12; skull crushers 4x8-12, not 4-6; overhead 3x10; incline DB skull crushers 3x8-10; French press 3x6-10 1x/week; 3-5x8-14.
status: contradicted — 2023: it "responds best to higher reps and endurance" vs it fatigues faster than the biceps, so use 6-12.

title: Long-head to lateral-head ratio of 2:1
statement: Three long-head movements overdo it. A novice needs only one long-head movement (lateral isolation optional).
numbers: 2:1 long:lateral; beginner 3 sets/week; he schedules 9-12 weekly sets; ~30 reps/week is too little for intermediates.

title: Choose tendon-friendly extensions that cover all three heads
statement: Top tier: lying extension with the bar behind the head (shoulder fully flexed), overhead cable extension (progress it for 2 years), kneeling cable extension, French press against an incline. Cables spare tendons but bore you, so mix in free weights; grip or balance limits cost points.

title: Skull crushers: let the shoulders flex past vertical
statement: Dumbbells beat the EZ bar for depth. Skull crushers and close-grip bench aren't interchangeable (long head vs lateral/medial); superset them with zero rest instead.

title: Skull crushers inside press giant sets made his presses stronger
statement: He credits long-head activation; supersetting two triceps moves is fine if they hit different heads.

title: JM press: from elbow-unfriendly to elbow-saving
statement: The JM press combines skull crusher and close-grip press, hits the lateral head, and is best on a Smith machine or SSB. Start very light.
numbers: SSB 8-12, Smith 10-15.
status: changed — 2020: an elbow-unfriendly hybrid; 2022-2024: helped his elbows.

title: Close-grip bench: a low-impact press, mostly chest
statement: Adds pressing volume and spares the shoulders; open arm days with it, not after the isolation.

title: Pushdowns: V-bar for heavy, rope for the long head and elbows
statement: Rotate V-bar and rope/reverse-grip/band pushdowns; don't do two pushdowns back to back.
numbers: Pushdowns 8-12.

title: Triceps menu (2023)
statement: His 2023 triceps options with rep ranges.
numbers: Pushdowns 8-12, cross-body cable 10-15, EZ skull crushers 8-12 or DB 10-15, SSB JM press 8-12 or Smith 10-15.

title: Poor triceps movements
statement: DB kickbacks, bench dips, Tate press, floor extensions, standing EZ overhead extension, dip machines.

title: Dips for triceps need a vertical torso and top-range work
statement: Normal forward-lean dips are mostly chest and shoulders; use a vertical torso and slingshot or top-range work for triceps.
numbers: 2020: 4x30 → 50 slingshot half dips; 2023: slingshot weighted +80 kg 4x5-8.

title: Never isolate triceps before dips or presses
statement: Superset presses with long-head extensions afterward instead.

title: Triceps NO and high-rep work
statement: For lagging triceps, light high-rep extensions on non-pressing days, never on bench days. Progress by adding reps, then slots, then days; add weight only once every day is capped.
numbers: Band or cable extensions 4-5x30-40 every 2 days; 2022 cycle 4x15 with 25 lb twice a week; a friend did 100-rep pushdowns after every session for 5 years.

title: Band and supinated cable extensions for cranky elbows
statement: They give a pump and ease triceps tendinitis.

title: Diamond or tiger push-ups for lagging triceps
statement: Finish with push-up variants to failure.
numbers: 2-3 sets to failure at the end; tiger push-ups in sets of 15.

title: Arm days: unnecessary for novices, eventually required
statement: To maximize arm size you eventually need an arm day. Open with a heavy curl (or a triceps press if triceps are the priority), not chin-ups; include other body parts to avoid junk volume (no 6-7 triceps exercises); keep it low stress and enjoyable.
numbers: A 4-set arm superset takes about 20 min.

title: Superset biceps and triceps; never two same-muscle moves back to back
statement: On arm days supersetting biceps with triceps is a must; never put two biceps or two triceps movements back to back. Templates are in the table below.
numbers: See table.

title: Long-armed lifters just have to get very big
statement: A "spider physique" is a matter of method, not fate.

title: Pulling doesn't build big forearms; isolate them
statement: Elite 600-900 lb pullers often have thin forearms. His raw-pulling years stalled his forearms; direct work made them "blow up". His big forearms come from years of isolation, not genetics.
numbers: About 13.5 → 15 in after direct flexion work.
check: Is there direct forearm isolation, not just pulling and grip work?

title: Use straps; strapless pulling doesn't build forearms
statement: Don't let grip limit big-muscle lifts. Going strapless or mixed-grip on back work doesn't build forearms; deadlifting for forearms is "the worst advice". Straps don't hurt forearm growth.

title: Grip strength and forearm size are separate
statement: Grip types are support, pinch and crush. Support grip (load stretching the fibers) builds size; crush grip gives no stretch and is least useful for size. Grip training is only one isometric function.

title: Train every forearm function, plus weighted stretch
statement: Train wrist flexion and extension, pronation, supination and elbow flexion, plus some holds. Judge an exercise by the function it trains; good ones stimulate only the forearm. What grows forearms in pulls is weighted stretch, not squeezing.

title: Forearm progression path (2023)
statement: Pick one movement you enjoy, then add 1-2, then cover every wrist/elbow function and rotate.
numbers: 1 → 2-3 movements → all functions.

title: Finger curls are his staple
statement: Replace wrist curls and grippers with finger curls (loaded negative, stretch): switch for 1-2 weeks "and never go back". They are forgiving on the wrist, an arm-wrestler favourite, and fixed his wrist pain. The dumbbell version is top tier.
numbers: 4-6 sets of 6-12, supersetted; start 1x/week, build to 2-3x; 2024: on a cable stack, rolling to the fingertips, sets of 15.

title: Wrist curls and extensions: 8-20 reps; drop anything felt in the wrist
statement: Do more extensions than curls if curls and chin-ups already load the inner forearm. Use standing wrist curls if seated ones hurt.
numbers: 8-12 (10-15 fine); 5x20 NO-style; reverse wrist curls 15-20; e.g. 6x12 extensions vs 2x12 curls.
status: contradicted — he also says to replace wrist curls with finger curls (FOR-06).

title: Do curls and extensions even if you already do hammer curls and carries
statement: Direct forearm work costs almost no fatigue; fat grips don't replace isolation.
numbers: 15 reps is "free volume".

title: Forearm frequency: from cautious to "spam them"
statement: Once work capacity is built, forearms recover fast; train them hard several times a week. "Forearms are the only thing to spam."
numbers: 2020: wrist flexion 1x/week then 2x; 2023-2024: 3-4x/week with modest volume.
status: changed — 2020: daily forearm NO is risky because tired forearms hurt curls and pulls; 2023-2024: spam them.

title: Don't let forearm work sabotage pulling
statement: Do grip work on lower or rest days, not before upper or deadlift days. Chin-ups pre-fatigue the brachioradialis, so isolate forearms fresh. Grip stamina is a currency; don't spend it all on holds.

title: Isometric holds: about 15 s, heavy
statement: Short heavy holds carry over better than long ones. High rack pulls held 5 s beat floor pulls for forearms.
numbers: 15 s × 4-5 sets (better than 25 s); towel holds 15-30 s × 3-6 sets (he reached 160 lb); rack-pull holds 5 s.

title: Dead hangs at the end of lower days
statement: Dead hangs give the most aggressive stretch and decompress the spine; not always to failure.
numbers: 2-3x/week; build to 2-4 minutes for visible forearms.

title: Brachioradialis needs neutral or pronated elbow flexion
statement: The brachioradialis is underdeveloped in most people. Use reverse curls, hammer and pinwheel curls, towel hammer curls, slow pronated preacher curls, riser curls and pronation twists.
numbers: Reverse curls 10x10 (2020), 3-6x8-15, 6-12 (2023); hammer/pinwheel 4 sets; towel hammer curls 3-4x6-10.
status: changed — 2024: direct work "not vital"; cross-body hammers suffice, but some neutral or pronated work is needed.

title: Top-tier forearm picks (2023)
statement: Preacher hammer curls (towel/hangman/rope, stop just below parallel), standing reverse curls, supinated forearm curls with sane range, pronation twist with a belt loop, dead hangs.

title: Copy arm wrestlers and welders, not strongmen
statement: They do huge volumes of loaded wrist flexion and get forearms that match their upper arms; copy their towel curls and pronation work but not their partial table-only ranges. He says strongman forearms come from bodyweight and systemic stress.
numbers: Forearms matching upper arms, 17/17 in.

title: Grippers are a low-fatigue accessory, not a size builder
statement: Do them between squat sets or anywhere. They rank C tier: no negative, only one lump.
numbers: 2022: 3-4 sets of medium reps 2-3x/week, or 5-6 sets 2-3x/week starting at the lowest gripper.

title: Fat grips and towels skew pulls toward the forearms
statement: Dropping them for 6 months shrank his forearms. They work on pull-ups, supinated/preacher curls, V-bar and skull crushers, but ruin hammer curls and don't replace isolation.
numbers: 6 months without them.
status: contradicted — 2020: he knew no one who built big forearms with fat grips vs towels and fat grips grew his forearms best.

title: Program farmer's walks like a squat or deadlift
statement: They build forearms and traps but are taxing; put them at the start of a session or on their own day, not in a superset.

title: Forearms take years
statement: The best natural forearms belong to older lifters; like calves, forearms are used all day. Small forearms are not a lifelong curse.
numbers: 1-3 years from stick to big.

title: Poor forearm movements
statement: Plate flips, newspaper twist, DB wrist twists, plate pinches, Zottman curls (pronation curls beat them), knuckle/fingertip push-ups.

title: Rice-bucket training is for conditioning and wrist health
statement: Not a size builder.
numbers: He did 20-30 min nightly for 2 months.

title: Big legs need a heavy knee flexion plus a heavy hip hinge
statement: Any squat pattern, hack, belt squat or leg press plus any heavy hinge. You can grow huge legs without squats or deadlifts specifically, but never without these patterns. The lower body needs few exercises.
numbers: Squat + RDL ≈ 80-90% of the gains; a leg day = 1 big quad move, 1 posterior-chain move, 1-2 isolations.
check: Does each week include a heavy knee-flexion (squat-pattern) lift and a heavy hip hinge?

title: Quads grow from compounds
statement: Naturals have big legs because they squat seriously. Quads are the easiest part to grow and a poor NO target.
numbers: He built 26-26.5 in thighs with almost only squats.

title: Don't be a bird-legged upper-body bro
statement: Even upper-focused lifters can fit in a little leg work. Train legs for long-term robustness, not a hormone boost.
numbers: At least 3 sets of squats and 3 of deadlifts a week.

title: His squat choice moved to heel-elevated and machine squats
statement: Heel-elevated, SSB, belt, hack and split squats replaced the back squat; he back squats about once a month. Elevated heels give more quad stimulus at less fatigue.
numbers: 2023: ~80% of his squat volume heel-elevated (20-45°); elevated heels cost ~15-30% of the load, the Platz squat ~50%.
status: changed — 2020: deep back squats are the best leg builder, "refusing to squat means small legs for life"; 2024: "do all squats with elevated heels".

title: Quad emphasis on squats
statement: A vertical torso, forward knee travel and a narrower, toes-forward stance bias the quads. A posterior-dominant 4-5 plate squatter may grow glutes and hamstrings instead; SSB squats are more posterior.

title: Pick the squat style by build
statement: High bar for most bodybuilders; low bar only if you can't high-bar (tall, long femurs). Low bar moves more weight through leverage, not more quad. Long-legged lifters whose squat turns into a good morning should hack squat.

title: Split squats: his favourite leg movement
statement: Best stimulus-to-fatigue of any leg movement. Treat them as heavy main compounds, third in the session, never closing a superset. Load them on an SSB, Smith or belt squat, not dumbbells. Forward lean biases glutes; belt-squat split squats are near-pure quad.
numbers: 8-12 or 10-15, never 30; balance caps dumbbells at ~75-80 lb.
status: changed — 2020: "not a fan of unilateral"; 2024: favourite.

title: Split squats for the VMO and teardrop
statement: Most bodybuilders, him included, have overdeveloped outer quads; split squats, box front squats or leg extensions bring up the VMO. Toes-out heavy squats build the outer sweep.

title: Leg rep ranges (2024)
statement: Machine and unilateral squats go higher; the barbell squat stays moderate because high reps are too taxing on cardio.
numbers: Hack squat and Bulgarian split squat 10-15 (6-10 is low); high-bar squat 6-10 (10-15 too cardio-taxing); 2020: 20-rep "widowmaker" squats best for leg size.
status: changed — 2020 favoured 20-rep squats; 2024 keeps barbell squats at 6-10.

title: Quad tier list (2023)
statement: Top: heel-elevated, Platz, feet-forward Smith squats, machine belt squat, pendulum hack/leg press, Bulgarian split squat, leg extensions, deficit sumo squat, SSB pause squat. A: high-bar, front, hack, barbell hack, sissy, split squats, seated leg press, low-box squat. B: low-bar, 45° leg press, improvised belt squat, reverse hack, Jefferson, Zercher. C or lower: shrimp, single-leg press, king squat, walking lunges, overhead/Bosu squats, vertical leg press, step-ups, DB/banded leg extensions, sumo deadlift.

title: Front squats: loved, but not worth it for most bodybuilders
statement: Too technical; hack or belt squats do the job better. Fine as the main squat if poor hip internal rotation forces a duck-footed back squat. The box front squat is the version he likes.
numbers: 4-6 reps, or after back squats.

title: Box squats are mostly poor for hypertrophy and novices
statement: They turn into a wide-stance hinge. Exceptions: box front squats, a close-stance parallel box squat for carryover, and a strict low box (A tier in 2023).

title: Pause squats are the best squat accessory
statement: The SSB is ideal for them, but they shouldn't be your only squat.
numbers: 4-8 reps.

title: Leg extensions: from knee-risky to top-tier isolation
statement: Leg extensions are true quad isolation. Never open leg day with them; leg press and extensions duplicate each other.
status: changed — 2020-2021: subpar, knee-risky "cherry on top"; 2023: top tier.

title: Leg press and hack squat are legitimate builders
statement: Only a minor gap to the squat. Hack squat for those avoiding squat technique, leg press for bad backs; never both in one day.
numbers: Hack squats 3x10-12 after deadlifts spare the lower back; extra hack/leg-press day 4x10-15.
status: changed — in 2021 he disliked the leg press (back pain).

title: Lunges: reverse lunges good, walking lunges worst
statement: The reverse lunge is top tier and can replace RDLs; walking lunges are the worst single-leg option. Load lunges; don't use them as pump finishers.
status: changed — 2020: he never did lunges because of knee inflammation; 2023-2024: reverse lunge is top tier.

title: Calisthenics can't build maximal legs
statement: Pistols and shrimp squats fall short; split squats beat them.

title: Trap-bar deadlift: fine for novices, weak for bodybuilding
statement: It reduces the hinge and is "useless for quads"; he dislikes it.
scope: Novices and athletes can use it.

title: Adductors are worth isolating
statement: They add size around the thigh.

title: Squats don't build hamstrings
statement: Heavy hip hinges and knee flexion do. Deadlifting gave him a hamstring sweep, but conventional deadlifts lack a stretched negative, so add RDLs and leg curls.

title: A hip hinge is necessary in every program; leg curls can't replace it
statement: Someone doing only leg curls ends up smaller and weaker. Any hinge counts, back extensions included.
numbers: 4 sets of RDLs beat 4 sets of curls.
check: Does the program contain a hip-hinge movement (RDL, deadlift, good morning, back extension)?

title: Do as much or more hamstring work than quad work
statement: He recommends this for knee health. Leg curls alone create an imbalance, so include heavy posterior-chain work.
numbers: Hamstring work ≥ quad work; 6x8-12 lying curls to balance quads.

title: The RDL became his king posterior-chain lift
statement: The deadlift became an accessory to the RDL; the RDL is top tier in every style.
numbers: 2023: he flipped an 80/20 deadlift/RDL split to 80% RDL; 2023-2024: deadlift ~once a month, RDL 2-3x/month for 6-12.
status: changed — 2021: floor deadlifts needed, RDLs not enough; 2022 onward: deadlift as accessory to the RDL.

title: Deadlift verdicts by year
statement: For hypertrophy he sees the deadlift as fatiguing for what it gives; drop it if your proportions don't suit it (strength view: see ch. 7).
status: changed — 2020: one of the best whole-body lifts; 2022: flaws real only if overprogrammed; 2023: B tier, no stretch; 2024: "energy vampire" with terrible stimulus-to-fatigue.

title: Deadlift programming: low reps, low volume, once a week
statement: Open the day with it, keep reps low and let RDLs take the higher reps. Never high-rep deadlifts (thoracic extension gives out first); twice a week is redundant; don't pair heavy deadlifts with RDLs on one day.

title: RDL and stiff-leg prescriptions
statement: RDLs strain easily at very high reps. They can go to failure as the only heavy hinge. Stiff-legs are more strength-oriented, RDLs more hypertrophy (stretch). His RDL is a full-range "reverse deadlift" from the rack.

title: Squat then RDL; never RDL and good morning on one day
statement: Squat followed by RDL is the "match made in heaven"; rotate RDL and good morning weekly. Don't pair good mornings with back squats (front squats are fine).
numbers: Squat 3x4-6 then RDL 3x8-12.

title: Good mornings are great in moderate reps
statement: More stretch than the RDL but worse risk/reward; never heavy 5s or 1RMs; the SSB is the best bar. Load caps like "two plates" are nonsense.

title: Hyperextensions are top tier
statement: They teach the hinge, are easy on the back, and progress for years (bodyweight → DB → barbell); loaded back extensions can be the main posterior-chain builder. Snatch-grip hyperextensions are on his every lower day.

title: Leg curls: from second-best to top-tier free volume
statement: The lying leg curl has a better per-hamstring stimulus-to-fatigue ratio, though he trains legs without curls himself. Curl after the hinge, never as the opener; pick seated or lying and progress it. GHR top tier, Nordics A, razor curls B, dumbbell leg curls bad.
status: changed — 2020: hinges preferred, curls hit the lower hamstring and knee; 2023-2024: top tier.

title: Hamstrings respond to high reps (2020)
statement: In 2020 he used high reps for hamstring work, supersetting curls with extensions.
numbers: Good mornings 3x20; curls at least 4x15; RDLs and hypers 4x8-12.

title: If glutes and lower back steal the hinge, bias the hamstrings
statement: Use hyperextensions, leg curls, and RDLs with the bar pushed into the quads or further forward; or pre-exhaust glutes and lower back with heavy rows before SLDLs.
scope: Hamstrings lagging behind glutes and lower back.

title: Underdeveloped posterior chain: open leg day with a hinge you enjoy
statement: Good mornings, any RDL, or hyperextensions.

title: The single-leg RDL is underrated
statement: His favourite hamstring lift in 2023: more stretch, little lower-back load, rehab-friendly. Use a band or belt squat for balance.

title: Kettlebell swings: heavy, not CrossFit style
statement: Heavy swings are top tier for hamstrings (2023); they don't build lats.
numbers: Heavy 6-8 reps.

title: Pull from the floor in one style that suits you
statement: Conventional, sumo, trap bar, Jefferson or block pulls; pick one and progress it rather than training sumo and conventional both. Tall lifters: sumo or blocks. He tried sumo for 8-12 months and dropped it. Above-knee rack pulls aren't a hinge.
numbers: 8-12 months of sumo.
scope: Lifters who pull from the floor.
status: changed — 2023: "you'd grow more from RDLs than sumo" (see LEG-23).

title: The snatch-grip deadlift is his favourite deadlift variation
statement: It is harder, with more upper-back stretch and more quads. Deficit pulls work posterior chain and quads deeper, block pulls more upper back; don't do both in one day.
numbers: Start ~two plates, narrow stance, 4-8 reps.

title: Heavy squats and hinges are the best glute builders
statement: Glutes can't really be isolated and any lower-body movement grew his; most men don't need glute isolation. Choose movements that force glute use rather than tweaking squats. Women squatting and hinging in a surplus will build big glutes.

title: Hip thrusts: from fine add-on to redundant
statement: By 2024 there is almost always a better option; split squats beat hip thrusts when time is short. Hip thrusts beat glute bridges (range); single-leg hip thrusts should be loaded.
numbers: 4x12-15, always >10 reps.
status: changed — top tier full-range off a bench (2023) → disliked as redundant (2024).

title: Best glute builders in his view
statement: Reverse lunges (SSB reverse lunges "destroy the glutes"), forward-leaning split squats, reverse hypers, butt blaster. Poor: donkey kicks, frog pumps, banded crab walks, lateral lunges/step-ups, abductor machine (adductor machine is better).

title: Big glutes are injury insurance
statement: He calls well-developed glutes protection against injury.

title: Calves stay small because they aren't trained
statement: Once trained, calves grow; small calves are bad training, not genetics. Squats don't grow calves.
numbers: His calves: 16 in (2020) → 17 (2022) → ~17.8 in; an inch a year is possible. He waited nine years before training them.

title: Calves need lots of load because they carry you all day
statement: Bodyweight raises add too little; overweight people grow calves from the load they carry.
numbers: Untrained calves already measure 13-14 in.

title: Train calves several times a week
statement: Once a week won't work; he prefers high frequency over high volume at low frequency.
numbers: 3x/week (his inch-a-year method, still 3x in 2024); 4-5x/week possible; 4-8 sets once a week just makes you sore.
check: Are calves trained directly at least 3 times a week?

title: Calf reps: mostly 10-20, heavy work 6-12
statement: Volume matters more than intensity; don't go very low because the Achilles is fragile. Sets of 10-15 must be weighted.
numbers: 4x20, 4x12-15, 3x20, 3x20-30, 15-20, 5x10; not below 10-15 (8-12 OK); weighted 6-12 with bodyweight 25-30; 2023: standing 8-12, seated EZ 10-15, DB block 15-20, 3x/week.

title: Calves heavy vs light
statement: By 2024: progressive overload on two loaded raise variations. A good calf exercise is easy to load, allows a deep stretch and slow tempo, and needs little balance or cardio.
numbers: 2022: NO-style 10-15 as the bulk.
status: contradicted — 2020: "don't train calves heavy" (Achilles, feet) vs a heavy calf day with loaded stretches the same year; 2024 settles on load as key.

title: Superset calves between other sets; never leave them for the end
statement: Calf work done "if I feel like it" never happens. He does most calf volume in upper-day giant sets; calves don't hurt squat or deadlift performance. Never open a session with calves.

title: Novices can skip calves; intermediates must start
statement: He waited nine years and regrets it: "The right moment is now."

title: Calf tier list (2024)
statement: S: standing two-leg raise with the foot elevated, slow tempo, high reps, machine or Smith; calf press on the leg press; weighted StairMaster on tiptoes. A: single-leg raise, 4-5 min tiptoe farmer's walk with straps. B: seated raise, biking with heels off, calf launcher. C/D: donkey raises, running/jump rope, plyometrics, bodyweight raises, DB hops. Padded standing machines are often too vertical.
numbers: Seated raise ~15 reps; tiptoe walk 4-5 min.

title: Calf variations
statement: Toshiki (explosive) and Piana (squeeze, slow negative) raises; seated EZ-bar or DB-on-knees finishers; seated leg-press raises; SSB and belt-squat raises. When two raises compete, the first one progresses most.
numbers: Toshiki/Piana raises 6-12; finishers 3-4 sets to failure.

title: Calf NO
statement: Most NO sets should go to calves.
numbers: Single-leg raises with ~10 lb, 70-100 reps/leg every 2 days; 100-rep seated EZ-bar stretches.

title: Calves should roughly match the upper arm
statement: He cites Reeves' proportion ideal; his own calves would need to reach about 20-22 in to look big.

title: Tibialis raises 2-3x a week
statement: Use a machine, slow negatives and a big stretch. The tibialis can't get monstrous but becomes visible from the side.
numbers: 15-20 reps with drop sets; start 2x/week, build to 3x; he does 50 lb/foot for 20.
status: contradicted — the same year his calf tier list rates tibialis raises C (rehab).

title: Abs need direct isolation
statement: Compounds and bracing don't build a six-pack; bracing gives an isometric contraction with no stretch. Ab isolation is "non-negotiable", and every program of his includes at least one.
numbers: ≥1 ab isolation per program.
check: Does the program include at least one direct, stretch-based ab exercise?

title: "Abs are made in the kitchen" is wrong
statement: Dieting only reveals abs; abs that show only when skinny are a "skinny pack". Trained abs stay visible year-round and at higher body fat.
numbers: At 220 lb and high body fat he still has a six-pack.

title: Train abs year-round, best during a bulk
statement: Abs grow under fat in a surplus, so a bulk is no excuse.

title: Ab frequency: 2-4 times a week
statement: Frequent ab work, but no longer daily; never once a week.
numbers: 2020-2022: daily (except Sunday); 2023: ≥3 sets every chest, shoulder or arm day; 2024: 2-3 exercises a week of ~3 sets is plenty; beginners 2x/week → 3x; 3-4x/week if possible; 2-3 sets per session.
check: Are abs trained directly 2-4 times a week?

title: Load abs and progress them at about 6-12 reps
statement: Weighted, progressively overloaded ab work replaced high-rep daily sets.
numbers: 2020: until you can't, 1 min rest, 5-6 min total; 2022 intermediate: 80-200 reps/week over 8-10 sets of 10-20, ≤4 sets/day; advanced 100-240 reps over 10-12 sets; 2023-2024: weighted sit-ups 6-12, decline sit-ups 6-10 or 8-12 (15-20 too high), 3x8-12 instead of daily 4x25.
status: changed — 2022: "going heavy does nothing", train abs like calves; 2023-2024: weighted 6-12 with real progression.
check: Is ab work loaded and progressed, mostly in the 6-12 rep range?

title: The stretch is the key ab-hypertrophy factor
statement: You already get the contraction from bracing. Crunches (thoracic-only flexion) and floor crunches with knees up miss the stretch; the sit-up pattern (fixed pelvis and feet, whole spine flexing) is "the exercise". Criteria: good stretch, high effective range, easy to load and progress.
status: changed — his reason for rejecting crunches moved from "they round the lower back" to "tiny range of motion, not danger".

title: Best ab exercises: weighted decline sit-ups and hanging raises
statement: Weighted decline sit-ups and crunches, hanging leg and knee raises, kneeling cable crunches and the ab crunch machine. Weighted knee raises (dumbbell between the feet) replaced leg raises once those got too heavy. Sit-ups built his abs the most.
numbers: Decline sit-ups from bodyweight to 60-70 lb, controlled negative, ~10-15° decline; 10-15 reps; machine crunch 10-15.

title: Leg and knee raises do train the abs
statement: Hip flexors initiate, but the abs catch the pelvis and legs on the negative; hip-flexor involvement is no reason to reject an exercise. Raises made the biggest difference to his lower abs and decompress the spine.
numbers: 2020: 60-100 leg-raise reps a day.

title: Few ab exercises, progressed
statement: Pick 1-2 bracing and 1-2 stretching ab exercises and progress them rather than many variations. Repeating only one movement can limit growth.
numbers: Max two ab exercises done regularly; 2020: 2 exercises a day.

title: Placement: after heavy lower compounds or supersetted, never left for last
statement: Abs left for the end or for home get skipped; if you must cut a block, move abs earlier. Superset them with presses and pulls (hanging leg raises with pull-ups or rows decompress the spine). Hack squats pair with abs better than barbell squats; do less ab work on heavy deadlift days.
status: contradicted — 2020: ab isolation belongs on upper days while fresh, yet he trained abs on lower days; 2022: after the lower compounds.
check: Is ab work placed after the heavy lower compounds or in supersets, rather than tacked onto the end where it gets skipped?

title: Pullovers before sit-ups pre-stimulate the abs
statement: Pullovers stretch the abs without draining their strength; he calls them an underrated core movement and does them weekly.

title: Planks: low value for size
statement: Planks teach novices to brace but become redundant with heavy compounds; prefer dynamic stretched movements. If kept, use long-lever planks, put them on upper days or in a circuit.
numbers: Beginners can split volume, e.g. 3 stretch sets + 3 plank sets; sphinx push-ups built to 20 strict reps.

title: Train the obliques; they won't widen the waist
statement: Waist width is hip bone structure and love handles are fat; bigger obliques tighten the side and make love handles look smaller. Wide-waisted lifters should isolate them all the more.

title: Oblique exercises: twists, suitcase deadlifts, full-range side bends
statement: Russian twists, twisting or slow-tempo sit-ups, suitcase deadlifts (unilateral load hits them harder with less weight), and full-range side bends on a hyperextension bench (top tier). Standing DB side bends, twister machines and windshield wipers are poor.
numbers: Russian twists 4x10-15.
status: changed — 2020-2021: twisting work unnecessary; 2023-2024: side bends top tier, and he admits he wrongly thought lateral flexion was dangerous.

title: Squats, deadlifts and pull-ups grow the obliques through stabilization
statement: His obliques got big early on without isolation.

title: A long torso or narrow frame makes the core the focal point
statement: A long torso, long abdomen or narrow frame makes the core the focal point, so prioritize it.

title: Lack of core development is the most common weakness he sees
statement: It is the most frequent weak point in his physique reviews.

title: Gymnasts get abs from constant core control
statement: L-sits, the hollow body and little rest between reps. Calisthenics abs look good partly because those athletes are lean; gaining weight exposes undeveloped abs.

title: Ab and lower-back days are idiotic
statement: Spread ab work across the week; an "abs and cardio" day is filler.

title: Everyone should train the neck directly
statement: The neck ties the physique together, helps facial aesthetics, and protects you in crashes and contact sports. It grows fast on little volume, shrinks fast if you stop, and compounds stall it. A pencil neck "costs nothing" to fix; the sleep-apnea worry is a myth.
numbers: His neck went from 16 to about 17 in.
check: Is there direct neck work at least once a week?

title: Use neck curls and extensions, not bridges
statement: Bridges carry too much fatigue and injury risk (wrestlers already bridge). A harness was far better than plates or bands. Front neck: lie across a bench with a slow tempo.

title: Neck variations
statement: Band neck extensions driven by a hip hinge feel safer; a bent-over harness extension while holding a bar adds mid and lower traps.

title: Neck reps: 10-20, for safety
statement: Keep neck sets in a moderate-high range; never below 10 or above 20.
numbers: 2020: 10-15 ("even a little low"), 8-15 for 4-7 sets; 2022-2024: 10-20 (10-30 too wide), 3x15-20; his 2022 sets were 25-35 lb for 40-50 reps; start with a 5 lb plate.

title: Neck frequency: 1-2x a week on lower days
statement: One or two sessions a week already gives great results; more than 3-4 is pointless and risks overuse.
numbers: 2020: daily NO, then 3x/week; 2021: every 6 days too little; 2022: 10-12 sets/week (100-180 reps), max 4/day; 2024: 1-2x/week, one exercise per lower day.
status: changed — daily/3x per week (2020) → 1-2x per week (2024).

title: Superset neck with leg exercises so it's never skipped
statement: The neck is almost never limiting; adherence is the real problem. Pair one neck exercise with the first lower-body lift.

title: Neck directions
statement: He now trains flexion and extension only; rotation matters only for drivers and combat athletes. Tuck the chin before flexion if your posture is poor.
numbers: 2020-2022: one function per day if training 3x/week.
status: contradicted — 2020-2022: train every direction; 2024: never side flexion.

title: Neck and trap work help each other
statement: Training one supports the other.

title: Don't overdo the neck on a square jaw
statement: A neck should roughly match the jawline.

title: Strength and size are different qualities
statement: Strength and size are different qualities with some crossover, and training for one is not training for the other. Two lifters who add the same amount to a lift end up different sizes, and the one focused on volume and tonnage is bigger.
numbers: example: two lifters taking a squat from 100 to 300 lb, or reaching a 250 lb bench
scope: all lifters, and especially bodybuilders choosing what to train for
check: Is the program built to add muscle (volume, tonnage) rather than to raise lift numbers for their own sake?

title: You can't grow without getting stronger
statement: Strength is not the bodybuilder's goal, but you will have to get stronger to grow. Size and strength both rise, one faster than the other.
check: Does the program expect loads or reps on its lifts to go up over time?

title: Within a person, strength reflects muscle
statement: For one person on long-practised lifts, strength gains reflect muscle gains (bigger legs mean a bigger squat), and small size increases bring surprisingly large strength increases. Between people, leverages dominate, so you can't read strength from size.
numbers: legs from 20 to 25 in means the squat went up; between people: 20 in legs squatting ~400 vs 22 in legs squatting 500
scope: comparing yourself over time; not for comparing different lifters
