status: changed — 2020: he rejected the idea that strength can rise while muscles shrink, and said size can't rise while strength stays flat; 2022: citing Candito losing size while his total rose, he said you can trade one for the other. Later view: correlated within a person, but tradeable.

title: Strength athletes train functions, bodybuilders train muscles
statement: A powerlifter squats to train his squat, and a bodybuilder squats to train quads, glutes and hamstrings. In his bucket picture, powerlifters drain the muscle buckets to fill the big nervous-system bucket, and bodybuilders do the reverse.
scope: choosing how to perform and judge a lift

title: Specialising in one costs the other
statement: No program maximises both size and strength. At equal bodyweight bodybuilders are weaker and powerlifters stronger, which he puts down to training, not genetics, and no natural bodybuilder holds powerlifting records.
scope: anyone tempted to chase both goals at once

title: Bodybuilders have "accidental strength"
statement: Bodybuilders are weaker than powerlifters but much stronger than average. Powerlifters are small for their strength and imbalanced: big legs, chest, front delts and traps, with small arms and parts of the back.

title: Strong lifters need a higher threshold before size shows
statement: Lifters gifted for strength have to get much stronger before size shows. They should use that strength to add sets and reps, not to max out. For a naturally weak lifter like him, strength gains turn into size.
numbers: e.g. a strength-gifted lifter's OHP of 195 lb for reps vs his 135
scope: strength-gifted lifters; naturally weak lifters (the opposite case)

title: Prefer rep strength over 1RM strength
statement: A 10RM tracks muscle mass better than a 1RM, which mostly reflects the nervous system, so bodybuilders should focus on rep strength. 1RM calculators built from strength athletes don't apply to them.
numbers: 10RM vs 1RM
check: Is progress tracked through rep performance (e.g. a 10RM) rather than 1RMs?

title: Size over numbers
statement: He would take a big chest over a 500 lb bench. He isn't proud of any lift and says he "doesn't care about strength".
numbers: 500 lb bench (example)
scope: his personal priority as a bodybuilder

title: Neural gains are front-loaded and capped
statement: Neural and technical gains on a new lift mostly arrive early. After that you are at 95-100% technical mastery, and further strength at the same technique is muscle. Saying all strength gains could be neural is "wrong and demoralizing".
numbers: ~6 months of weekly practice (2020); "a month to a year" (2021); 95-100% technical mastery
scope: any lift practised regularly, past the learning phase
status: current — the window was refined from ~6 months (2020) to a month to a year (2021), with the same conclusion
check: Once a lift has been practised for ~6-12 months, is further strength at the same technique and bodyweight treated as muscle gain?

title: Learning or rotating lifts gives artificial progress
statement: Progress on a new or rotated lift is mostly relearning, not muscle. A box lets you think you are stronger at the squat. A second +100 lb on the bench brings far more muscle than the first.
numbers: his SSB box squat 185→365 lb in under a year, mostly relearning

title: Strength is largely skill
statement: Strength is largely the skill of recruiting motor units in a pattern, and it needs a fresh nervous system. High-frequency programs (daily squatting, Bulgarian or Wisconsin-style) raise one lift without much muscle, and he never prescribes them for size.

title: Big strength jumps without visible change are a red flag
statement: Past the novice stage, a big percentage strength gain with no muscle gain is biologically impossible. Strength that jumps while nothing visibly changes is a red flag.
numbers: +100 lb on chin-ups, dips and OHP should visibly change you
scope: past novice; judging your own or others' claims

title: Strength detrains faster than size
statement: Time off costs strength and work capacity well before it costs size. Presses, especially the OHP, regress quickly when not practised.
numbers: a month without a gym: legs barely changed, ~60 lb lost on lifts

title: Fat-driven strength isn't real progress
statement: Mass moves mass, but strength gained by adding mostly fat raises absolute strength, not pound-for-pound strength. It is leverage, and it disappears on a cut.
numbers: +20 lb on the bench with +20 lb bodyweight = no real progress; +100 lb of mostly fat raises absolute strength only
check: Is strength progress judged at a stable bodyweight (or alongside lean gain), not credited when it only follows fat gain?

title: Bodyweight helps presses far more than hinges
statement: Extra bodyweight helps pressing through leverage (a shorter range of motion) and helps hinges much less. In a deficit, hinges barely suffer while bench and OHP drop a lot.
numbers: "put 50 lb on your frame, add ~100 lb to your bench"; he benched 315 at ~220 lb, 335 when fatter, and lost it when the fat came off
scope: pressing vs hinging lifts across bulks and cuts

title: Pure strength needs mass, preferably muscle
statement: For pure strength, carry as much mass as possible, preferably muscle. Getting really strong means letting bodyweight rise, so staying very lean ("otter mode") means never getting really strong or reaching full size.
numbers: 400 lb at 10% body fat beats 400 lb at 20%
scope: lifters whose goal is maximal strength

title: You can get stronger without gaining weight
statement: Strength can keep rising at a stable bodyweight. He uses his own lifts as proof.
numbers: all his lifts rose at ≤210 lb (2020); in 2024 he beat his old 240 lb lifts at 220 lb, except the bench

title: Pound-for-pound matters
statement: Relative strength matters. Wilks-type scoring favours light lifters, and without it big frames that bulk would dominate. Being lighter also makes calisthenics easier.
numbers: his handstand push-ups were easy at 160 lb, impossible at 220 lb

title: Leverages dominate lower-body numbers
statement: Long femurs or a long torso make squats hard and deadlifts easier, and arms past the knees would make a deadlift world-record holder. Tall lifters have more absolute strength and shouldn't compare themselves with short ones, but short lifters keep a squat advantage through range of motion. A bigger structure (wide hips, big joints) means more strength potential.
scope: comparing squat and deadlift numbers between people

title: Strength work is a year-round pillar
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: A small dose of heavy strength work is the backbone of hypertrophy training and stays in all year, not only in a block. It is little tonnage, but its high-intensity peaks drive progression.
confidence: medium — ~10 videos, 2020→2021 (strongly stated early, less emphasised later)
status: changed — 2020-21: the backbone, "the one cornerstone you never cut"; 2024-25: high-bar squat and bench only 3-5 times a year, he "doesn't care about strength", and his heavy work moved to dips and weighted pull-ups. Later view: keep getting stronger, through less risky movements.
check: Does the program keep some heavy, low-rep work all year rather than only in phases?

title: Strength work opens the session
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Strength work comes first, and a day with zero strength work is bad, with occasional exceptions. Pre-activation must be light: an explosive opener taken short of failure (a kettlebell swing) primes you, while a leg-curl opener only fatigues. A small dose fires up the nervous system for the accessories.
check: Does the heavy strength work come first in the session, after only light warm-ups?

title: Strength work is a minority of the tonnage
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Strength work is a small share of total tonnage, and the rest is hypertrophy work. Strength exists to drive tonnage. Switching back and forth between strength and hypertrophy phases is "like living with divorced parents".
check: Is heavy strength work a minority of weekly tonnage, with most work in hypertrophy ranges?

title: Strength sets are solo sets
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Never superset or giant-set heavy squats, deadlifts or top sets. At most pair them with neck or calves. His bench depends on focus.
numbers: exception: bench and rows can be supersetted at 4x6-8
status: contradicted — he also says the bench is the one lift you can get away with not treating as strict strength work, and he allows bench/row supersets, while elsewhere it needs full focus and no supersets
check: Are heavy squats, deadlifts and top sets performed as solo sets, not in supersets or giant sets?

title: Plan strength-work progression carefully
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Plan how reps and sets evolve more carefully for strength work than for volume work, because it opens the session and affects everything after it.

title: No strength blocks for bodybuilders
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Bodybuilders don't need strength blocks. "Build a strength base first" is a lie, because strength grows on a bodybuilding program anyway. Bodybuilders don't peak, so peaking practices don't transfer, and speed work at 40% 1RM is junk volume.
numbers: speed work at 40% 1RM = junk volume
status: changed — 2020: most bodybuilding "is really powerbuilding", and 1-2 mesocycles of a powerlifting program to raise compound strength ("The Bridge") is "a good use"; 2022-24: rejects strength blocks and powerbuilding (see STR-63).
check: Does the program avoid separate strength-building or peaking phases?

title: "Get strong" must name the lifts
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Advice to "get strong" must say which lifts. Unless the answer is every lift for every muscle, ignore it. Trying to get as strong as possible, with good form, on every movement for every muscle *is* bodybuilding.

title: Bodybuilding progresses strength more slowly
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: A bodybuilding program raises strength more slowly, because effort is spread over more muscles and the goal is different, but it develops every body part. Powerlifting maximises strength, while bodybuilding keeps it stable to support steady tonnage.

title: The 85% rule doesn't maximise strength on purpose
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: His 85% rule deliberately doesn't maximise strength gains, because doing so would minimise volume accumulation.

title: Train weak points, not flattering variations
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Train your weak points, not variations that flatter your strengths.
numbers: his deadlift weak point is the top, not the floor

title: Approach the bar certain it goes up
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Walk up to the bar certain that the programmed weight will go up. Since adopting this, he has never failed a squat or deadlift recorded in his notebook.

title: Swap the main lift occasionally
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: Swapping a main lift for a while (squat → good morning, bench → weighted push-up) is fine, and a week off won't cost strength.

title: Chasing numbers was his worst period
section: Strength work inside a bodybuilding program
statement: His worst years were the ones spent chasing numbers: constant injuries, poor gains, and a rounded-back pull when he was obsessed with the number.
scope: his experience; a warning against number-chasing

title: Deadlift: few sets, never more than 5 reps
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Deadlift for 1-3 sets of 2-5 reps, never more than 5, and a single heavy set of 5 is often enough. 3x3 works very well if you leave reps in the tank.
numbers: 1-3 x 2-5; often 1x5; 3x3 with reps in reserve; 3x5 is a good volume for floor pulls; back-offs 4x3 at a comfortable triple or 3x3 submax
scope: heavy floor pulls, intermediate and up
check: Are heavy deadlift sets kept at 5 reps or fewer, for only a few sets?

title: Novice deadlift: sets of 6, no high-rep maxes
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Novices can deadlift sets of 6. Don't do 12-rep maxes on the conventional deadlift, where cardio and structure give out before the muscles.
numbers: 2x6 (12 reps)

title: Deadlift rarely; let other hinges do the work
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: His later practice is to deadlift from the floor rarely and get most posterior-chain volume from RDLs, good mornings and hyperextensions.
numbers: 2024: deadlifts about every 40 days, with a PR each time; ~95% of posterior-chain volume from RDLs, good mornings and hypers
status: changed — 2020-21: he pushed the deadlift hardest with 2-rep maxes, said they gave zero back pain and more progress than any other lift, and called a 2RM done for hypertrophy hypertrophy training; 2024: low-frequency deadlifts and no max testing. (His 2RMs also sit uneasily with STR-44; they are consistent only if a 2RM is not a 1RM.)

title: Squat: 4-8 reps, never singles to triples
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Squat in the 4-8 rep range, never singles, doubles or triples, to avoid knee valgus and the back tipping forward. Ramping single sets of 5 to a top set beats 3 sets at the same intensity.
numbers: 4-8 reps; 3x4-8 on one heavy day; 3-6 or 3-8; ramp 1x5 at RPE 6, 7, 8
check: Are heavy squat sets kept at 4 reps or more?

title: Bench: never below 4 reps
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Never bench below 4 reps, and keep to 4-8 if your shoulders are temperamental. Close-grip bench is his favourite variation and progressed very fast.
numbers: 3x4-6 flat barbell; 4x6-8; 8-10 fine; paused 6-10; Spoto press 8-12; close-grip 4x6-10
scope: bench and its variations; shoulder-friendly benching
check: Are bench press sets kept at 4 reps or more?

title: Overhead press: low reps, never supersetted
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: As strength work, the overhead press is done for low reps and never supersetted. 12-15 reps is too many when it opens the day, and 3x3 gives less volume than he wants.
numbers: 3-6 sets x 2-5 reps; 4x4-6 also given; not 12-15 as an opener; 3x3 too little volume
scope: OHP as the session's opening strength lift
status: contradicted — 2020: "a safe lift" you can even take to 1-2 rep maxes, vs 2020: it progresses too slowly and strains some lower backs when maxed daily (different contexts, a mild conflict)

title: 3x3 for strength lifts only
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: 3x3 is a favourite strength scheme: it leaves little room to sandbag and is very intense. Use it for bench, squat, pull-ups and deadlift, not for tonnage lifts like rows or RDLs.

title: Weighted pull-ups: low volume, heavy
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Weighted pull-ups are done for very low volume and high intensity. After leg day they also decompress the spine. His own loads are in ch. 1 and Appendix C.

title: Strength isn't only low reps
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: Mix rep ranges, because strength isn't built only with low reps. Successful powerlifters train varied ranges. Switching from high to low reps spikes strength short term, but long-term progression is what counts.

title: Reps at a given %1RM are individual
section: Rep schemes for the main lifts
statement: How many reps you can do at a given percentage of your 1RM varies between people, so online percentage and RPE calculators mislead.
numbers: e.g. 2 vs 4 reps at 90%

title: Never test 1RMs as a bodybuilder
statement: Maxing out is a powerlifting skill for peaking and brings no hypertrophy benefit. 1RMs don't even build strength (2-3RMs or 1 rep in reserve might), and every max-out uses up muscle-building capacity.
check: Does the program avoid 1RM testing?

title: Estimate your max from reps
statement: Estimate your max from rep performance and program by intensity. A double just under your max beats a single: double the tonnage, with less risk and fatigue.
numbers: e.g. 200x10; 485x2 vs 500x1; by 2021 he hadn't tested a 1RM in ~4 years

title: Constant max testing stalls progress
statement: Testing your max often "smashes the piggy bank": it spends what you have built instead of building more.
numbers: testing a deadlift 1RM every 2 weeks kept him at 465-485 lb for a year

title: Specificity wins
statement: The best way to bench more is to bench, and the best deadlift accessory is more deadlifting.

title: What carries over to the bench
statement: Close-grip bench carries over and skull crushers barely do. Push-ups and ring push-ups don't build bench strength, but dips carry over a lot. A slingshot carries over little to raw benching, and using only a slingshot for 2 months could cost raw strength.
numbers: he was advanced at push-ups yet benched ~145 lb the first time; a lifter hit a 4-plate bench after 6 weeks thanks to dip strength

title: Dips as the pressing strength lift
statement: He believes not everyone can reach a 4-plate bench, but everyone can reach a 4-plate dip. Dips don't hurt him, so far heavier dips feel achievable.
numbers: 4-plate dip for all; 5-7 plates feels achievable to him; "get to a 10-plate dip" before complaining about human limits
scope: pressing strength, especially for those whose bench stalls or hurts

title: What carries over to squat and deadlift
statement: Front squats carry over to the back squat less than people think, and pause squats carry over more. Front squats barely help the conventional pull beyond upper-back rigidity. A stronger squat helps the deadlift only up to a point. The SSB box squat in deadlift stance may be the best conventional-deadlift accessory, and sumo carries to conventional better than the reverse.

title: Pause reps are a variation, not a replacement
statement: Pause reps build strength but force lighter weights and can't replace touch-and-go reps, so use them as variations. Even top lifters use variations, so pure minimalism fails.

title: Partials and odd lifts mask true strength
statement: Partial range of motion can help the full lift, but partials and unusual lifts hide your true strength.
numbers: a 1000 lb rack pull vs a 500 lb deadlift; his 500 lb front-rack holds vs Olympic lifters' 700
scope: judging strength from partials and odd lifts

title: Machine numbers don't transfer
statement: Machine numbers don't transfer to free-weight lifts. Leg presses of 500-600 lb are simply the kind of load legs should handle.
numbers: a 500 lb leg press usually means a ~300 lb squat

title: Squats are more taxing than deadlifts
statement: With proper technique, squats are more taxing than deadlifts. Big deadlift-to-squat ratios come from sloppy pulls and timid squats.

title: Where heavy lifts fail
statement: In hinges and squats you fail on the way up or at the turnaround, never on the way down. Many "mid-squat" failures are really a failure to build speed out of the hole. A rounded ("fishing-rod") position makes the lockout harder.

title: Grip: mixed, hook, straps and thick bars
statement: A mixed grip can beat straps for some lifters. Powerlifters should give the hook grip a real try first, and thick-grip training makes a normal bar feel easier.
numbers: him: double overhand caps him at a ~330 lb single vs 470 lb with mixed grip

title: Strength standards are C-tier
statement: He ignores strength standards unless you compete. They rest on unverified self-reports or powerlifter data and round plate numbers, and they ignore leverages, experience, the nervous system and timeline. They compare you to weak people and turn hypertrophy training into number-chasing. If you compete, use your sport's competition standards.
scope: non-competing lifters; competitors use their sport's standards
check: Does the program avoid generic strength standards as targets (unless the lifter competes)?

title: Size-from-strength standards are illogical
statement: Standards that promise size from strength ("a 200 lb OHP gives big shoulders") are illogical; flip them and you get nonsense like "20 in arms means a strong curl". A 3-plate bench goal can keep a bodybuilder's chest small.
numbers: 200 lb OHP; 3-plate bench (examples)

title: The 1/2/3/4 standard only fits novices
statement: The 1/2/3/4-plate standard roughly holds for novices because the loads are low, but beyond novice, leverages make fixed numbers meaningless. The OHP step is far harder than the others.
numbers: 135 OHP / 225 bench / 315 squat / 405 deadlift; OHP 135→225 is far harder than the rest; a 3-plate bench is much easier than a 2-plate OHP

title: Minimum baselines he endorses
statement: A trained adult man should never drop below 20 push-ups. The average man can't do a pull-up or deadlift his bodyweight, and every able-bodied man should. A year of training should get you past a few push-ups and a light OHP, and any lifter can reach a ~400 lb pull.
numbers: ≥20 push-ups; 1 pull-up; bodyweight deadlift; a year should beat a 60 lb OHP at 140 lb; untrained man pulls ~200 lb, any lifter can reach ~400
scope: trained adult men; able-bodied men in general

title: Strength targets he links to growth
statement: The strength gains he cites as signs of growth are rep targets on hypertrophy lifts, not 1RMs.
numbers: strict EZ curl 60→100 lb x6 grows biceps; ~300 lb per leg on split squats for a heavy lifter; +50 lb on the bench "makes you look like a different person"

title: Round numbers create plateaus in your head
statement: Beliefs like "a natural can't bench 400" and idolising round numbers create mental plateaus.
numbers: 400 lb bench (example)

title: Rejects powerbuilding
statement: Heavy big-three work plus high-rep accessories usually delivers neither size nor strength. It trains one narrow kind of strength (1RMs on three lifts) that has to dominate and drains energy, and most powerbuilders never compete. The fix is to drop the 1RM training, and then you are just bodybuilding the silver/bronze-era way. He debated Dr. Milo Wolf on this.
status: current — see STR-26 for his earlier, more favourable 2020 view
check: Is the program free of 1RM-focused big-three work bolted onto high-rep accessories (powerbuilding)?

title: Train like a powerlifter, look like one
statement: Training like a powerlifter makes you look like one: bottom-heavy and not aesthetic. Lifters chasing the big three often stay skinny-fat (the "Starting Strength problem"), and most powerlifters wrongly expect aesthetics. You don't need a 700 lb deadlift for a big back.
numbers: powerlifting volume ~70-80% lower body; 700 lb deadlift (example)
check: Is training volume spread across all muscles rather than concentrated on the big three and the lower body?

title: The big three are a small part of strength
statement: The big three are a small part of the body's strength potential. Big naturals may be weak on them but strong on isolations and back work. The big three should express strength, not pigeonhole you.
numbers: big three ≈ 1/10 of strength potential; maybe 5% of Arnold's volume

title: "Strength copers"
statement: He claims that lifters who chose strength because they couldn't build a physique, or who say "the best way to get big is to get strong", are lying to themselves.
scope: his opinion of a type of lifter

title: What bodybuilders can learn from powerlifters
statement: Powerlifters who stall add volume and run hypertrophy blocks, because strength eventually needs bigger fibres, and many have huge quads. Their peak-drop-peak cycle works for strength, not for tonnage.

title: Strength sports are minimalist, bodybuilding maximalist
statement: Strength sports are minimalist by default and bodybuilding is maximalist. The more specific the need, the more minimalist the method. Bodybuilding and powerlifting are "cousins who shouldn't mix".

title: Strongman is a better strength test
statement: Strongman tests strength better than powerlifting, and a strength athlete who never competes isn't one. Former strongmen and powerlifters in their 30s-40s fit well into bodybuilding.

title: Modern strength athletes carry lean muscle
statement: Modern strength athletes recomp into lighter classes and carry lean muscle, and a fluffy lifter loses to leaner lifters in his class.

title: Unverified lifts don't count
statement: A lift with no video, witness or record doesn't count, and neither does one with bands, chains, boxes, cambered bars, above-parallel squats or unweighed plates. Weigh and load plates on camera, ideally at a sanctioned meet, and claim records only in competition.
numbers: technical plates can fake ~100 lb; a deadlift-bar, deadlift-only event adds ~20-30 lb at 600

title: Strength claims need bodyweight
statement: A strength claim means nothing without the lifter's bodyweight. In his view, IFBB pros at 250-270 lb pulling ~600 lb are weak.
numbers: e.g. a 260 lb lifter mocking a 200 lb one; 250-270 lb pros pulling ~600 lb

title: Fighters: hypertrophy helps, max testing doesn't
statement: Lifting doesn't make you a fighter, but hypertrophy carries over to fighting, while fight training does nothing for size. Strength matters more for grappling than striking. Fighters shouldn't test 1RMs (higher reps, less injury), and their staple is any floor pull for low reps.
numbers: floor pull 1-3 x 5 (or 1-3 x 2-5), any style

title: Muscle multiplies power, if it's the right muscle
statement: Muscle multiplies power, but only the muscle the sport uses. Olympic lifts are counterproductive for athletes (bad racks, 1RM testing), and a rugby player should keep lower-body compound volume low.

title: Manual workers still need strength training
statement: Blue-collar workers still need strength training, because the job trains only certain qualities. Even with a grip-heavy job, use straps or a brief heavy hold.

title: Women should strength train every pattern
statement: Women should strength train every movement pattern. They get very strong without ballooning.
numbers: e.g. 1-plate to 2-plate squat

title: Male maximal strength peaks around 35-40
statement: Male maximal strength peaks around 35-40, going by most past Olympic lifters and powerlifters.
numbers: ~35-40 years

title: Bodybuilding is beauty through illusion, not mass
statement: Bodybuilding pursues beauty through illusion, not a pile of mass or big measurements; flow, insertions and posing beat raw size.

title: Train with aesthetic intent or get an accidental physique
statement: Pure strength, big-three-only or compound-only training gives an "accidental" physique: big trunk and quads, small arms (spider, fridge, frog). A minimalist strength routine won't build an aesthetic body. His own 2020 big-three-only experiment confirmed it.
scope: Anyone whose goal is the look, not strength alone.
check: Does the program include work chosen for the look (isolation for arms, delts, traps and other visual muscles) rather than only the big compound lifts?

title: Training for looks is legitimate, not vain or feminine
statement: Anyone who trains for looks is a bodybuilder. Wanting to look good is legitimate, and calling it vain or feminine is shaming that pushes men toward neglecting themselves.
numbers: stage pros are under 0.1% of bodybuilding
scope: All men and women training; includes calisthenics and "functional" trainees, many of whom he calls closet bodybuilders.

title: No purely aesthetic stimulus exists
statement: You train function and orient it toward looks; a developed muscle always functions, and a stronger curl means a bigger biceps.

title: Maximizing form costs function, and vice versa
statement: Pick form or function as the priority and accept getting only some of the other. Size and function correlate only when the sport dictates size; he accepts being slower and less athletic.
scope: Lifters choosing between physique and athletic goals.

title: Athleticism isn't a look
statement: A six-pack shows leanness, not athletic ability; strongmen and fat athletes have strong cores under the fat. His "sumo test": a sumo wrestler's legs are athletic.

title: Have a dream physique, ideally a fictional one
statement: Pick a dream physique and build your program around it, preferably from statues, paintings, manga or comics rather than real people. Dreamers' results skew toward their dream; an anime physique can be approximated by matching its muscle distribution.
scope: Goal-setting for anyone training for looks.

title: Physique preference is subjective
statement: Any goal is valid (small legs, a slim beach body); ideals exist to be broken and you need no permission. Push the muscles that serve the goal and maintain the rest.

title: Imbalances must be deliberate
statement: Most imbalances are accidents, and "bodybuilding should not have accidents". Legs so small they detract from the physique have no merit, and long legs are no excuse.
check: Is every lagging or dominant body part a deliberate choice tied to the stated goal, rather than a by-product of exercise selection?

title: Natural powerlifters and bodybuilders look alike for a reason
statement: They look alike only because natural bodybuilders train like powerlifters. Aesthetic programs must include isolation and give presses more volume; squatting as much as pressing builds a big lower body.
scope: Natural lifters with an aesthetic goal.

title: Natural ideal is about 12-18% body fat
statement: A natural should carry about 12-18% body fat with lots of muscle; stage condition is pointless for naturals. Old-school naturals and physique competitors 100 years ago were in this range and looked tremendous.
numbers: 12-18% (old-school naturals); 10-16% (era competitors); abs look good at 10, 15 or 17%; 15% looks good; 6-8% "achievable but not reasonable"; 5% is masochism; 8% standards make men look like skeletons
scope: Naturals training for looks, not stage competitors.
check: Is the target condition in the 12-18% range rather than stage leanness (5-8%)?

title: His own body fat sits around 16-18%
statement: He keeps a visible six-pack and oblique and serratus separation at 16-18% and credits direct core training, not genetics. People guess 12% because of his muscle-to-fat ratio.
scope: His own physique (see ch. 1 for full stats).

title: He never cared about being very lean
statement: Being very lean was never his priority. Fat on the arms helps them look big when relaxed; by stage standards he is fat, but normal people see a six-pack.
status: contradicted — 2020 he said his aim was to be as big as his body allows at the lowest body fat possible; 2024 he says he never cared about being lean and still doesn't.

title: To look big at rest, carry some fat
statement: Muscle plus some fat is what makes a physique look big at rest; stripping it just makes you look small. Most admired naturals carry a fair amount of fat, and on a skinny man muscle plus some fat transforms the look.
numbers: dropping ~20 lb of intramuscular and surrounding fat would make him look small
scope: Naturals wanting to look big day to day.

title: Too much fat ruins the look; a gut kills big limbs
statement: There is no point being big at too high a body fat. If your stomach protrudes past your chest you aren't in shape; excess fat goes to the waist and love handles.
scope: All; the upper bound on AES-14.

title: More muscle makes the same body fat look leaner
statement: Two people at the same body fat look different; on a large lean mass, trading fat for muscle at the same weight looks far better. Fat loss during recomposition is hard to judge by eye.
numbers: two people at 17% look different; at higher bodyweight a 2% change is far more fat

title: People underestimate body fat by about 5 points
statement: Subtract about 5 points from body fat claims. Knowing the exact figure is useless; norms are built on untrained people and no measuring method is best, so look and feel good.
numbers: subtract ~5 points (e.g. a claimed 10-12% is ~15-16%)

title: Visible detail needs muscle size, not just leanness
statement: What shows depends on muscle size and fat pattern as well as body fat. Lower abs and serratus need size; to get striking abs, "grow them" rather than shred.
numbers: upper/lower pec separation shows below ~10-11%, flexed only; visible arm and leg separation suggests ~10-12%

title: Veins come from muscle growth
statement: Existing veins enlarge around muscles as they grow (his biceps, lats, shoulders); you need to be fairly lean but not extremely lean.
numbers: not below 10% needed

title: Apollonian V-taper vs Herculean X-taper
statement: The Greek tradition has two branches: Apollonian (wide shoulders and lats, small waist, smaller legs, low fat) and Herculean/Farnese (thicker waist, big limbs, legs and core). He prefers the Herculean, ancient "bear mode"; the Farnese Hercules is closer to his ideal.
scope: Goal-setting; he has written programs for both.

title: His "Berserker" ideal: big limbs, strong core, upper back
statement: Massive arms, forearms and legs slightly out of proportion with the trunk, a strong core, developed upper back and smaller shoulders. Big limbs pull attention from the torso, an illusion.
status: changed — 2020-22 the trunk and chest stay comparatively small (2021 "Buddha physique": big limbs, small shoulders and chest, very developed core); 2023 the Berserker includes a big chest; 2025, being narrow, he chases a Bizu-style physique with huge traps.

title: Arms should look bigger than the shoulders
statement: He dislikes big round delts on smaller limbs; the arm should dominate the shoulder.
scope: His preference; others may prefer dominant shoulders (see AES-41).
status: changed — 2020-22 he kept delts deliberately small and cut shoulder tonnage because they were getting too big; 2023-24 shoulders became his weak point to bring up (rounder via vertical presses and isolation) and top tier in his list, while he still likes them small next to the arm. Later view: grow them, keep arms dominant.

title: Classical/silver-era alternative
statement: A classical look has smaller legs and posterior chain, a tight waist and a V-taper from shoulders and lats; the silver era didn't chase glutes or hamstrings. Use upper/lower plus arm/upper hybrids instead of two lower days.
numbers: Reeves' rule: neck = arms = calves

title: Steve Reeves is his top natural reference
statement: Reeves followed Greek proportions and stopped training calves until his arms caught up. His target is slightly bigger than Michelangelo's David.
numbers: Reeves: 6'1", 210-225 lb, 18.5-19 in arms, 29 in waist, 26 in thighs, ~10% body fat; arms = neck = calves

title: As one area grows, its neighbours must follow
statement: Growing arms need a growing chest or it looks flat; big pecs with spaghetti arms look bad; fix lagging arms without swinging to huge arms on a small torso. Flow dies with big quads and small calves, or big biceps and small forearms.
check: When a muscle is prioritized, are its visual neighbours (e.g. chest for arms, forearms for biceps, calves for quads) also trained enough to keep up?

title: Flow matters more than muscle size
statement: How the whole frame connects matters more than individual size. The core makes or breaks it, while neck and calves can lag without hurting it much.

title: Cheerleader effect
statement: One outstanding muscle makes the weaker ones around it look better.

title: Novices grow everything; advanced lifters must choose
statement: Beginners can grow every muscle at once. Past a point, assess objectively where you can slack off to put volume elsewhere.

title: Limbs make the bodybuilder
statement: No real bodybuilder has small arms, and big arms are what normal people lack. A big back and chest without arms looks big but not like a bodybuilder; only a huge V-taper gets away with small arms. Arms and forearms are always visible in a T-shirt.
scope: Men training for looks; exception: a huge V-taper.
check: Are arms and forearms given direct priority rather than left to compound lifts?

title: Isolate the arms or become a "spider"
statement: Powerlifter-written hypertrophy programs neglect the triceps long head, biceps, forearms, rear delts and traps, producing a big torso on spaghetti arms. Add isolation for them.
numbers: ≥1 isolation exercise for forearms, ≥1 for traps, ≥2 for biceps, ≥2 for triceps long head
check: Does the program include at least 2 isolation exercises each for biceps and triceps long head, and at least 1 each for forearms and traps?

title: Triceps long head is top tier
statement: The long head is the biggest part of the arm and visible from every angle relaxed. It props up the biceps and its peak, adds width and back-pose thickness, and links with lats and rear delts (the "pitbull" look).
numbers: a long sweep makes a 17 in arm look like 19 in

title: Forearms are top tier
statement: Forearms are always exposed, don't depend on flexing, carry little fat and look vascular even when fluffy. A big wrist makes them look blocky; deadlifts build forearms less than people think.

title: Biceps are only second tier; brachialis adds thickness
statement: Everyone trains biceps, sleeves hide them, they depend on flexing and give less thickness than triceps. The brachialis is the hidden MVP of arm thickness.

title: His arm and forearm targets
statement: He aims for 19 in arms, since 20 in is "mythical" for him, and 15 in forearms. Long arms need about 2 extra inches to give the same effect.
numbers: arms ~18 in pumped (2020-01) → goal 19 in; forearms 13-13.5 in on 6.5 in wrists → goal 15 in; long arms +~2 in

title: His own biceps-triceps balance
statement: His biceps outgrew his triceps; once the long head caught up he re-emphasised biceps, and he now accepts biceps dominance may never change.
status: changed — 2020 biceps dominant; 2022 long head caught up, so he deliberately re-emphasised biceps; 2023 he accepts biceps dominance may be permanent.

title: V-taper toolkit
statement: A V-taper comes from lats and shoulders: pullovers for the ribcage, pull-ups for outer lats, lateral raises and face pulls for side and rear delts, later upright rows and weighted pull-ups. Without lats you get a T-taper; pullovers and core work also fix an hourglass look.
scope: Lifters with a narrow shoulder-to-waist ratio.

title: Shoulders are top tier for daily looks
statement: All three delt heads give the most width and look good at any body fat; the rear delt gives the shoulder its pop and 3D look. "Shelf muscles" (delts, traps, upper chest) give the bodybuilder look.
status: current — this is his later view; see AES-22 for how it evolved.

title: Aesthetic lifters over-hammer shoulders
statement: Heavy shoulder focus is a habit borrowed from enhanced bodybuilders; naturals can have capped delts but not the bulky popping delts of steroid users.

title: You can never have too much upper back
statement: A thick upper back marks a seasoned lifter; traps are top tier and growing them does not make you look narrower (he disagrees with Gironda here). "Bear mode" needs shrugs and more rows.
scope: General; Apollonian/classical goals favour less lat flare (goal-dependent, not a conflict).
check: Does the program train the upper back and traps directly (rows, shrugs) rather than avoiding traps for fear of looking narrow?

title: Width vs thickness
statement: Width comes from outer lats and medial delts; thickness from mid/lower traps, lower back, chest and arms. Fix a flat-looking physique with chest, arms and traps. Erectors are second tier and show in clothes; ignore the lower-back "smile", which needs extreme leanness.

title: Chest is second tier, upper chest third
statement: The chest fills the shirt; the upper chest is hidden by it, and he doesn't care about it. A flatter chest with dominant shoulders is a valid preference.

title: A better front usually means more front training
statement: A front that outshines the back usually reflects training priority; golden-era aesthetics prioritised the front (chest and arms).

title: The core ties the physique together
statement: The eye goes to the midsection first, and weak abs make everything look worse; without his abs, he says, his physique would look terrible. Never skip core, especially with a wide waist.
scope: All, especially shirtless looks and wide waists.
status: changed — 2020-23 the core is key (2021: the most important thing for aesthetics); 2024 tier list puts abs bottom tier for everyday clothed looks, while he still says never skip core. A refinement by context (clothed vs shirtless).
check: Is the core trained directly?

title: Waist width is mostly bone structure
statement: Ab and oblique training won't ruin a V-taper; it only thickens the wall a little. Bodybuilders with thick obliques often had fat there first, and waist fat goes when you cut.
status: current — (a 2020 tension: he said he doesn't care about a tiny waist, yet keeps the waist as tight as possible; probably "can't be tiny, keep it tight".)

title: With a wide waist, build big abs and everything around it
statement: Big abs read as a strong waist. Add a beefy back, delts for width, big arms and legs; with a poor structure, pack on mass rather than chase being shredded. Wide hips → obliques, lats, chest, shoulders.
scope: Lifters with wide waists or hips.
check: For a wide-waisted lifter, does the plan add size around the waist (abs, obliques, back, delts, limbs) rather than rely on getting very lean?

title: Abs only count on a muscular body
statement: The abs obsession produces over-dieting skinny guys (the Zyzz-era ab chasers) and guys who justify a gut. Abs matter only on a muscular body.
numbers: ~90% of young men want abs

title: Do heavy squats and hinges thicken the waist?
statement: He said heavy knee flexion and hip hinges develop the waist somewhat, so don't overdo them if you want it tight, though a few sets won't bloat you.
status: contradicted — 2022 he says they develop the waist; the same year he calls the idea that heavy pulls thicken the waist "mostly nonsense".

title: A big stomach at low body fat is usually bloating
statement: Poorly digested food, water, two huge meals or breathing cause it. Building the core makes the stomach look smaller; vacuums only help with enough mass on top.
scope: Lean lifters with a protruding stomach.

title: Neck standard: in line with the jaw from the front
statement: From the front the neck should line up with the jaw; much bigger looks like a ball. Of three stages (pencil, intermediate/aesthetic, monster), intermediate is enough. Long necks need more work, and big traps on a pencil neck look wrong.
numbers: 2020: neck ≈ arm size (≥18 in for 19 in arms); 2022-24: in line with the jaw
status: changed — 2020 the neck should be wider than the jaw and about arm size; 2022-24 in line with the jaw is enough, more looks like a ball.
check: Is the neck trained directly toward roughly jaw width?

title: A thick neck is the #1 facial upgrade
statement: A thicker neck gives a squarer jaw, a leaner-looking and more masculine face; a pencil neck makes a face look worse. Even non-lifters should train it; it is top tier. For a baby face: lift, train neck, grow a beard.

title: Jaw training isn't worth it
statement: The jawline is mostly genetic and depends on leanness; jaw training stresses the teeth and causes tension.

title: Looksmaxxing: lifting is the base stat
statement: Your body is the base stat and clothes and grooming are "buffs" on it; nothing requires paying anyone. Tailored jeans are worth it, and elastic athletic jeans suit big legs.
numbers: lifting ~80% of looksmaxxing, hair ~40%

title: His thigh-size scale
statement: He grades male thighs by circumference but warns not to obsess, since leg size depends on leg length. In 2020 his calves lagged too far behind his thighs.
numbers: thighs 20-22 in small, 26-27 in big, 29-30 in very big; his 26-27 in thighs vs 16 in calves (2020)

title: Big legs make the waist look smaller
statement: He likes big legs: they make the waist look smaller, are rarely developed and get noticed. Big male legs aren't feminine, and muscular legs can't be too big.

title: Legs shouldn't dwarf the upper body
statement: The "frog physique" (big legs, small top) comes from PR-driven, squat-heavy or powerlifting training. Squat volume can be reduced, and training legs minimally once a week is fine for an upper-body goal.
numbers: legs once a week, minimal, for upper-body goals
check: Is lower-body volume kept in proportion to upper-body volume, so legs don't outgrow the upper body unintentionally?

title: Glutes are top tier for men
statement: Glutes are the most 3D muscle, visible through pants and not lean-dependent; male glutes are square, store little fat and never hurt a male physique. Women look at them a lot.
status: changed — 2022 he noted the silver era didn't chase glutes and the posterior chain was optional; 2024 glutes are top tier (already in 2021 he said they can't hurt a male physique).

title: Calves and quads second tier, hamstrings third
statement: Calves and quads show in shorts and pants; hamstrings show only from behind. Obsessing over the VMO is "small guy syndrome".

title: Use genetic gifts to save time
statement: If a muscle grows well from compounds (his quads from squats), skip extra work for it and isolate weak parts instead.

title: Rank muscles by how they look relaxed in clothes
section: Muscle tier list for everyday looks (2024)
statement: Muscles that show in clothes without flexing and regardless of leanness rank highest (see table). Abs are bottom tier because clothes hide them and they depend heavily on leanness.
numbers: four tiers (see table)
scope: Everyday clothed looks, not the stage or shirtless.

title: Judge a physique relaxed, in everyday clothes
section: Muscle tier list for everyday looks (2024)
statement: Relaxed poses in everyday clothes are the real test, because you can't hide weaknesses there; stage flexing is not the reference.
check: Is the physique judged relaxed and clothed rather than only pumped and flexed?

title: Being short is an advantage for looking big
statement: Shorter segments look more 3D and bigger with less muscle. On stage, though, tall freaks with good insertions usually win.
numbers: the same arm looks huge at 5'5" and flat at 6'5"; 200 lb at 5'4" looks like a tank, wiry at 6'4"

title: Frame is clavicles, waist, hips and joints
statement: Frame means clavicle width, waist, hips and joint size. Small joints make muscle bellies look bigger: thick wrists shrink forearms, thick elbows blunt peaks, big knees stop the quad sweep. Greek proportions were scaled from the wrist.
numbers: a 15 in forearm looks smaller on a thick wrist

title: Narrow frames: build the outline
statement: With a narrow or small frame, build the outline (triceps long head, medial and rear delts, traps, neck) and big limbs that extend sideways, and use open poses. Narrow clavicles → prioritise arms and as much delt as possible.
check: For a narrow-framed lifter, are the outline muscles (long head, side and rear delts, traps, neck) prioritized?

title: Short stocky vs tall lifters
statement: Short stocky lifters shouldn't chase shoulders and mass for their own sake; tall lifters need everything big, especially thickness from squats and deadlifts.

title: Mass tolerance depends on frame
statement: A great frame wants minimal excess mass; a poor frame needs size even with some fat.
numbers: a 5'7" small-framed man with wide hips can't carry over ~200 lb and look good

title: Real-world size perspective
statement: Average gym-goers are lighter than people assume, so a relatively lean 200 lb already looks like you lift. A lifter training 10+ years for aesthetics shouldn't look early-intermediate, and a lean 165 lb lifter at 5'8" can look huge.
numbers: average gym-goer 170-180 lb; ~200 lb relatively lean looks like you lift; 220 lb lean natural is big; lean 165 lb at 5'8" can look huge

title: Pump, light, angle and posing change the look hugely
statement: Window-light mirror shots flatter; at 220 lb he doesn't look it unpumped, and 20-30 lb lighter but pumped, people would say he grew.
numbers: 220 lb bodyweight; 20-30 lb lighter pumped looks bigger

title: Measurements: objective but misleading
statement: Tape measurements track progress objectively, but pump and fat inflate them and big numbers can look worse than smaller ones. Use a locking tape and measure on dates fixed in advance. He claims Blaha's "18 in" arms are really 14-15 in and that Blaha wears a belt shirtless to fake a V-taper (his unverified opinion).
numbers: +10% body fat raises all measurements; measure one part every 2-3 months on pre-set dates (e.g. 6 months); 22 in arms can look worse than smaller ones

title: His physique review method
statement: Identify strong and weak points; estimate body fat to choose cut, recomp or bulk; spot undeveloped high-potential parts; fix the program toward the goal. People misjudge their own strengths, and even stage physiques have at least two weak areas.
numbers: at least two weak areas even on stage physiques
scope: Reviewing a physique; he asks for training history, program, goals, lift numbers and many angles.

title: His grading scale
statement: He grades each muscle S/A/B/C. He rates himself 6.5/10 and has never met a 10; he graded a top French natural 6/10 and was accused of unrealistic standards.
numbers: S/A/B/C per muscle; himself 6.5/10

title: Posing matters
statement: A nice physique without posing skill is wasted. Pressing a limb against something makes arms look bigger and leaner; lats push out the delts and triceps in poses.

title: Archetypes describe where the mass sits
statement: He uses animal archetypes (spider, frog, otter, bear, whale, barbarian, hippo, lobster) to describe physiques by mass distribution and body fat (see table).

title: Otter mode is what most women pick
statement: The otter look (Fight Club Brad Pitt) is what most women pick and what most people can reach; getting too big or strong takes you out of it. Stopping there stalls progression, but you see size coming and can stop.
numbers: ~155 lb (Fight Club Brad Pitt); reachable in 1-2 years

title: Calisthenics builds statues but stays light
statement: Calisthenics gives the most statue-like bodies outside bodybuilding, but its athletes stay light and need heavy pulls, shrugs, rows, legs, calves and arms to look like bodybuilders. Olympic lifters look aesthetic through core, shoulders and upper back.
numbers: calisthenics athletes 160-170 lb; Olympic lifters 160-190 lb classes
scope: Calisthenics and other athletes wanting a bodybuilder look.

title: Muscle is the best way for a man to look better
statement: Muscle changes how people treat a man (halo effect); looking strong is effectively being strong socially, signalling work ethic and protection. "Looks don't matter" is a cope; he felt the shift at 15 and around 19, when at a party men greeted him and ignored the woman beside him.
numbers: ~19 years old at 170-180 lb (his anecdote)

title: Women like muscle, not mass monsters
statement: Women like muscle (chest, shoulders, arms, abs, glutes) but not mass monsters or shredded steroid looks; many prefer bulky to shredded. "Too big" usually means enhanced or posturing; no woman ever told him he was too big, and strength numbers don't impress them.

title: Lifting makes women more feminine, not bulky
statement: Most women look better heavier with more muscle. Women's usual goals (lower body, toned arms, abs) need different programs.

title: Muscle alone doesn't fix dating
statement: Personality still counts: average-looking funny, confident men do fine, and bragging about muscle puts women off.

title: The look takes years
statement: Changes take months to show and years before people notice. A natural with 5-10 years of training looks far better than anyone on a beach, and a man's physical prime can run to about 40-45 if he keeps lifting.
numbers: 5-10 years; prime ~40-45; Kratos-type look (smaller version) 10-15 years

title: Cosmetic surgery is a cop-out
statement: Surgery is a cop-out except for loose skin and gynecomastia; work for a few years first. He reads ab implants from abs on a protruding gut that never change year to year, and butt implants from glutes out of line with squat strength.
numbers: ~2-plate squat expected for real developed glutes; implants need replacing about every 10 years

title: Injuries are preventable, not bad luck
statement: Injuries come from variables you failed to control, so they are preventable; calling them bad luck is lazy and irresponsible.
scope: All lifters. Only things like being tackled mid-lift are truly out of your control; skipping a warm-up or slipping on ice still counts as yours.

title: Volume/intensity mismanagement is the top cause
statement: Ego, too much load and forcing the extra rep cause most injuries; together with poor positioning they account for the "vast majority". Perfect form cannot save poor volume/intensity management.

title: Injury = load and fatigue exceeding tissue capacity
statement: An injury is pressure exceeding what the tissue can handle, a failure to adapt to a cycle of stress. Risk depends on load and accumulated fatigue together.
numbers: 50% of max is "baby weight"; 5 reps at 80% to failure every day raises risk daily as fatigue builds.

title: The "red zone" is where injuries happen
statement: Acute injuries happen where the negative reverses into the positive; almost nobody gets hurt at lockout. Negative-first lifts (squat, bench) are the most dangerous at high intensity, and a controlled negative is injury prevention.
numbers: "99%" of injuries in the red zone (2020); 95-98% (2021).
scope: All lifts, especially heavy squat and bench.

title: Grinding the last rep causes most injuries
statement: Most gym injuries come in the last grindy reps of heavy sets. With no grinding, staying in the rep range and no last-rep chasing, risk is "almost zero". All his own past injuries came from grinding reps he wasn't capable of.
numbers: Cutting 3-4 grinder squat reps gave him 3 years with no squat injury.
check: Does the program avoid grinding ugly reps and chasing the extra rep on heavy sets?

title: Overuse comes from repetition, not frequency
statement: Overuse injuries come from repeating the same movement, angle, stance and load. Frequency itself is not the cause. Back-off sets in the same style as the main lift, minimalist HIT and Big-3-only training all feed tendinitis.
numbers: A quad can be trained every 48 h if the stance varies.
scope: All lifters; see INJ-46 for the rotation rule.

title: Muscle should give out before tendon
statement: Mechanical failure with weak technique shifts tonnage onto skeleton and tendons and causes tendinitis. Maximize stress on the muscle and minimize it on tendons; tendons are never fully spared, but there is a sweet spot.

title: Never high volume, frequency and intensity together
statement: You can combine two of high volume, high frequency and high intensity, never all three; the trifecta "summons injury".

title: Life stress and sleep affect tendons
statement: Life stress, poor sleep and alcohol promote tendon inflammation; his old tendinitis flares on stressful days with no training change.
status: changed — 2020-2021 he said stress may matter as much as form; late 2021 he said diet-driven inflammation is only minor and movement matters far more.

title: Form is "where", programming is "when"
statement: Form is awareness in the moment, programming is awareness over time; injuries become predictable when a weak "where" meets a bad "when". His early videos covered only form.

title: Injuries come from autopilot and surprise
statement: Most injuries happen on autopilot or from unexpected motion or timing, so stay present and do the most dangerous lift first while fresh (see INJ-50).

title: Partial-only training leaves deep ranges unprepared
statement: If you only train partial range, a failed rep that drives you deep finds the muscle unprepared, and that is when pecs, backs and biceps snap. Train full ROM at least sometimes, deep, controlled and light.

title: Freak injuries come from freakish choices
statement: Freak injuries are rare and come from doing something "freakishly stupid", such as attempting a weight you've never approached. Structural failure mid-lift is "entirely avoidable".
numbers: If you squat 275×4, don't load 315 for a single.

title: Most real injuries happen outside the gym
statement: Most real-world injuries are domestic (boxes, lawnmowers, ice), not heavy gym lifts, because in the gym you're warm and primed.

title: Tall, lanky lifters get hurt more
statement: Tall lifters get hurt more because their strength outpaces recovery and longer levers put more torque on the lower back and knees.

title: No lift is inherently dangerous
statement: Danger depends on how, by whom and at what load a lift is done; rounding risk exists only for a given intensity, lift and person. Inactivity is more dangerous than heavy squats or deadlifts.

title: Injury-prone people should adapt the stimulus
statement: Some people are more injury-prone; if hard training keeps hurting you, change the stimulus rather than hoping your body changes.

title: Injury prevention is the best way to grow
section: Why it matters for a natural
statement: An injury is a gap in tonnage, which means no growth, plus a mental-health hit; preventing injury is the best growth strategy.

title: Bodybuilding should be injury-free
section: Why it matters for a natural
statement: You should be able to train 10 years with zero injuries and stay mobile to ~80; bodies wrecked in their 40s come from lifting badly. He claims Coleman's body came from not letting injuries heal.
numbers: 10 years injury-free; mobile to ~80.
scope: Naturals training for the long term.
status: contradicted — he also says "pushing the limits will sometimes injure you; that is acceptable" {{5Nhv3cgzrAg@442}}.

title: Tendons, not muscles, limit older lifters
section: Why it matters for a natural
statement: Pain-free bodybuilding is how you keep growing with age; with training age, tendons become the limit (triceps limited by elbows, quads by knees).
numbers: Joint-friendliness ranks ~7th for him but 2nd-3rd for a lifter in his 40s.

title: Tendons and spine need loading
section: Why it matters for a natural
statement: Tendons and the spine exist to be loaded; underloading atrophies them and they fail in old age. There is no "tendon capital" to save, though overload gives tendinitis.

title: Push through discomfort, never through pain
section: Why it matters for a natural
statement: The cautious lifter goes further than the one who pushes through pain: "pushing through pain = ER, through discomfort = PR". Step back from a set that feels sketchy.
numbers: Prevention might cost 3 weeks, a cure 3 months.

title: Never train through joint or tendon pain
statement: Joint/tendon pain is a warning; pushing through turns minor issues into lifelong ones, and joint pain never goes away by itself. If a movement hurts, stop and re-check form; if form changes don't fix it, drop the lift, since there is "always a way around".
scope: All lifters; applies to tendon/joint pain, not muscle soreness (INJ-24).
status: changed — 2020: absolute "never lift through pain; if it hurts, stop". 2021: graded pain scales where minor pain can be pushed aside (INJ-26). 2022-2025: tendon/joint pain is still a stop signal.
check: Is any lift that causes joint or tendon pain modified or dropped rather than pushed through?

title: Muscle pain is fine, tendon/joint pain is an alarm
statement: There are two kinds of pain: pump and muscle soreness (fine) versus tendon, ligament or joint pain (alarm). Tendons have more nerve endings because they repair poorly. Tension in the muscle is "more painful than dangerous"; pain at the tendon insertion is not.

title: Hurt is not injured
statement: Pain is not injury and doesn't tell you the degree of damage; judge by function, not sensation. Most times lifters think they're injured it is nothing, and an unnecessary break hurts them.

title: Graded pain scales: occurrence and aftermath
statement: He grades pain during the lift (occurrence) and after the session (aftermath), each with a matching response; see the table below.
numbers: Level 1 in-set pain: one more rep; if it persists, stop, walk 2 min, do another set ("99%" gone). Aftermath level 3+ is usually injury.

title: Pain is partly learned (nocebo)
statement: Expecting pain on a lift creates it and obsessing makes it grow. Assess small pains and push them aside so you can spot real injury (music helps), but don't swing to "all pain is imaginary". After his ribs healed he still felt squat pain until he "unlearned" it.
scope: All lifters, especially after an injury.

title: Joint noises rank low as warnings
statement: Pain or a feeling that something shifted matters more than noise. Painless elbow clicking after tendinitis or sternum cracking on dips is fine.

title: Judge a lift by next-day pain
statement: Tendon and back irritation shows most the next morning (blood leaves the tissue overnight), so judge a lift by its aftermath, not by how it felt.
scope: All lifters, especially tendon and back issues.

title: Recurring pain fades or worsens
statement: Recurring pain rarely stays the same: it either fades or worsens as a warning. Long-standing pain that never snapped is likely structural and under control.

title: A low-back "pump" is SI overuse
statement: A burning low-back or SI "pump" after deadlifts or squats is not a pump but SI-joint/tendon overuse from bad programming; stop before it sets in. He felt it every session on BBBS and no longer does with proper volume.

title: Tendinitis is a spectrum ending in rupture
statement: Tendinitis is the most common lifting injury, ranging from occasional pain to deep all-day pain. Ruptures (biceps, patellar, hip labrum) usually follow months or years of ignored tendinitis.

title: Rest does not cure tendinitis
statement: Rest only seems to cure tendinitis; it returns because the movement cause is unchanged. Immobility "fossilizes" the tendon and atrophies the muscle that shares its load. Take at most 1-2 days off when pain is bad, mainly to get over the emotional hump; longer builds a fear association.
numbers: Max 1-2 days off; 3-4 weeks is far too long; 2 weeks off still re-flares.
check: Is tendinitis handled with at most 1-2 days off followed by modified training, rather than weeks of rest?

title: Avoid painkillers and anti-inflammatories
statement: They mask the signal you need, and in his view anti-inflammatories weaken tendons and block adaptation ("not medical advice"). If you are on them anyway, avoid max singles and stay high-rep. He claims a powerlifter on painkillers squatted through months of hip pain until the labrum tore.
scope: Lifters with tendon or joint pain.

title: Train in the pain-free "valley"
statement: Train between inactive moderate pain and acute pain; this widens the pain-free window. End the session before pain turns acute. Warm-up blood flow eases pain, but if it returns mid-session you are re-aggravating it. Rehab is never painless; the pain becomes dull.

title: Tendinitis is "a game of angles"
statement: Find which movements load the painful tendon and switch to variations that work the muscle without pain. Reintroduce the painful movement unloaded; if it always hurts, ban it, because there are always equal alternatives.

title: Blood flow and surrounding muscle fix tendons
statement: Send blood to the tendon with light, high-rep pump work, and build the surrounding muscles and the antagonist, since an aggravated tendon is doing too much work. Only corrective work that stresses the tendon enough to adapt ends tendinitis for good. A pump matters more for tendon health than for growth.

title: Fix the environment first
statement: For tendon recovery, fix stress, sleep and badly managed rest in the program first. He also mentions MSM powder and more water.

title: Pain gone after a deload = too tendon-heavy
statement: Tendon pain that disappears after a deload means training is too tendon-heavy; the deload is only a band-aid.
scope: Lifters relying on deloads for joint pain.

title: Cold and pressure changes worsen tendinitis
statement: Tendinitis worsens in the cold, with pressure changes (flying) and when not warmed up. Healed injuries linger as tendon damage felt after poor sleep, on waking or in the cold.

title: Prevent tendinitis rather than heal it
statement: Preventing tendinitis matters more than healing it; this is his lesson from chronic elbow tendinitis.

title: Ice helps tendinitis but won't cure it
statement: Ice helps tendinitis, especially the exposed patellar tendon, but won't cure it alone, and it rarely reaches the rotator cuff/AC joint. In 2024, "despite the current consensus against icing", he says ice saved him every time.

title: Icing rules
statement: Use a reusable gel pack with a thin cover, never directly on skin. Build duration gradually, then stay still as long as you iced; never ice before or during activity.
numbers: 5 → 10 min, 15 min max, never over 20 (permanent damage risk). Up to 5×/day; 2× on squat days (e.g. train 6 pm, ice 9 pm and before bed); 3×/day 10 min (2020-08); 3-4×/day 15 min (2020-10); 10-15 min on, 5-10 off (2024).

title: Ice timing after training
statement: Let the tendon cool after training before icing, then move slowly afterwards.
numbers: Wait 2-3 h after leg training (2020); ice 10-15 min, move slowly ~10 min later (2021).
status: contradicted — the 2-3 h wait (2020) sits beside a 2024 phrasing of icing ~10-15 min after training {{bRKQIOYo2u4@1469}}; the 2024 wording is ambiguous.

title: Cold and contrast showers help
statement: Cold showers and contrast showers help sore tendons and the low back.

title: Rotate variations, grips and stances
statement: Rotating variations, grips and stances prevents overuse and is how he gains year-round; small joint-angle changes shift strain while training the same muscle. On machines, rotate grips and machines too.
check: Does the program rotate variations, grips or stances rather than repeating one identical pattern for long?

title: Risky lifts at higher reps
statement: Put risky lifts in higher rep ranges so you can sense the bad rep coming. A 1RM concentrates risk into one all-or-nothing rep; an injury on rep 3 at 70% is milder, and a rounded 8RM deadlift is far less risky than at 1RM. 3RM and 10RM give the same hypertrophy, so pick the one you can progress safely.
numbers: 10-15 reps instead of 3-5; burnouts with ~20RM weight, never an 8RM; lunges and good mornings never below 8; hypers ~15, never 3×3.
check: Are injury-prone lifts (good mornings, lunges, pullovers, weighted dips/chins, etc.) kept at moderate-to-high reps rather than low-rep maxes?

title: Small muscles and fragile structures get higher reps
statement: Small muscles and tendon-heavy movements skew to the volume end; don't carry low isolation-style rep choices onto the wrong lifts.
numbers: Biceps: no 2-5 (2020-11); 3-5 only for very experienced lifters, carefully (2020-09).
status: contradicted — biceps low reps: allowed for very experienced lifters (2020-09) vs no 2-5 at all (2020-11).

title: Strength work at ~1 RIR
statement: Stopping strength sets at ~1 RIR cut his strength-work injuries to almost zero; strength sets taken to failure carry the highest injury risk.
numbers: ~1 RIR.

title: Dangerous lifts first, stabilisers fresh
statement: High-danger lifts open the workout when you're fresh. Don't pre-fatigue stabilisers (abs, hamstrings, lower back) right before a compound that needs them.
check: Does the riskiest lift come first in the session, without stabilisers pre-fatigued?

title: No heavy squat then heavy deadlift
statement: Heavy back squat then heavy deadlift in one day is a "death combo": squat fatigue rounds the thoracic spine on the pull. Don't progress squat and deadlift simultaneously; a heavy low-back lift followed by a floor pull, or barbell rows after deadlifts, is how people get hurt.
check: Does the program avoid heavy squats and heavy deadlifts on the same day?

title: Pull more than you press
statement: Balance the body: pull more than you press, more posterior chain than quads, and hinges at least equal to knee flexion. There is no perfect ratio (not necessarily 2:1), but heavy pressers must pull roughly as much, and the type of pull matters, since weighted chins and plate rows don't train the scapular girdle.
check: Does pulling volume at least match pressing volume, with hinges at least equal to knee-dominant work?

title: Repetitive Big-3 programs injure novices
statement: Grease-the-groove and highly repetitive Big-3 programs (back squat 3×/wk, no variations) cause injuries in novices; the big lifts need rest between sessions.
numbers: Back squat 3×/wk with no variations.

title: Train antagonists and opposite movements
statement: Train opposite movements and antagonists, such as hand opening, wrist extension, and curls on triceps days.

title: Imbalance = undertrained partner
statement: Strengthening a muscle prevents injury; an imbalance is an undertrained counterpart, not a "too strong" muscle. Keep feeding the big muscle and train its partner more.

title: Train joints in all directions
statement: Train joints in every direction they move and fix weaknesses (e.g. unstable knees in a hinge) in the gym rather than avoiding them.

title: Start light after changing stance, grip or equipment
statement: When changing stance, grip or equipment, drop the load a lot at first; big changes are mainly dangerous when you jump to unfamiliar heavy weights.
numbers: A 500 lb squatter narrowing stance drops to ~250 (~50%); SSB under 70% of max squat at first.

title: Warm up before anything heavy
statement: Cold heavy sets cause strains; he strained a pec benching 135 cold after already handling 225-plus. Injuries at heavy weight are far worse than warm-up injuries.
numbers: 2020 bench: empty bar, then 25-30 reps with 25s; knees needed 35-40 min in sub-zero gyms. 2025: 1-2 warm-up sets are enough to ready tendons.
status: changed — 2020 long warm-ups; 2025 1-2 sets suffice for tendons (a refinement, possibly different contexts).
check: Is every heavy lift preceded by at least 1-2 warm-up sets?

title: No static stretching before lifting
statement: Static stretching before lifting is useless and risky on cold tissue; stretch only when warm or after training. Test 2 weeks without it, and keep a favourite stretch if you love it.
numbers: 2-week test without pre-lift stretching.

title: Ramp back after a break
statement: After a break, ramp back stepwise; jumping back to old weights is how he strained his patellar tendon and got sore knees.
numbers: 2 months off then the same weight leaves knees sore.

title: State your injuries when asking for critique
statement: Injuries are critical programming information; include them when asking for program critique.

title: Equipment and setup hazards
statement: Flat soles only (banana-soled sneakers roll the ankles in and cause knee cave); bulky squat pads are more dangerous than bar discomfort; inflated Smith loads carried to free weights cause injuries; never re-rack by stepping forward before lockout; put heavy split squats in a rack with safeties, a Smith or a belt squat.

title: "Strength restoration" between sets
statement: Tiny, non-invasive band or light exercises in specific reps and angles target problem tendons, supersetted between sets of main lifts at almost no recovery cost. Never schedule them outside training or you'll skip them. Next-day soreness means you did resistance training instead. Start with one routine for your worst area.
numbers: 2-3 movements under a minute (later 2 movements on different planes; 3 was overkill); ~10-15 reps; 4-8 sets with a very easy band. He runs 6 routines (3 S + 3 R), 2-4 per day.
status: contradicted — he also said (2023) direct tendon training is a waste of time for aesthetics {{M2yqxp4IHXg@943}}; partly reconcilable, since rehab and aesthetics have different goals.

title: Dead hangs to decompress the spine
statement: Decompress the spine with dead hangs or pull-ups at the end of squat/deadlift/lower days. Be warm (not cold before deadlifts), never jump into a hang, and avoid fully relaxed hanging, which can trigger SI spasms.

title: Hypers + leg raises for back pain
statement: Back hyperextensions plus leg raises is the "golden combo" for back pain (decompression, hip health).

title: Hip-flexor stretch after leg days
statement: Post-workout hip-flexor stretching after leg days is the only stretching he kept. Long sitting tightens them, which strains the low back and impairs squats and deadlifts; it fixed his bad hip-flexor pain. Stretch cautiously, since cold, short hip flexors can tear.

title: The lower back is the top injury site
statement: The lower back is the most common injury site in squats and deadlifts, from bad technique and too much frequency; low-back pain is the #1 reason people can't squat or deadlift for years.
numbers: Ranking: lower back > shoulders > knees.

title: Squats hurt backs more than deadlifts
statement: Squats cause more lower-back injuries than deadlifts (often via butt wink). Done properly, the deadlift is one of the safest lifts: it starts with the positive, you see form breakdown coming and you can drop the bar. "Deadlifts aren't bad for your back; deadlifting with bad form is". He has never been hurt deadlifting.

title: Next-day back pain = wrong deadlift
statement: Next-day low-back pain after deadlifts means a style you're not built for or improper deadlifting, regardless of load.

title: Lower back as a stationary bridge
statement: Use the lower back as a stationary bridge and drive with the legs; dynamic flexion under load injures, not a fixed angle. Pulling rounded from start to finish is less risky than a neutral spine that rounds mid-lift. Leg damage grows back; spinal/structural damage only deteriorates.

title: Keep the thoracic spine neutral
statement: Thoracic rounding leads to lumbar rounding (the spine gives up in stages), so keep the upper back neutral; strong thoracic extension is in his view the most important thing for staying healthy. He opposes rounded-back pulls for bodybuilders; elite outliers like Konstantinovs prove nothing for average lifters.

title: Most "back injuries" are SI, nerve or muscle
statement: Discs are hard to destroy; most "back injuries" are SI-joint, nerve or muscle issues. The SI joint needs recovery, so don't hit it every session; only lower-day programming and recovery fix it, and a belt does nothing for it.

title: After a back tweak, keep moving
statement: After a low-back tweak, keep moving: unweighted good mornings/squats, then find a pain-free lower movement (leg press, hypers, DB RDLs), then return to squats and deadlifts light. Complete rest atrophies the protective muscles; rehab with hyperextensions rather than good mornings.

title: A strong back and core protect
statement: "A stronger muscle is a safer muscle": lower-back isolation is recommended, and deadlifting/squatting is the best prevention for back and knee injuries. Someone who deadlifts 400 lb won't hurt his back picking something up; people in their 30s with back pain mostly have weak backs/cores.
scope: All lifters and the general population.

title: Good mornings: high risk, high reward
statement: Good mornings top his danger list, since failure pulls you into loaded lumbar flexion with no safe bail, but they remain high-risk/high-reward, not banned. Never do them with a fatigued lower back. Deadlift negatives are also risky because you lower while fatigued.
numbers: Never below 8 reps (see INJ-47).

title: Never AMRAP a deadlift
statement: Pulls from the floor make ugly reps too easy to grind, so never AMRAP a deadlift.

title: Daily posture carries into lifts
statement: Sit tall, use a lumbar pillow, keep the head neutral and don't slouch; slouching carries into lifts and causes back, shoulder and disc problems. Decline starts at the head, then thoracic spine, shoulders, lower back, so fix it in that order. Don't hyperextend into a rigid spine; change positions often.
numbers: Bad posture takes as many years to fix as it took to develop.

title: Scoliosis is no reason to stop lifting
statement: Back and core muscles act as a brace, and he deadlifts heavy with scoliosis; posture can't fix bone. He believes his came from a one-shoulder backpack, and the asymmetry overloaded his lower shoulder, which was repeatedly injured on bench.

title: Machines don't prevent back injuries
statement: Smith squats can't self-correct, so you end in a loaded good morning, and leg press and lever machines can still hurt the back.
scope: Lifters swapping to machines for back safety.

title: Patellar tendinitis: pattern, frequency, muscle
statement: Patellar tendinitis is fixed in three parts: correct the movement pattern, manage frequency and tonnage, and build the muscles that unload the tendon. Never by rest. Even perfect form wears tendons if frequency is too high.

title: Box-squat and widowmaker rehab
statement: His knee rehab: box squats progressed by reps then load, then "widowmakers"; stay in the widowmaker phase as long as possible and keep the rebuild maximally conservative. See the table below.
numbers: Every 2-3 days, never daily; details in the table.

title: Knee rehab habits and wraps
statement: Morning knee extensions from small to full range, then knee bends; avoid impact sports, running on concrete and cat-style stretches that overextend the knee. Use short elastic wraps angled onto the tendon, not sleeves or hole-braces, and never too tight: X-shape for pain below the kneecap, around the kneecap for kneecap pain, wrapped inside → out. He still tapes his previously torn left knee when it flares.

title: Signs of patellar tendinitis vs tear
statement: Signs: pain at the knee break (not the rest of the rep), worse going up stairs, a warm/tender knee, sudden "giving way" when walking. Pain that fades once warm suggests tendinitis; pain that keeps rising suggests a tear.

title: Squats aren't bad for knees
statement: "Squats are bad for knees" is a boomer myth; deep squats are fine with controlled knee travel. Knee pain comes from bad form, too much frequency, fat and inactivity; the danger lies in knees shooting forward or caving out of the hole.
numbers: Squatting 2-3×/wk with the same stance eventually brings overuse knee pain (2024).

title: Posterior chain protects the knee
statement: Weak hamstrings and too-vertical, quad-only squatting prime knee injury; posterior chain work and hip hinges protect the knee.
status: contradicted — 2020-2021 he said growing his quads (~23 in), "not glutes or hamstrings", cured his patellar tendinitis {{KMcJAERb9Dk@1059}} {{9kIIW251uiI@190}}; 2020 he also blamed big quads relative to posterior chain {{j5PP3gx7DC4@0}}; 2022 relearning the squat and building hamstrings/glutes fixed it {{yoROLGGUPXU@1150}}.

title: Knee-unfriendly options
statement: Sissy squats, leg extensions (for some), pad-on-knee calf machines, Platz-style narrow toes-out squats and locking the knees every rep are knee-unfriendly. His own patellar injury came from jumping 225 → 275 in a narrower Platz-style stance after a break.

title: Frequent heavy flat bench injures shoulders
