statement: Frequent heavy horizontal pressing is the main cause of shoulder injury regardless of form, unless you're an outlier. Injuries are almost always to the rotator cuff/AC joint, not the delts; he claims they are the #1 injury in retired powerlifters. The tell is an achy soreness between pec and shoulder the next day.
numbers: Benching 3×/wk (or 10×10) smoked his shoulders; 3×/wk flat bench = shoulder pain for many intermediates.
check: Is heavy flat bench kept infrequent (not 3×/wk) or rotated with other horizontal variations?

title: Vertical pressing is shoulder-friendly
statement: Vertical pressing done properly is easy on, even restorative for, the shoulder; end push days with it and press on top of you, not in front. Heavy OHP after bench made his shoulders "feel amazing".
numbers: Replace one horizontal day with seated OHP 4×8-12 submax + face pulls; DB overhead press 3×6-10 for women.

title: Rotate horizontal presses, don't cut them
statement: Don't cut horizontal volume for sore shoulders; rotate variations: push-ups, paused/Spoto/close-grip/slingshot/floor press, DB bench, rings, and alternate push-ups and dips.
numbers: Very high-volume push-ups every 2 days are "amazing" for shoulders and pec tendons.
status: changed — close-grip bench: a shoulder-friendly swap (3×6-10) in 2020 {{hT4zgNcMOBY@501}}; dropped in 2023 after elbow tendinitis and posterior shoulder pain {{43F9unmSc_I@1634}}.

title: Touch-and-go bench wrecked his shoulder
statement: Touch-and-go bench protracted his right shoulder until at 24 he could barely raise his arm; paused bench, Spoto press and the Slingshot let him bench pain-free again.
numbers: Rehab to raw full-range bench in 4-5 months. Typical 2021 session: slingshot up to 315, then 205-235 paused/Spoto/close-grip. Touch-and-go plus scoliosis cost him ~3 weeks off repeatedly over two years.
scope: His own history; benchers with shoulder pain.
status: changed — 2020-2022 he kept benching via Slingshot/paused/Spoto; 2024 he dropped flat-back, full-range bench because it destroyed his shoulders {{ZLheQPgEfoA@4943}}.

title: Fix bench mechanics for shoulder pain
statement: For shoulder/AC pain fix the arch, slow negative, bar path and elbow tuck, keep both scapulae on the bench (narrow benches cause issues), and use a hand-off or lift-off rather than a traumatic solo unrack. He uses an in-between elbow angle, not a 90° flare; pain near the armpit means tuck the elbows.

title: External rotation and upper back for pressers
statement: External rotation, rear delt and upper-back work keep shoulders healthy, and heavy pressing needs it directly: an upper-back movement every push day. Keep rehab movements in even when pain is gone.
numbers: Face pulls 15-20+ or AMRAP with a band (2020); 4×15-20 (2022); 20-25 between pressing sets (2023).
status: changed — front delts: 2020 front-delt isolation fixed his shoulders and a strong front delt prevents injury {{KMcJAERb9Dk@1123}}; 2022 overdeveloped front delts versus weak rear/side delts invite injury, and shrinking them stopped his injuries {{yoROLGGUPXU@710}}. Both views value rear delts.
check: Do push days include direct rear-delt/external-rotation/upper-back work (e.g. face pulls)?

title: Train shoulder end ranges light
statement: The shoulder is weak at its end ranges: train high-mobility ranges light, never heavy. Sloppy heavy or internally rotated raises cause impingement; upright rows aren't inherently dangerous, the danger is a big-mover mindset.
numbers: Lateral raises/upright rows 12-15, no lower (2023-01); upright rows 10-15 (2023-08).

title: Avoid behind-the-neck and neck presses
statement: Avoid behind-the-neck and guillotine/neck presses; going too deep disengages the lats and causes impingement.
status: contradicted — 2021 he called the behind-the-head snatch-grip press a valid hypertrophy variation, just never heavy if unconditioned {{jAnfGqpsK38@1360}}.

title: Don't stack shoulder-heavy work
statement: Don't stack shoulder-heavy work: incline + weighted dips, heavy dips + heavy bench, or bench + OHP supersets.

title: Kipping and overweight pull-ups hurt shoulders
statement: Kipping pull-ups are a top source of shoulder/rotator cuff injury; overweight lifters also hurt their shoulders on pull-ups.

title: Pullovers high-rep with shoulders supported
statement: Keep pullovers high-rep with the shoulders supported; pain usually reveals pressing-tight shoulders.
numbers: Never below 6 (2020-2021); 4×12 (2020); 8-12 (2022); restoration pullovers 12-15, not taxing.
status: changed — rep floor refined upward from ≥6 (2020-2021) to 8-12 (2022).

title: Lifters who can't press can still grow shoulders
statement: Lifters who can no longer press can still grow shoulders with raises, especially cables, including people over 50.

title: Warm the shoulder before squat and bench
statement: Warm the shoulder before squatting or benching (band dislocates once warm, rotations, raises); pain present at the start tends to stay all session. Shoulder pain in the squat setup may come from benching, not mobility.

title: Watch shoulder fatigue at high weekly volume
statement: At high weekly volume, watch shoulder-joint fatigue; if pain starts the whole program goes down.
numbers: e.g. 18 sets/wk.

title: Never overextend the elbow under heavy curls
statement: Never fully extend or overextend the elbow under heavy load in curls; stop the negative short and keep a slight bend. Bouncing off the tendon at full extension does nothing for growth and causes distal tears. If the shoulder moves with the arm, overextension is safe; with the shoulder frozen (preacher curls) it is not.
numbers: ~45° short of extension on concentration-type curls.

title: No heavy supinated pulling, no mixed grip
statement: No supinated/Yates rows, supinated shrugs, or mixed-grip deadlifts or rows: the biceps gives before the back. Bodybuilders should use double overhand, then straps; straps prevent tears and asymmetry. He claims he's never seen a tear with double overhand; mixed grip also causes bar rotation, uneven traps and lower-back torsion. Vertical supinated pulls are generally fine.
numbers: If you insist on supinated rows: 4×10-12, not 3×6-8.
check: Are heavy pulls done double overhand or with straps, never mixed grip or heavy supinated rows?

title: Distal biceps tears are permanent
statement: Biceps tears at the distal attachment need surgery, and the biceps never looks the same.

title: Pull-ups are limited by tendons
statement: Pull-ups are limited by the elbow, biceps tendon and shoulder, not the back. Rotate grips and implements, and don't drop into a disengaged dead hang and rebound. Weighted chin-ups are the riskiest pull-up (supinated overextension under load). Going unweighted for elbow pain is only temporary.
numbers: Weighted chins 6-10.
status: contradicted — neutral grip: he says neutral-grip DB pressing wrecks his shoulders and neutral curls/pulls can overextend the rotator cuff {{VXwYO2qG9ZY@384}} {{du7JYCA2pa4@620}}, yet lists neutral grip as a fix for elbow pain on pull-ups {{C4CnYbHCCGo@691}}.

title: Light band curls for biceps tendon health
statement: Light, low-anchored band curls (as many reps as possible, noticeable but not hard) keep the biceps tendon and elbow healthy and keep the deep range. Use them as a finisher on arm days or after heavy push days; never cold or explosive.

title: Biceps tendinitis: stay pronated
statement: With biceps tendinitis, stay pronated and reintroduce supination gradually; the cause is often presses, dips or pull-ups. Use an EZ bar if a straight bar hurts.

title: Causes of elbow tendinitis
statement: Elbow tendinitis comes from repetitive triceps-heavy pressing (close-grip bench), locking out every rep, deep French presses and skull crushers. He never locks out on bench. Avoid close-grip and football-bar pressing on back-to-back days.
numbers: Weighted dips + French press 2×/wk "will wreck your elbows".

title: Elbow-friendly triceps choices
statement: Prefer cables over EZ bar/dumbbells, rope or plate overhead extensions, DB or shoulder-extension skull crushers, the JM press, and high-rep, high-frequency band pushdowns; vary grip width. The JM press cured his elbow tendinitis (Todd Hutchings' advice).
numbers: JM press 12-15 (2020); Smith JM press at 5-8 is "asking for injury" (2024).

title: Prime cranky elbows first
statement: Prime cranky elbows with light triceps isolation (band extensions, hammer curl + pushdown) before dips, pressing or chin-ups.
numbers: Band triceps extensions 30-50 reps.

title: Train lighter and short of lockout with elbow tendinitis
statement: With elbow tendinitis keep training lighter, stop short of lockout/full extension, work up to the painful point and extend gradually. Pops are fine, but don't force through pain.

title: Avoid arm wrestling
statement: Arm wrestling carries a high elbow-injury risk; pros commonly have 2+ surgeries, and he avoids it.
numbers: 2+ surgeries common among pros.

title: Band hand-opening for grip overuse pain
statement: Elastic-band hand opening (finger extensors) fixes wrist, finger, elbow and forearm pain caused by constant gripping; do it as often as possible, especially after gripper work.
numbers: 3×/wk, then daily.

title: Wrist curls carry overuse risk
statement: Wrist curls (especially pronated, high-volume, or with a fixed dumbbell) carry overuse risk; they "destroyed" his wrists. Pain-free beats heavier: for curl-related forearm pain, go lighter and do more reps.

title: Press with a stacked wrist
statement: A cocked-back wrist under heavy load leads to overuse injury and the bar landing on the neck or collarbone; strengthen with rack holds and arm-wrestling-style work.

title: Fixes for wrist pain
statement: The band wrist-traction stretch (Uncle Nick) cured his wrist pain; he does it between front-squat sets. For wrist pain from pressing overuse, change variations, use rings or an EZ bar, add high-rep wrist curls and rice-bucket work.

title: Callus care
statement: Shave or clip calluses right after training (never after a shower), the day before a rest day, and moisturise hands nightly with a balm; this stopped tears that used to happen every ~3 weeks. Lift normally 2 days later.
numbers: Every 2 weeks; balm absorbs over 6-7 h.

title: Pec tears come from unprepared stretch
statement: Pec tears come from stretching through a range the muscle isn't prepared for; train the chest in more than one plane and stretch it deeply under low load. He claims PED users tear tendons while naturals tear near the armpit.
numbers: Severe tears rarely heal past 80-85%.

title: Flyes light and comfortable
statement: Flyes should be light, high-rep and comfortable, with the arm bent if needed.
numbers: Machine flyes 8-15, not 5; cable flyes 12-16.

title: Pec strains usually heal alone
statement: Pec strains usually heal on their own; pain when breathing or bracing points to the ribs/intercostals instead.

title: Dips: progress them, stop on sternum pain
statement: Stop dips if they cause sternum pain (especially young lifters); painless sternum cracking is fine. Don't do dips twice a week with one unprogressed; replace one.
numbers: Weighted dips 6-10, not 3-5.
status: changed — 2020: dips usually worse than bench for bad shoulders, ring dips "double the risk" {{np9LdwTPfNs@762}}; 2023-2024: avoiding dips while doubling down on bench is where shoulder injuries happen, and dips help shoulders {{ZLheQPgEfoA@2036}}.

title: Spotting rules
statement: Take the bar the moment the lifter asks and never jerk it out; bench without safeties needs a spot.

title: Hamstring pulls are nearly 100% avoidable
statement: Train the lengthened position under control (RDLs, hypers, GHR, leg curls, paused lifts) at higher reps; deadlift-only lifters train only the positive. RDLs nearly eliminated pulls in athletes he advised; no foam rolling needed.
numbers: Leg curls 4×10-15 for strongmen.
check: Does the program train the hamstrings in the lengthened position (RDLs, leg curls, hypers)?

title: Uncontrolled hamstring stretches can tear
statement: Uncontrolled Nordic/GHR stretches and ballistic toe-touch stretches can tear hamstrings, especially in heavy lifters new to them.

title: Hip/glute pain rebuild order
statement: For hip or glute pain, pause the painful lift, train the least painful lower movement, rehab glutes with thrusts/bridges/hypers at low intensity, then reintroduce squats, then deadlifts.
numbers: With a fragile hip, squat 2 plates instead of 3, for high volume.

title: Wide stances injure many
statement: Wide stances (sumo, wide squats) injure many, including him; for hamstring pain at the hip, drop wide-stance and lunge-type moves.

title: Neck: high volume, never heavy
statement: Train the neck with high volume, never a 3RM; prefer controlled neck curls or bands over bridges/plates. Warm up the neck and keep reps in reserve if pressing triggers neck pain; OHP to failure gave him days of shooting neck pain. A thick neck protects in car crashes and against concussion.
numbers: 10RM weight, then pause reps, slow.
scope: Neck training; pressers with neck pain (see ch. 6 for neck training).

title: Hernias come from twisting under load
statement: Hernias come from fast twisting under load; keep the trunk still in lower-body lifts and one-arm rows.

title: Spinal flexion is safe done properly
statement: Sit-ups and spinal flexion/twisting are safe done properly (hinge at the hips, use the abs); if flexion hurts, use hanging leg raises.

title: Rib and intercostal rehab
statement: For ribs/intercostals: serratus punches, pullovers and his R3 routine every lower day, years after the break. He broke ribs on a heavy squat and re-aggravated them with allergy sneezing (accounts of the event vary).

title: Heavy bodyweight slows ankle healing
statement: Heavy people's ankle/Achilles injuries heal slowly; don't start calves heavy and avoid high-impact sport. His rolled ankle wouldn't heal at 240 lb but healed fast at 220 lb.
numbers: 240 lb vs 220 lb.

title: Keep training what you can
statement: Keep moving and train what you can the next day; only a broken bone or torn tendon justifies stopping. An unrehabbed injury spreads, and compensation injures the other side. After shoulder surgery keep training everything else and do cardio; moping for a month brings nothing.
scope: Any injury short of fracture or tendon rupture.
check: After an injury, does training continue around it (rather than stopping entirely) unless a bone is broken or tendon torn?

title: Return slowly; twice makes it chronic
statement: Return slowly and methodically; rushing to regain lost time, or letting form slip again, causes reinjury. Once is okay, twice the same way creates a chronic pattern. Every one of his injuries came from impatience about a target weight and cost months.
check: Is the return from injury gradual rather than a jump back to pre-injury loads?

title: The psychological milestone
statement: The psychological side matters as much as the physical: the weight you got hurt on is the key milestone, and it should be retaken only when it feels non-challenging. Small rehab wins create a virtuous circle.

title: Take responsibility, don't blame the lift
statement: After an injury, find what you did wrong instead of declaring the lift evil.

title: Return order after an upper-back injury
statement: After upper-back pain take 2 days off, then avoid painful lifts, and see a doctor if everything hurts. Return order: squats and good mornings first, then vertical then horizontal presses, then deadlifts, rows last.
numbers: His rib timeline: upper-back machines at 1 month, DB rows at 2, deadlifts with two plates at 3.

title: Serious injuries need doctors
statement: Serious injuries need proper rehab and doctors; he is not a doctor and doesn't advise on surgical cases. He also says GPs wrongly prescribe rest and painkillers (see INJ-33, INJ-34).

title: The body re-adapts
statement: People who think they'll never squat or deadlift again are usually wrong, though robust mobility after a serious injury can take years.
numbers: 5-7 years for robust mobility after serious injury.

title: Training matters more than diet for naturals
statement: For a natural lifter, training drives muscle growth and diet only fuels it; the "diet is 70-80%" line is nonsense that comes from drug users. Nutrition only matters once training is on point.
numbers: Training is "at least 50%" (2020), "80% or more" (2023)
scope: Naturals, all levels; training's share grows as you advance
status: changed — 2020: training is at least 50%; 2023: training is 80% or more
check: Does the program treat training, not diet, as the main driver of muscle gain?

title: Diet is the top factor for longevity
statement: Diet matters more than cardio or lifting for longevity and disease; it is overrated for muscle and underrated for a long, healthy life. He puts longevity ahead of pure hypertrophy and says the two go together when the diet suits you.

title: Diet determines most long-term health
statement: Diet can be the difference between dying in your 60s and your 80s; fixing diet and training would remove most health problems, yet people take pills for symptoms instead.
numbers: Diet + training would remove ~90% of health problems

title: Food builds mass; training directs it to muscle
statement: Food is anabolic only if you train. Extra food or protein without training just makes you fat, and without calories and sleep no amount of hard training builds mass.

title: Make diet an automatism; push training instead
statement: Once a diet works, keep it stable and put the effort into training. Constant diet tweaking feeds doubt and anxiety; the diet should not be the struggle, the training should.

title: Check diet before deloading after a strength drop
statement: If strength or tonnage drops unexpectedly, look at your diet before deciding you need a deload.
scope: Lifters with an unexplained performance drop (see ch. 4 for deloads)

title: Nutrition is his self-declared weakest area
statement: He calls nutrition his least-researched area and avoids diet videos because the topic is emotional and industry-funded.
scope: Context for weighing his nutrition claims

title: Calories in vs out sets weight; food sets composition
statement: Energy balance governs weight change for everyone, but macros and food choice decide what kind of weight you gain or lose. You can lose fat eating junk, but that misses the point; claiming otherwise hands overweight people an excuse.
scope: Everyone; macro or micronutrient quirks matter only in rare cases
check: Does the plan control total calories while also specifying food quality?

title: A calorie is not just a calorie
statement: The source of calories and how they are combined (e.g. protein with carbs) affect insulin and where fat goes; an all-junk intake is not equivalent to whole food at the same calories.

title: You need a surplus to build mass
statement: No muscle is gained in a constant deficit; eat until the scale moves. Elsewhere he says maintenance is all most people need for gains.
scope: Lifters trying to gain (see ch. 11 for bulking)
status: contradicted — "eat until the scale moves" vs "maintenance is all you need for gains" (both 2021)
check: Is the lifter out of a chronic deficit while trying to build muscle?

title: Stalled scale: add a small snack
statement: If the scale isn't moving, add one small snack such as a bowl of rice with chicken.
numbers: ~200 kcal snack (2021); he forced a ~300 kcal daily snack to hold 210-211 lb while getting stronger (2020)
scope: Lifters gaining or maintaining while getting stronger

title: Maintenance rises slowly as you grow
statement: Maintenance calories rise as you recomp or gain muscle, and appetite usually signals it; needs climb very slowly unless activity or climate changes.

title: His own intake: about 2,000-2,400 kcal
statement: At 6'2" and ~210 lb he eats roughly 2,000-2,400 kcal and calls his metabolism slow; 4,000 kcal would make him gain fast.

title: Huge calorie claims are miscounted or drug-fuelled
statement: Claims of 4,000-10,000+ kcal a day are miscounted, drug-fuelled or specific to very active athletes; Phelps' intake reflects hours of swimming, not lifting. Eating huge and burning it off (G-flux) is no better than not eating the excess.
numbers: 4,000-10,000+ kcal; 5,000 kcal at 5'7", 225 lb, ~25% fat "just maintains fat"

title: Depressed? Eat at maintenance
statement: If you are depressed, don't diet; eat at maintenance rather than bulking.
scope: People in a low mental state

title: Protein needs are vastly overrated
statement: He eats far less protein than commonly recommended and still grows; eating much more gave him health problems and no extra gains.
status: changed — his own intake fell from 120-140 g (2020) to 50-70 g (2021-22), then rose to ~100-120 g (2024); the view that high protein is unnecessary never changed
check: Does the plan avoid prescribing very high protein (e.g. 2 g/kg or more) as necessary for growth?

title: 2 g/kg or 2 g/lb is a waste
statement: Intakes like 2 g/kg, 2 g/lb or 200 g/day at 180 lb are wasted; past a point protein is just burned as fuel. Mainly steroid users can use that much, and supplement sellers push the overshoot.
numbers: 2 g/kg, 2 g/lb, 200 g/day at 180 lb = too much

title: ~0.8 g/lb is near optimal, but more than needed
statement: About 0.8 g/lb is "close to optimal", yet even the low end of the optimal range exceeds what he needs. Studies don't test lower intakes, so "suboptimal" may still give most of the gains; missing 10 g a day won't stop progress.
numbers: 0.8 g/lb; "suboptimal" may give 94-95% of gains; 10 g/day shortfall is irrelevant

title: Novices especially need little protein
statement: Beginners lack the anabolic capacity to use high protein, so the extra is expensive calories better replaced by carbs. He ate less than prescribed early on and still grew.

title: High protein isn't needed even when bulking
statement: Protein matters only until you have enough, bulking included. He aims for the smallest protein and calorie intake that still lets him grow; old-school lifters ate less, from steak and eggs.

title: Raise protein slowly when raising calories
statement: When adding calories, add protein slowly. Animal protein is so satiating that skinny lifters on high-protein diets fail to eat enough.
numbers: ~1 g protein per 100 kcal added
scope: Lifters increasing intake, especially skinny ones

title: Bioavailability makes or breaks a protein source
statement: How much of a source's protein your body can use matters as much as the label. Cooking meat raises it; red meat's value lies in its other nutrients, not its protein.
numbers: Whey ~100%; eggs ~90%; crickets ~90%; sardines ~80%; turkey ~80%; cooked tofu ~70%; lentils and mushrooms poor

title: Diversify protein sources
statement: Fish, fatty fish and plant proteins should complement animal protein. By 2022 his sources were chicken, turkey (now mostly), sardines, salmon, eggs, tuna and lentils.

title: Insects are valid protein, not a revolution
statement: Insects are a usable protein source but "not a nutrition revolution": they carry parasite risk and were never a staple anywhere. Buy only tested products.
numbers: 9-35 g protein/100 g vs 16-20 g for meat; 244 of 300 farms infected, 81 with human-transmissible parasites; cooking kills most

title: Macro balance is individual
statement: The right carb/fat/protein balance differs per person; find it by trial and error and by looking at your ancestry. A past high-fat, high-protein, lower-carb diet made him fat, sluggish and weak; others get fat on his diet.

title: He thrives on a high-carb, low-fat diet
statement: Most of his calories come from carbs, with low fat and moderate protein. Carbs improve his recovery, work capacity, endurance and look; he is leaner and more vascular on them, and fatter when he swaps carbs for fat.
numbers: 60/20/20 carb/protein/fat (2021); ~80% of kcal from carbs (2024)

title: Beginners manage calories, not macros
statement: Beginners only need to manage calories. He ignored macros for his first five years; balancing macros is easy, the hard part is choosing foods that agree with you.
numbers: He ignored macros for 5 years

title: Carbs don't make you fat; processed sugar does
statement: Low-fiber, high-sugar processed products make people fat, not carbs as such. Carb tolerance depends on digestion, body fat and ethnic background, and carbs can inflame some people. "Earn your carbs": most people eat pasta, rice and bread they don't need.

title: Keep fat low, but never near zero
statement: Naturals need some dietary fat for hormones; enhanced-style diets that cut fat almost completely would crush a natural's testosterone. His fats come from olive oil, fish, oat milk and occasional butter; avoid palm oil.
numbers: A fatty ramen broth left him lethargic for 4 h

title: White rice is his staple carb
statement: White (sticky) rice digests easily, and its low satiety lets him eat more and fill glycogen. Not everyone digests it; if it constipates you or insulin sensitivity worries you, swap to brown rice, sweet potato, quinoa or lentils, and avoid wild rice if it bothers you.
scope: Him; others if it agrees with them

title: Exercise changes how sugar acts
statement: Insulin sensitivity depends on exercise: sugar after training acts differently than sugar on the couch. He could keep his physique on processed carbs, but his health would suffer.

title: Cycle carbs by training day
statement: Put more carbs on some training days and fewer on others. Which days get the most has changed: in 2021 it was lower-body days (hungry heavy squats kill a workout); in 2024 it is upper-body days, with fewer carbs and more animal protein on leg days and carbs the day after legs.
status: contradicted — lower-body days get most carbs (2021, 2023) vs upper-body days (2022, 2024); the 2024 version is the latest

title: Rest days: less food, carbs near zero
statement: On rest days eat less, mostly protein and non-starchy vegetables, with carbs near zero unless you are a hardgainer. In 2021 he ate carbs only on training days, first to cut and then as a discipline so he never skips a session.
numbers: Carbs ~0 on rest days

title: Carbs the day before training fill glycogen
statement: Eating carbs the day before a session fills glycogen (Reeves' practice and his). Carbs on press day don't directly improve pressing, only through weight gained over time.

title: Meal timing is "D tier"
statement: When you eat matters little next to what and how much; distribution only affects how you get through the day. OMAD isn't inherently bad for hypertrophy.

title: There is no anabolic window
statement: Protein timing doesn't matter: synthesis runs for about a day and earlier meals already supply nutrients. The window was a protein-powder marketing tactic; protein or fat after training doesn't slow absorption, and a sugary post-workout drink is optional and mostly placebo.
numbers: Protein synthesis runs ~24 h
check: Does the plan avoid treating an immediate post-workout window as necessary?

title: Pre-workout: carb meal 2-3 h before, never fasted
statement: Eat a carb-rich meal 2-3 hours before training, plus a banana if hungry; be fed but not full. He never trains fasted and eats on waking.
numbers: 2-3 h before training
status: changed — 2020: a pre-training meal mostly helps psychologically unless it's fast carbs; 2023-24: carb meal 2-3 h before, never train fasted
check: Is training done fed, with a carb-rich meal a few hours before?

title: Six meals a day is a myth
statement: 1-3 meals a day are fine if calories and nutrients are met; six big rice-and-chicken meals came from steroid users. Novices eating 2-3 times will see calories rise naturally.
numbers: 1-3 meals fine; "not even 5%" of naturals need six meals

title: His pattern: two big meals plus snacks
statement: He eats two big sit-down meals with snacks or a breakfast between, sometimes one meal; he can't do OMAD because it would mean ~2,500 kcal in one sitting.
numbers: First meal ~10:30 after a 9 pm last meal, a de facto 12-14 h overnight fast

title: Distribute calories around hunger tolerance
statement: If you can't sleep hungry, start eating later and save calories for an evening meal; if you can't function hungry, eat most early and keep the post-training meal light and high-protein. He trims the post-workout dinner, not the pre-workout meal.

title: Some train best full, others hungry
statement: Some people train best on a full stomach, others hungry and aggressive. He likes being full on lower-body days because hunger hurts his focus.

title: The body burns fat before muscle
statement: Fear of muscle loss from fasting is a myth created by supplement companies: muscle is expensive and preserved, and true muscle breakdown comes only deep into starvation. Muscle lost during fasts comes from training performance dropping.

title: Fasting has no hormonal magic
statement: Fasting doesn't boost testosterone or growth hormone; intermittent fasting just extends the overnight fast. Its value is mental toughness and easier calorie control; "starvation mode" is mostly an excuse.
numbers: Strength drops a lot after 48 h of fasting

title: He doesn't fast; it darkens his mood
statement: Fasting makes him unproductive and gloomy, and puts many people, especially the overweight, in a dark place. A binge-then-fast cycle signals imbalance; if you struggle to eat enough, fasting isn't for you. In 2021 he said fasting helped him rein in his appetite after over-bulking.
scope: Him; people who struggle to eat enough

title: Very short eating windows are impractical
statement: 1-2 hour eating windows don't work: satiety makes large intakes near impossible, going to bed hungry hurts sleep and next-day work, and they invite junk binges.
numbers: 1-2 h windows; even 5,000 kcal near impossible in that time

title: Water fasts need minerals; dry fasting is dangerous
statement: If you water fast, add vitamins and minerals; dry fasting is dangerous.

title: Ramadan: aim for maintenance and train fed
statement: During religious fasting aim for maintenance, not a surplus. Prep the pre-dawn meal the night before and train 2-4 h after it (or at lunch), never late afternoon or evening while dehydrated. Pre-dawn: soft pasta or sticky rice and water with a pinch of sea salt; break the fast with protein and fats, then carbs, plus lots of vegetables. Gains continue, just not optimally.
numbers: Eat ~4 a.m., train ~6 a.m. or 2-4 h after the pre-dawn meal
scope: Lifters observing Ramadan or similar fasts

title: Eat mostly whole foods you cook yourself
statement: Most of what you eat should be home-cooked whole food; restaurants and delivery only occasionally. You control salt and condiments, get more satiety and micronutrients, and pay far less. Every man should learn to cook; cooking badly beats outsourcing.
numbers: Takeout ~5x the cost; his meals take ~10 min
check: Is most of the food whole and home-cooked rather than restaurant or delivery?

title: Minimize processed food; no processed meats
statement: Processed means anything prepared for you, and it's worse with more steps; makers optimise for taste and addiction. Poor food quality damages your hormonal profile even with perfect macros and may feed anxiety and depression. Nobody should eat processed meats.
check: Is processed food a small minority of the diet, with no processed meats?

title: Micronutrients are the hard, underrated part
statement: Judge foods by micros, not macros. Calories, protein and fat are easy to hit; vitamins and minerals are what junk misses. Covering micros from whole foods usually covers calories too; potatoes and cake have similar macros but very different micros.

title: Plants should be most of your food volume
statement: Eat lots of vegetables; he is "plant-based in the old sense", not vegan, using animal products for bioavailable protein. Leafy greens, onions, garlic, peppers, tomatoes, mushrooms, carrots; oats almost daily plus fruit.
check: Do vegetables and other plants make up most of the food volume?

title: Improve diet by subtraction, step by step
statement: You improve more by stopping bad foods than by adding good ones; there's no point taking an antidote while still drinking poison. Introduce changes gradually, since removing all junk at once can backfire (acne, feeling bad).

title: Junk food is empty calories
statement: Junk food helps nobody's health; only very-high-TDEE hardgainers benefit. Cake won't kill you in a big surplus, but the more junk you eat, the more the rest must cover micros. He sees the "junk food doesn't exist" camp as possibly worse than clean-eating cultists.

title: No food makes you big; no superfoods
statement: Once macros are met with healthy food it's just calories; organ meats for size are an old gimmick. Some foods (kiwi, garlic, onion, ginger, olive oil) are simply rich in micronutrients.
numbers: Organ-meat gimmick is 60-70 years old

title: Supermarket produce is low in micronutrients
statement: He believes supermarket produce is depleted (poor soil, early harvest), while admitting he has no source. Buy organic and local from farms that rest their soil, favour hardy roots like potatoes, or grow your own.

title: Fruit instead of processed sweets
statement: Use whole fruit (bananas, apples) as snacks rather than processed sweets. Fiber supplements are pointless; get fiber's value from vegetables and fruit.
numbers: In summer, two mangoes a day plus other fruit; bowel movements beyond 1-2/day signal GI problems

title: There is no universal diet
statement: Nutrition is even more case-by-case than training: amounts, ratios, timing and micros differ. Reject absolutes and cookie-cutter plans and experiment by removing and adding foods; by your 30s-40s you should have most of it figured out.
numbers: ~80% figured out by your 30s-40s
check: Is the diet tailored to the individual rather than a cookie-cutter plan?

title: Use family history and ancestry to choose foods
statement: Ask what relatives on both sides died of, protect your family's weak organ and copy your healthiest relatives. He built his diet with a longevity nutritionist from family history (no DNA test); without such help, use credible sources on which foods aggravate or protect against a condition.

title: Drop foods that disagree with you
statement: Remove foods that disagree with you, even "healthy" ones (broccoli wrecks his stomach); don't trick the body with lactose pills. For bloating, find the trigger (dairy, red meat, gluten, oats, pasta); clean foods with similar macros are interchangeable.

title: No food is universally good or bad
statement: Dose matters per person: an amount that helps one person may harm another. Beef and milk aren't bad in themselves but may be bad for you.
numbers: E.g. 100 g may help and 300-400 g harm one person but not another

title: Remove foods gradually, before a recomp
statement: Eliminate foods one at a time and do the experimenting before a recomp, not during it. He dropped milk, then cow cheese, then goat cheese over two years, and pork before beef.
numbers: Dairy removed over ~2 years

title: Stubbornness costs more in diet than in training
statement: Being stubborn with diet costs more than being stubborn with training, because hard work compensates less for a bad diet.

title: Dropping dairy transformed his physique
statement: Quitting dairy, especially milk, removed his love handles, facial bloat and water retention at the same bodyweight, revealing separation and veins; he links this to estrogen in milk. If you are lean but have stubborn love handles or unexplained bloat, try cutting dairy.
numbers: 215 → 210 lb in ~2 months but much leaner (2020); no milk for 3 years and butter 1-2x/week as his only dairy (2024)
scope: Him; lean lifters with stubborn love handles or bloat
status: changed — milk only (2020, still ate goat cheese) → all cheese gone (2022) → butter the only dairy left (2024)

title: Dairy isn't good for most people
statement: Being able to digest lactose doesn't make dairy healthy; most people do poorly on it, though some groups (Scandinavians) thrive on it. The "other species' milk" argument is a nature fallacy.

title: Red meat shouldn't be anyone's main protein
statement: Red meat rarely helps any condition and isn't needed for gains; he has cut it close to zero after relatives who ate it died early.
numbers: Limit 1 lb/week, don't overcook (2020); beef eliminated (2022); beef ~every two months, meat from 2x/day to ≤1x/day (2024)
status: changed — 1 lb/week (2020) → eliminated (2022) → beef ~every two months (2024)

title: Cutting animal products cost him nothing
statement: Each removal of animal products improved his health and physique with no loss of strength or muscle. He now eats mostly plants and carbs with modest animal products; eggs and fish can replace meat.
status: changed — 2020: calories "largely from animal products"; from 2022: mostly carbs and plants, modest animal protein

title: Eggs: a few a week, whole, pasture-raised
statement: Eat whole pasture-raised eggs with deep orange yolks, where the vitamins are; eggs are a micronutrient bomb, but their protein is overrated. Twelve a day is ridiculous and can't be used.
numbers: 12/day in his early bulks → 4-8/week (2020) → 4-6/week (2024); ~90% bioavailable; 12 g protein/10 g fat per 100 g

title: Fish: limit canned tuna, favour sardines
statement: Limit canned tuna and salmon for mercury; sardines are safer; eat fatty fish like trout twice a week. Source locally.
numbers: Canned tuna/salmon ≤2x/week; fatty fish 2x/week

title: Soy and tofu are fine
statement: Soy has had no negative effect on him. Studies test normal intake, not overconsumption, and estrogenic effects depend on genetics and receptor sensitivity.

title: Raw garlic and onions daily, as food
statement: Eating raw garlic and onions daily changed how he looks and feels: pumps hours later and vascularity without fat loss. By 2024 garlic is the only food he credits for vascularity (mostly it is training and leanness); tolerance builds, and it won't cure illness, only support general immunity. For his dosing protocol see SUP-23.
numbers: Pumps 4-5 h later; 3 cloves stopped working after ~1-1.5 months

title: Salt is not the enemy
statement: Lifters who cook their own food should salt it: sodium is needed for contraction and intramuscular water, and water without minerals "just passes through". Use sea or pink salt and get blood pressure checked.
numbers: Supermarket food has ~5x the sodium of his rice

title: Hydrate by urine colour; drink filtered water
statement: Judge hydration by urine: clear, without constantly peeing pure water. Vegetables and salads supply much of your water. He believes tap water carries hormones and toxins, so he drinks only filtered water (filter, reverse osmosis) and no coffee, tea or soda.

title: Cut sodas, juices and energy drinks
statement: Drink water instead of sweet drinks; this change alone can drop several pounds. He drinks water (sometimes with lemon), oat milk and occasional orange juice.
numbers: −5-10 lb from cutting liquid calories; oat milk ~1 L/week

title: Alcohol impairs muscle building
statement: Alcohol hurts muscle building and performance, though occasional drinks won't kill gains. Daily "moderate" drinking is addiction, a binge wrecks next-day training, and liquor is worst. He rarely drinks and calls alcohol poison.
numbers: He has a beer or two a year

title: A diet must be sustainable for life
statement: Build your diet from foods you enjoy and can repeat for life. Bland bodybuilder food is "theatrics" that breeds misery and eating disorders; spices make dense food easier to eat.
check: Could the person eat this way for life, from foods they enjoy?

title: No cheat meals
statement: Needing a weekly binge means the diet is wrong; he "doesn't eat clean", so there's nothing to cheat from. Planned refeeds for performance are different from cheat meals for feelings, and weekly rich binges stress stomach and skin.

title: Extreme diets suit only a minority
statement: Keto, carnivore, vegan, zero-fat and raw-meat diets suit a small minority; humans are omnivores and no diet should ban whole food groups. Carnivore and vegan mostly help by removing processed junk.

title: He doesn't count calories; count if it helps
statement: He doesn't count calories or macros because he is already obsessive about training; counting is a legitimate tool if it helps you. In 2020, eating purely by appetite during a recomp backfired on him: dropping dairy led to unnoticed weight loss and lifts going backwards.
status: contradicted — recommends eating by instinct, yet appetite-only eating during his 2020 recomp backfired

title: Keep a professional relationship with food
statement: Treat food as sustenance and diet as a tool, not a personality; eating only for pleasure is close to addiction, though pleasure is fine as a by-product. Fix a bad relationship with food early.

title: Clean-eating obsession can become a disorder
statement: Obsessive clean eating can become an eating disorder, though calling healthy eating "orthorexia" pathologises it. Judge foods by whether they agree with you, not by labels; eating with others reduces disorders.

title: Remove temptation rather than test willpower
statement: Keep tempting food out of the house instead of proving willpower; for a craving, wait it out. If you grew up food-insecure, an empty fridge can cause heavy stress, so he instead makes a month's snacks last a month.
numbers: Wait ~15 min on a craving

title: Eat until satiated, not full
statement: Pause briefly mid-meal and pack away the rest if hunger is gone; don't eat the instant you feel hunger, and don't overeat to compensate for extra activity.
numbers: Pause ~30 s mid-meal

title: Limit sugar, but don't ban it
statement: He keeps sugar limited with fruit first, but calls banning all sugar too extreme; he eats a sweet breakfast he enjoys. Avoid palm-oil spreads like Nutella.
numbers: 3-4 croissants with jam/peanut butter + whey for breakfast (2023-24)
status: changed — 2021: restricted sugar except fruit; 2023-24: sweet croissant breakfast, banning sugar "too extreme"

title: Artificial sweeteners aren't harmless
statement: The problem with sweeteners is addiction to sweetness. Banana test: if a banana doesn't taste very sweet, your taste buds are ruined.

title: Hardgainers must prioritise eating
statement: Skinny and tall lifters usually just don't eat enough (no proven link to low testosterone). They need a surplus and scheduled meals, never just 1-2 a day; because appetite shuts off quickly, more meals help them, and tall lifters need patience.
numbers: Appetite shuts off in 5-6 min; six meals can help hardgainers

title: Hardgainers: drink calories, skip the bro diet
statement: Skinny lifters on chicken-and-broccoli diets don't grow; drink calories through homemade blender shakes (peanut butter, milks, avocado, blueberries) sipped through the day or before bed, or eat cake or pizza if needed while keeping the diet balanced. Quick dense snack: oats with bananas and honey.

title: GOMAD is idiotic
statement: A gallon of milk a day brings excess fat and calcium, puts all your eggs in one basket and has hidden long-term costs; any growth comes only from protein and calories.

title: The vertical diet is for Efferding's athletes
statement: Red meat plus white rice, low fiber and no onions or garlic suits Efferding's strength athletes, not non-athletes or teens; the orange juice is meant to boost appetite, not replace vegetables. He notes Brian Shaw quit it.
scope: Non-athletes and teens should avoid it

title: Women: moderate surplus by appetite
statement: Women should run a moderate surplus guided by appetite; their gains tend to go to legs and glutes.

title: Fat loss: swap processed food for whole food
statement: Replace processed foods with vegetables and whole foods instead of crash dieting; fiber-rich food satiates and calories fall on their own, while rapid loss risks loose skin. Stop snacking and eat only planned sit-down meals (even 4-5 instead of 3); salad-starving dieters out-snack it.

title: Snacking within macros is fine unless overweight
statement: Snacks within your intake are fine unless you are overweight; people with a low metabolism do better on snacks plus occasional big meals than on six big meals.

title: Shop smart and plan the week
statement: Shop with a list, after a meal, local and seasonal; buy perishables only as needed and plan the week.
numbers: Hungry shoppers buy 15-20% more; French households waste ~30% of food bought; tips save up to ~$1,000/yr; a cabbage ~$0.28 lasts two days

title: Healthy food is not expensive
statement: Eating healthy is affordable; he lived on a small monthly budget in the US and got jacked. Dorms without kitchens make gaining hard.
numbers: $690/month

title: Cook chicken in oven or pan, well seasoned
statement: Bake or pan-cook chicken with heavy seasoning; never boil or steam it and avoid rotisserie. Garlic and onion powder go on anything. Use oven and pans rather than the microwave or ready-meals; he credits that switch with better body composition and hormones.
numbers: Bake 25-35 min with poultry seasoning

title: Cook fresh rather than weekly meal prep
statement: He stopped weekly meal prep: budget prep made him hate his food, and dry chicken and rice followed by a Sunday binge is "weak-minded". He cooks fresh with a few precooked dishes.
status: changed — 2021 recipes batch-cook rice for 7-15 days; by 2022 no meal prep; 2024: weekly prep wasted food

title: Skin and acne follow diet
statement: For acne, stop harsh face washes, drink water, cut soda, refined sugar, dairy and fast food, and sleep more. Saturated fat, junk or spices cause body odour.

title: Post-meal brain fog may signal too many carbs
statement: Brain fog lasting over 30 minutes after a meal may signal too many carbs or gluten. He gets sleepy for an hour after meals, so he puts his last meal near bed.
numbers: >30 min of fog

title: After a big meal: salad or lemon water
statement: He ends a big meal with salad and balsamic, or drinks water with a squeezed lemon before bed.
numbers: ~1 L water with a lemon

title: Supplements are near-worthless for muscle
statement: Food, training and sleep build muscle; supplements are "D tier", worth maybe 1%, and the least important part of a bulk. Programming is "100 times more important", and most products are nonsense, some dangerous.
numbers: ~90% nonsense (2020); worth maybe 1% (2023)
check: Does the plan treat supplements as optional extras rather than a driver of progress?

title: Supplements only concentrate what food gives
statement: A supplement gives what food gives in concentrated form, so eat real food first; healing needs habits, not pills.

title: A supplement that builds muscle is a steroid
statement: Any supplement that truly builds muscle is a steroid; everything else is a dud. The "miracle" products that worked were banned as hormonal, and a flashy tub that works may hide illegal substances. There are "no natural steroids".

title: Supplements stand in for lifestyle changes
statement: Pills replace harder habits: vitamin D replaces sun, ashwagandha replaces dealing with stressors, organ-meat pills replace eating organs. The funnel moves you from a hard habit to an easy, pricier pill.

title: Vitamins: crutch or worth taking?
statement: In 2022 he said a balanced diet removes the need for vitamin supplements ("crutches"); in 2024 he listed multivitamins and vitamin D among the few supplements worth anything.
status: contradicted — 2022: vitamins are crutches a balanced diet removes; 2024: multivitamins and vitamin D are among the only four worth taking

title: Joint and recovery supplements beat muscle ones
statement: Supplements for joints and recovery matter more than those sold for muscle.

title: Try cheap ones; drop what shows nothing
statement: If you try supplements, pick cheap ones not marketed at beginners and drop anything that shows no improvement.

title: Take half the label dose
statement: Take half the recommended dose of any supplement: results are the same and you buy half as much. Natural stacks are copied from PED users; cut yours down (he cut ~80% of his). He exempts creatine, which he takes above label (SUP-12).
numbers: Half the label dose; he cut ~80% of his stack
status: contradicted — "half the label dose" vs his own creatine above label dose

title: His stack is about three items
statement: He keeps only about three cheap, sustainable supplements; cutting 80% of his stack changed nothing. The only ones worth anything, he said in 2024, are whey, creatine, multivitamins and vitamin D; the rest is a bonus at most.
numbers: 2022: creatine, MSM, bee pollen (pollen 6 months/yr); 2024: creatine, MSM, protein

title: Prefer tonic herbs to supplements
statement: He prefers raw garlic and ginger, as "tonic herbs", to bought supplements.

title: Creatine works, but the effect is small
statement: Creatine is natural, cheap and one of the most proven supplements; for him it brings longer, higher-volume workouts and intramuscular water. In 2020 it also stood in for the red meat he minimises.

title: Creatine daily, no loading, no cycling
statement: Take creatine every day without loading or cycling; loading phases exist only to make you finish the tub, and megadoses don't scale gains. He takes more than the label dose for work capacity.
numbers: ~1 tablespoon/day
check: Is creatine (if used) taken daily without loading or cycling?

title: Creatine side effects vary by person
statement: Some people get hair loss (DHT), bloating or water retention, or kidney stones; he gets none and his hair is thicker than ever. Stop if it causes hair loss.
numbers: He got bloodwork every 6 months to check creatine (2020)

title: Whey is a convenience, not a necessity
statement: Whey only makes protein easier to consume and was the first hyped "magic potion"; you don't need it to be jacked. He used whey or pea protein for convenience (low appetite, 1-2 meals a day, avoiding animal products). In 2024 he called powder not worth the money at current prices while still using and recommending it.
status: contradicted — 2024: whey is among the few worthwhile supplements and he uses it, yet powder is "not worth the money"

title: At most one scoop a day
statement: Use at most about one scoop of protein powder a day; if shakes make up most of your protein, your diet is wrong. Test it: stop or cut powder for a while, and 9 times out of 10 nothing changes. Stockpiling and bulk discounts breed dependence and overconsumption.
numbers: 3 shakes/day → ~2 scoops/week with no loss (2021); 1 scoop/day (2023); 1 scoop 3-4x/week (2024)
check: Does protein powder supply only a small share of daily protein (about one scoop at most)?

title: Pick plain powder; gainers are garbage
statement: Choose a powder that is mostly protein, without added carbs or sugar, and don't dry scoop. Weight gainers and carb powders are sugar and industrial by-products sold far above the cost of the food they come from; make your own shake or eat rice.
numbers: Gainers cost ~10x the food they come from

title: Small or slow shakes; night shake if short
statement: He claims only a limited amount of whey is absorbed per hour, so sip shakes slowly or take smaller ones. A night-time shake is fine if protein falls short, as during Ramadan.
numbers: ~20 g whey (30 g cricket) absorbed per hour; an 80 g shake is only ~30% used

title: MSM is his key joint supplement
statement: MSM powder is his favourite joint supplement and the only thing that fixed his knees; it is anti-inflammatory, cheap and horribly bitter, takes weeks to work, and his joints suffer quickly when he stops. He saw little difference from pricier glucosamine.
numbers: ~1 tsp/day in juice, starting lower (2020); also "1-2x/week" (2020); daily nonstop for 5 years by 2024
scope: Lifters with joint or tendon issues
status: changed — 2020: ~1 tsp/day vs 1-2x/week in the same month; 2024: daily, nonstop

title: Collagen in his whey for tendons
statement: He adds collagen to his whey shake for tendon health.

title: He takes bee pollen daily
statement: He started bee pollen to treat his spring pollen allergy without antihistamines and now takes it daily because he finds the benefits too large to stop. It gives him euphoric, almost manic energy and may worsen anxiety; he believes it helps skin, hair and digestion. Pollen without hard training builds nothing.
numbers: Six months a year (2022) → every day (2024)
status: changed — six months a year (2022) → daily (2024)

title: Bee pollen protocol: microdose up
statement: Allergic people risk anaphylaxis, so microdose from early April and raise slowly; stop if you react. Take it on waking on an empty stomach, after lunch and after dinner, letting it dissolve in saliva, with a spoon of farm honey.
numbers: 1-2 pellets once a day at first; ~¼ tsp by end of April; adult male 3 tsp/day; breakfast ~90 min after the morning dose
scope: Bee pollen users, especially allergy sufferers

title: Buy local organic pollen pellets
statement: Buy local organic pellets, not capsules, creatine blends or Amazon products; local pollen helps local allergies, and paying more than a modest monthly cost is a scam.
numbers: ~€10-15 or up to $20/month; 1 tsp ≈ 15 kcal, 1.2 g protein

title: Raw garlic: low dose, every other day
statement: Eat 1-2 raw cloves every other day, starting with half a clove twice a week, always with a meal; never a whole bulb (vomiting, effect lost). He says studies show one clove per 24 h maximises allicin.
numbers: Start ½ clove 2x/week; target 1-2 cloves every other day (2023); earlier 3-6 cloves/day in two servings, under half a bulb, starting at 1 clove (2020)
status: changed — 3-6 cloves/day (2020) → 1-2 cloves every other day (2023)

title: Garlic prep: raw, thin, rest, chew, at lunch
statement: Always raw (cooking destroys allicin), sliced very thin, rested briefly, chewed thoroughly; eat it at lunch, not before bed, since evening trainees feel it in their session. He calls the 10-minute rule a myth. Buy organic garlic that is hard, strong-smelling and unsprouted; never garlic pills.
numbers: Rest 60 s after slicing

title: Garlic benefits and downsides
statement: Raw garlic gives pumps through blood flow, steady all-day energy, immunity and vascularity; a cheaper, healthier "stimulant" than spike-and-crash pre-workouts. It lowers LDL and blood pressure; the pump fades with habituation but better circulation stays. Downsides: breath and body odour, gas, stomach pain, heartburn; some can't digest it.

title: Ginger every 48 hours
statement: Start with a small piece of ginger every 48 h and build up. He credits it with better focus than nootropics, better insulin sensitivity (full muscles instead of fog after carbs) and libido; downsides are sour armpit odour and diarrhoea. He cycles garlic on upper days and ginger on lower, higher-carb days. Buy dry, hard, mould-free ginger with yellow flesh from Asian markets, never store-bought pickled ginger.
numbers: Small piece every 48 h → he now eats 4-5 sizeable pieces every 48 h; pickle peeled ginger in fruit juice 4+ days (replace the juice) or honey and a little water 10-15 days in the fridge

title: Fish oil did nothing for him
statement: He stopped fish oil because it did nothing, and his doctor said too much omega-3 was bad for his condition; he also limits fatty fish.

title: Minor compounds he has tried
statement: Turmeric in every dish while healing (he rates it despite debated absorption); taurine before bed gave him vivid dreams and deeper REM sleep; B12 made no noticeable difference.
numbers: Taurine ~$10 for 6 months

title: Filtered water needs minerals from elsewhere
statement: Filtered water lacks minerals, so get them from diet or a mineral supplement.

title: No sleeping pills; fix the cause
statement: Don't take sleeping pills; fix whatever is disrupting sleep (see ch. 4).

title: Anti-stimulant: no coffee, no pre-workout
statement: He takes no caffeine or pre-workout; needing them to train is a weak, compromised relationship with lifting, and motivation from a spike stops when tolerance or supply runs out. Using caffeine to start out is fine, but not as a crutch; pre/intra-workout supplements are "C tier".
numbers: He works 15-20 min after waking without coffee
check: Can the lifter train hard without depending on stimulants?

title: Caffeine borrows energy and wrecks sleep
statement: Caffeine borrows energy, builds tolerance and replaces natural wake-up hormones; even a noon cup affects sleep, and an evening pre-workout ruins recovery. Viewers who quit for two weeks lost headaches, fatigue and shaking. If you use it, take regular breaks.
numbers: None at noon or later; a 7 pm pre-workout for an 8-9 pm session ruins recovery; 1-2 week break every two months

title: Want a stimulant? Drink coffee, not pre-workout
statement: If you want a stimulant, drink coffee; a $40 pre-workout is a scam because only caffeine and beta-alanine matter. One morning coffee is a ritual; coffee all day is addiction. He still abstains himself.
numbers: $40 pre-workout
status: changed — 2020-21: coffee is an addiction and sleep-wrecker; 2024: drink coffee instead of pre-workout, one morning cup is a ritual

title: Intra-workout: water or a carb drink
statement: During training a carb drink is enough; plain water is fine.

title: Smelling salts are a meme
statement: Needing smelling salts to lift isn't sustainable.

title: Test boosters are scams
statement: Test boosters are disguised steroids or junk, placebo at best; nothing natural raises testosterone or simply grows muscle. He notes tongkat ali has been eaten for centuries in Southeast Asia without producing muscular populations, and deer-antler testosterone claims were debunked.
numbers: Deer-antler "+200% T" claim debunked

title: Turkesterone and ecdysterone do nothing
statement: Any gains people report on turkesterone or ecdysterone come from placebo, training harder, newbie gains or muscle memory; he never took them, and the names deliberately evoke steroids. Vegans eat quinoa without getting huge: "show me the monsters".
numbers: Ecdysterone costs ~300x spinach, about six tubs of creatine (~$60 at ~200% margin)

title: Pump products, fat burners and nootropics don't deliver
statement: Pump supplements, fat burners and fat-loss creams don't work; nootropics pushed to uneducated audiences are risky "smart pills".

title: Never buy from fitness YouTubers
statement: Never buy supplements or programs pushed by fitness YouTubers; the industry is a hydra with replaceable heads, and the best creator stance is never to mention supplements. Creators who sell or take supplement money lose integrity, even if the company is good (see ch. 13).

title: Marketing sells image transfer to teens
statement: Supplement marketing runs on social proof, newbie-gain testimonials, image transfer and teen audiences; buyers expect to look like the seller, and "might as well try it" funds the industry. Prices bear no relation to ingredient cost and are padded with fluff ingredients.
numbers: He estimates 70-80% of buyers were teens using their parents' money; tongkat extract ~$10 vs a branded product at $50-60

title: Bunk-supplement buyers partly scam themselves
statement: Buyers of bunk turkesterone partly "scammed themselves" by trying to dodge hard work; whatever they felt came from training harder, so the placebo defence fails. He predicted a new magic muscle supplement (perhaps a black-pepper or capsaicin extract) within 6-12 months.
numbers: New fad predicted within 6-12 months

title: Default for naturals: small permanent surplus
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Men who are not very over- or underweight should stay in a small surplus for their whole career ("perma-bulk"), unless they start out fat; overshooting body fat once ruins it.
numbers: "permabulk from day one for 15 years"
scope: Natural men not at a bodyweight extreme; fat starters cut first (BLK-04).
check: Is the default plan a small, continuous surplus rather than repeated bulk/cut phases?

title: Who should bulk: from extremes only to most
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: In 2020 only extremes should bulk or cut (very skinny bulk, very fat cut, everyone else near maintenance). By 2024 lean, small and formerly chubby lifters must lean bulk, and maintaining or cutting is a mistake for them; moving past the lean "auto mode" physique requires an awkward bulking phase.
numbers: example lean-but-small lifter: ~15% at 190 cm/81 kg (2024)
scope: Naturals who are lean but not big, including escaped skinny-fat and formerly chubby lifters.
status: changed — 2020: only very skinny people should bulk; 2024: lean/small lifters must bulk.

title: Skinny naturals must gain weight, slowly
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Skinny naturals should slow lean bulk on a small surplus, never dirty or aggressively (they just turn skinny-fat). You must gain weight to gain muscle; building muscle at maintenance at 130 lb is a meme. Skinny women need to gain too.
numbers: a skinny novice transforms in 2-3 years
status: changed — 2022: "you do not need a caloric surplus" (he had gained at maintenance); 2022-2024: for skinny/lean lifters a surplus is required and "your best weapon".

title: Fat people: lift while you cut
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: If you start fat, cut while lifting: it keeps muscle, makes the cut easier and keeps skin firmer. A high-fat, low-muscle novice can still build muscle on a cut. Cut until skinny-fat or skinny, then build.

title: Skinny-fat: recomp at maintenance, never cut
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Skinny-fat is not a body type but metabolic distress. Stay at maintenance (or a very slight surplus or deficit) and put the effort into training; cutting skinny-fat is a mistake.
check: Does a skinny-fat lifter stay near maintenance and train hard instead of cutting?

title: No cutting in the first years unless fat
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Unless fat or obese, don't cut during your first ~5 years: you haven't built anything to reveal. Teens shouldn't cut, though overweight teens can.
numbers: first ~5 years
scope: Beginners and teens who are not fat.
check: Does a non-fat lifter in their first ~5 years avoid cutting?

title: After big weight loss: maintain before surplus
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Someone who lost a lot of weight but is still soft should recomp at maintenance before adding a surplus, because waist fat returns first. Someone overweight who stress-eats should fix the emotional eating and learn to hold maintenance, then cut slowly.
numbers: ~18 months at maintenance; example 12 kg over

title: Formerly very fat: stop cutting, then bulk
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Very fat people often keep cutting past need. Once fat is under control, lean bulk; if dysmorphia makes you want to cut, cut once, then lean bulk.

title: No upside to bulking into the 20s
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Sitting around 22% body fat has no upside except for strongmen chasing every pound; bulking up to ~20% is a bad idea for most.
numbers: ~20-22% body fat

title: Tie bulks and cuts to a goal
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Bulks and cuts make most sense tied to a performance goal (a lift, a show, one-arm pull-ups). Athletes shouldn't bulk for a bench or cut for abs; diet serves the sport.

title: Tall lifters and bulking speed
section: Who should bulk, cut or recomp
statement: Tall lifters need more mass to look impressive. He has said both that slow, patient bulking works for them and that more aggressive gaining can be justified.
numbers: example 75→95 kg in 3 years (2024)
status: contradicted — 2023-12: slow, patient bulking (tall lifters who dirty bulk get fat); 2024-12: aggressive gaining can be justified.

title: Keep the surplus small
statement: Bulk on a small surplus; a few hundred calories is enough and more is pointless for a natural past beginner.
numbers: +200-400 kcal (2020); under 10%, "4% beats 40%" (2021); his own +300 (2022); ~500 kcal gets ~95-98% of possible gains (2022); 200 kcal "enough" (2024-09); 300 "plenty", 500 "pointless" (2024-12)
scope: Naturals past the beginner stage; see BLK-15 for the hardgainer exception.
status: changed — the advised surplus shrank: 10-15% ceiling (2020) and ~500 kcal near-optimal (2022) → 200-300 kcal, 500 "pointless" (2024).
check: Is the bulking surplus around 200-300 kcal rather than 500+?

title: Big surplus = fat; big deficit = muscle loss
statement: A big surplus doesn't build more natural muscle, only fat; a big deficit burns muscle as well as fat. Protein synthesis is limited, your capacity to get fat is not.
numbers: no muscle benefit above ~10-15% surplus (2020); 1000-2000 kcal does not double muscle (2022)

title: Novices start at maintenance
statement: Novices should eat at maintenance and raise calories slowly as appetite grows; a big surplus is a waste.
numbers: +500 kcal or more is a waste

title: Hardgainer exception: eat more
statement: Very skinny, fast-metabolism lifters who stall on a small surplus should eat more aggressively.
numbers: perhaps double the surplus
scope: Very skinny lifters with fast metabolisms who have stalled.

title: Raise calories slowly, then hold
statement: Raise calories slowly and hold them steady until the bulking intake becomes your new maintenance (proof you gained muscle), then raise again. Constant swings in intake disrupt training.

title: Small daily surpluses beat huge days
statement: A steady small surplus beats occasional huge eating days, which are mostly stored as fat. Force-feeding makes you lethargic and diet-fixated.
numbers: a 3,000 kcal surplus day is mostly fat; +1000 kcal/day force-feeding criticised

title: His own method: bare-minimum surplus
statement: He bulks on the smallest surplus that still moves the scale; for him an extra bowl of rice is enough because his metabolism is slow. He admits this instinctive method may not suit hardgainers.

title: Gain about 0.5-1.5 lb per month
statement: Bulk slowly; past the beginner stage, more than a pound or so a month is mostly fat.
numbers: under 4 lb/month (2020-08); 1-2 lb/month (2020-12); 0.5-1 lb/month or ~10 lb/year (2023-07); ~1 lb/month (2023-10); 1.5 lb/month "good" on a lean bulk (2024-11)
scope: Intermediate and advanced naturals; true beginners can gain faster (BLK-21).
status: changed — 1-2 lb/month (2020) tightened to 0.5-1 lb/month after his own too-fast 2023 bulk (20-30 lb in a year); 1.5 lb/month called good in 2024.
check: Is the target gain about 0.5-1.5 lb per month (less if advanced)?

title: The more advanced, the slower
statement: The more advanced you are, the slower the bulk must be. An advanced lifter gaining 2 lb a month is just gaining fat.
numbers: he gained 5 lb in a year from 210 (<0.5 lb/month); 10 lb lean mass in 2-3 months at 200 lb is impossible

title: Judge gain relative to bodyweight
statement: Judge monthly gain as a percentage of bodyweight; fast gain is justified only for true beginners filling out.
numbers: at 180 lb, several lb/month is too much to be muscle for an intermediate

title: Spread gains over years
statement: Gain your mass over years, not months.
numbers: over 5 years rather than 8-10 months (2020); 20 lb over 3 years beats 20 lb in 1 year (2023); 14 kg in 4 years is good (2024); 50 lb in 3 years too fast unless dangerously skinny (~20 lb of it avoidable fat)

title: Fast fat-free gains are a lie
statement: Never try to gain 20 lb fast "without fat", even if skinny; anyone claiming 20 lb of muscle with no fat is lying, and no one bulks 100 lb and gets 90% muscle.

title: Slower gain is more likely muscle
statement: The same weight gained faster may give the same strength increase, but the slower gain is far more likely muscle.
numbers: 10 lb in 2 months vs 5-6 months; an inch on the arms in 3 months is fat

title: Each bulk more conservative
statement: Each bulk after the first should be more conservative ("first bulk is like a first love"); lifters tend to do the opposite.
scope: Lifters on their second or later bulk.

title: Teens have time
statement: Teens can slow bulk for up to 10 years. Forcing large gains (e.g. for a sport season) backfires: it is mostly fat and fosters eating disorders.
numbers: +25 lb for a season at 18 criticised; 3,500→4,300 kcal (+22%) for 1 kg/month or +60% for 3 kg/month called miscalculated

title: Training dictates diet
statement: Calories can't become muscle by themselves. Training creates growth and the surplus only fuels recovery, so extra calories must coincide with rising volume, workload and intensity, or they are stored as fat.
check: Are calorie increases matched by rising volume, workload or intensity in the gym?

title: A bulk must raise work capacity
statement: A bulk should raise work capacity and volume; if volume regresses on a bulk, there's no reason to bulk. Eat to fuel progression, not to gain weight.

title: Progressing? Don't add calories
statement: If you are progressing without a surplus, don't add calories. Raising his surplus while still progressing was his "first mistake" in 2023.
scope: Anyone still progressing at current intake.

title: Bulking helps but isn't required
statement: Novices and intermediates can gain without bulking; a surplus only makes progression easier, and its main advantage is faster visible gains, which help adherence.
scope: Novices and intermediates; for skinny lifters see BLK-03.

title: Food explains many program results
statement: Running a demanding strength program at maintenance vs eating everything feels "night and day" for leverage and recovery; many program results reflect noob gains and food, not the program. Energy-demanding programs (e.g. his Doom Slayer) should be run on a bulk.

title: The calisthenics check
statement: If bench rises while push-ups regress, or rows rise while pull-ups drop, you're gaining fat: slow down or stop the bulk. Keep calisthenics in while bulking.
check: Do push-ups and pull-ups hold or improve while the bulk continues?

title: Strength in proportion to bodyweight is a bad trade
statement: Strength rising only in proportion to added bodyweight is a bad trade and mostly not muscle; heavier scale and heavier bar don't equal muscle ("mass moves mass", better leverage).
numbers: +20 lb bench for +10 lb bodyweight = bad trade

title: Watch the waist
statement: Rising lifts and bodyweight with a growing waist means fat, a trap for bodybuilders using powerlifting principles. A rapidly growing waist means visceral fat, and every inch there looks bad.
check: Is the waist staying roughly stable while bodyweight rises?

title: Mirror as often as the scale
statement: Check the mirror as often as the scale: "bulking hypnosis" or size goggles hide fat gain, and on a cut "lean goggles" hide size loss.

title: Signs to stop or slow a bulk
statement: Stop or slow the bulk when bloat appears with no visible muscle (go to maintenance or a small deficit), when extra calories no longer improve gym performance, when your face gets chubby, or when you no longer like your body.

title: No target bodyweight
statement: Don't set a target bodyweight; it becomes an obsession and forces overeating. Set a time frame instead. He once aimed 180→225 lb to hit 100 kg.
numbers: his old target 180→225 lb
status: contradicted — he repeatedly rejects goal bodyweights, yet in 2023-01 praised Hamza's 180 lb target as "good nuanced advice".

title: Weigh in every few weeks
statement: Weigh only every 2-4 weeks; earlier he weighed every month or two, or not at all, judging by strength and mirror.
numbers: every 2-4 weeks (2023)

title: Calorie tracking: optional, personal
statement: He has never tracked calories on a bulk because it feeds his obsessive tendencies, but tracking is the easiest way to know you're gaining, suits people who need regimentation, may be needed to get shredded, and he would count if he cut.

title: Body-fat numbers are unreliable
statement: Body-fat scales are inaccurate, nobody can eyeball body-fat % accurately, and knowing the number is nearly useless.
numbers: scales always read 12-14% for him

title: Dirty bulking is mostly fat
statement: Dirty bulking adds mostly fat and leverage, not muscle. Junk food is low in protein and micronutrients, so you feel sluggish and bloated; whatever muscle you keep would have come from any surplus. Big naturals got big in spite of it.
status: contradicted — 2020: dirty bulking builds less muscle because junk lacks protein; 2021: the muscle difference is "negligibly small, if it exists".
check: Does the bulk avoid dirty bulking and force-feeding?

title: There is always more fat than you think
statement: After a dirty bulk you must cut and lose the "size and strength" you thought you had. Everyone who cuts finds more fat than expected, and you can't predict your shredded weight by subtracting fat. Some people never lose the love handles.
numbers: fat you think is 20 lb is really 40; plan 20 lb, need 40-60
scope: Lifters who over-bulked; anyone planning a cut.

title: GOMAD is stupid
statement: A gallon of milk a day overshoots into a large surplus with no room to manage calories, and brings too much milk fat and protein. At most it suits very skinny or very active athletes, and it can promote dysmorphia.
numbers: a gallon of milk/day
scope: Bulking lifters; possible exception for very skinny or very active athletes.

title: Excess fat is anti-anabolic
statement: Excess fat lowers testosterone, so the fatter you get the less anabolic you are; obese naturals might even lose muscle. Visceral fat and the tendon load of extra bodyweight aren't fully reversed by leaning out.

title: Force-feeding harms your relationship with food
statement: Force-feeding can trigger eating disorders the way crash diets trigger anorexia. If you hate your food, the bulk fails.

title: Hard bulking works only if you track
statement: Performance lifters who compare old numbers at the same bodyweight, and aesthetic lifters who track measurements, can bulk hard; most people don't track, so it fails for them. In his view their strength-driven mass doesn't prove you must dirty bulk.
scope: Examples he gives: Alpha Destiny, Geoffrey Verity Schofield (2022).

title: Slow is a default, not a law
statement: Some people need faster bulks or cuts; if slow cycles stop working, go a bit more aggressive. Slow is a conservative default.
scope: Lifters whose slow approach has stopped working.

title: Whole foods first, then dense extras
statement: Base the bulk on whole foods, then top up with enjoyable calorie-dense foods. Pure clean eating is hard for hardgainers; junk is fine only if very skinny. Eat more vegetables on a bulk than on a cut, and avoid foods that bloat you.

title: For mass, calories over macros
statement: For mass, total calories matter more than macros; eat carbs, which are easy to eat and not filling.

title: Appetite tricks
statement: To eat more: small, frequent meals (a huge meal kills appetite); drink calories (morning shake of ice cream, milk and nut butter); a few pieces of raw ginger before bed; sandwiches with butter, peanut butter, honey or mayo; keep a go-to high-calorie meal ready.

title: The bulk must be enjoyable
statement: A bulk must be enjoyable and sustainable (rituals, food you love); there's no need for 15 meals a day. Consistency of the surplus is what counts.

title: "Can't gain" means not eating enough
statement: Skinny people who "can't gain" aren't eating enough; there is always a cheap way to eat more, and appetite is only a signal you can disobey.

title: His rest day is his only non-surplus day
statement: On his weekly rest day he eats low or no carbs and fewer calories; it is the only day not in a surplus.
numbers: 1 rest day/week

title: Recomp is real but slower than a bulk
statement: A recomp is its own thing, not a bulk/cut hybrid: heavy training at maintenance makes the body draw on fat stores, like sculpting a statue. It is slow but real; for growth, a slow bulk beats it.
numbers: his recomp: 3 years at 210 lb (2019-2022)
scope: Lifters with both muscle and fat (BLK-55).
status: changed — 2020-2021: recomp is "the future", better than bulk/cut, planned 4-5 more years; 2022-08: recomp growth "minimal compared" to a bulk, switched to a slow lean bulk; 2024: "perma-bulker is the way to go unless you start out fat".

title: Recomp needs fat to trade
statement: A recomp needs both muscle and fat. Skinny people have nothing to recomp; the higher the body fat, the easier the trade. Ideal candidate: someone after bulk/cut cycles, happy with size, wanting to redistribute (best started when fluffier).

title: Recomp body-fat floor
statement: Don't recomp below a body-fat floor; very low body fat tanks hormones and costs muscle.
numbers: recomp 18-19% → ~12-13% (2020); not below ~14-15% (2022); hormones tank below ~8-9%
status: changed — 2020: recomp down to ~12-13%; 2022: stop at ~14-15%.

title: Commit at least a year
statement: Commit to a recomp for at least a year; two months then switching wastes time. What a week of bulking or cutting gives can take a month or two on a recomp.
numbers: ≥1 year; 2% body fat (~4-5 lb fat→muscle at his size) takes 3-7 years

title: Keep everything stable
statement: No big diet or training changes before or during a recomp. The only changes: a gradual calorie increase as muscle is gained (or you slide into a slow cut) and a small tonnage increase.

title: Judge a recomp by gym performance
statement: A working recomp shows tonnage and strength rising at the same bodyweight. Getting weaker means untracked weight loss or wrong diet, training or hormones; feeling depleted means it's failing. Measurements may drop the first year, so use the mirror (cuts, veins).

title: Monitor by weight, not body-fat tests
statement: Monitor a recomp by bodyweight every few months, not by body-fat tests every two weeks.

title: No recomp without training
statement: You can't recomp without training; sedentary maintenance gives a "reverse recomp" (lose muscle, gain fat).

title: Recomp is for sculpting, not size
statement: A recomp is slow when advanced and suits sculpting specific body parts rather than chasing overall size; long-neglected muscles grow even without a surplus.

title: Stalled recomp: widen the window
statement: When a recomp stalls, don't cut deeper: run a very slow bulk ("widen the window"), then recomp again, even if the cycle takes 5 years. When strength stalls for a long time, the recomp is over.
numbers: cycle up to 5 years

title: Maintain to recomp, not recomp to maintain
statement: A recomp that only holds mass is wasted time. A heavy lifter for whom more gaining adds only fat can recomp for a year or two.
numbers: 1-2 years

title: Miserable stalled cut → recomp
statement: If a cut has stalled and you're miserable on very low calories, switch to a recomp at maintenance.
numbers: below 1900 kcal (example)

title: Body-fat set-point window
statement: Each person has a body-fat window where they're most anabolic; push it slowly. The window shifts with age, training and hormones and may shrink to a true set point.
numbers: example window ~14-18%

title: Cut slowly
statement: Cut slowly. If you got fat, accept being fat for a long time and lose it slowly.
