numbers: 1 lb/week is too fast; 2-3 month cuts too fast unless a mini-cut or a few lb

title: No crash cuts
statement: Crash ("suicide") cuts are dangerous to health, cost strength and muscle and feel awful. Use one only if body image is hurting your mental health, knowing it's not optimal.
numbers: his crash cut: 240→205 lb (love handles stayed, strength lost)

title: Don't cut training volume on a cut
statement: Don't preemptively cut volume, reps, sets or strength work when dieting: start the cut on your current program and let failure show where to adjust. Switching to more volume at lower intensity is a "fallacy".
numbers: cutting tonnage 30% programs strength loss
check: Does the cutting phase keep the same program, volume and loads as before the cut?

title: Strength loss means the deficit is too big
statement: Strength dropping on a diet means the deficit is too large. Losing some strength from weight lost is normal, but not from the deficit itself; early in a cut glycogen isn't depleted, so big drops aren't diet-caused.

title: Muscle loss in a deficit
statement: In a deficit the body prioritises organs, so some muscle loss may be unavoidable. Advanced lifters lose muscle mainly because they get weaker and can't produce their usual stimulus; naturals avoid this through patience.

title: Building muscle in a deficit
statement: Building muscle in a deficit is possible but slower than at maintenance, which is slower than in a surplus.
scope: Naturals (fat novices are the main exception, BLK-04).
status: changed — 2020: a deficit makes new muscle "almost impossible"; 2024: possible, just slower.

title: Don't wait for a strength goal to cut
statement: An overweight lifter shouldn't wait to hit a strength goal (e.g. a 3-plate bench) before cutting; lose fat while gaining strength and hit it lighter. While dieting, the diet is the priority, not strength chasing.

title: Managing hunger on a cut
statement: Fight cut hunger with low-calorie filling foods and protein, and save calories for the evening; he says a spoon of bee pollen kills mild hunger.

title: Mini-cuts
statement: A mini-cut makes sense if injured for weeks during a bulk. Mini-cuts "never really hurt", but a young lifter shouldn't do many.
scope: Bulking lifters sidelined by injury; young lifters.

title: Fasting works only via the weekly deficit
statement: Fasting works only through the weekly deficit it creates ("volume fast" vs "frequency fast"); a weekly 24 h fast plus a surplus isn't an "ultimate recomp" strategy.
numbers: 24 h weekly fast

title: He defers on cutting advice
statement: He defers on cutting advice because he has spent almost his whole career bulking, with only one (bad) cut.
numbers: 14 of 15 years bulking
scope: Context for all cutting principles above.
status: contradicted — "bulked 14 of his 15 years" vs a 3-year maintenance at 210 lb.

title: Avoid bulk/cut cycles
statement: For non-extreme naturals, bulk/cut cycles become yo-yo dieting: the same 10-20 lb up and down forever, no progress, metabolic stress and bad habits ("bulk-cut purgatory"). In his view, cycles come from pro (enhanced) bodybuilding.
numbers: +20/-15 lb; the same 10-15 lb forever
check: Does the plan avoid repeated bulk/cut swings for a natural who is not at an extreme?

title: If you cycle, make cycles long and gentle
statement: If you do cycle, make phases as long as possible with the smallest calorie difference (even a six-month bulk is short), and avoid micro-bulk/micro-cut zigzags around a target weight.
numbers: six months still "short"

title: Naturals live at roughly 12-18%
statement: Naturals should live in a moderate body-fat range, presentable year-round; he prefers the upper half for himself.
numbers: 14-18% (2020); 12-18%, some at 10-12% or 18-20% (2020); 12-16%, up to 18% (2021); he prefers 15-18% (2022); looks/performs best at 15-16% (2023); 12-15% year-round "presentable" (2024); 10-12% advised for an "otter mode" look (2023)
check: Does the plan keep body fat roughly within 12-18% year-round?

title: Year-round shredded is a trap
statement: Year-round shredded leanness keeps you catabolic, creates your own "natural limit" and small lifters, and harms hormones. Naturals should be very lean only for a few weeks before a show; in his view natural shows should judge at 13-14%.
numbers: 13-14% for natural shows (his proposal)

title: Limits of natural leanness
statement: Natural competitors need about 10%; much lower costs so much mass you may not look like you lift. 10% is reachable while staying big only if done slowly.
numbers: ~10% for competitors; below ~8% big mass loss; 5% impossible without looking skeletal
scope: Natural competitors and very lean dieters.

title: Shredded means hungry, weak and small
statement: Being shredded means hungry, unfocused, weaker and smaller. He never wants it and would cut only to see his body without fluff, or when he has little gym time.

title: Big naturals spent years in a surplus
statement: Every natural who reached 180-200+ lb spent years in a sizable (not necessarily dirty) surplus, and any big, strong natural carries some fat at some point. An aesthetic physique still starts lean.

title: More muscle carries fat better
statement: More muscle lets you carry more fat and still look lean; muscle spreads fat and veins show. Some subcutaneous/intramuscular fat and water make naturals look fuller and bigger.

title: Abs: built in the gym, revealed by diet
statement: Train abs on a bulk so they show sooner; natural abs can stay visible year-round at moderate body fat. Don't use the six-pack as a cutting gauge, since fat distribution varies.
numbers: he has abs at 15-17%; abs possible at 20%

title: "Ab anxiety" keeps lifters small
statement: "Ab anxiety" or small guy syndrome means clinging to a skinny six-pack and refusing to gain weight. Adding weight raises total fat but not necessarily body-fat %.

title: Maingaining is a rebranded lean bulk
section: Maingaining, seasons and his current plan
statement: "Maingaining" is lean bulking rebranded, and recomp isn't "gaining" because bodyweight stays the same. In his view marketing it to skinny beginners (often by enhanced people) leaves them recomping and never growing; say "lean bulk" or "recomp" instead.
numbers: 2024: maingaining at 11-12% "perfectly doable"
status: contradicted — 2021-2023 rejects the term; 2024 calls maingaining at 11-12% "perfectly doable".

title: Bulk in winter, maintain in summer
section: Maingaining, seasons and his current plan
statement: Bulk slowly through winter and spring, and maintain or recomp in summer when appetite is low; cut only if competing. Alternating bulk and maintenance phases is "smart".
status: changed — replaces both his 2020 "no cycles" stance and his 2023 continuous-bulk plan.

title: His status in early 2025
section: Maingaining, seasons and his current plan
statement: At 220 lb and higher body fat he was recomping while still progressing, planning to resume the bulk.

title: No spot reduction
statement: Fat comes off in an order you can't control (core and face first, legs and lower back later; already-lean areas don't lose more). Creams and pills are marketing, and local high-rep work is trivial next to diet. Love handles come off only by slowly using fat stores.
numbers: local work vs diet ~1 vs 100

title: Yo-yo dieting scrambles fat distribution
statement: His repeated bulk/cut swings made his fat distribution go haywire with new deposits, and dirty-bulk fat is stubborn.
numbers: his 210→240 lb dirty bulk, then crash and slow cuts

title: Lungs must never end a set first
statement: Never end a squat or deadlift set out of breath with reps left in the muscles. Getting winded after one rep, on curls or after a bench set means poor conditioning; fix it with conditioning work or a slower tempo.
numbers: he squats 8 reps to failure and deadlifts 5 heavy without breathing hard
scope: All lifters, especially on lower-body compounds.
check: Can the lifter finish hard squat and deadlift sets limited by muscle rather than breath?

title: Poor conditioning costs size
statement: Poor conditioning means unfinished sets, lost tonnage and ultimately lost size. You can't build high lower-body tonnage without stamina; many people fail intermediate programs this way.
numbers: gassing after four reps means never getting big

title: Balance heart and muscle endurance
statement: Balance cardiovascular and muscular endurance. Extra conditioning won't hinder growth, but being out of breath while lifting means cardio is limiting the muscle work, so fix cardio or methods.

title: Puking is low work capacity
statement: Vomiting in training signals low work capacity, not a good session; improve conditioning.
numbers: if 10 squats make you vomit

title: More than 5 reps is not "cardio"
statement: People who call anything over 5 reps "cardio" lack work capacity, and avoiding reps reinforces it. High reps for legs are a requirement.
numbers: >5 reps

title: Lifting alone rarely taxes the heart
statement: Lifting isn't metabolically demanding (you rest as long as you like), so you must actively seek breathlessness. Mostly-upper-body machine training barely taxes the heart; older machine-only lifters should add lower-body work.
scope: All lifters; machine-only and older lifters.

title: Fitness is separate from looking big
statement: Being big, lean or vascular doesn't mean fit, and stamina and cardiovascular health are separate qualities. You should be able to talk for 40 minutes without breathlessness and climb stairs without getting winded.
numbers: talk 40 min without breathlessness

title: Conditioning is easy to keep
statement: Once built, cardiovascular endurance is easy to maintain; it recovers fast between sessions and matters mainly within the workout.

title: Cardio done right helps gains
statement: Cardio doesn't kill gains or testosterone. Good cardio boosts gains through more volume, better pumps and faster recovery.
numbers: biking 30 min each way to the gym didn't hurt his squat/deadlift; low-intensity running 2x/week for 20-30 min doesn't hurt
status: changed — 2020: cardio kills gains indirectly via calories; 2024: good cardio boosts gains.

title: Cardio's real cost is calories
statement: Cardio doesn't cannibalise muscle but uses calories meant for recovery, so how much you can do depends on intake. Skinny men prioritising muscle should avoid cardio-focused activity; long slow distance limits growth only through calorie shortfall.

title: Cardio isn't needed for leanness
statement: Cardio isn't needed to be lean or to recomp; it burns calories but can raise appetite, so weigh the trade. With his low appetite he never used cardio to burn calories.
status: contradicted — elsewhere he says losing weight "just means stop overeating and do more cardio" and that leanness depends on cardio and calories; his 2023+ advocacy also supersedes the 2020 stance.

title: Count cardio in your recovery budget
statement: Cardio also loads joints and muscles, so factor it into frequency and recovery. Weighted cardio has a recovery cost but is time-efficient and synergistic with lifting.
numbers: 2 h/day swimming tires shoulders, back and legs

title: Heavy legs can hurt endurance
statement: Low-intensity cardio barely touches a lifter's recovery, but heavy leg training can hurt endurance, so fighters must program legs carefully.

title: 5-15 hard minutes after lifting
statement: Do a short block of high-intensity cardio after each session (it replaces pump finishers), plus low-intensity walking, hiking or swimming.
numbers: 5-15 min after every session (2023-11); 10-15 min HIIT + low-intensity hikes/swims (2024-11); his own ~10 min
status: changed — 2020-2021: no conventional cardio for 3 years, all conditioning through weights, cardio "not necessary"; from 2023-11: cardio is "S tier" and "makes you a better bodybuilder".
check: Does the program include roughly 5-15 min of hard cardio after lifting (or on separate days)?

title: Never cardio before lifting
statement: Never do cardio before lifting; it lowers lifting intensity. Do it after, on another day or at another time, and warm up by ramping the lift (wear layers), not with cardio.
check: Is cardio placed after lifting or in a separate session, never before?

title: On a cut, cardio in a separate session
statement: On a cut, do cardio separately (e.g. in the morning) because energy is too low to pair it with lifting; on a bulk, right around the lifting session is fine.

title: Program sprints like deadlifts
statement: Treat sprints like deadlifts: intense, well warmed up, infrequent and far from heavy squat/deadlift days. Hamstring strain risk means warming up and doing weighted stretches.
numbers: 1-2x/week ("already a lot")

title: Cardio on leg days
statement: Hard cardio on top of leg training now counts as a plus for recovery and conditioning.
numbers: 2020: sprints/longer cardio 2-3x/week on days off, after leg day before a push day, or on light days
status: changed — 2022: avoid intense leg cardio on leg days; 2024-12: hard cardio on top of leg training boosts recovery and conditioning.

title: His 2024 cardio routine
statement: Hard cardio twice a week (a threshold mile on a self-powered treadmill, or a stair stepper on tiptoes with a heavy backpack) plus outdoor weighted carries on his days off.
numbers: 2x/week; 1 mile (10 min/mile, aiming for 7) or 10 min stepper with an 80 lb pack; 20-30 min carries on his 2 days off

title: Joggers need several runs a week
statement: Joggers typically need several runs a week to benefit.
numbers: 3-4 runs/week

title: Giant sets are a bodybuilder's GPP
statement: Supersets and giant sets of non-interfering movements, done non-stop, tax the heart without separate cardio or hurting strength, and conditioning rises with working weights. Giant sets are "passive cardio with almost no cost" as long as they don't become a circuit.
numbers: giant sets rated B tier (2024)
check: Does the program use supersets or giant sets that keep the heart rate up?

title: Giant-set examples
statement: Examples: a lower-body move → weighted carry → ab move; start with a squat then easy exercises; end upper days with push-ups + lateral raises + face pulls until quality drops; pull-ups + dips for novices. If a pull-up/face-pull superset kills performance, your conditioning is poor.
numbers: 10 reps of the lower-body move
scope: Bodybuilders; novices for pull-up + dip pairing.

title: Lower-body lifts build work capacity best
statement: Heavy high-rep squats and deadlifts are "compressed HIIT". High-rep lower-body work plus giant sets give enough moderate conditioning; if you skip legs, add supersets to compensate.

title: Conditioning is specific
statement: High-rep squats carry over to breathing under heavy squats better than sprints. Find your most cardio-taxing lift and make it easier over time (variations, shorter rests, giant sets). Strongmen use farmer's walks or hikes; powerlifters use squats or rack/isometric pulls.

title: Don't rely on weights alone
statement: He doesn't recommend doing cardio only through weight training; add an activity you like, such as swimming or hiking.
status: contradicted — in the same era he did all his cardio with weights and said high-rep work and giant sets "already provide enough" conditioning.

title: AMRAP compound sets: use sparingly
statement: Very high-rep AMRAP compound sets are limited by heart and lungs and hard on joints; use them sparingly. A few sets of paused squats beat a long treadmill session for leg size and strength.
numbers: 30-40 rep squats = C tier; 3 sets of paused squats > 30 min treadmill

title: GPP menu for lifters
statement: Good GPP for lifters: pull-ups, push-ups, ab work, plate carries, traps, bodyweight hyperextensions, sandbag carries/tosses, sled drags. Nothing that fries you for the next session.

title: Walk daily; lifting isn't enough activity
statement: Lifting alone isn't enough activity: walk daily, walk instead of riding, carry groceries. Sitting still breeds muscle and tendon pain, and desk workers need more cardio than blue-collar workers.
numbers: walk 40-50 min/day

title: 10k steps: fine, but slow
statement: 10k steps gets people walking, but in his view its promoters forget that desk workers lack the time. Walking is low in impact and fatigue but time-costly.
numbers: 10,000-20,000 steps; walking = B tier

title: Minimal-effort cardio does nothing
statement: Minimal-effort "cardio" (slow pedalling while gaming, a very slow treadmill walk, under-desk steppers) does essentially nothing.
numbers: 1 mph treadmill for 30 min

title: Any hard method works; he prefers HIIT
statement: Any method works if your heart rate is up and breath short. It's boring but necessary, so link it to something you practise. His preference is HIIT (sprints, beep tests, giant sets): time-saving and fun.

title: Best picks: fartlek, StairMaster, rucking
statement: His top conditioning tools for bodybuilders are fartlek, the StairMaster, heavy rucking, the rowing machine, crawling, sandbags and rebounding.
numbers: fartlek: jog ~1 min (1-2 min) / sprint 5-10 s, repeat to exhaustion; StairMaster ≤20 min high pace or 50% bodyweight backpack 10 min; rucking 15-30 min; rebounding 15-50 min/day

title: Running ranks low for bodybuilders
statement: Running is hard on the lower back, shins and knees and interferes with leg training; long-distance running requires losing muscle and costs too much time and energy. Sprints and fartlek stay highly rated.
numbers: running C tier, long distance D tier (2024)
status: changed — 2020: uphill running "unmatched" for cardio; 2024: running C tier, long-distance D tier.

title: Treadmills weak; manual ones the exception
statement: The motorised treadmill is weak because it does part of the work; self-powered treadmills are much harder because you create the momentum. Outdoors, run on dirt, grass or sand, never pavement or stone (knees).
numbers: treadmill D tier (2024)
status: contradicted — he says the best cardio is outdoors on soft ground (2020) yet runs on a self-powered treadmill (2024); the manual treadmill is his stated exception.

title: Steppers and jump rope
statement: The StairMaster is now his best cardio machine; jump rope is poor for bodybuilders (high coordination cost, low tax once learned).
status: changed — 2020: prefer stepper or jump rope over treadmill; 2021: never steppers; 2024: StairMaster S tier, jump rope poor.

title: Swimming: noble, not a physique shortcut
statement: Swimming is relaxing and builds shoulders, but it is not a physique shortcut: it takes far more time than lifting for the same stimulus and builds a disproportionate physique. It beats running for slimming while building muscle.
numbers: 5-10x the time of an OHP stimulus

title: Cardio machines don't build muscle
statement: Rowing machines and air bikes don't build legs or back ("chicken/Peewee tier" as muscle builders), even though the rower is top-tier cardio. Running does nothing for his muscles and can't replace lifting during a break; uphill running is tough on hamstrings and glutes.

title: Athletes: the sport covers conditioning
statement: An athlete's sport already covers conditioning, so lifting should target the fibre damage the sport leaves. You can do plenty of health cardio, but you can't be both a competitive endurance athlete and a high-level bodybuilder.

title: Combat conditioning in short intense pockets
statement: Fighters should condition with 30-40 min sessions of intense pockets with rest, not long runs. An optional conditioning day is safer than a third lifting day. Each day combines cardio, thoracic extension, abs, posterior chain and carries or pulls.
numbers: conditioning day 35-40 min; boxing 3-5 dashes of 3 min at max sustainable pace (progress by distance); MMA 5-min dashes or sled drags; strikers 10x10 m sprints; grapplers rope climb 3x5 m or sled pull 15 m, plus pull-ups and dead hangs

title: Rugby and cycling conditioning
statement: For rugby, fartlek "Indian runs"; for a cycling-focused day, short dashes paired with leg and ab work.
numbers: rugby: jog ~60 s, sprint 5 s; cycling Day C: 3x500 m dashes + single-leg calf raises AMRAP, shiko 5x10-25 + bicycle crunches AMRAP

title: Keeping leg size as an athlete
statement: To maintain leg size as an athlete, train legs once a week with a little strength work, or squat/deadlift every 15 days and do cardio otherwise.
numbers: 1x/week, or every 15 days

title: Anything works, so choose for the long term
statement: Almost any program works for novices. That should free them to pick what sets up the rest of their career, not justify random programs, and novice results prove nothing about a program, coach or channel.
scope: novices; it becomes "a game of inches" only later
check: Is the novice phase judged by skill, habits and base built rather than by how fast the numbers rise?

title: Build a base and habits, not performance
statement: Novice status is short but you are an intermediate or advanced lifter for life, so use the novice period to build a base, prevent injuries and form habits rather than to chase numbers.
numbers: noob gains may be only 3-4% of your lifting time

title: Don't rush out of the novice phase
statement: Treat the novice phase like childhood and prolong it. The noob-gain "poison" and the "noob" stigma make people rush.
numbers: 1-2 years as a novice "doesn't matter" over a 20-year career; 6-12 months costs nothing; strength novice status can last up to 2 years
status: changed — see BEG-10 (2020-04 "no more than 4-6 months" → 2020-11/2021 prolong to 1-2 years → 2024 done within a year for many)

title: Noob gains are a quantity, not a window
statement: Noob gains are an amount of development, not a time window that closes. A bad program wastes time but not potential.
numbers: they last ~6 months to ~2 years; 6-8 months on machines is followed by fast growth after switching to compounds
scope: anyone untrained without a hormonal deficiency

title: Novices need only the bare minimum
statement: Novices are built to grow from very little, so do the bare minimum and don't add volume you don't need. "Optimal" means adding complexity only once the simpler thing stops working.
scope: novices; minimalism would hurt an advanced lifter like him

title: Novice is about experience, not strength numbers
statement: Novice status depends on experience, not strength. Strength standards are worthless for classifying lifters.
numbers: he dislikes the 225/315/405 x5 rule, though any healthy male should eventually reach it; some bench 225 lb after two weeks, others take two years; he knew a near-4-plate bencher (5-plate squat, 6-plate deadlift) who was "still a novice"

title: Novice ends when you can write your program
statement: You stop being a novice when you want to, and can, write your own program.

title: What makes an intermediate
statement: An intermediate can overload by means other than adding weight and knows what they want and where their weak points are. Intermediates struggle because volume becomes a new overload variable.

title: Training stage is per body part
statement: Training stages apply per body part: a 600 lb deadlifter can be a novice at arm training.
numbers: 600 lb deadlift example

title: How long the novice phase lasts
statement: His estimate of the novice phase's length has moved around. His latest view is that many are done within a year, but bad programming and program hopping stretch it to years.
numbers: 2020-04: no more than 4-6 months; 2021: ~6 months (stretch to a year), 1.5-2 years is fine; 2024: within a year for many, 3-4 years with program hopping and bad programs; repeat novices who quit and restart can stay novices for 5 years
status: changed — 2020-04 "4-6 months max" → 2020-11/2021 prolong to 1-2 years → 2024 within a year for many

title: Three full-body days a week by default
statement: The novice default is 3 full-body days a week, 48 h apart (Mon/Wed/Fri); 2-3 days works.
numbers: 4 days is the high end; 5-6 days is "very hard to justify"; 2024: "tremendous results" on 2-3 days of ~1 h; floating rest days are for advanced lifters
status: contradicted — elsewhere he prefers "full body every day" with one heavy compound per day and says novices can recover from daily calisthenics, while also saying full body needs programming knowledge novices lack
check: Does the novice train 2-3 (at most 4) full-body days a week?

title: Build frequency before sets, sets before weight
statement: Of volume, intensity and frequency, complete beginners should first build frequency (2x/week → 3x), then add sets rather than weight.
numbers: 2x/week → 3x/week

title: Novice frequency mainly prevents injury
statement: For novices, frequency matters more for injury prevention than for hypertrophy.

title: Sessions of about 45-60 minutes
statement: Novice sessions should last about 45-60 min and lengthen as you advance; 1.5-2 h sessions are junk volume for a novice.
numbers: 2020: ≤60 min, 45-60 min; 2020-12/2021-01: 40 min, adding ~10 min "here and there"; 2021: 25 min 3x/week for complete beginners; 2022: 45-60 min; 2024: ~1 h
check: Do novice sessions last about an hour or less?

title: Novices lack work capacity, not recovery
statement: Novices don't recover faster than advanced lifters. They lack work capacity and mental stamina, can't exert themselves as hard, and burn out mentally before physically.
scope: novices; the gym itself is mentally taxing for them

title: Small additions can wreck a novice
statement: A few extra sets can wreck a novice for a week; some even get sick.
numbers: 2-3 extra sets, or 2 extra sets of 10, can wreck them for a week

title: As much as possible from few hard sets
statement: Get as much as possible from as few hard sets as possible and stay shy of maximum recoverable volume. Overshooting sets is for experienced lifters.
numbers: two hard sets can grow a novice muscle; 18-20 weekly sets is "brainwashed" bodybuilding-channel thinking
check: Does the novice program use few hard sets per muscle, well under 18-20 weekly sets?

title: Start around 3 sets per muscle per week
statement: A novice muscle starts at about 3 sets a week, rising to 4-6 only when needed.
numbers: ~3 sets/week, then 4-5-6; 3 curl sets/week is enough to start isolation; 2022 shoulder example: OHP 8-12 plus lateral raise 10-12, 3-4 sets each, once a week (6-8 sets) is "all a novice needs"

title: About 12 sets a day in bi-sets
statement: A novice day is 1-2 bi-sets of 3 sets. Start with bi-sets before tri-sets and avoid heavy giant sets, which are too hard on a beginner's cardiovascular system.
numbers: ~12 total sets per day; giant sets fine only for abs, neck, calves, forearms and push-ups

title: Accessories at 3 x 8-12
statement: Three sets of 8-12 are enough for novice accessories.

title: No deloads for novices
statement: A novice program that needs a deload is too much; novices must learn to manage fatigue instead.
check: Does the novice program run without planned deloads?

title: But don't train too easy
statement: Novices must experience high intensity; the "number one beginner mistake is training too easy".
numbers: 2024: pick 4-5 movements per day, take them to failure, overload, add complexity later
status: contradicted — elsewhere he says to lower intensity and volume at first and never struggle

title: Novices need written, rigid structure
statement: Novices need a written, fixed structure; flexibility is earned. They can't be trusted with lift rotations or optional exercises, and should start on an established program because they lack the data to program for themselves.
scope: novices; training by template or instinct comes later

title: Leave some room for choice and mistakes
statement: Within that structure, leave some room for choice (rep ranges rather than fixed numbers, a small choice of lifts) and for first mistakes, which can't be catastrophic. His novice program is "deliberately open-handed".

title: Full body is the best novice split
statement: Full body is the best novice split; a novice wanting 3 days is better served by full body than by half a PPL. No gentleman splits.
numbers: 2022: a 3-day push/pull/legs-arms is also "enough"

title: His template: supersets, few compounds, rest isolation
statement: His novice template is 3 full-body days with supersets throughout (they build work capacity), 2-3 compounds per day and the rest isolation.
numbers: 2-3 compounds/day; 2021 alternative: one heavy compound per day with the rest hit lightly

title: Don't stack heavy compounds in one day
statement: Don't pile several heavy compounds into one day (squat + row + deadlift + bench); novices "overdo compounds".
numbers: 5x8 squat then 3x8 deadlift would wreck a novice; cut squats to 3-4 sets

title: Isolation from day one
statement: "Compounds cover small muscles" is false. Compounds build the centre line, while arms and delts need isolation; skipping it leaves big quads and chest with "toothpick arms" after 2 years.
status: contradicted — once said he "would never prescribe that much isolation to a novice"
check: Does the novice program include isolation work (at least arms and delts) from the start?

title: No dedicated arm day for novices
statement: A novice arm day is a waste; add one curl and one triceps movement to existing days and add forearms later.

title: Catch weak points and small muscles early
statement: His current view is that "just grow everything" is bad advice: dormant weak points cost years of catch-up, so train small parts, including forearm isolation, from day one.
status: changed — 2020: calves, neck, traps and rear delts can wait until you have a solid physique; 2023: forearm isolation optional (gripping during pulls does most early work); 2024: forearms from day one, catch weak points early

title: Introduce every movement pattern
statement: A good novice program introduces every movement pattern and builds a wide base: slower progress but a higher ceiling. The squat, bench and deadlift alone don't cover every pattern.
status: changed — 2020: a wide base of all patterns (one video: focus on squat, bench, deadlift before hypertrophy work); 2023: a real base is push-up and pull-up proficiency and there is "no reason to waste years building a 'base'"

title: Don't force a style on novices
statement: Novice programs shouldn't force a style (powerlifting, rings). Start with a broad strength-and-size goal and specialise later, since most people only discover what they want after lifting a while.
numbers: ~95% of lifters are beginners

title: Powerlifting novice programs work only because anything works
statement: Starting Strength, StrongLifts, GreySkull and 5x5/3x5 are powerlifting programs that lack isolation and catapult novices into weights they shouldn't handle. They work only because anything works for novices.
numbers: 10x10 breaks novices
scope: novices whose goal is hypertrophy; 2024: StrongLifts is "garbage for hypertrophy", use free natural-bodybuilding programs instead
check: Does a hypertrophy-focused novice avoid a pure powerlifting program (Starting Strength, StrongLifts, 5x5)?

title: Run the program until it stops working
statement: Run a novice program until it stops working, not for a fixed 4, 8 or 12 weeks, and don't program-hop. A fixed timeline is a red flag.
numbers: most novice programs are too short: spend about double the usual time
check: Is the novice program run until progress stalls rather than for a fixed number of weeks?

title: Template users: 6-12 months per template
statement: If you train from templates, run one for 6-12 months before alternating with a second.
numbers: 6-12 months

title: Monotony is fine; fancy methods come later
statement: Repeat the basics with close variations. Fancy lifts, drop sets and lift rotations come later; master variations before rotating them.
numbers: no complex program at 6 months
status: contradicted — elsewhere beginners should explore, "tossed into the sea"

title: Close variations are allowed
statement: Variations close in specificity are fine, so novices needn't repeat an identical lift 3x/week; they help reach deeper ranges.
numbers: people told to squat 3x5 3x/week quit after ~2 months
status: contradicted — elsewhere "no variations for novices", with the paused squat as the only exception (BEG-55)

title: Keep it fun and keep them hungry
statement: Keep novice training fun and give "just enough to keep them hungry". Endless squat, bench and deadlift makes novices quit.

title: His own beginner program ladder
statement: His ladder runs from a novice/"beginner" version to Greek Statue / Adam / Baki / Tokita Ohma, then intermediate programs. After graduating, he points to the full-body hypertrophy program in his "natural apogee" playlist.
numbers: beginner version = his novice program with 2 sets per exercise and no variations; harder programs need ≥2 years on a novice program

title: Start light and accumulate quality reps
statement: Start light, even with the empty bar, and accumulate quality reps without struggling or compromising the next session. Repeat a hard weight before adding more; no PR is worth an injury.

title: Fixed schemes first, evolving ranges on accessories
statement: Fixed schemes (5x5, 3x5) are fine at first; use evolving ranges on accessories, then spread them. If every lift uses evolving ranges, tonnage collapses when all hit their low point at once.
numbers: evolving ranges 6-10, 8-12; turning a 3x3 into a 3x3-5 takes ~2 weeks to learn
status: contradicted — "evolving ranges are not suitable for beginners" vs "teach them early so they become second nature"

title: Use rep ranges where form stays clean
statement: Novices should use higher reps in a range where form stays clean; back work that loads the lower back and hamstrings needs at least 6-10 reps.
numbers: ≥6-10 reps; 3x6 rows get butchered; 4x8 squats are risky because of grinding and ugly reps

title: Early bar progress is mostly neural
statement: Early strength gains are mostly neural and technical, not muscle.
numbers: 5-10 lb per session for a long time; +10 lb/week is mostly neural; 60 → 200 lb squat in year one is "a given"; adding 200 lb in 6 months is pointless

title: Skill first; strength never exceeds skill
statement: Strength should rise but never outrun skill; real training starts once you can perform the big lifts.

title: Teach other overload methods early
statement: Teach novices to overload by manipulating reps, sets and volume, not just load.

title: New lifts: start easy, then go to failure
statement: For unpracticed lifts or rep ranges, start easy without failure, then push to failure.
scope: anyone learning a lift or rep range

title: Free weights and bodyweight before machines
statement: Novices should learn on free weights and bodyweight; machines, cables and the Smith are for advanced lifters. Novices on machines "stay small for years", and a machine-and-cable novice program is a bad sign.
scope: novices; exception from 2024: the Smith vertical press, which handles stabilisation
status: changed — 2020-2023: the Smith is useless or harmful for beginners (never learn squat or bench on it); 2024: novices should lean on the Smith vertical press
check: Does the novice learn the main lifts with free weights or bodyweight rather than machines or the Smith?

title: Calisthenics is an ideal entry point
statement: Calisthenics is an ideal entry and perhaps the best base for bodybuilding: learn to move your body through space without needing a gym, rep ranges or plate math.
numbers: 2023: a "real base" is push-up and pull-up proficiency; his novice program has more push-ups than bench

title: Pull-ups over pulldowns; vertical over horizontal
statement: For novices, vertical pulls matter more than horizontal pulls and pull-ups beat pulldowns, which are accessories. Vertical pulls decompress the shoulders and spine when benching often.
numbers: anyone who can do 3+ pull-ups should do them

title: Pull-up progression for novices
statement: Use negatives if you can't do a pull-up, then many low-rep sets or AMRAP sets, and stay at bodyweight until a clean 15. No weighted chins for novices.
numbers: many sets of 2-3 (novice max ~5); 3 sets AMRAP; negatives 3 x 5-8 (can go first in the session, straps for grip); 15 clean reps before adding weight; 1-2 grips (pronated plus chin-up)

title: No barbell or Pendlay rows for novices
statement: Novices can't pull from the floor well yet, so use cable or dumbbell rows; cable rows teach the lower back before it must bridge a row. Most intermediates should skip barbell rows too.

title: A full-ROM floor pull, at low volume
statement: A full-ROM pull from the floor is mandatory for novices, but deadlift volume stays low. Any full hip hinge counts (conventional, sumo, trap bar, Atlas stones).
numbers: 1x5 is "excellent"; 1x5, 3x3 or 3x5 is enough; 3-4 x 6-10 or 4 x 6-12 is too much; once a week keeps novices coming back for PRs
status: contradicted — one video says novices should squat and deadlift several times a week (with deloads), while his own routine deliberately deadlifts once a week
check: Does the novice pull a full-ROM hip hinge from the floor about once a week at low volume (about 1x5 to 3x5)?

title: Deadlift entry points and grip
statement: Ways in: trap bar (high → low handles → conventional), rack pulls to learn the hinge, deficits to teach leg drive, dumbbell deadlifts. No Jefferson or snatch-grip deadlifts for novices; grip double overhand with straps (see EQP-07).
numbers: no mixed grip at least until a 300 lb deadlift

title: Squat free; no box; parallel is enough
statement: Novices should squat free and unsupported, to parallel. A box fixes depth instead of mobility and box squatters can't reach parallel later, so squat higher and deepen over months; mobility is innate, just unpracticed.

title: Paused back squat is the one variation
statement: The paused back squat is the one novice variation. No front squats, which need thoracic mobility and front-rack time, unless the lifter loves them.
numbers: squat 2x/week (once regular, once paused); 1-3 heavy sets of 4-8 plus 3 back-off sets

title: Goblet squats first, heel-elevated later
statement: Learn the normal barbell squat before heel-elevated squats. Goblet squats are a good start (B tier); bodyweight squats are C tier.
numbers: goblet squats useful until ~120-130 lb dumbbells

title: Several horizontal presses a week
statement: Novices need several horizontal presses a week; prefer paused and close-grip bench to floor press. Too much overhead plus incline pressing overloads the shoulders, and range you can't control should be trained with an easier pressing mode.
numbers: 2020 weekly budget: 2 knee flexions, 2 hip hinges, 2 horizontal presses, plus a curl, a triceps movement and a hyperextension

title: Incline or knee push-ups, not wall push-ups
statement: Beginners who can't do push-ups should use incline or knee push-ups, not wall push-ups.
numbers: 10 clean push-ups is a benchmark

title: Strict standing dumbbell curls first
statement: Start with strict standing dumbbell curls; cheat curls only later and very light. No heavy partials, and never curl daily.

title: Novice shoulders: face pulls; lateral raises added later
statement: Face pulls are great and cheap for novices. In 2020 he said side raises were unnecessary (OHP plus face pulls was enough); by 2022 his novice example includes lateral raises.
numbers: 2022: OHP 8-12 plus lateral raise 10-12, 3-4 sets each, once a week
status: changed — 2020 no side raises → 2022 lateral raises in his novice shoulder example

title: Back hyperextensions for novices
statement: Back hyperextensions teach novices to use their legs and build the lower back; they waste tonnage for advanced lifters.
numbers: 3-4 x 12 (4x15 in his 2020 modified Fierce 5)

title: Abs: bracing first, then stretch work
statement: Beginners should start abs with bracing only, then add stretch exercises; pullovers once a week, building range gradually.
numbers: bracing only ~3 months; pullovers 1x/week, 3 sets

title: Learn by modifying the program you run
statement: Learn to program by modifying the novice program you run, then use it as a skeleton: copy its rep ranges, match its tonnage, stay minimalist. The first draft will look terrible; if the base program is very bad, start from scratch.
numbers: run it 3-6 months with fixes; drafting your own while on it may take a year
status: changed — 2020: novices shouldn't write programs (theirs are almost always bad); 2021: draft your own while running the novice program; 2024: start on an established program, then write your own and have a coach review it (a refinement, not a flip)

title: First self-written programs are too greedy
statement: First self-written programs almost always have too many exercises, sets, reps and too much frequency, and the jump from novice to intermediate volume crashes people. A bridge program, or a novice program that already ramps volume, helps ("novices are not made of sugar").
numbers: sessions jump from 45 to 90 min

title: Only following programs keeps you a novice
statement: Novices who only follow programs never learn to program, so they plateau, quit and restart as novices. His novice program exists to launch people into self-programming.

title: Everyone should eventually write their own
statement: Everyone should eventually write their own programs; from 2024 he adds having an experienced coach review them.

title: Experiment early, but don't wing it
statement: Beginners should experiment, not optimise, to build instinct, but without winging it too much.

title: Novices don't need optimisation or coaching
statement: Optimising is "the surest way for a novice to stay a novice". Knowledge is a small part of the value and application the rest, so eat more and run a free program instead of paying a coach, and spend less time on fitness YouTube.
numbers: ~90% of his audience are novices; knowledge ~10% of value, application ~90%

title: "Optimal" is relative: start with what you can
statement: For a very weak beginner, 5 minutes of knee push-ups is optimal. Doing something beats waiting for the perfect workout; avoid paralysis by analysis, since anything B-S tier works.
numbers: 5 minutes of knee push-ups; 30 push-ups beat nothing

title: About 90% of lifters quit, mostly as novices
statement: Most people who start lifting quit, mostly in the novice phase.
numbers: 90% (2020, 2021, 2022); 95% during the novice-to-intermediate move (2020, "made up"); 80-90% as novices (2023)

title: "Novice syndrome": overdoing it is the main crash cause
statement: Overdoing it, not lack of potential, is the top reason novices crash, and it is mostly mental. Burnout is over-stimulation (e.g. 2 h sessions), not overtraining; a program that stops you training for a full week is bad for you.
numbers: a year mildly intense beats six months super intense
check: Is the novice workload modest enough that it never forces a full week off training?

title: Newbie gains spoil people
statement: Fast early gratification and easy linear progression spoil lifters, who crash when progress slows; many quit on reaching "intermediate" expecting magic.

title: Adherence is the number one principle
statement: Adherence is the first program principle: remove barriers (meal prep, any structured program, planned transport) and use "floaters". Lower volume and intensity at first so the habit lasts.
numbers: for many, travel time equals training time

title: Avoid the "Arnold effect"; set modest goals
statement: Avoid the "Arnold effect" (credited to Zack Telander) and draconian pro lifestyles; set modest, real goals.
numbers: e.g. 20 push-ups; jumping from junk food to chicken and broccoli lasts two weeks

title: Many novice programs are filters
statement: Many novice programs are filters that only outliers survive; injured novices indict popular programs. Most novices fail to reach intermediate because of injuries, plateaus and boredom.

title: Imperfect form is OK at tiny loads
statement: Imperfect form is acceptable for novices because loads are tiny, as long as they stay in a safe rep range. Still master the objective form rules, warm up with as many sets as needed, and never jump straight to heavy weight.
numbers: 3-5 warm-up sets

title: Novices miss early injury signals
statement: Novices follow programs to the letter and miss pain that signals an injury in the making.

title: Beginner wrist pain often comes from pull-ups
statement: Wrist pain in beginners mostly comes from pull-ups done by gripping hard and pulling with the wrists.

title: Deadlifts tax beginners as much as advanced lifters
statement: Relative to their weaker muscles and nervous system, deadlifts are as taxing for beginners as for advanced lifters.

title: Novices should just eat more
statement: Novices should eat more and gain weight; diet barely matters unless they are very skinny or very fat. No perfect macros or supplements needed, though he still recommends whole foods.

title: Skinny novices bulk; average novices maingain
statement: Skinny novices should bulk rather than recomp; average novices can maingain from day one; for skinny-fat novices the approach hardly matters. Avoid extreme bulk/cut cycles and dirty bulks.
numbers: tiny surplus or maintenance

title: Strength programs push teens to bulk for leverage
statement: Strength-centric novice programs push teenagers to bulk for leverage instead of for muscle.

title: Kids can start conservatively around 10
statement: Children can start conservative training around 10 (goblet squats, pull-ups, push-ups), heavy squats and deadlifts at 15-16. He rejects "don't lift before puberty ends"; teens should prioritise form, work capacity and enjoyment over muscle.
numbers: ~10: conservative work; 15-16: heavy squat/deadlift; his routines are for 16+; 14-17: form and enjoyment first

title: Teen training plan
statement: Teens: no ego lifting, moderate-to-high rep ranges with some low-rep work, and every body part trained semi-frequently. A 14-year-old boxer should do 2-3 full-body sessions, not 4 days.
numbers: 6-10, 8-12, 10-15 reps with some 5s; starting at 15 beats 20; by 18-19 you will have a huge advantage

title: It's never too late to start
statement: It's never too late to start; using past inaction as an excuse is a "reverse sunk-cost fallacy". Elderly, disabled and amputee people benefit (e.g. with unilateral work).
numbers: examples: 23, even 80

title: Realistic timelines take years
statement: Going from skinny to big takes years, not months; being small at 17-20 is normal.
numbers: 6-12 months transforms almost anyone; looking like you lift took him 3-4 years; 5 years makes you a different person

title: Combat athletes and laborers: low lifting frequency
statement: Combat athletes and manual workers should lift 2-3 compound-focused sessions a week plus grip, core, neck and bridging work. No Bulgarian-style training.
numbers: jiu-jitsu 5x/week → 2-3 lifting sessions; a wrestler cuts to 2 lifting days with less volume; a laborer doing judo trains 2x/week, 45 min, 2 compounds + 3 isolations

title: Obese beginners: balanced resistance training
statement: A heavily overweight beginner should avoid calisthenics (joints) and powerlifting (a slippery slope to staying fat) and use a balanced resistance program. Bodyweight templates suit light people and frustrate heavy ones.
numbers: example: 120 kg 20-year-old

title: Returning after a long break
statement: After a long break, return with short, low-volume sessions of favourite exercises and let muscle memory work. No hard programs (e.g. his Guts program) for returners.
numbers: 2 x 45 min/week, ~2 sets; after 6 months off, 1-2 submaximal sets

title: Women: same physiology, different goals
statement: Women respond like men physiologically but have different goals; "just train like men" is lazy. They need muscle for health and should avoid doing too much and burning out. A reluctant partner can start with bodyweight work at home or light bar and dumbbell work framed as time together.
numbers: examples: bar box squats, 5 lb dumbbell presses
scope: women beginners; to be taken seriously in a gym: dress to train, train hard, pick a hardcore gym

title: Fear of being mocked is unfounded
statement: Fear of being mocked is a fragile ego: nobody notices you, and everyone good once looked foolish. Fear of getting "too big" is laughable for a natural.
scope: anxious beginners; he sees plate math as a gatekeeper

title: Trust and test, don't copy
statement: Build your own judgment and understand everything you do; copying someone's methods won't give you their body. Your first program or guru seems best only for lack of comparison.

title: Strap up when grip limits a pulling set
statement: Use straps as soon as grip limits a back or pulling set, and spend the saved grip on direct forearm work. "Letting grip limit the back is criminal"; straps let you isolate the back better and don't hurt forearm growth.
numbers: forearm isolation costs only 10-15 min/week
scope: non-powerlifters with a hypertrophy goal, once grip limits (not novices at first, see EQP-04)
check: Are straps used on back and pull sets where grip would otherwise end the set, with forearms trained directly?

title: Bodybuilders should strap their pulls
statement: Every non-powerlifting bodybuilder should use straps on pulls (deadlifts, rows, shrugs); there's no reason not to, and they are "essential for deadlifts".
confidence: medium — ~6 videos, 2020; the principle continues later through EQP-01

title: Straps are worth 20-30% on back work
statement: Without straps he would lose 20-30% performance on back work; straps can multiply upper-back gains.

title: Don't strap when grip isn't the limit
statement: Do warm-ups bare-handed and skip straps where grip doesn't limit (for him, pull-ups and dumbbell rows). Novices don't need them at first, and overuse steals forearm work.

title: Straps on dumbbells can disrupt the path
statement: On dumbbells, straps restrict wrist rotation and can disrupt the path and recruitment.

title: If you dislike straps, use them for volume work
statement: If you dislike straps, use a regular grip for most working sets and straps for volume work.

title: Hook and mixed grip are powerlifting dogma
statement: Double-overhand grip limits floor pulls "100% of the time". The hook grip is a "biological strap" that differs from straps only by ego and discomfort, mixed grip is terrible, and the double-overhand → mixed/hook progression is powerlifting dogma irrelevant to hypertrophy.

title: Anti-strap arguments are silly
statement: Claims that straps cause injury, ruin form, feed ego or are "cheating" are silly. He points to strongmen who pull and carry huge weights in straps without wrist injuries; a year of strap use gave him only bruises, and a bruise isn't an injury.
numbers: strongmen pull ~1000 lb and carry ~800 lb in straps

title: Remove stability or grip so the target limits the set
statement: Removing the stability demand (Smith) or the grip demand (straps, wrist cuffs for laterals or triceps extensions) lets the target muscle alone limit the set.

title: How to choose straps
statement: Pick grainy straps (IronMind) over silky ones, long enough to loop 2-3 times; pay more than $5 and stick with one pair. They stiffen and improve with sweat (he never washes them).
numbers: loop 2-3 times; >$5; his lasted ~2 years

title: No lifting gloves
statement: Gloves let the bar slip, smell and need replacing; bare-hand discomfort goes away within about a week.
numbers: ~1 week to adapt

title: Callus care
statement: Rub a lotion bar into your hands every night (chalk dries them) and shave calluses with a nail clipper about every 2 months.
numbers: shave ~every 2 months; he went from monthly tears to none in ~4 years

title: Gear only on heavy sets, never warm-ups
statement: Gear is fine if it doesn't change the lift's strength curve and helps recovery or strength. Do warm-ups raw and add gear from about 75-80% intensity ("don't belt up for one plate").
numbers: add from ~75-80% intensity
check: If supportive gear is used, is it kept off warm-ups and added only from about 75-80% intensity?

title: Elastic gear isn't for novices
statement: High-poundage elastic gear (wraps, slingshot, bench shirt) has a learning curve, isn't for novices, and is useless worn as fashion.

title: Belts add rigidity, matter little for hypertrophy
statement: A belt adds rigidity, not stored energy; it takes some lower-back stress, helps leg drive and adds weight for most people, so powerlifters should use one. Its effect on abs is negligible for hypertrophy. No shame in using one unless it hides bad form; he tried one once and never again.

title: Sleeves and wraps are mostly placebo
statement: Sleeves and wraps are mainly psychological and placebo unless very rigid, but still worth buying, since "a placebo effect … is still an effect". He wears cheap elbow and wrist wraps for warmth.
status: changed — 2020: they add poundage for almost anyone and keep tendons warm; 2021: mostly placebo, ~10-20 lb

title: Slingshot: useful once, now dropped
statement: The slingshot takes weight off the bottom of the bench, deloads shoulders and chest and keeps elbows tucked; buy the size for your bodyweight. By 2025 he no longer uses his and is selling it.
numbers: takes ~30-40+ lb off the bottom
status: changed — positive reviews 2020-2021 → 2025 no longer uses it

title: Squat shoes: from heels to flat
statement: His current view: he squats in flat shoes with no difference and keeps lifting shoes only for high-bar. He calls wrestling shoes the best general shoe (2023).
status: changed — 2020: heeled weightlifting shoes for all squats/knee flexion (more depth, like extra ankle mobility), flat thin soles for everything else → 2024: squats flat, heels only for high-bar

title: Shoe rule: wide toes, one shoe for anywhere
statement: The sole should be at least as wide at the toes as at the heel. Barefoot is great, but if you are later forced back into shoes you lose strength, so pick one shoe you can wear anywhere.
numbers: forced back into shoes you may lose ~40 lb on deadlifts
status: contradicted — in 2020 he says avoid sneakers/Jordans for lifting, yet also calls LeBron lifestyle sneakers his favourite lifting shoes

title: Commercial gyms are optimal; train hybrid
statement: His current view is that commercial gyms are optimal for building muscle. He trains about 50/50: legs at home; pull-ups, overhead and isolation at the gym. He joined a gym because home limits explained his lagging triceps and delts.
numbers: ~50/50 split; 6'4" basement ceiling; look for an uncrowded mom-and-pop gym at $40-50/month ($100/month is expensive)
status: changed — 2020-2021 home gym unlocks progress (EQP-21) → 2023-2025 commercial gyms optimal, hybrid training

title: Owning your space can increase gains
statement: Owning your training space lets you train as aggressively as you want (drop weights, grunt, music, shirtless); he progressed far more after building his own gym. In 2020-2021 he said "eventually you need your own personal gym".
status: changed — later softened into the hybrid view of EQP-20

title: Commercial gyms have hidden time costs
statement: Travel and overhead add up, and walking between machines, hunting for clips and waiting for equipment kill focus and pump.
numbers: ~70 min overhead per session even with a gym 10 min away; 3 h training + 3 h travel per week; at $15/h ≈ $45/week lost

title: Pick a gym that lets you train hard
statement: Other gym-goers slow progress most (shared racks, chatty members, staff policing deadlift lowering, pop music). Leave a gym that bans grunting or dropping weights; "intimidating" hardcore gyms are better.

title: Home gym economics
statement: You can start a home gym cheaply, and owning equipment creates commitment. The usual "it saves money" argument is weak, though quality gear resells well.
numbers: start with $300-400; $3000 home gym vs $300/year membership takes 10 years to pay off; plate-loaded gear resells at 70-80% after 3-4 years
status: contradicted — 2020: a home gym is like owning a house, even overpriced gear saves money; 2021: used gear loses value and isn't an investment like stocks

title: Don't build during a price crisis
statement: Don't build a home gym during a crisis when prices spike; do calisthenics meanwhile.
numbers: COVID 2020: prices doubled; 2021: competition had cut prices, a good time
status: current — the 2020 → 2021 shift is a change in context, not a reversal

title: Pool money for a shared gym
statement: If you need company, pool money with friends for a shared neighbourhood gym.

title: Core minimal kit: pull-up bar, rings, bands
statement: A pull-up bar, wooden gymnastic rings and bands are enough for excellent gains; rings are invaluable without a gym. Add a dip station.
numbers: wooden rings ~$30 (metal or plastic slip)

title: Calisthenics alone limits legs and size
statement: Calisthenics is a valid program you can run for years, but legs respond far better to barbell compounds and getting big is very hard without free weights, so mix them.
check: For leg growth and real size, are free weights (barbell compounds) included alongside calisthenics?

title: Build a home setup in stages
statement: Build gradually: pull-up bar → small rack or squat stands → Olympic bar → plates. With no room for a rack, get a dip/pull-up station plus compact squat stands. A bench and squat rack are non-negotiable for full chest and legs; a barbell-only setup struggles with small muscles and risks a "spider physique".

title: Rings: wrist-friendly, upper body only
statement: Rings are easy on the wrists and key for underrated horizontal pulls, but upper-body only; ring-only arm training is foolish.
numbers: he runs 2 ring days per 8-day cycle

title: With only bars: weighted pull-ups and dips
statement: With only pull-up and dip bars, weighted pull-ups and dips are the staples; kettlebells beat plates for loading them (compact, less dangling).
numbers: a 25 lb plate is ~$20

title: Light loads: reach failure, not 50 easy reps
statement: With little weight, keep reps higher, combine weights and bands to reach failure at lower reps rather than doing 50 easy pump reps, and superset movements for the same muscle. Not optimal, but it works.
numbers: ~130 lb available → higher reps; ~30 kg → weights + bands, supersets

title: Improvised loading ideas
statement: Load push-ups with a sturdy backpack, do heel-elevated dumbbell squats for high reps, use ring rows with feet far back as an upright-row substitute, or run a light kettlebell circuit.
numbers: 70 lb in a 200-lb-rated backpack; 50 lb per hand on high-rep DB squats is hard; 2 kg kettlebell circuit (swings, uphill lunges, RDLs, goblet squats)

title: Kettlebells are inferior for hypertrophy
statement: Kettlebells are inferior for hypertrophy and acceptable only as minimalist training; sandbags aren't practical for hypertrophy.
status: changed — 2022: any resistance is valid if used well (no personal experience) → 2024: inferior for hypertrophy

title: Mindset beats equipment
statement: Lack of equipment is no excuse: he cites African lifters in scrap-metal gyms, medieval peasants, Apollon's homemade railway-wheel bar and a bamboo gym.
numbers: Apollon's bar: 366 lb

title: Only buy what you'll use weekly
statement: Only buy equipment you will use at least once a week; later he sells anything not used weekly.
numbers: ≥1x/week; his last purchase (a tibialis station) gets 3x/week use; adjustable dumbbells only if used ≥3x/week (2024)
check: Is each home-gym purchase something that will be used at least once a week?

title: Buy nice or buy twice
statement: Buy high-end but not luxury gear; boutique bars cost double for no gain. Quality bars, racks and brand-name stations resell easily; knockoffs don't.
numbers: knockoffs ~40% cheaper, often with missing parts

title: Ways to save money
statement: Buy cosmetic seconds (Rogue Boneyard), wait for sales, call manufacturer sales reps for non-commercial models, and bundle orders to hit shipping thresholds without buying unwanted pieces.
numbers: Ohio Power Bar for $180 at the Boneyard (~$100 saved); sales-rep models at ~half price with free shipping; thresholds: Rogue $5000, plate sellers $500; expect 2-3 months of shipping waits

title: Delivery logistics
statement: Check bundle stock (ask for missing items to ship later), be present for delivery and have heavy items brought inside, and rent a truck plus a strong helper for plywood and mats.

title: Cheap DIY substitutes
statement: Use hardware-store wooden blocks instead of fitness-brand ones, spring clamps instead of collars, a cheap mirror instead of expensive quotes, and pay a welder for cuts.
numbers: fitness-brand blocks ~5x the price; $1-2 spring clamps (not for dumbbell triceps work, nor one-arm implements above ~200 lb where plates tilt); $40 mirror vs $1000 quotes; ~$20 for welder cuts

title: Gradual build vs full bundle
statement: Building gradually spreads the cost; buying a full bundle at once saves shipping and gives peace of mind.

title: Barbell and rack are the centrepiece
statement: Start a home gym with one quality Olympic bar and a rack, not a collection of specialty bars. A bar without a rack mostly limits you to floor pulls; never clean a bar onto your back to squat.

title: Buy the best bar you can
statement: A good bar lasts decades and flexes back under load, while cheap bars bend permanently.
numbers: ~$300-400 for 10-20 years (~$30/year); cheap $80-100 bars bend at ~300-400 lb

title: Try a bar model before buying
statement: Train with a bar model for weeks before buying, and test stiffness if you dislike stiff bars. His favourite is the Rogue Ohio Power Bar, plus a cheap Boneyard beater bar for rack pulls.
numbers: Ohio Power Bar ~$400; beater bar $180; he used his for 2 years

title: Bar care
statement: Stainless bars need no upkeep; non-chrome steel rusts, so oil and brush it often. Brush chalk out after every session and store the bar horizontally on a wall or vertically, off cold humid floors.

title: Always set safeties when alone
statement: Always set safety arms when training alone; you need total trust in your safeties.
check: When training alone in a rack, are safety arms always set?

title: J-cups: roller cups solve both problems
statement: Plastic-lined J-cups resist sliding but the liner wears at heavy loads, after which steel damages the bar; steel cups wear the knurling. Roller cups fix both; his hack was another brand's roller cups with the rear guard cut off, secured with a strap.
numbers: liner wears at 300+ lb; near-impossible to shift ~400 lb; roller cups $300 retail vs ~$30-50 hack; used 5 months without slipping

title: Rack-mounted monolift arm
statement: A rack-mounted monolift arm costs far less than a dedicated monolift; he uses it weekly for bench lift-offs without a spotter. Chalk-mark the holes. He walks out squats and OHP by choice and loves 3x3 racks.
numbers: ~$100-120 vs thousands; the arm swings only above ~135 lb

title: Chalk-mark pin heights
statement: Chalk marks on the rack let you repeat pin heights for partials, pin presses and squats.

title: Weight is weight: buy cheap plates
statement: Buy the cheapest plates in good condition; closing mom-and-pop gyms are the best source.
numbers: he bought ~1000 lb of mismatched brands
scope: home gym builders below ~400 lb loads

title: Calibrated plates for very heavy loads
statement: At very heavy loads, buy calibrated plates, because cheap "45s" vary enough to create a dangerous side-to-side imbalance. He recommends Vulcan (cheapest marked calibrated).
numbers: at 400-500 lb; cheap 45s weigh 38-48 lb (~20 lb imbalance); he spent $2-3k and needed extra 5s and 10s for dumbbells

title: Build your own platform
statement: Don't lift on bare concrete (drops damage it, and it's hard on knees and stability); build your own platform for a fraction of retail.
numbers: DIY <$150 vs ~$1000 retail (2020); $100 at Home Depot vs $1000 Rogue (2023); his 16x8 ft platform ~$500 vs ≥$4000 custom (Feb 2020); his 16x9 ft one $800-900 vs $5-6k contracted (Dec 2020); ~$3000 saved

title: How to build the platform
statement: Plan on paper and do a mock assembly; buy plywood in person (online stock is warped). Use mid-quality wood for the base and the best wood for the top; glue the base layers but screw the mats and top wood so damaged pieces can be swapped. Shim sloped garage floors, add a vapour barrier in arctic climates, and use wood screws if bolting a rack.
numbers: plan 1-2 months ahead; top wood ~3x the price; glue dries ~40 min; swapping a damaged piece ~$30

title: Horse stall mats, with drawbacks
statement: Horse stall mats are the best and cheapest mats; avoid online puzzle mats. Use two layers or screw them to wood on sensitive floors. Drawbacks: slippery for squat, OHP and bench leg drive (wood is "night and day" better), they crease, shift and collect moisture.
numbers: the wood under his deadlift spot sank after ~7 months

title: Platform first, gym on top
statement: Build the platform before installing the gym on it; a large platform becomes immovable.

title: Plan the space months ahead
statement: Chalk the footprint, number every item on a paper map, measure to the inch and leave 3D clearance for loading plates. Don't overpack, because a cramped gym kills enthusiasm. Put the rack in first, near the back rather than in the middle.
numbers: his whole gym fits in 16x8 ft and took 3-4 months to plan and build

title: Live through a winter before a garage gym
statement: Cold is a major drawback: heaters only take the edge off, bands freeze and steel numbs hands. Live through a winter before building a garage gym; he tolerates it but wouldn't recommend it.
numbers: if 40-50 °F bothers you, don't build one; his garage ran 15-30 °F for 6-8 months a year
scope: garage gym builders in cold climates

title: Shelter an outdoor gym
statement: For a garden gym in a rainy climate, build at least a crude shed; a wet bar is a squat hazard.

title: Good machines rethink the movement
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: Machines are all-or-nothing: the best ones rethink the movement and adjust to anthropometry, but machines often can't replace free weights. Converging presses are "Gorilla tier" and may beat the bench; diverging presses are really shoulder presses; the Nautilus pullover is top tier; cable rows and triceps pulleys are good.
status: changed — 2020 "barbell purist" who didn't need guided machines → 2022-2024 rates good machines, Smith machines and cables highly

title: Home machines: plate-loaded and multi-purpose
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: If you buy a machine for home, it must be multi-purpose and plate-loaded (easy to move and resell); internal weight-stack stations are a nightmare at home.

title: Respect the Smith machine
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: The Smith machine was invented by Jack LaLanne for safe heavy loading, every serious bodybuilding gym has one, and mocking it is ignorance. The fixed path lets you apply full strength.
scope: intermediate/advanced hypertrophy work (see BEG-47 for novices)

title: A belt squat is worth buying
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: A belt squat gives quad tonnage with near-zero lower-back load, plus rows, single-leg RDLs and the best shrugs. Plate-loaded beats cable-loaded.

title: Safety squat bar is a game changer
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: A safety squat bar belongs in every gym. He recommends the Elitefts Yoke SSB (thick pad); its thinner sleeves need clamps.

title: Trap bar for shrugs and carries
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: The trap bar is "Leonidas tier" for shrugs, power shrugs and carries (upper traps).
numbers: most trap bars max out at ~500 lb

title: No cable stack: use bands on the rack
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: Without a cable stack, loop a band on the rack with a rope through it, or put a stick in a band loop (better than any V-bar), for pushdowns, rows and face pulls.

title: Accommodating resistance is unnecessary
section: Machines, Smith, cables and specialty bars
statement: Chains and bands as accommodating resistance are unnecessary for bodybuilding, and useless if set up wrong (chains that never touch the floor, chains on machines).

title: Dumbbell-only training is less efficient
statement: Dumbbell-only training is limited: you outgrow them on deadlifts, goblet squats aren't back squats, and isolating legs and triceps is hard. Cables are a big upgrade, and barbells offer more than dumbbells (load aside).
numbers: you outgrow 100 lb DBs on deadlifts

title: Adjustable dumbbells are a trap
statement: Adjustable dumbbells are a "trap" (pricey base and plates), worth it only with frequent use. Buy used dumbbells from closing gyms or private sellers instead, but avoid cheap junk dumbbells, which can cause wrist tendonitis.
numbers: worth it only if used ≥3x/week (2024); junk DBs ~$30-50 a pair
status: changed — 2020: adjustables make sense vs a full fixed set costing thousands → 2024: a trap unless used ≥3x/week

title: Loadable dumbbell handles: niche
statement: Loadable dumbbell handles are worth it only for frequent isolation work, arm wrestling or outgrowing rack dumbbells on rows. They are bulkier with a different strength curve (start light); leave room for the collar.
numbers: DB-10 ~$80, DB-15 >$100; 4-6 isolation movements/week

title: Rope-plate loading replaces dumbbells
statement: A plate on a rope is a cheap dumbbell substitute that needs no collars and feels heavier than its weight; bring a rope to the commercial gym for giant sets.
numbers: ~10 ft of 0.5-1 in rope for ~$10; 25 lb on a rope works like 40-50 lb on a DB

title: Benches: try before buying
statement: A "fat pad" bench stops sliding and keeps the scapulae on the pad but limits depth and elbow tuck, so try before buying. He uses a flat bench (adjustables are flimsier and he never inclines). Ab benches aren't worth it; pads are indispensable for hip thrusts.
numbers: ab benches ≥$800

title: EZ bar; calves don't need a machine
statement: A quality EZ bar is worth it for heavy curlers; for occasional curls a cheap one is fine. An EZ bar, a bench and a block make a home seated calf raise, so calves don't need a machine.
numbers: quality EZ bar $150-200 (Rogue, 30 lb, thick); $20 bar for occasional curls

title: Use a slant board, not plates under heels
statement: Buy a sturdy slant board instead of putting plates under the heels.

title: Neck training: get a harness
statement: Plates and bands work for the neck up to a point, then a harness is needed; he now says a harness is far better and regrets not buying one sooner.
numbers: plates/bands up to ~45 lb, then a harness
status: changed — 2020-2022: plates and bands are enough for an aesthetic neck → 2023: a harness is far better

title: Bands for tendon and joint work
statement: Use bands for tendon and joint "nucleus overload" work at high volume and low intensity.

title: Bands feel better than plates
statement: Bands feel more comfortable and, he believes, more hypertrophic than plates; mix both for variety, joint health and adherence.

title: SPRI tubes vs looped bands
statement: SPRI tubes have rotating handles (better for curls and OHP), don't freeze and last a lifetime; buy the lightest first and never anchor them under a bench for barbell bench. Looped bands are better for barbell accommodating resistance (known tension).
numbers: start with the lightest (yellow)

title: A few key grip tools, progressed
statement: Pick a few key tools per grip type and progress them rather than buying every gadget; loading pins allow easy overload. Start with the easiest gripper and thinnest extensor bands and move up only once the level is mastered.
numbers: Captains of Crush grippers last 4-5+ years; IronMind extensor bands ~$9

title: Fat grips: from skipped to A tier
statement: Fat grips are "A tier": pick a size where the fingers barely touch. Axle bars are B tier (fixed thickness); a thumbless grip gives a similar benefit. Thick bars do cut the load on target muscles.
status: changed — 2020: complementary, and he wasn't using them → 2023: A tier

title: Towels upgrade any implement
statement: Use a short, coarse, non-absorbent towel (a dish towel); wrapping any implement upgrades it for forearms. Beyond dumbbells, rope and towel are the best forearm tools.
numbers: towel rows go from C to B tier

title: Forearm tool tier notes
statement: Wrist rollers beat spring forearm twisters; finger-curl machines are C tier (do isolation light with free weights); grip-sport tools are A tier but costly; rings are C tier for forearms; a light mace is enough for forearm raises.
numbers: grip-sport tools $50-60; 5 lb mace (20 lb unusable)

title: Lifting knowledge should be free
statement: Charging for knowledge you got for free is unjust; all his own programs are free, and he likens paid plans to selling festival water when free water is hidden nearby.
numbers: ~30 free programs by 2023; a $50-100 non-personalised program or ebook is "ridiculous"; $1000 for plans is overpriced
status: changed — he stayed opposed to selling generic programs, but from Dec 2024 runs a paid personalised tier (see IND-21)

title: Learn to program for yourself
statement: A program you build and beta-test yourself is "ten times better" than a bought one, and knowing how to program protects you from exploitation; gurus who discourage self-programming keep you dependent so they can sell.
numbers: His planned $40 program (BBBS) would have been "garbage" marketed, so stop buying programs
scope: All lifters, novices encouraged to explore programming early
check: Does the lifter understand and control his own program rather than depend on a seller for it?

title: Most YouTube program sellers are scammers
statement: He claims most people selling programs on YouTube are scammers; a "custom" program that is really a copy-paste template is a scam every time, and most influencer programs are cash grabs written in minutes.
scope: Paid programs; free templates are fine, and charging for a truly individual program is understandable

title: Buying a program is a waste, with a few exceptions
statement: Paying for a program is a waste, especially for a novice; if you do buy, he named a few he thought worth the money and others he thought not.
numbers: Worth it in his view: Jeff Nippard's ~40-page programs (scalable for years with more sets), Peter Katcherian's $27 program; not worth it: Kinobody's $80 program
status: contradicted — "paying is a waste" / "stop buying programs" sits beside recommending specific paid programs

title: No pre-written program fits you exactly
statement: Every pre-written program, even a paid custom one, must be modified by the lifter; if changing one thing "breaks" a program it is a bad program, and forbidding changes is ego.
scope: All programs; only you can choose your own frequency
check: Can the program be adjusted (exercises, frequency) without falling apart?

title: Most lifters don't need a coach
statement: Beginners and advanced lifters alike mostly don't need a coach; he calls coaching "a scam about 99% of the time" and says coaches profit from keeping clients helpless, for example by changing the program weekly to justify fees.
numbers: Top reasonable price $200-250/month for an excellent powerlifting coach (2020); $500/month to shuffle a program is a scam (2024)
scope: Exceptions: advanced competitors and very specific needs
check: Does the coaching aim to make the lifter independent rather than keep him paying?

title: What a good coach or PT looks like
statement: A good coach has the abilities he claims to build, or a track record of struggling clients who got there; he prepares sessions, stays off his phone, corrects form, is excited by a client's talent, and teaches the client to stop needing him.
scope: Choosing a coach or personal trainer; also check credentials and any history of lying

title: Working out is not training
statement: "Working out" means getting tired; "training" means getting better toward a goal. Many coaches just exhaust clients so they feel worked.

title: The supplement industry exists to empty your wallet
statement: He describes the supplement industry as a conglomerate with one shared goal, your money, which has infiltrated every fitness sphere through sponsorships; ignore anyone who earns money or a cut from a supplement.
numbers: His figures: ~$35B/yr sales, ~3%/yr growth, ~$140B valuation (2021); US fitness industry ~$30B/yr (2022)
scope: All supplement advice from sponsored or selling creators

title: The supplement marketing playbook
statement: Marketing creates a need, then plants suggestion ("you might not get enough protein"), then FOMO and fake scarcity; viral campaigns piggyback or sponsor memes, and the less an ad looks like an ad, the stronger it is. Understanding this makes you immune.
numbers: Ad potency: TV 1, YouTube ad 2, influencer 3, grassroots paid campaign 4; influencers act neutral, then launch their own product 3-4 months later; fake out-of-stock notices drive buying three tubs
scope: Consumers; he cites turkesterone and ecdysterone as sponsored virals

title: High-protein dogma was manufactured by sellers
statement: In his view the high-protein dogma and the urgency of the post-workout meal were created by supplement sellers and magazines; protein pushers are often sponsored, and 1970s Weider magazines sold whey next to drugged pros.
numbers: Missing a meal or waiting 2 h after training won't hurt unless chronic
scope: Nutrition marketing; the nutrition itself is in ch. 10

title: If it must be bought, it probably doesn't work
statement: Hard work can't be sold, so a routine that requires buying something, especially something expensive, probably isn't effective. Lifting is a cheap hobby, you can't pay your way to a good body, and people built great physiques 50-60 years ago without supplements, special programs or diet plans.
numbers: Examples: vein and six-pack products, electric ab stimulators, plastic forearm developers (~$50, D tier), CoolSculpting, ab implants
check: Can the method be followed without buying anything beyond gym access and food?

title: The guru "switcheroo"
statement: Gurus give a sensible free tip (sleep, sunlight, whole food) to earn trust, then sell a lazy paid replacement for it.
numbers: Examples: a $300 light instead of sunlight, liver pills instead of organ meat

title: They sell the cure to the illness they created
statement: "When someone sells you the cure, they likely created the illness": influencers create body dysmorphia, low-T anxiety and fear, then sell the fix. Since your progress means you stop needing them, they profit when you never progress.
scope: Influencers and their products; he calls YouTube fitness "a factory of demoralization"

title: Fast-result promises are scams
statement: Promises of results in under a month or "get big in two months" are scams that feed fear, insecurity and impatience and push PED use and dysmorphia; real progress takes years.
numbers: Any promise under 1 month; "six-pack in two weeks" is garbage; a special method to gain 20 lb of muscle "smells like a scam"; novices can't get big arms in two weeks
scope: Programs and products sold to novices
check: Does the program avoid promising visible results in weeks?
